en: The beloved of Śrī Janakī is known [as the subject]. Victory! This is the introduction (*bhūmikā*) to the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*. May that Blessed One Rāma, who is honored even in the forest by the wielder of the Pināka bow (*Pinākin*) accompanied by the daughter of Dakṣa (*Dakṣasutā*), and who is dear to the daughter of the Earth (*Mahītanayā*), bestow auspiciousness upon us. 1.

In the year one thousand five hundred and eighty of the Śālivāhana era, this work—which is for the most part intent upon refuting the methods of Śrī Bhāskara in rivalry with Munīśvara (whose secondary name was Viśvarūpa), the author of the *Marīci* commentary on Bhāskara’s *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*—was composed by [the author], the grandson of Śrī Lakṣmaṇa Daivajña (the chief minister of King Mahārājādhirāja Jayasiṃha and the author of numerous works such as the *Bījakalpalatā*), and who himself authored many treatises including the *Vāsanāvārttika* and the *Saurabhāṣya*.

This astronomical treatise entitled *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, which consists of a discernment of the principles of the solar system (*sauratattva*), was indeed composed by the one named Śrī Kamalākara—the son of the creator Śrī Nṛsiṃha Daivajña, and the younger brother of his elder brother Bhāskaravirodhin, who was himself a devotee of Bhāskara—out of devotion to Bhāskara and for the sake of the intellectual discernment of his own elder brother, Adidivākara.

Having understood the calculation of the palāṃśas (latitude degrees) [234 pages, lines 14–15], and having known the sum of the sines of the latitude and the obliquity of the ecliptic, one calculates the declination sine (*krāntijyā*) by means of the repeated method [265 pages, verses 178–180]. From that, one obtains the knowledge of the degrees of the interval between the *dhruvaka* (polar star) and the *bāṇa* (arrow) produced in the two halves of the horizon; from that, the knowledge of the *akṣāṃśas* (co-latitude degrees) [3–201 pages, verses 58–15]. For that purpose, we have acquired several books; having obtained from the library of the Śrī Saṃskṛta Pradhāna Pāṭhaśālā a manuscript of a very ancient composition, and having selected its primary readings—though they contain specific errors yet are ancient—we have, with the permission of the noble and eminent Principal of the Śrī Kāśī Saṃskṛta Pāṭhaśālā, Mr. Yīthīb Mahāśaya, undertaken this work.

In the Śaka year measured by the [number of] tongues, enjoyments, and the earth-born (1756), this Siddhānta—adorned with investigations into the latencies of moral conduct (*śīla-vāsanā*) and consistent with various other methods—is now studied by scholars of the science of Siddhānta in Bhāratavarṣa, who, out of a desire for knowledge of its specific alternative methods, approach it in comparison with the ancient Siddhāntas composed by Ācārya Thībhāskara and others.

People consider themselves to have accomplished their purpose by having studied some portion of this Siddhānta after reaching the further shore of the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*). However, due to the rarity of manuscripts for the study of this Siddhānta, there was [formerly] a lack among scholars; now, by this very method, the fourteenth proposition of the second chapter on geometry (*rekhāgaṇita*) has been reached. This is indeed the constant excellence of the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*. Now follows the table of contents (*anukramaṇikā*) of the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*.

(5) At the time of taking the square root of a number ending in zero, [the following rule applies]: *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, Chapter on Square Roots (Spaṣṭādhikāra), Verse 18–19: "Take the square root of sixty times the square of sixty (3,600). Whatever integer root is obtained, multiply it by sixty, add one, and divide by two. The quotient is the fractional part of the root not yet reached; this is the square root with its fraction, being itself an approximation. Now, for numbers other than those ending in zero, the square root consists of the integer part and the remainder. [Note: The calculation involves finding the nearest integer square root of 3,600, which is 60. This is multiplied by 60 to get 3,600, plus one makes 3,601, and dividing by two gives 1,800.5. This represents the fractional component used to approximate the square root of the original number.]

Thus, there exists among many who are deluded a misconception regarding this matter. Listen now to the true nature of that investigation concerning the method of extracting square roots, as it was previously established by Āryabhaṭa, Bhāskara, and others. To begin with, the square root is of two kinds: rational (rekhātmaka) and irrational (asamaka). Those numbers whose square roots are rational are squares themselves; those whose square roots are irrational are not squares, such as 5, 4, and 8, which correspond respectively to the earth, the Vedas, and the sky.

Those for whom no root exists whose nature consists of consonants (varga) are the second, third, and fifth [classes], namely: 2, 3, and 5. Therefore, there are two *pada*s for the class *jha*, and one *pada* for the non-class (*avarga*), which consists of the letter *ra*.

Among non-square numbers, just as the square of five (25) is greater than the square of four (16), so too the square of a number with a remainder is greater than the square of a whole number. Thus, when calculating the square root, if one assumes a value slightly less than the actual root, the resulting square will be deficient; whereas if one assumes a value slightly greater, the resulting square will be excessive. Since it is logically impossible for the square to be equal [to the original number] without that intermediate value, and since there exists some fractional part within the range of the integer, one should carefully consider this with a subtle intellect. Even in that case, it would be equal to five.

If it is asked how that is so when their roots are impossible there due to a lack of logical consistency, listen: regarding what is called the root of the square of two (2), three (3), and five (5)—is that root distinct or non-distinct? Since these [numbers] are of the nature of squares of distinct numbers, whereas those [roots] are not of the nature of squares of distinct numbers, the possibility of a non-distinct root exists. Furthermore, since it is well-established by the reasoning that "a distinct number multiplied by itself does not lose its distinctness," the distinctness of the square-roots of two, three, and five is inevitable; thus, for these [numbers], even the possibility of a distinct root exists.

Furthermore, the statement "He who carries away someone entirely also carries away that person's group entirely" is contradicted by the certainty derived from its opposite: "He who does not carry away someone entirely does not carry away that person's group entirely. For example, since "this one does not carry him away entirely," the value obtained in the first part is 2; thus, it is a refuge for the particular (viśeṣaśaraṇaḥ). It is a refuge for the particular.

When performing multiplication according to the method of partial products by arranging the digits in successive rows from bottom to top for the purpose of finding the square of a number with parts, if the square of the last digit divided by sixty is subtractable, then there is a subtraction of that lower part. In this case, such a part (2) is contained within six; it does not exceed three. Since its square divided by sixty is subtractable, there is a subtraction of the final part, yet no subtraction of the penultimate part.

The square root of that product multiplied by the area yields the measure of the side (*bhuja*). This side, however, is with its fractional parts: 7; 20; 55. And this diameter (*vyāsa*) is 20; 3; 12. In this manner, it should be calculated even for *iñca*-hands by the wise. (13) The area is five. This [area] together with the *kuṇḍa* is divided by 180. From the quotient obtained by dividing by 107, the square root shall be the diameter here. (137) [The result is] zero, five fires, and kings: 0; 25; 16. This is the multiplier with its fractional parts.

In this case, by calculation, Vyāsa itself becomes the side (bhuja). (138) Now, for a pentagon with one unit side, the side length here is approximately 1.17557; thus, in a fire-altar (kuṇḍa) of seven units, the diameter (vyāsa) is 218 and the side (bhuja) is 18. (139) The square root of 220 multiplied by 821 results in 181,220. O friend, from that, the diameter (vyāsa) and the side (bhuja) in a heptagon are likewise obtained. (140) Zero, twenty-six, earth (one), and six arrows (five)—this is the multiplier: 126,156.

The sides (bhuja) here are 12, 35, and 21; the diameters (vyāsa) are 29, 7, and 56. Thus ends the method for calculating the *kuṇḍa*. Now, the methods for its construction [are given] in the *Sphuṭādhikāra* of the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, verses 159 and 158: "One should first draw an octagon using the diameter and the sides as described. The circular *kuṇḍa* shall be formed by measuring from the center to the midpoint of its own side. Then, indeed, it is bound from the center by means of that segment of the arm."

A semicircle is a segment drawn with a radius equal to half its own diameter. Alternatively, it is a circle drawn above, below, or on all sides. When constructing fire-pits (kuṇḍas) of three, four, five, six, seven, or eight units in size, one should divide that [diameter] into four equal parts and take the second part. One should draw a circle starting from the midpoint of that [second part], and the respective divisions should be made. From the two points at the ends of those divisions, lines should be drawn according to the measurement of the many petals; then, equal lines should be drawn for each division, and thus the circles are formed.

By rotating [the circle], a fish is produced; its mouth is held outside of that [circle]. (154) By means of that, there shall be the strength of the sacrificial offering (*pūṇījyābala*), having the shape of the *khavakuṇḍa* and the *stukā*. Whatever exists therein, by those two lines which are divided and joined, or by the arms [of the figure] being attached to the circle, it should be given here according to that influence. Then, equal to those segments on all sides, by that it shall become so. (155) The *kuṇḍa* born from the sky, the sky, and the thread shall be according to the oblations of the sacrificer. (145)

The pit known as *padma* (lotus), consisting of eight petals, is auspicious like wisdom (*prajñā*). Since the divisions [of the sides] therein are irrelevant when the result is established through the very attainment of the manifest and unmanifest, I have not described them; for by such knowledge of the divisions, those sides remain irrelevant. Even in the case of the second lotus-shaped pit, one should first construct an equilateral triangle with equal altitudes. Then, from the two ends of its sides, using the measurement of the unequal sides, [one proceeds]. (vv. 156–157)

Then, from the center of the three arms at the *yonikuṇḍa*, one should rotate two arms outward. Having drawn a circle with a radius equal to one-third of that [distance], one should then divide it; three half-circles (*maṇḍalārdha*) are to be drawn here by rotating the arm. That which is situated outside, being a fragment, is indeed the petal itself. From the center of that [circle] and toward the sides, reaching the tips of the arms on the bank, thus for each arm there is a petal, making it like an eight-petaled lotus.

Having abandoned the working line (kārya-rekhā) and the bow attached to it, the remainder shall become a lotus-shaped pit (padma-kuṇḍa), supreme through the ritual application of both the manifest and the unmanifest. The first type of pit is the Yoni-kuṇḍa, resembling the root of the Aśvattha tree. In these pits measured in cubits (hasta), one should subtract the respective arms. Thus, having made a circle with half that extent, a four-armed [figure] should be formed; indeed, by those two [lines], according to the stated rule, using the sacrificer’s finger-breadths (yajamānāṅgula). There, with sides equal to the arms, from the desired angle on both flanks— || 148–150 ||

In this [section on] Kha-khasrākṛti (the shape of a kite), sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) arise; from half the side and the radius of the circle, by increasing half the side—[this applies] to the sacrificial pits known as one-cubit (hasta) and so forth. One-sixth part of the fruit and root [should be applied], and outside the side, another [portion] should be made. Or, having conceived an inch (aṅgula) there, [it is done] by the method of the water-vessel (toya-bhāṇḍa). This is the clear exposition in the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*. One should accomplish it precisely by means of the width and sides stated for the one-cubit [pit].

162 || Now, as for the half-moon-shaped *kuṇḍa*, it is a semicircle. Therein, due to a lack of understanding of the underlying principle (*vāsanā*), many dry scholars, having assumed the area of the circle to be double [the area of the semicircle], calculate that half of that—the area of the semicircle—would be its own area. Therefore, the calculation they have made for the diameter of the half-moon based on doubling the area results in very gross *kuṇḍas*; that is not my opinion. || 163 ||

The square of the desired result is four times the square of the result (4 × *pha*²), which is thirty-two times the square of the result (*32 × pha*²). Divided by five, this becomes *pha*²/5. This correctly accords with the stated result. Its square root is the diameter; thus, what was stated is established. That very *kuṇḍa* is indeed measured according to its proportions. Now, in the case of an equilateral triangle, if one were to produce two [triangles] on either side such that their bases are equal, and if they are joined in reverse order, the resulting figure would be a rectangle. Its area is the one intended here, and not any other, even though it has been mentioned by the Lord of Sages (the *Munīndra*), because it is already understood.

The *bhuja* (side) protects that [area], and the *koṭi* (perpendicular side) is the vertical drop (*lamba*). These two are directly perceived; indeed, they are not established by verbal testimony alone. (14) [It is] of the nature of the square root of the difference between the squares of the *bhuja* and the *bhujārśva* (the side of the *bhuja*). Because of the extraction of the square root, the *kuṇḍa* (sacrificial pit) arising from the inner and outer angles is indeed the *bhuja*. When the rectangular area in the form of the product of the *bhuja* and the *koṭi* is being calculated, this color of the result is indeed [determined] by the *bhuja*s numbering twenty (twenty fingers).

In this context, the calculation of the result in reverse order is as follows: the [square root] derived from dividing by three that which was struck by the sine of the arc, and then taking the square root of that [result], is what has been stated by some as the "arm" (*bhuja*). This is established by those who say "eight and the earth" (i.e., eighteen). Furthermore, the hypotenuse (*adhyakṣaka*) is likewise brought forth. In a circle, this arm is twice the sine of sixty degrees. The sine of sixty degrees is equal on all sides to the simple chord of the angle. This is a square form: 3. And the triple-sine (*trijyā*) is indeed the radius; thus it may be 3. These are established through the application of the *bāḍha* (firm) rule.

In this context, the root is the day multiplied by four; or rather, the root is equal [to that], as it is the same as the four limits. Thus, up to the three, five, six, and eight corners, that root is the side of the triangle. One who stands at Naimiṣa does not indeed know the squares of the sides in reverse order in this way. (16) The square of the side increased by its own square, divided by four and then multiplied by four, has its root manifested in the form of the square-root itself. Now, the rationale for the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is stated: "It shall be the diameter"—this is established as it was explained.

When the diagonal of an equilateral quadrilateral is equal to the square root of the sum of the squares of its two equal sides, it is indeed well-known that the result is one. For the sum of the squares of two equal sides is twice the square of one side; the square of this [sum] is four times the square [of one side].

That [area] is equal to twice the square root of the result; its square root is the chord. The square root of the result divided by three is the side, or its square is the *varṇavarṇa* (the square of the color). Or, sixteen times [the area] divided by nine—thus it is established as stated in the *Camurbhaja*. Its square root, and again the square root of that, is the diameter (*vyāsa*); this is very clear to those who know the underlying principles (*bāsanā*). Now, the area of the circle is equal to the square root of five times the square of the diameter minus one. Furthermore, in the first *yonikuṇḍa*, there is one equilateral triangle; from one of its angles, the diameter is obtained by reversing that process. Thus it is established as stated in the *Vṛtta*.

In the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, in the chapter on the *spaṣṭādhikāra* (263), it is stated: "The result [derived] from the square of the hypotenuse (*karṇa*) is known as its own result; therein, by another method, the result is likewise. Thus, when the measure of the side (*bhuja*) is four, six, and nine, the square root of that [sum] is the diameter; half of that is the side, and its square is the area. (Note: The mathematical intent appears to be that for a right triangle with sides 4, 6, and 9, the hypotenuse is √(4² + 6²) = √52, and the diameter of the circumcircle is √52. Half of this diameter is the radius, which serves as the side of a square whose area is the square of that radius.)

The square of the fruit (*phalavarga*) resulting from the division by sixteen is multiplied by four (the "ocean," *abdhi*); thus, for me, it is *yāva* 14355. For you, it is *yā* 9. From this, the area of the equilateral triangle is *yā* 3944. The result of the subtraction of these two areas is the area of the quadrilateral: *yāva* 15335 *ve* *va* *m*. Since this is equal to its own product, the equation is *yāva* 5539 = *yāva* 0 *pha* 4. Here, since the divisor is not divisible by four (the "ocean"), the dividend and divisor are multiplied by zeroes and nines (009), resulting in a multiplier (*guṇa*) of 4800 and a divisor (*hāra*) of 7003; thus, what was stated is established.

In the second case, however, there is one [figure] with equal sides and four equal angles, and likewise another circular-like figure situated at one corner; the sum of these two forms a circle. Having understood their respective areas according to that method, the area of the quadrilateral is thus: let its side be *yā* (yāvat-tāvat). The square root of half this [square] is the side of the quadrilateral; therefore, in a quadrilateral with equal sides, it is *yāva* (yāvat-tāvat-squared). Its square root is the side of the quadrilateral, and thus it is equal to the side. *yāva* (0).

47. 26) The result of the arc. The sum of the two results is established. Now, it is well known that when the side is twenty-two and thirty minutes (22° 30')—that is, twice the sine of eight degrees—the hypotenuse exists [as the radius]. In that case, the square of the sine of five degrees and forty minutes (5° 40') is 1 li-va (1). Its square root is the sine of five degrees and forty minutes, namely 0;42;23. Subtracting this from the radius (trijyā), the result is the versed sine (utkramajyā) of five degrees and forty minutes, which is 0;17;34. 1 - 4/3. 807 - 5 - S - G.

The chapter on the determination of the three questions regarding the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) [ends here]. (9) The general proof for this is as stated in the *Āryabhaṭīya*; furthermore, the proof for the lost [parameters] is as follows: From the degrees of the equinoctial shadow (*viṣuvāṃśa*), one determines the degrees of the amplitude (*bhujāṃśa*).

Alternatively, when the right angle is at any point on the circle, the measure of one of the two sides forming that angle is the same as the measure of the arc between that side and the hypotenuse, and also the measure of the arc between that side and the hypotenuse. It is stated that the degrees of the side-arc, the degrees of the declination-arc, and the degrees of the equinoctial-arc constitute three types of measures. When the equinoctial-arc and the degrees of the zenith-distance (jināṃśa) are known at that point, the degrees of the side are determined; for instance, the angle formed by the intersection of the declination-circle and the meridian-circle is the gnomon, and its sine is the *bala-koṭi-jyā*.

The sine of the oblique ascension (*āyana-valana*) at the point where the planet is on the ninety-nine-degree circle is derived from the sine of the oblique ascension at the point where it crosses the meridian. Now, in the direction from the junction of the sphere (*gola-sandhi*), the complement of the stated arc is in the opposite direction; this is the equatorial latitude (*viṣuvāṃśa*). The hypotenuse (*karṇa*) and the perpendicular (*ṛti*) are the sides; one side is the sine of the oblique ascension on the ninety-nine-degree circle, and the other side is the sine of the equatorial latitude corresponding to the equal-numbered degrees of the oblique ascension. This is the declination sine (*krāntijyā*).

Therefore, if the chord of the arc produced by the first [latitude] is equal to the chord of the arc facing it—the chord of the equatorial degrees—then, by the proportion "if the radius (trijyā) is this, what is the chord? we obtain: *jyabhu* × *jyavi* / *ijyāvi* = *tri* × *vi* × *ka* × *yu* × *ko* / *śuviṣuvāṃśakoṭisavardhinīpujyā*. Thus, the derivation is established. From that, the determination of the longitudinal distance from the point of intersection on the sphere is easily understood. [Note: The symbols and numbers at the end appear to be marginal annotations or references.]

Chapter 16: The Section on the Three Questions. The declination at the point where the celestial equator intersects the meridian of the zenith is the line of the *kadamba* (the axis of the celestial sphere). Likewise, there is a difference at the end of the quadrant (*pada*). This difference between those two exists at the end of the quadrant. (97) In the section on the rising of planets, the wise should understand the obliquity of the ecliptic (*krānti*) and the latitude (*savana*). Now, there is no difference between the equinox (*viṣuvat*) and the method for the declination; it is not so by its own nature. Therefore, in the form of the meridians (*nāḍī*), it is due to the degrees of the equinox (*viṣuvāṃśa*). (98)

The obliquity situated on the sūtra called the horizontal meridian (tiryagdhvā) is the obliquity according to the rule of the ecliptic (bhavṛtta). In the first case, that very [obliquity] is here [defined] from the equatorial degrees (viṣuvāṃśa) within the ecliptic; the other obliquity, situated on the sūtra of the vertical axis (kadamba), is according to the rule of the hour-circle (nāḍikāvṛtta). Because of that, whatever becomes the initial obliquity of the planet, that alone is named the equatorial degree (viṣuvāṃśa); the other obliquity would certainly be different. By virtue of that, those which are the degrees born of the [ecliptic] sector and situated on the equatorial circle (viṣuvavṛtta) should be understood as being situated on the circle of declination (krāntivṛtta) by one who knows the nature of the celestial sphere.

The sine derived from the equinoctial degrees (viṣuvāṃśa) is multiplied by the maximum declination and divided by the trijyā; that [result] is again divided by the dyujyā of the equinoctial degrees. (103) That same [sine] is multiplied by the trijyā and then divided by the sine of the maximum declination. Then, it is multiplied by the trijyā and [divided] by the sine of the maximum declination and the trijyā. (104) Since the multiplier and the divisor are equal, when they are both cancelled, everything stated [in the preceding verses] is established according to the sequence of the steps for the equinoctial degrees. (105)

That which exists between two [points] situated on a horizontal line is divided into three parts; by means of those degrees of arc and half-chord values (*ardhajyā*), that which arises from the sides of a triangle would be produced. However, such a triangle cannot exist in reality because it is not perceived; therefore, its establishment here is somehow problematic. Those of small intellect call it a "complete chord" (*pūrṇajyā*) and consider it a "natural" (*jāti*) figure, but that is not my view. Because of its subtlety, its proof is established otherwise; likewise, we shall explain it according to the method of the sphere of declination (*krāntikṣetra*).

The sines of the [two] sides in the [right-angled] triangle are the [two] sines of the desired [arcs]; the hypotenuse is the equinoctial sine (viṣuvatī). Having thus conceived another [triangle] according to one's desire and investigated it through the principles of the sphere with one's own intellect: here, from the square root of the difference between the squares of those two sines which are the [two] sides, multiplied by the radius and divided by the sine of ninety degrees (the co-sine), that arc shall be the measure of the unknown side. Or else, the co-sine situated as the hypotenuse here, multiplied by the radius and divided by the known co-sine—[that result is the sine of the unknown side]. || 109–111 ||

The mark of the arrow on that bow would be equal to the visible portion of the ten-fold [diameter]; for the drinking of the night is indeed great. He who, knowing the time of night marked by the hundred-petaled [lotus], does not understand the reduction of Hari and Hara... (112) ...the base and then the pair of circles, their sum; those two being situated on that circle, the arm and the side are situated between them. (106) The chord of that triangle and its arc, as well as the sine, would be three times the radius in the sky within the celestial sphere.

(1) A right-angled triangle cannot be formed by the full chords (*pūrṇajyā*) of an arc belonging to a circle of arbitrary radius; however, it may be formed by such chords in certain cases, as follows: one part is twice the number of degrees of the arm (*bhujāṃśa*) on the circle of the ecliptic nodes (*golasaṃdhi*). The second part is the arc of the great circle from the point of intersection of the arm-circle and the ecliptic circle up to the limit of the second node (*dvitīyapāta*). The third part is the arc of the great circle between the second node and the intersection of the arm-circle and the equator (*krāntivṛtta*).

For these [sines], the area of a straight-sided natural sector is indeed produced by the full chords (*pūrṇajyā*). This is because the angle formed by the union of two full chords in a circle is a right angle. (33) [See verse 23 of the *Udayarātrādhikāra* in the *Viśeṣaśataka*. (262) In the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, the *Tripraśnādhikāra*: (263) "Thus, when both are known, the square root of the sum of the squares of the sine (*jīvā*) of one and the corresponding cosine (*koṭijyā*) of the other, divided by the radius (*trijyā*), is the sine of the arc where that sum occurs."

113–115. Furthermore, the sine of the arc [of the hypotenuse] is clearly produced here by the subtraction of that [sine of the complement]; or else, when the other [sine] is divided by the radius (trijyā), the result is the sine of the complement. Thus, the sine of the aspect (aśā) is diminished by the sines of the [complementary] arcs. In this context, there are other divisions of the hands (karaprabheda) based on the differences of the oblique ascensions (krāntikṣetra) as stated. Now, O best of the learned, when the sine and the hypotenuse are at the sides of the sphere, that which is seen is a ten-sided quadrilateral (daśacaturasra).

116–119. One of its angles is attached to the tip of the chord; that is called the "uneven" (viṣama) angle. The other three angles are equal, starting from the angle designated as uneven. Those two arms situated on the sides, which are attached to the tip of the chord, are unequal with respect to the equal angles; those two arms situated on the sides are designated as "equal" (sama). Having subtracted the square of the chord from the square of the arm on one side, the square root of that result is the bow (cāpa), which is necessarily located on the other side.

That unequal side would indeed be the arm; thus, the chord of that unequal [side] is divided by three and multiplied by another known as the "unequal" [coefficient]. (120) [Commentary]: For the purpose of illustration, consider one such quadrilateral. Suppose a planet is at some point above the entry into a circle of equal radius (*sama-maṇḍala*). Above that, a solid cube is constructed, pierced through its center from the east and west, and made of burnt clay. Then, on the plane of the equator (*sama-maṇḍala*), there is a pair of arms; one arm is on the equatorial plane, and the second arm is likewise on the equatorial plane.

The third [side] is north-south, and the fourth is called the arc at the eastern *svastika*; thus it is a quadrilateral. In the *ṛgvṛtta*, the depressed angles are the diagonals; the sum of two such arc-type triangles forms a quadrilateral—all this must be considered. Then, with that arc as the hypotenuse, the other side is equal to the arm; this is the calculation for such a case involving a straight line. (121) In the circle centered on the pole, this is the equinoctial circle (*viṣuvanmaṇḍala*); likewise, there are indeed small circles which are the daily paths (*ahorātravṛtta*). (122)

Even when the sphere is divided, the number of those degrees remains the same for both [the ecliptic and the equator]. At the equinox, those which are the equinoctial degrees (viṣuvāṃśa) between the two solstices [are the same]. (123) On the circle called the diurnal arc (svāhorātravṛtta) as well, the degrees are measured by that same amount. These are declared to be the minutes of arc (asavaḥ-tatkalaḥ) for the purpose of establishing the knowledge of time. (124) From sunrise to sunrise is the day of the fixed point [the sun]. The trijyā (radius) is the equatorial circle, and by means of the yujyā (sine of the colatitude), it is called the diurnal circle (yuniśā). (125)

If the [sine] of the arc is greater than the sine of the maximum [latitude], then the area covered by the right-sine (dhujyā) is to be subtracted from that very area where the twelve signs [are situated]. (226) From fixed Aries (sthirameṣa) onwards, those [degrees] on the equatorial line related to the planet are to be known as the degrees of the area; at the equinox, these are the equinoctial degrees (viṣuvāṃśaka). (227) Now, regarding the knowledge of the rising-time degrees of the signs from fixed Aries according to their area-degrees at the non-axial location (nirakṣa): by which means the area-degrees beginning with the rising of Aries on the ecliptic go toward their rising.

In that [place], the degrees of the non-axial (vyakṣa) emergence and the degrees of the parts (kalā) are to be understood as being exactly the same as at the equator. || 128 || In the circle of the zodiac, those degrees of the fields (kṣetra) belonging to the three signs beginning with Aries which have arrived at the meridian—those are the equinoctial degrees; they are the degrees of rising (udayāṃśa) in one’s own non-axial location. || 129 || That which was previously established by subtraction is here simply the measure of the time of rising (udayakāla). And thus, the triad of signs beginning with Aries is from the east, while the triad of signs beginning with Cancer would be from the west. || 130 ||

This [equinoctial shadow] is indeed that which, by subtracting the six signs beginning with Aries, becomes the six signs beginning with Libra. The equinoctial sine multiplied by the shadow in *palas* becomes the earth-sine (*bhūjyā*). That [earth-sine], multiplied by the radius (*trijyā*) and divided by four, is the degrees of ascensional difference (*carāṃśa*). Thus, the degrees of ascensional difference arising from the rising and setting of the zodiacal signs should be calculated by the wise according to this method. *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, Chapter on the Three Questions (Tripraśnādhikāra), verse 132.

One should multiply the three *cara*-values by the third parts of the *palas* [of the respective signs] to obtain the *carakhaṇḍakas*. These *palas*, arising from the [signs] beginning with Aries, are coarse for the purpose of common worldly usage. Now, the knowledge of the time-parts (*kāla-aṃśa*) of the rising of each degree of the signs in one's own locality: the *caras* of the degrees of the signs starting with Aries are to be subtracted from the [rising times] at the non-axial place (*nirakṣaja*). When those are added [to the rising times] in reverse order, it is thus the *rāśipaka* (the rising time of the sign) for the triad of signs beginning with Cancer. The six signs beginning with Libra are the reverse of that; these are their respective rising time-parts for each degree.

Because it lies within the interval between its own meridian and the horizon of its location, it possesses its own [northern] carakhaṇḍa (ascensional difference) alone. || 135 || Furthermore, that portion of the celestial sphere which is situated higher [in the north] rises in a shorter time due to its smallness, while that which is situated lower [in the south] rises in a longer time; such indeed is the perception by the observer. || 136 || Since the deer and other [northern] animals rise at a point depressed by their respective oblique ascensions, they are exceedingly inclined; therefore, due to the southern latitude, they rise in a short time, and likewise [the southern stars]. || 137 ||

In the northern solstice (*udaṅnate*), whatever [period] such as the house of Cancer (*kīṭagṛha*) there may be, it attains its end through that [northern course]; then, after some time, its emergence occurs from that [point]. Therefore, the risings are not equal. From the end of Libra (*dhanvan*) to the end of Pisces (*jhaṣa*), or from there to the end of Gemini (*mithuna*), at the equator (*vyakṣa*), it rises with fifteen *nāḍīs* increased by its own [local] motion (*cara*). In the same way, the end of Virgo (*kanyānta*) rises from the end of Gemini; from that point, the end of Libra rises with fifteen *nāḍīs* increased by the respective *cara* of those two in due order.

140. And because the center of the [celestial] sphere is always below, and because of that [position], the path is below; whatever [planet] rises at a particular time, by that very time its seventh [counter-position] surely sets. 141. For it has been stated here that this [calculation] applies to the objects of the senses of those who are within [this] range; it is prior to the six flavors (rasas), and not beyond them. 143. Furthermore, that which has been declared by the gods beginning with the Sun, and by the independent great sages, regarding the activity [of the planets] as determined by direction, place, and time—[that is what follows].

(1) Viśvanātha: At the location of Ekāṅkalapalabha, the carāsavas at the end of Aries are 60; at the end of Taurus, the carāsavas are 108; and at the end of Gemini, the carāsavas are 128. Thus, because there is no difference between the sine and the arc of these [sines], the subtle carakhaṇḍakas for the beginning of each sign are obtained by dividing [the respective carāsava] by six and subtracting from the value below it. However, in the location of Jyadhakapalabha, because there is a difference between the sine and the arc, it is indeed appropriate to state them as gross values.

(2) Viśvanātha: Regarding that segment of the zodiacal circle (*bhamaṇḍala*) which is transverse—specifically in the *Jyotiṣasiddhānta* and especially in the *Tattvaviveka*, where the term "transverse" (*tiryak*) is used to denote the form of a perpendicular—it should be understood here that the word "transverse" indicates an oblique state. In effect, from the junction of the sphere (*golasandhi*), as each respective segment of the ecliptic situated above the meridian passing through the celestial pole becomes increasingly inclined, forming angles less than right angles, so too does every [point] related to that segment [move].

On the equatorial circle (*nāḍīvṛtta*), the degrees are small. Now, up to the horizon of the celestial sphere (*golasaṃdhi*), there are no degrees of declination (*vayaṃśāḥ*). The sine of the oblique ascension at the end of Aries (*meṣāntadyujyā*) is thirty degrees on the ecliptic (*krāntivṛtta*). In this [circle], the sine of the oblique ascension (*jyāpayujyā*) is equal to the sine of thirty degrees (*jyā 30*). Thus, from the sine of the oblique ascension (*jyādyaḥ*) and the sine of the oblique ascension (*jyāme'dya*), here ‘*ya*’ refers to the gnomon (*khūpa*), and ‘*jyoma*’ refers to the shadow. That is the sine of the arc produced on the ecliptic from the meridian zenith distance (*dhruvaprotakrāntivṛtta*). This is the maximum sine of the oblique ascension (*paramālpapayujyā*). Even by the method of addition for that which is greater, since the oblique ascension of Taurus is greater than that of Aries, the oblique ascension of Gemini is greater than that of Taurus.

In this system, liberation is not merely the rising of the ascensional difference (*nirakṣodaya*); rather, everything such as this is entirely in accordance with the teachings of Bhāskarācārya. That [liberation] has two types of results: the seen (*dṛṣṭa*) and the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*). The seen result arises from the surface of the earth for those situated on the back [of the globe], and from the center of the earth’s curvature (*kukendra*) for those situated behind. The unseen result arises by that same logic from the hemisphere of the celestial equator (*kṣitija*) at the center of the earth; for while one half is accepted as visible, the other half below it is invisible.

Now, another [method] regarding the movement of the ecliptic: on the circle above and likewise below, they remain constantly situated. On that circle, the khāpna-arteries (khapanāḍikā) are such that, when reduced by the khāni, there are five and one (five hundred and one) nāḍīs in a quarter of the ocean (one-fourth of 360 degrees). (1) Note: Here, the reading *dhanvatāt* is correct, based on the authority of the rule "with *dhanus*, [the suffix] *dhan* and a nasal dot" (*bindu*), and so forth. This concludes the Chapter on Tripraśna from the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*.

267. When the Sun is always in the northern hemisphere (saumyagala), it is non-decreasing; when it is in the southern hemisphere (yāmyagala), its own arc is decreasing. The difference between these two on the circle of time (kālavṛtta) is the carā (ascensional difference). That which is in degrees, divided by six, becomes the nāḍikās. In the northern hemisphere, those [nāḍikās] added to or subtracted from the half-day respectively result in the half-night. When the half-night is subtracted from twelve, those two results are the measures of the carā and the āyu (daytime). ॥147-148॥

That portion of the day which lies above the equatorial plane (kṣitija) and that of the night which lies below it—on the northern hemisphere (saumyagola), the day is greater and the night smaller; on the southern hemisphere (yamya), the day is smaller and the night greater. In those cases, the measure of the night is respectively greater or less than the day, due to the equality of the path of the meridian (vadhara-dhva-sāmya). Thus, there is always an equality of day and night when situated below the northern and southern poles (dhruva). That [day] is solar (sāvana) by virtue of the sun; the distinction is that it is half of four (two) according to the fixed revolutions (sthira-śna).

Where the degrees of the colatitude (*lambāṃśa*) are equal to the degrees of the maximum declination (*parāpamāṃśa*), there the appearance is that of the apamaṇḍala (the ecliptic). At the time of the rising of Aries, Mars is there; otherwise it is not, and there it faces the sign of Cancer. Due to the constant eastward revolution of the earth, Mars always revolves below [the horizon], and likewise it faces Capricorn. Whosoever has a northern declination greater than the colatitude remains above the horizon for as long as that duration; likewise, one with a southern declination exceeding the colatitude remains below the horizon for that same duration.

(1) Where the first [ascendant] degrees are clearly 19° 30', and where the [maximum] altitude is always seen to be 15°, that place is situated on its own meridian behind [the prime meridian]. (2) In that place, the latitude is 69° and the palabhā (equatorial shadow) is 20 units; there, Aries and Taurus are never seen, while Cancer and Gemini are indeed always visible. Furthermore, Scorpio is never seen there, nor are the four signs beginning with Libra (Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius), as their maximum altitude is 78° 11'.

And it is observed that there is a set of four oxen (the signs), while the axle is fixed at ninety [degrees] in the reed (the equator). Wherever the auspicious actions and so forth are seen, the scales and so forth are certainly not always present. By virtue of the southern and northern axles, they declare the expenditure; indeed, it is by the southern and northern axles. In their respective solstices, situated below and above the earth, the measure of night and day exists through the mutual appearance and disappearance [of the sun] from the nadir and zenith. 158.

When the Sun is at the zenith of the local horizon, there would be day above and night below; or rather, when the Sun is visible, it would always be day, and when that destroyer of darkness is not seen, it would be night. (159) If day were situated below, how could it be said to belong to the Four-faced One (Brahmā)? (1) Vi0: The degrees of latitude (akṣāṃśa) are the interval between the zenith and the position of the celestial pole. Those at the zenith rise from the point where the local horizon and the celestial equator intersect; above them, at a distance of a few degrees, lies the local horizon behind.

Therefore, even for a planet whose true arc of the shadow (jyācchāyāstabhā) is always visible from latitudes less than twenty-four degrees, this is consistent with Bhāskara’s *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*, in the chapter on the conjunction of planets (*bhagrahayuddhādhyāya*) within the *Grahaṇita*. The only distinction here is that the observer is situated on the curved surface of the earth (*kupṛṣṭhasaṃsthā dṛṣṭiḥ*). (2) Viśvanātha Śarmā states that because the four signs beginning with Aries are not seen [from the poles], all of this is indeed in accordance with Bhāskara. (3) Regarding "two Indras," these are the two poles (*dhruvendrau*).

Thus, the latitude (*pradeśarāji*) is derived from the point situated below the intersection of the *dhruva* (celestial pole), the *dhū* (the meridian), and the *indu* (the ecliptic). Indeed, there is no distinction here between the *dhruva*, the *dhū*, and the *indu*; rather, such usage is employed in many places merely for the sake of completing the meter. (4) Viśvanātha Śarmā—If, according to the first method, [the latitude] is obtained as stated in Siddhāntatattvaviveka, Chapter on Tripraśna, verse 268: "If it arises from observation, then from the mark of the observed point, it is below the terrestrial back-surface (*pṛṣṭhakuja*). (Verse 160).

Regarding that which was indeed stated—that the day [of the conjunction] is when there is no visibility from Bhadrakūpa—how can that be? To this it is replied: what was stated based on visibility is the result of the aspect (*dṛkphala*) according to the method of Ādhārī. (161) This was stated for the sake of the results taught in the *Adṛṣṭatantra*; thus there is no fault even regarding the two lunar fortnights (*pakṣa*). However, the solar day (*brāhmaṃ dinaṃ*) found in the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi* has not been mentioned here at greater length. (162) Just as, by relying on the Earth itself, [the calculation] arising from the visibility of the Sun occurs between sunrise and sunset at Bhadrakūpa...

I shall now correctly describe the measure of the day for those situated at points above the curved surface of the earth. (163) The difference between the squares of the two [sines of] the latitudes of the two points where the sun is heard [to rise] on the curved segments is divided by their product; that result, diminished by the terrestrial segment, gives the distance in *yojanas* from the back of the earth. (164) By means of those very subtle parts of a *yojana*, whatever point of observation exists upon the surface of one's own land, the sun situated on the horizon at the center of the earth is indeed visible from that very point. (165)

In whatever manner this [point] is situated above or below the terrestrial sphere (*kugarbhakṣitija*) within the celestial sphere (*khagola*), in that same manner the Sun, located at a point beneath the observer's position, becomes visible according to the power of the observer's terrestrial latitude. (16) I shall state the calculation for that: the arc-seconds arising from the Earth's obscuration (*kucchanna*) of the Sun, multiplied by the cosine of the co-latitude (*dyujyāṃśajakoṭi*) and divided by the radius (*tribhajyā*), is the segment of the Earth (*kukhaṇḍa*). (167) The height above the Earth's surface, diminished by that segment of the Earth, will be the mark of one's own visual horizon (*nijadṛṣṭicinha*) measured in *yojanas*.

From this, the knowledge of the horse-portion (*hayāṃśaka*) [is obtained]; furthermore, for those situated below the equator (*garbhabhuja*), it would be the reverse of the *rīyā*. (168) Even for those situated below the North Pole (*dhruva*), it should be calculated in this manner; even below one's own local meridian (*svagarbhayana*), it is called the "nāḍī" [measure]. Here, the sequence of calculation arising from the end of a single sign (*ekadirāśyanta*) of the Sun is to be multiplied by the minutes of arc of its obscuration (*kṛcchannaliptā*). (169) Then, the segment of the earth (*kukhaṇḍa*)—which is the product of the radius (*trijyā*) and the girth of the waist (*kaṭigrīvya*)—minus that segment, results in the measurement in *yojanas* and so forth.

Thus, in three ways, the result arising from the limit of two signs [of the arc] shall be by means of seventeen, ten, and five; likewise, by sixty-six and seventy-six consonants. The marks visible here for the two signs and three signs, respectively, up to the limit of the degrees of the circle's diameter, are similar to those. When the Sun is situated below the horizon at twice the nadis [of its own declination], its appearance occurs on its own sphere.

Indeed, when the Sun is situated in its own direction within the celestial sphere (*golā*), its shadow always exists; from that shadow, the measurement of the Sun’s altitude (*unnata*) shall be determined. By means of the calculation of the *tara* (parallax) and the *kila* (sine), wherever the intersection of the line of contact (*vidhasparśarekhā*) and the solar radius occurs, the visible degrees (*dṛśyāṃśāḥ*) are conceived up to the local horizon (*garbhakṣitija*). Likewise, below the local horizon, one should calculate the visible degrees at the solar orbit (*ravicakṣā*). From that, it is possible to know even the measurement of the terrestrial latitude (*pṛṣṭhagaṇḍalaya*). For that purpose, the method of calculation beginning with "the minutes of arc (*liptāḥ*) which would be... is indeed appropriate.

(1) vi0 śa7—Thus, relying on the reasoning demonstrated above and having clearly established the *ḍaṭī*, one should praise the investigation into the duration of day and night, beginning from the observation of the sun in Aries and extending through the months of one, two, and so forth.

Regarding the statement beginning with “syādinam” (it would be a day), which suggests that what has been stated [as a day] might instead be the day of the four-faced Brahmā, measured by a thousand *yugas*—to the question of how this could be so, the author raises an objection with the words “here it is said” (*atrocyate*) and so forth. Having established the point through the latter half of the one hundred and sixty-first verse, he expresses his own reflection on the matter of the agreement between observation and calculation. By explaining the definition of a day in two ways—through the methods of the visible and the invisible—he settles the argument that there is no fault. Thus, Bhaṭṭa’s investigation into the day of Brahmā is particularly distinguished.

(1) From the intersection of the celestial equator and the ecliptic, a line parallel to the terrestrial equator is extended until it meets the lower meridian. An observer situated along that line necessarily perceives the sun as being on the celestial equator. Therefore, the distance in *yojanas* from that point to the surface of the earth is established by the formula beginning with "the segments of the earth and the sun's auditors" (*kukhaṇḍārkaśravaṇau*), which calculates the elevation above the surface. If one assumes that the observer's vision extends even further upward, then the sun would be visible even when situated below the celestial equator.

12) Viśvanātha Śarmā: Regarding that which was established by the verse beginning with "kukhaṇḍakākeśravaṇa" in the Siddhāntatattvaviveka, chapter on the Three Questions (Tripraśnādhikāra), verses 270–271: "The small segment (kukhaṇḍaka) is indeed the upward-pointing mark on the surface of the earth at the end of the small segment. When joined with the small segment, it is the downward-pointing mark; the small segment multiplied by three is the distance from the zenith. That [distance] subtracted from ninety degrees (90°) is the visible portion of the arc. (vv. 182–183)

When the lord of the sign is conjoined with [the Sun] and is greater than Mars, and when the degrees of the ascendant are moving upward from the point of conjunction, then there is the sight of the face and neck; otherwise, the order is reversed. (18) Now, for the purpose of explaining this, here is the illustration of the diagram: "From the mouth of Pisces to the end of Libra, from the mouth of the one named Aquarius to the end of Virgo, and from the mouth of the one named Capricorn to the end of Sagittarius—this is the measure of the day according to the shadow of the sun. (173)

In this context, by that same sequence, for those traveling toward the north, the remaining portion here would be night; [the day] would end at the face of Virgo (Kanyā), the mouth of Leo (Siṃha), and the shoulder of Taurus (Vṛṣabha). The day would be obscured and its song stifled, ending at the face of Cancer (Kīṭa) and the conclusion of Gemini (Mithuna). Thus it is for those situated behind their own land, at a distance of three yojanas. That which is said here regarding the rising [of a planet] occurs only when Mars (Kuja) is within the womb [of the sign].

The point on the terrestrial horizon known as *astodaya* (rising-setting) has been described previously; it is not otherwise, as the wise should understand. (176) This [point] is stated to be at a distance of one-quarter of a day from the eastern horizon. Therefore, here too, for the duration of a day, it is as previously stated. (177) Wherever the visible degrees—equal to the sum of the degrees of the colatitude (*lambāṃśa*) and the degrees of the sidereal longitude (*sidāṃśaka*), increased by twenty-four (*jināḍhya-kukṣu*)—are greater than the obscured degrees, there, according to the aforementioned method, the mark of its own terrestrial surface will be found. (178)

It is a marvel that by those very *yojanas*, through their influence, the sun remains perpetually risen there; for, by means of the *yojanas* of its own orbit and day, which arise from a small visible portion at the edge of the earth's shadow, it is seen everywhere—even at the location of all eyes—beneath the terrestrial horizon, within the sphere centered on the lords of the planets. That this visibility exists is indeed a wonder here. It is said that by those parts of the visible arc at the edge of the earth's shadow, situated beneath the terrestrial horizon, [the sun is perceived].

If the visible degrees situated above the horizon should be greater than the degrees of the earth's shadow (kucchanna-bhāga), then [the calculation proceeds as follows]: the radius of the sphere (trijyā) divided by the cosine of the sum of the earth-shadow degrees and the visible degrees results in the sine of the zenith distance (ḍa"sthā). [From] the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*: 272. From the point on the surface of the perfectly spherical terrestrial globe marked by the observer’s location, that which was stated regarding the Sun based on the visible degrees does not hold true when [the Sun is at the zenith]. 273. [This is because] the center of the Earth is located at the center of the sphere. [Note: The commentary clarifies that the geometric model fails when the Sun is directly overhead.]

On the circle known as the horizon (kṣitija), within the sphere formed by the equinoctial colure (masvastika-dṛgbhava-maṇḍala), there are degrees of direction (digaṃśa) corresponding to their own latitudes (bhujā); likewise, the degrees of the oblique ascensions (agraka) are determined by the limits of day and night. In this same manner, the directions of the planetary spheres situated on the celestial sphere (bhamaṇḍala) apply even to the meridian (yāmyottara-maṇḍala). However, those degrees of declination (akṣāṃśa) are always southward from the center of the sky up to the equator (viṣuva). Similarly, the degrees of the planet's sphere in the nadir (adhaḥ) are directed toward the circle known as its own day-and-night (svadyuniśā-vṛtta) from the meridian.

Thus, the parts of the zenith-distance (khamadhyāntabhāga) would be greater than those in the case of the declination (dhruvaśrava-vṛtti). Therefore, here, when the directions are the same, there is a sum; when they differ, there is a difference—this is indeed due to the method of their correction. From the correction of the latitude and the colatitude, the ascensional difference (anata-śas), the amplitude (stanakhaḍḍa), and the meridian distance (udayonnata-śas) are obtained. By the correction of the ascensional difference and the latitude, the oblique ascensions (apamabhāga) are obtained. When this is done for the Sun, then from the oblique ascensions, the right ascensions (bhano-bhuja-aṃśāḥ) situated in their respective places are obtained.

In the first quarter, the sun indeed occupies the *āgha* position; in the second quarter, however, it is in the *tadana* position. In the third quarter, it is joined with the *rasa* [position], and in the fourth quarter, it is displaced from the *cakra*. (191) In the first quarter, the *palabhā* decreases and the shadow (*chāyā*) becomes small. In the second, the shadow increases. In the third, the shadow becomes greater and increases further. But in the fourth, it is subject to decrease and the *lipakā* [measure] is lost. (192)

If the shadow moves toward the south, even so, it shall be the first *pada*; but if you observe it moving toward the north, know that it is the second *pada* of the sun. (193) This was stated by the ancient sages as being applicable everywhere; however, it applies only to the shadow of a bad poet, not to the shadow of the sun. (194) When the orb of the sun is attached to the eastern part of the horizon, that very degree of the ecliptic is the ascendant (*lagna*).

Therefore, at the end of the [ecliptic] quarter, the ascendant will be exactly eight signs away; likewise, when moving upward toward the south or north, it will be the culminating point (*lagna*). (195) The civil time (*sāvana*) is determined by the desired moment from the calculation for that specific time; if it is sidereal (*nākṣatra*), one should calculate it here using the [local] rising times (*udaya*). (196) Viśvanātha Śarmā: Now, the method for determining the solar position with precession (*sāyana-ravi-pada*) according to Bhaṭṭa is indeed distinct. However, this does not invalidate the method for determining the solar position as demonstrated by the venerable Bhāskarācārya.

Just because seasonal signs do not appear in certain regions, such as Kashmir and other Himalayan areas, it does not follow that the seasons are not present there; rather, let the method for determining the seasons as shown by Bhaṭṭa be considered superior. By this much, the criticism of the bad poets regarding the description of seasons serves merely to bring out the greatness of Bhaṭṭa. *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, Chapter on the Tripraśna (Chapter 274): "If the Sun and the Ascendant are both small [in value], then the desired time would be negative. (275)

Then, the time prior to the rising of the [true] Sun would be from the point of its [mean] rising; that [time] would be determined by the force of the *cakṣuḥ-savana* accumulation. Whatever is desired as the current [longitude] here, at that time it is equal to that. The degrees traversed from the Sun corrected for motion are those [already] gone; however, the degrees yet to be traversed belong to the forward and backward motions respectively. For the purpose of calculation, those two are joined with the current rising; when divided by sixty, they become the two times known as past and future.

198–201. Now, whatever time in *ghaṭī*s and so forth is here [indicated], that is multiplied by three (*tri-guṇita*). From that, the elapsed and the remaining portions are to be subtracted for the purpose of calculating one's own limbs (*svāṅga-sādhana*). Likewise, those *udaya*s that have elapsed and those yet to come are indeed to be understood there; in the remainder, they become respectively produced in direct and reverse order (*krama-anukrama*). When those [results] are not pure (*aśuddha-udaya-bhakte*), one should apply the fruit arising from the sequence (*kramaja-phala*) which resides in the results beginning with the *kalikā*. 198 || atha ghaṭyādiko yo'tra kālaḥ tri-guṇitaśca saḥ | tataḥ śodhyau tu tau yāta-gamyau svāṅga-sādhane || 199 || tathā yāta-iṣya-kā ye ca sva-udayās-te'pi tatra vai | boddhavyāḥ śeṣe bhavetāṃ te yukta-anukrama-janite || 200 || aśuddha-udaya-bhakte te paṭṭināṃ kalikādike | phale rataḥ kramajaṃ yacca phalaṃ tat kila yojayet || 201 ||

That which arises from the direct order [of signs] in the case of pure sign-divisional positions (rāśyaṃśaka), and that which arises from the reverse order in the case of impure sign-divisional positions, is to be subtracted [from the ascendant]. The ascendant thus obtained is to be corrected by the degrees of motion (calāṃśa) in reverse order for the purpose of knowing the auspicious and inauspicious results, according to the methods of the various Tantras using the true planets. If the elapsed or remaining time is small, then the desired results will be small. The minutes [of arc] are multiplied by sixty and divided by their own rising times (udaya); these are then increased or decreased by three.

The desired time is obtained by subtracting the [longitude of the] Sun from the [longitude of the] ascendant in reverse order. The elapsed and remaining portions of the moving [sign] corrected for precession, in their respective order, are the two times; these added together, along with the degrees of the mid-heaven (madhyodayāṃśa), and divided by six, yield the desired ghaṭīs according to the sequence previously stated. If those two [lunar nodes] are situated in different signs of the movable, fixed, or dual [categories], the difference between them in minutes should be multiplied by their own [respective] ascensional differences (svodaya). 205–207.

The equinoctial degrees (viṣuvāṃśaka) are those portions of the [ascendant] fields which remain when the circle of the Bhaṭṭatanāḍas is subtracted from the respective positions of the planets; these are to be calculated here first from the true Sun. Having added those [degrees] to the desired fivefold ghaṭīs, they become the equinoctial degrees arising from the ascendant. Thereafter, the field-portion (kṣetralava) is to be calculated as before; those degrees of the ascendant (lagnabhāga) become the "ajata" [degrees]. Divided by thirty, starting from the house, that [result] is the "nirakṣacala" [correction] to be applied once.

Thus, one obtains the degrees of the equinox (viṣuvāṃśakāḥ) here according to the method described. The difference between those two, divided by six, gives the ascensional difference (upeṭikā) from its own oblique ascension; this is established as the desired ascendant. Those degrees of the equinox which exceed twelve signs are subtracted from twelve signs. From the remainder, the ascendant should be calculated as before; from that, the desired time will be obtained. If the ascendant arises after the sun, it is above the sunrise; if it is less, it is below.
