But at the time of night, the shadow of the sun along with the signs should be known as corrected for precession (āyanasaṃskṛta). From the method of calculating the ascendant described above, the desired [ascendant] for one's own purpose shall be obtained by reversing the process.

The equinoctial degrees of the Sun, diminished or increased by the sixfold natāṅgulīs (sine of the altitude), are the mid-heaven (madhyalagna) from the meridian. Then, those who know [the science] take the degrees of the ascendant (kṣetrāṃśaka) multiplied by zero (i.e., set aside) as the true ascendant (khalagna). Or rather, having calculated the ascendant from the time of the Sun at the equinox, one should determine the tenth house from that ascendant increased by six signs; that, when added to the right-ascensions (vyakṣodaya) [of the intervening signs], becomes the water-ascendant (ambulagna). The sine of the altitude of the ascendant (lagnāgrakaśajyaka), multiplied by the sine of the altitude of the true ascendant (khalana natāṃśajīvā), is then divided [by the radius].

The degrees of the apsis of the aspect (dṛkcāpa) are the many degrees obtained from the difference between zero and the degrees of the arc of the result [of the sine] divided by the radius (tribhajyā). || 223 || The sine of the ascensional difference (nata-bhāga) of the aspect multiplied by the radius and divided by the sine of the interval between the ascendant and the sun—those are the degrees of the apsis of the aspect-motion (dṛggati-cāpa-bhāga). || 224 || And those shall be the degrees of the apsis of the aspect at the zenith; they are subtracted from sixty (kha-aṅga) here according to the same method. The sine of the altitude (unnata-bhāga) of the true ascendant multiplied by the radius and divided [by the sine of the co-latitude]—|| 225 ||

The sine of the zenith distance (*koṭijyā*) for those [spheres] whose latitudes are negative and whose declinations are variable shall be the ascensional difference (*akṣepaka*); its direction is determined by the degrees of the sun's meridian altitude. (226) According to the method of the *Tripraśna*, the remaining time from sunset should be calculated as the time of depression (*nata*) of the tri-uneven horizon (*trirāśilagna*). Viśvanātha: According to the method of the *Tripraśna*—that is, the method described in the ancient astronomical Siddhāntas regarding the *Tripraśna*—the time of depression of the tri-uneven horizon (*vitribhalagna*) is to be established; thus, Bhaṭṭa seems to be deceiving us in reality.

It should be investigated by the learned whether the effort required to determine the remainder of the *cugu* (ascensional difference) for the *vitribhalagna* is as great as that for calculating the *ṭakṣepa*. Now, if the *nata* time is sought, then the *lambaśaṅku* (sine of the altitude) is measured from the zenith to the celestial pole; the *vidhibhā* (complement of the latitude) is the *vidhibhayujyā* (sine of the complement of the latitude). As stated in the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, in the chapter on *tripraśna*: "The time [is not derived] here from that, nor is its sine (*tajyakā*) [derived] from the *dhujīvā* (sine of the hour-angle) of the *vitribhalagna*. (Verse 227).

The ascendant’s *agrajā* (sine of altitude) multiplied by the sine of the latitude and divided by the cosine of the declination is the horizontal parallax (*dṛkkṣepaka*) for that direction. Alternatively, it is obtained by the formula: "the square root of the sum of the squares of the sine of the desired deity’s position and the sine of the co-latitude. By this [method], the wise man should calculate the measure of the horizontal parallax as divided according to the appropriate [direction]. The degrees of the ascendant’s *agrajā*, the degrees of the co-latitude, and the degrees of the *bāhu* (sine of the amplitude) should be understood in sequence. The degrees of the direction for the tri-quadrant ascendant increased by the degrees of the direction, and the degrees of the co-latitude, should always be known [in this manner].

The wise declare that the horizontal parallax (*dṛkkṣepa*) situated at the meridian of the ecliptic (*citribhalagna*) is derived from the latitude (*akṣajyā*). [Verse 231] The sine of the latitude (*viddhibhā*) multiplied by the sine of the co-latitude (*akṣajyā*) and divided by the radius (*tri*), and then multiplied by the sine of the [longitude of the] meridian point (*trimavya*), and finally reduced to arc (*cāpa*), shall be the clear horizontal parallax in its own direction. [Verse 232] Alternatively, the horizontal parallax (*serokaṭakṣepa*) should be calculated; that, multiplied by three and divided by the cosine of the difference between the [longitude of the] meridian point and the [longitude of the] ecliptic point (*khacitribhāṅgabhedasya koṭijyā*), shall be the clear [parallax].

Herein is the proof: First, having assumed the point of the sphere’s junction (the vernal equinox) to be one’s own ascendant (lagna), from that point, O Bhaṭṭa, the meridian circle and the ecliptic are established; here, the degrees between the ascendant and the sun are indeed the solar degrees measured from the assumed junction of the sphere. The horizontal circle arising from the non-trigonal ascendant (vitribhalagna) is called the solstitial colure (ayanamaṇḍala); and there, the visual path which is equal to the degrees of depression (natabhāga) is the maximum declination (paramāpama), which is to be calculated from the maximum declination.

Thus, when the two celestial spheres are observed at the non-trigon (vitribha) point, their respective latitudes are always the maximum declinations at the meridian. When the distance between the non-trigon and the desired point is divided by the sine of the meridian zenith distance, those degrees of the field become the degrees of the oblique ascension (ṭakoṣaka) known as the equinoctial degrees (viṣuvāṃśaka), corresponding respectively to the right ascensions of the signs situated at the non-trigon. (235–237)

Thus, everything produced in the non-arc-field (*apakṣetra*) is immeasurable compared to the nature described for the arc-field (*krāntikṣetra*). Therefore, the knowledge of the degrees of the sword-defect (*khaṅgadoṣa*) derived from its half is easily understood by the learned, as previously stated. (238) Whatever fields known by the name "born" (*jāya*) arise from the connection of sines situated within the sphere (*gola*), through those very [fields] the supreme knowledge is attained. (239) Since the fields called arcs situated on the surface of the sphere certainly arise from straight lines, I shall explain them correctly and without doubt. (240)

They describe the east-west thread as that which passes through the eastern and western *svastikas* (fixed points). Likewise, the north-south thread is said to be that which passes through the northern and southern markers. The degrees of the arc between the *trivibha* (three signs) point and the local zenith are the degrees of the visible altitude (*dṛśyeṣāṃśāḥ*). When this is known, the calculation of the declination (*dakṣapadāna*) by means of proportion is easily understood.

(1) Viśvanātha Śarmā: Or, by the thirty-fourth verse of this very chapter, "The latitude of the ascendant minus three signs [is found] by means of the cosine of its dig-aṃśas," the measurement of the ascendant minus three signs is easily understood, just like the "half-day minus degrees" (*dinārdhanatāṃśa*). Alternatively, for the sake of clarity regarding the term *sva-lagnaprakā* in the previous verse, it might be argued that it ought to be "by means of the cosine of the dig-aṃśas of the ascendant minus three signs"; however, this does not seem entirely satisfactory.

(2) Viśvanātha Śarmā: "The sine of the angle between the intersection of the remaining [meridian] circle and the horizon is the *lagna-yujyā* (the sine of the oblique ascension); the shadow of the gnomon at that time is derived from the half-diameter," and so forth—this proof of the verse by Bhāskara cited in the *Praha-gaṇita* is easily established. *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, Chapter on Tripraśna (282). 283. When the celestial equator and the local horizon intersect, those two points situated in the east and west are fixed; that [line] shall be known as the *udaya-asta* (rising-setting) line. It is the intersection of the celestial sphere and the day-and-night circle (the meridian) at the unmandala (equatorial horizon). //242//

Those who know the science declare that the instruction for those two situated at the east and west [meridians] is fixed there; likewise, the *ūrdhvādharasvastika* (vertical-horizontal cross) is bound, and thus the *ūrdhvādharasūtra* (vertical-horizontal line) is described. (243) In this same manner, the *nirakṣajordhvādharasūtra* (the vertical-horizontal line of the non-axial observer) is established; likewise, the *bhūsthakoṇasūtra* (the diagonal line situated on the earth) is indeed fixed by the diagonal lines of the moon and the sun, as well as the other celestial bodies. (244) Furthermore, whatever line should run transversely between both of these, the interval situated along that line is to be understood here.

When two sūtras are situated at equal intervals from each other and are both bent in this manner, the distance between those two sūtras known as *śvaparā* (east-west) will be equal to the *agra* (apex) everywhere; that which is called the diameter (*vyāsa*) is the interval between the western and eastern [ends]. Likewise, the sine of declination (*krāntijyā*) is the diameter of that [circle], and the distance between the earth-sine (*kujyā*) and the fourth [term] is the carajyā (ascensional difference sine) in the form of the *yujīva* (sine of latitude), which is called the triple-sine (*trijyā*). The base of the gnomon (*śaṅku*) is on the western-eastern sūtra, extending toward the directions of the globe from the limits of rising and setting.

From the tip of the gnomon (*śaṅku*) to its base, and from that base to the shadow-tip (*śaṅkutala*) in whichever direction; from the tip of the northern shadow to the north, and from the tip of the southern shadow to the south [is the distance]. During the day it is toward the north, and at night during the long nights it is toward that same direction; by moving from that direction, on the meridian line, it is in that very direction. The arm (*bhuja*) is known as the *śaṅkutalā* correction (*saṃskāra*), and through that refinement, it becomes the true arm (*bhuja*) here.

The hypotenuse (hara) is the distance between the eastern and western *svastika* points; likewise, the sine of co-latitude (*trijyā*) is the side (*bhuja*) at the observer's own meridian, and the cosine (*koṭi*) is the distance from east to west. Here, the degrees of the latitude (*akṣāṃśāḥ*) extend from the observer's own meridian to the limit of the circle at the eastern and western *svastikas*. Similarly, the declination (*apama*) exists on the prime vertical (*unmaṇḍala*), and by that same method, the ascensional difference (*cara*) is established. At the north-south *svastikas* which resemble those [east-west ones], the degrees of latitude always remain exactly midway between them.

In the same way, the degrees of altitude (*lambāṃśaka*) are always constant within the sphere between the observer and the zenith. Just as a planet, by its revolution in another direction, reaches the horizon (*dṛgvṛtta*) while remaining fixed there, so too the celestial meridian (*kuta*) joined with the zenith becomes the fixed horizon for those two [the planet and the observer]. (248) When that planet is situated on the equator (*samamaṇḍala*), it takes on the nature of the east and west; and when it is situated in the southern or northern cardinal points, it takes on the nature of the south and north, being attached to the center of the earth. (249)

Then, the horizontal [line] is that which is grasped; and the line called "man" (*narasūtra*) is at the intersection of those two lines. (1) Regarding those two circles of the earth and the sky: this is from the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, Chapter on the Three Questions (Tripraśnādhikāra), verses 284 and 285. Now, the planet, having moved by its desired degrees from the center of the earth, is not at the intersection of the horizon-circle and the meridian-circle. (256) Because it is not struck [by the vertical], it does not appear as if depressed; for the plumb-line does not point toward the center of the earth. (266)

The gnomons (śaṅku) at the meridian and the zenith are those which, by their own shadow, take the form of the vertical and horizontal threads; these are the degrees of altitude (unnatāṃśa) here in the visual circle, and the degrees of time (kālabhāga) are the degrees of depression (natāṃśa). Thus, from the center of the sky, the degrees of depression are the degrees of time of depression at midday. [257] The sine (bhujā) is not joined; the result is the hypotenuse (śravaṇa), and that which arises from the great visual thread is the perpendicular (koṭi). [267] The previously mentioned gnomon-shadow (śaṅkutala) is the base (bāhu); it should be divided by the hypotenuse arising therefrom.

That sūtra which was extracted by Vyāsa from the *Ugra-sūtra* and known as the *Kalā-sūtra* has been explained here [as follows]. (268) The height (*unnata*) in the celestial sphere at night and day, the *kujyā*, the *carajyā*, and the *nara*—these are not stated here as being equal to the *lambajyā*. (269) Those gnomons (*śaṅku*) situated along the east-west and north-south directions on the level circle (*samamaṇḍala*) and the horizon circle (*dṛgvṛtta*) are well-known; they should be understood by their respective names. (258) The *bhuja* is the *akṣajyā*, and the *koṭi*-like *upakā* is the *lambajyā*. (269)

The eternal field (kṣetra) arising from the ear (karṇa) and the hypotenuse (iyakṣaja) is described as follows: the arm (bhuja) is the equinoctial shadow (akṣabhā), the base (kaṭi) is the sine of the amplitude (kaṭula), and the hypotenuse (śruti) is the palāśa. That field arising from the ear and the hypotenuse is devoid of falsehood. In that [field], the base (kuja) is the equinoctial shadow (apama-bhā), the arm (bhuja) is the sine of amplitude (agrā), and the hypotenuse (śruti) is the radius (kāṣṭhā). The arm (bāhu) is the radius of the unmaṇḍala (unmaṇḍala-nara), the base (koṭi) is the segment starting from the sine of amplitude (agrādi-khaṇḍaka). From that, the sine of amplitude (apamajyā) is likewise the arm (bāhu), the segment starting from the sine of amplitude (agrāgra-khaṇḍaka) is the base (kaṭi), the radius of the unmaṇḍala (unmaṇḍala-nara) is the hypotenuse (śravaṇa), and the equinoctial shadow (kṣitijyā) is likewise the hypotenuse (tathā).

In this case, the *agra-bhuja* (the base arm) is the side (*koṭi*), and the *samanā* (equal latitude) is its hypotenuse (*śruti*). Similarly, the *apama-ya-kā* (declination-related arm) is the side, and the *kujyā-nata-dhṛti* (earth-sine and meridian-distance support) is the hypotenuse. || 263 || Likewise, the *bāhūraga-thakhaṇḍa* (segment of the distance from the base arm) is the side, and the *sama-śaṅku* (equatorial gnomon-shadow) is the hypotenuse. Similarly, the *ūrdhva-ta-śakuna* (upward-pointing bird/altitude) together with the *sama-śaṅku* becomes the hypotenuse. || 264 || The *kujyā-nata-dhṛti* (earth-sine and meridian-distance support) is likewise; indeed, these are the values arising from the *akṣa* (latitude). In the same way, O wise one, other [values] such as the *dṛgjyā* (sine of altitude) and *akṣaja* (arising from latitude) also arise. || 265 || [These are] those which exist within the sphere of vision (*dṛśya-maṇḍala*) and the interior of the house (*gṛha-bhañjālaya*). || 266 ||

For Khaṭa, that [shadow] is indeed of the nature of the *jyā* (sine) of the altitude. (1) Viṣṇuśarman accepts the shadow at the center of the earth (*ku-garbha*) as the *śaṅku*, but Bhāskara, in the *Tripraśnādhikāra* of the *Golādhyāya*, while discussing the rationale for the calculation of the abbreviated shadow (*saṃkṣipta-śaṅku*), states: "The *śaṅku* is not the *nara* (the horizontal distance), because it is vertical; therefore, the *śaṅku* is similar to the true [vertical]. From this, the *jyā* of the altitude of the *śaṅku* would not be obtained, because that [shadow] stands at the center of the earth facing toward the center of the earth (*ku-garbha*). Therefore, the *śaṅku* is defined as being of the nature of a plumb-line (*avalambaka-sūtra*) extending from the zenith (*khasvastika*) downward.

The statement by Bhaṭṭa—that it is improper to say that those [sines] are not perpendicular, and thus his description of the gnomon as being in the form of a plumb-line is incorrect—is indeed appropriate. For in the science of geometry (*rekhāgaṇita*), the definition of a perpendicular is well-established as being upon a plane; likewise, in spherical astronomy (*gola*), the definition of a plumb-line is prevalent as being upon the horizontal plane (*dhara-tala*). Therefore, the gnomon of a planet situated above the horizon-plane (*dṛk-kuja*) or the earth-plane is certainly not defective. This is because, from the twelve-finger gnomon, the sine of the altitude (*madhyajyā*) is derived through the calculation of the hypotenuse (*karṇa*). Thus, the gnomon is established as being twelve fingers in length.

Śaṅkara states here that the *koṭi* is the versed sine (*utkramajyā*) of three signs minus the arc of the perpendicular drawn from the line of the planet's apogee and the Earth; thus, like Bhāskara, even Kamalākara is not at fault for repeatedly singing this same verse when refuting the *valana*. (Siddhāntatattvaviveka, Tripraśnādhikāra, verse 286). The sum of the segments of the shadow-tip and the hypotenuse is the base (*bhuja*) on the plane of the shadow; it is called the *kalā*. From those two [the *kalā* and the hypotenuse], the *kaṭi* shall be the *yaṣṭi* in what is known as the *akṣaja* [shadow]. (Verse 287).

270. When the *kujyā* (sine of co-latitude) is multiplied by the arm (*bhuja*) and divided by the hypotenuse (*karṇa*), the results are the two segments of the *agrā* (equinoctial shadow) starting from the tip; their sum shall be the *agrā*. 280–281. Those two segments of the *krāntijyā* (sine of declination) and the *agrā*, when multiplied respectively by the arm and the *koṭi* (co-latitude), shall be the *śrujyā* (sine of altitude) and the *śaṅku* (gnomon-shadow) when the sun is situated on the *unmaṇḍala* (prime vertical). 282. Those two segments of the *kujyā* and the *agrā*, when multiplied by the *koṭi* and divided by the *bhujyā* (sine of latitude) and the arm (*bhuja*), shall be the *nara* (horizontal distance) when the sun is situated on the *udagvalaya* (meridian).

In this case, *ghuśyavaśa* is a *kalā*, and that same term, by virtue of having three vowels (*tri-pavaśāt*), may be designated as *mūtraka*. Thus, many [terms] arising from syllables come into being in the sphere (*gola*) through their separation and combination. (271) The sine of the latitude (*bāhu*) and the cosine (*kaṭī*) are respectively multiplied by the radius (*trijyā*) and divided by the hypotenuse (*karṇa*). These two are the sines of the latitude and the colatitude (*palalambau*). (272) Alternatively, here the sines of those [angles] are the sine of the complement of speech (*vāṅkoṭī*) and so forth; and these two are mutually related to the sine of the latitude and the cosine of the complement by means of proportion (*anupāta*) for one of sound intellect. (273)

The sine of the ascensional difference (krāntijyā) multiplied by the hypotenuse (karṇa), and further multiplied by the co-latitude (koṭī) and the sine of the amplitude (doṣṇā), yields two results: the first is the *agrā*, and the second is the equinoctial shadow (samaśaṅku) multiplied by that same [sine of amplitude]. When divided by the co-latitude (bhū), the quotient is the *dhṛti* of that [shadow]; or otherwise, the *agrā* multiplied by the hypotenuse and divided by the sine of amplitude would be the *dhṛti*. Those two quantities known as *agrā* and *dhṛti*, when multiplied respectively by the sine of amplitude and the hypotenuse and divided by the co-latitude and the hypotenuse, shall result in the equinoctial shadow (*samaśaṅku*) subtracted from the radius.

That product of many factors may be divided by *kavya* (the square of the cosine of latitude) or otherwise; the upper segment resulting from that division would be the divisor for the *koṭi* (sine of the co-latitude). Less than that is the equal segment of the same [divisor]; the sine of the amplitude (*bhujaphla*) divided by that divisor gives the *agrā*, and subtracting that from the divisor yields the *kujyā* (sine of the colatitude). The division of that [result] and the upper segment of that divisor are known in various ways by the learned; these should be understood in the sphere (*golaka*) through the intersection of the multiplier and the divisor.

The *hṛti* (the hypotenuse) is the square root of the sum of the squares of the base (*bhuja*) and the perpendicular (*koṭi*). When this is divided by the ear (*śravaṇa*, the hypotenuse), the result is obtained through that division. Here, the base is the gnomon (*yaṣṭi*), and the second [term] is the product of the arm and the hypotenuse divided by the ear. In the first case, it becomes the area of the shadow-base (*śaṅkatala*); in the second, the area would be the sum or difference of the segments of the tip of the shadow (*agrāgrakhaṇḍa*). Or else, the *hṛti* should be established by those proficient in calculation through the inversion of the multiplication of the shadow and the gnomon. How can the square root of the sum of the squares of the arm and the perpendicular be found? Thus [is the method].

The square root of the difference between the squares of the arm (*bhuja*) and the ear (*karṇa*) is the hypotenuse (*koṭi*); likewise, the hypotenuse is the arm. (287) The square root of the difference between the squares of the hypotenuse and the ear is equal to the measure of the other [side]. Thus, by means of two [sides], the knowledge of the third is produced; this has been declared by the wise. (288) And because of the absence of all three—the arm, the hypotenuse, and the ear—the result would be impossible; therefore, it never occurs otherwise. (289) Next, having separately observed the sines of the latitudes (*krāntijyā*) of the equatorial points, they should be multiplied respectively by the sine of the arm and the sine of the hypotenuse, and divided by the sine of the arm. (290)

The *āya* shall be the *kujyā* (versed sine of the altitude), and another segment shall be from its division; the sum of those two segments shall be that divisor for what arises at the end of the day. (279) In the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, Chapter on the Three Questions (Tripraśnādhikāra): The first [value] may be derived from the eternal field or reduced by simplification (*apavartita*). An operation of proportion (*anupāta*) must be applied everywhere, so that there is no deviation. (290) The midday shadow, the other [shadow], and likewise the gnomon—these three, when multiplied by their respective names, are designated as the "desired" (*iṣṭa*) values arising at the specific time. (291)

291–294. When the Sun is situated in the six signs beginning with Aries (Meṣa) and is moving northward, it is in the northern hemisphere; when in the six signs beginning with Libra (Tulā), it is in the southern hemisphere. At that time, the rising shadow (udyacchaṅku) is obtained by multiplying the equinoctial shadow (yaṣṭi) by the sine of the latitude (akṣajyā) and dividing by the radius (trijyā). Alternatively, the other [shadow] is found by taking the product of the equinoctial shadow and the sine of the colatitude (yujyā) and dividing by the radius. From this, the divisor (hṛti) should be understood as the result of the multiplication of the multiplier and the divisor. Or, the divisor may be the square root of the difference between the squares of the hypotenuse (śaṅku) and the equinoctial shadow. Alternatively, the other [shadow] is obtained by multiplying the equinoctial shadow by the sine of the latitude and dividing by the sine of the colatitude.

295–298. A man who eats at midday [should calculate] the fruit by means of the sine of the seventh degree [of the sun's amplitude]. Likewise, when the day-measure is multiplied by the twelvefold sine of the colatitude (*lambajyā*), and divided respectively by the hypotenuse of the shadow (*palakarṇa*) and the radius (*trijīvā*), the result is the midday gnomon. That same result, when further divided by the hundredth part of the base and the hypotenuse, becomes the multiplier. (1) Now, the sine of the degrees of declination (*apamāṃśu*) in reverse order, or the sine of the colatitude (*lambāṃśu*) divided by the radius (*tribhajīvā*); that same value, diminished by the quotient, becomes the degrees of the oblique ascension (*vilambabhāga*), which serves as the multiplier for the midday gnomon.

In this context, as previously stated, the hypotenuse (bhuja) is the arc-sine of the meridian altitude (madhyadṛgjyakā); or else, by means of the "support" (dhṛti) obtained through addition and subtraction according to the sequence of the celestial sphere: || 299 || The product [of that support] with the equinoctial shadow (palabhā) is divided by the equinoctial hypotenuse (palakarṇa). Then, the result is multiplied by the day-half-hypotenuse (dinārdhakarṇa), and likewise by the arc-sine of the complement of the latitude (nṛcotkramajīvā). || 300 || Subtracting this from the radius (trijyā), the resulting arc-sine of the altitude (dṛgjyā) is obtained; from this, the human [shadow] is likewise determined. The arc-sines of the sun's altitude and zenith distance, when divided by ten, are the respective shadows. || 301 || The radius multiplied by the equinoctial shadow is the mean support (madhyamā dhṛtiḥ) for the horse [the sun].

The sines of the maximum shadow and the hypotenuse are multiplied by the sine of the latitude; when divided by the sine of the latitude, they become the [sine of the] hypotenuse and the sine of the maximum shadow, respectively, in the case of the equinoctial circle (samamaṇḍala). When the sine of the hypotenuse is diminished by the sine of the observed shadow and divided by the sine of the maximum shadow, it becomes the sine of the altitude of the sun at the time of observation. When the sine of the altitude of the sun at midday is multiplied by the sine of the latitude and then divided by the sine of the colatitude, [the result is the sine of the declination]. When that [sine of declination] is multiplied by the sine of the latitude and then divided by the sine of the colatitude, [the result is the sine of the ascensional difference].

By means of the light of the midday sun, those two [the shadow and the gnomon] are respectively equal to the sine of the ascensional difference (śravaṇa). For the remaining [half-day], the small portion arising from its own hemisphere is the altitude (unnata), and the depression (nata) situated there is the complement; that depression shall be subtracted. Now, in this manner, the calculation of the shadow-hypotenuse (chāyākarṇa) at the desired time is as follows: from the time of the end of the day-and-night, the cosine of the ascensional difference (cara-jyā) is multiplied by the radius (jyā) according to the sequence of the sphere (gola); that product becomes the sine (sūtra). || 306–308 ||

(1) Viśvanātha-śiromaṇi: The midday shadow is the base (*bhuja*), and the gnomon (*śaṅku*) is the perpendicular (*koṭi*); the square root of the difference between these two is the side (*karṇa*). This is similar to the triangle of latitude (*akṣakṣetra*). Depending on whether the sphere is northern or southern, the hypotenuse (*karṇa*) and the perpendicular (*koṭi*) will be greater or less [than the midday shadow]. Therefore, from the center of the equatorial circle (*ahorātravṛtta*), the upper segment from the foot of the gnomon-staff (*yaṣṭi*) situated at the midday shadow is the "gnomon-shadow" (*śaṅkuchāyā*). Thus, whatever the gnomon-staff may be, it is the perpendicular, and the square root of its difference is the side; this is similar to the triangle of latitude.

Now, for half a day, where the versed sine (lamba) from the zenith of the non-polar point is the declination-sine (krāntijyā), what is the horizontal [sine] from the base up to the pole of the sphere? How is it derived? Therefore, from the base of the declination-sine, that which is the perpendicular upon the equatorial line is the measured co-latitude (koṭi); on the equatorial line, the arm (bhuja) is of the same nature as the triangle of latitude. From the non-polar celestial point (svastika), the radius (trijyā) is the hypotenuse, while the versed sine and the latitude-sine are the co-latitude and the arm, respectively.

Here, by constructing a right-angled triangle (*kamya*) above the vertical radius (*lambajyā*) which is the square root of the product of the trijyā and the sine of the obliquity (*krāntijyā*), the versed sine of the obliquity (*krāntyutkramajyā*) becomes the base (*kaṇa*), the vertical radius (*lambajyā*) becomes the hypotenuse (*koṭi*), and the gnomon (*hamba*) becomes the side (*bhuja*); thus, everything is clear. From the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, Chapter on the Three [Questions] (Tripraśnādhikāra): When that thread, equal to the minutes of arc, is multiplied by the trijyā and divided by the product of the earth’s diameter and the sine of the ascensional difference (*carajyā*), the result in minutes is multiplied by twelve (*ravi*). Divided by the shadow-hypotenuse (*palakarṇa*), it shall be the desired gnomon; then, the thread [is determined].

The sine of the desired [arc] multiplied by the radius, or divided by the radius according to the sine of the desired [arc], is the sine of the desired [arc] in the sphere; this, added to the sine of the horizon [sine] in the thread, becomes the sine of the desired [arc]. Thus, the minutes [of arc] added to or subtracted from the sine of the desired [arc] become its own gnomon. Here, the desired gnomon added to or subtracted from the radius becomes the other gnomon. The arrow of the versed sine of the depressed [arc] is subtracted from that, and the other [gnomon] becomes the desired arrow; likewise, the desired [arrow] and the other [arrow] joined and divided by three are the [resulting] weapon.

That quotient obtained by him is subtracted from the divisor; thus it becomes the desired divisor (*iṣṭahṛti*). The quotient multiplied by twelve and divided by the sine of the ascensional difference (*palabhā*) gives the desired sine of altitude (*iṣṭakṣepaka*). By dividing the sine of the desired altitude (*udvṛttaśaṅku*) by the sine of the ascensional difference, the result is the desired *carajyā* (sine of the hour-angle). The midday gnomon (*madhyamaśaṅku*) diminished by that [sine] becomes the desired gnomon (*iṣṭaśaṅku*). In this same manner, the desired *antyā* (sine of the meridian zenith distance) is derived from the desired gnomon or from the division by the desired divisor. The calculation of the gnomon at the desired time should be performed like that for midday. Likewise, the visible gnomon (*dṛśyaśaṅku*) shall be found, and from that, the shadow (*chāyā*) and its hypotenuse (*tacchuti*) are determined.

In any procedure for correction (*śuddhi*), if that which is to be corrected does not subtract [from the other], then the wise should perform the correction in reverse (*viloma-śodhana*) according to the rule stated therein. However, in the case of addition, subtraction should be performed; likewise, in the case of subtraction, addition should be performed. The *nata* (ascensional difference) is multiplied by five and divided by the moon (one); if it is greater than that, then the *nata* is [further] diminished by five and one. The sine of its arc (*kujyā*) is divided by the radius (*tribhajyā*). When added to the *nata*, it becomes the inverse sine (*atarkramajyā*). Then, the *nara* (sine of the altitude) is derived from the *udvṛtta* (ecliptic).

In the southern hemisphere, when Mars is below the horizon, its visible altitude cannot indeed be diminished by that [latitude]. Therefore, for the sake of subsequent proportionate calculations, it is multiplied by the wise according to its suitability. When the Sun reaches the meridian, that gnomon-shadow which arises through the previously calculated method shall indeed serve for the determination of the other [parameters]. For one whose declination is less than the degrees of latitude, the circle there is not touched by the equator; its true nature is here described as being like the shadow of the equatorial gnomon.

At one's desired time, having divided the night by three, one should lead the cord upward; likewise, the urine, the self-measure, and the cut-off [measure] prior to the arrow-throw. That which is seen as equal to the tip of the arrow and the cord leading upward—when that cord is joined with the thread, it becomes the equidistant line (*samanā*). From the union of those, the thread is likewise known as *hṛti* and *dhṛti*; thus it is declared, regardless of where one is situated within the day and night.

The sine of the latitude multiplied by the equinoctial shadow is the hypotenuse arising from three parts of ten degrees; it should be calculated likewise by the half-chord of the oblique ascension, and then divided by the product of three [sines] in sequence. Now, the first [result] is the sine of the altitude of the meridian-transverse; the second would be that pertaining to the oblique ascension; the third would be that pertaining to the circle of results. From these, by reverse order, one does not obtain the sine of the latitude. (1) Vi0 Śa: Above the level surface, the vertical and horizontal lines have their own distinct forms.

The *hṛtisūtra* (perpendicular line) is drawn from the southern axis toward the south; from that, the angle produced by the intersection with the equatorial line (*samasūtra*) is the arc of the plumb line (*lambāṃśa*). Then, according to the established technical terminology of the *rekhāgaṇita* (geometry), such as "the product divided by the base" and "the sum of the perpendicular lines," the application of this geometry is clearly evident in the treatises of Kamalakara and others. This concludes the chapter on the *prinā* (latitude/declination) in the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*. The circle situated at the east-west meridian line, reaching the depressed degrees of the horizon-circle (*dṛgvṛtta*), is known as the *phala* (resultant/arc).

The versed sine of the degrees of the position of the fruit-form (phalarūpaṭhattasthana) shall be known as *hara*. When multiplied by the radius (*trijyā*) and divided by *hara*, the results are the two sines of the amplitude (*apamajyake*) called "arm" (*bhujā*) and "fruit" (*phala*). The difference or sum of these two—depending on whether they are of the same or opposite directions—shall be the declination (*krānti*) and the latitude (*akṣa*) respectively. The sine of the zenith distance (*dṛgjīva*) is the cosine of the degrees of the direction; ninety minus that is the degrees of the direction. The product of the degrees of depression (*namrāṃśa*) called "fruit" and the sine of the latitude (*viṣaudya*), when divided separately by twelve (*dyu*) and ten (*bha*), [yields the respective results]. 329–330, 335.

The square of the sine of the latitude multiplied by the square of the hypotenuse (karṇa) gives the two factors of the product; from these two, the quotient of the sine of the co-latitude divided by ten million is indeed the result. The sine of the complement of the latitude multiplied by the sine of the complement of the hypotenuse, divided by the radius (trijyā), shall be the *nara*. The sine of the complement of the hypotenuse multiplied by the sine of the complement of the arm, divided by the sine of the latitude, shall be the sine of the degrees of the azimuth (*diglava*). The square root of the sum of the squares of the sine of the latitude and the *nara*, multiplied by three and divided by the sine of the latitude, [is the desired value].

Then, by means of that diagonal of the direction (*digjyā*) through the reverse order of procedure, there is a separate conjunction with the two [sines] of the latitude (*dharā*). From those two, the accomplishment [of the desired result] shall occur according to what was stated. Likewise, from the sine of the altitude (*natajyā*) and the half-circumference of the equator (*vāsārdha*), which have been previously established, it is also thus. Furthermore, I shall explain again that very method for the determination of time which was previously taught by the Lord of Men (*Naraśrī*) according to the rule of the directions; for it is the sole path for those desiring the excellence of calculation, even when distinguished by the various circles arising from the earth, the four quarters, the six seasons, and the twelve months. (337–338)

The mandala situated in the directions is the terrestrial circle; there, from the center of the sky, as far as two nāḍīs [of latitude] and as far as the degrees of latitude (akṣabhāga) extend here, and as far as the lord of birds [the sun] moves from the meridian, the degrees of the bow [arc] are the subtracted hours (natāsava). The degrees of latitude (akṣāṃśaka), corrected by the degrees of the arc of the result of declination (krāntiphala), are the degrees of the arc of the result of the sine (doḥphala); and when well-corrected by the addition or subtraction of those degrees of latitude, the degrees of the arc of the result of declination are to be known. 332–333.

The sine of the degrees of depression of the horizon-circle known as the arm (bhujā), when multiplied by the square root of the difference [of its square from the radius], is the sine of depression (natajyā). The product of the sine of the degrees of depression known as the result (phala) and the sine of the degrees of depression known as the subtracted tripartite result (tribhataphala) is said to be the "stated" [product]. (334)

(1) Viśvanātha Śarman, in his *Graha-gaṇita*, [states]: "The *palabhā* should be as derived from this; having clarified the measure of the *nata-śaṅku* by means of a demonstration of that diagram, Bhāskara has shown the measure of the angle produced by the intersection of the equinoctial and ecliptic circles—known as *parā*—in the 343rd verse of this very chapter. From that, the desired shadow at night can be easily calculated. [End of] the Chapter on Tripraśna in the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*. 37.294.

O Lord, those degrees of the arc [of the ecliptic] which correspond to the sleep (setting) of one's own natal sign and its portions, as well as the directions, would not be the same degrees traversed by the planet from the center of the sky. The circle of the zodiac situated at the center of the sky, when its diameter lies upon the local meridian, forms a cross. From that cross, the degrees of direction for the planet are those by which it lies toward a particular direction; these directional degrees are north-south relative to the prime vertical, and they are indeed southward when measured from the southern point.

In the southern hemisphere, those [sines] are always southern; they become the parts of the desired latitude and the parts of the declination. When the northern [latitude] is equal to its own directional part (the colatitude), it is otherwise. Or, when the sine of the latitude is greater than the sine of the amplitude, then the calculation of a single shadow should be performed as previously stated. Otherwise, when the desired degree of latitude is made such that it is less than fifteen degrees, then from those two [values], by calculating according to the rule stated above, the first shadow shall indeed result from the desired declination itself.

Thus, having calculated the [longitude] exceeding three signs (*tripala*) in the *vicaryama* [sphere], one should correctly determine it in the *ayamasamyagola*. If, at the equinox (*samya*), the sine of the latitude (*dilavajyā*) is found in the degrees of declination (*apamabhāga*) corresponding to the tip of the shadow (*agrakalpa*), then this first shadow is produced there due to the division of the hemisphere (*kapālabheda*). At that time, the first shadow exists only in the northern hemisphere (*bhavaṃdakakapāla*), as established by the distinction of time. However, at the equinox, the sines of the earth’s shadow (*kujadhvaja*) move toward the south and north.

If the *dig-aṃśas* (directional degrees) are situated in a *khaṭaka-pāla* [sign] belonging to a certain direction, then the planets situated in that other sign will belong to that same direction. Those situated in any other sign are fixed as belonging to their own respective directions. By means of the calculation of the *dig-aṃśa-khaṇḍas*, one should multiply the degrees to be traversed (*laṅghāṃśa*) by the divisor and divide by the sum of the parts; the resulting arc-parts are equal to the number of *khaṅkas*. Then, that [result] multiplied by the sine and divided by the radius— (Note: The provided text contains fragments of astronomical calculation rules regarding planetary directions and traversed degrees, specifically concerning the determination of directional sectors based on zodiacal signs and the computation of longitudinal distances using trigonometric proportions.)

By dividing [the radius] by the sine of the latitude, the desired values for the shadow and the gnomon-shadow are obtained there; and when the desired latitudes here are equal to those [sines], the sines of the altitude and the zenith distance are derived from them. Likewise, from that, the elevation and the light are found; the hypotenuse is the sun's gnomon divided by one hundred. (344–345)

[1] Viśvanātha Śarmā: Here, for the purpose of determining after how much time the second shadow will occur from the first shadow, there is this specific rule: The degrees of the arc of the result, obtained by dividing the co-latitude (koṭi) multiplied by the radius (trijyā) by the sine of latitude (yujyā), when divided by three (hutāśa), become the ghaṭīs and so forth; these should be added to the well-known [time]. The justification for this is as follows: From the intersection of the equatorial circle (nāḍīvṛtta) and the horizon circle (ḍagvṛtta), the desired latitude (akṣaśā) is measured up to its own celestial point (svasvastika). By subtracting the latitude of the celestial point (khaaindu), the second latitude is obtained.

The second meridian altitude is calculated as being below the horizon; therefore, the first shadow is near the horizon. Consequently, the first *natāṃśas* (zenith distances) are $180^\circ - a - \text{ikrāṃ}$, and the second *natāṃśas* are $\text{ikrāṃ} - a$. Thus, the difference between the two zenith distances is established in the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, Chapter on the Three Questions (*Tripraśnādhikāra*), verse 296. In this manner, when there is the occurrence of two [solar] disks due to the non-ecliptic deviation (*ayuddhakṣavaśāt*), that shadow which belongs to the planet situated in the southern direction shall arise from its own non-ecliptic deviation. (Verse 351)

For the sake of the horizontal movement of the ecliptic, [the shadow] is cast toward the northeast and southeast; thus, up until midday, it is seen in reverse order, and from midday onwards, that same [order] should be understood. (1) Their own declination and their own latitude are small; they do not become greater degrees on the sphere. (2) When the sun is slightly more than half [the day], then the shadow will be equal to the successive parts of the quadrant.

When the *agra* (the sine of the amplitude) is greater than the equinoctial shadow (*sadottara*), two units of the first [digit] are independent; even when the *agra* is smaller than the equinoctial shadow, there may be the occurrence of even a single unit of light. When the other [shadow] is equal to the degrees of the equinoctial shadow (*svāpama*), then the desired [result] is fifteen hundred and sixty-nine. In that case, the degrees of latitude (*akṣabhāga*) are nine; thus, by a wise person, one should investigate the celestial sphere (*khagola*) regarding the arising of the moon from the circle of the earth's shadow.

Thus, when two shadows are established upon a single gnomon, that shadow which occurs at the end of the day shall be the light arising from the *ayuddhakṣa* (the non-conflict point). In this case, the light arising from the *vidhraddhākṣa* (the conflict point) for one situated at a distance is calculated as previously stated. However, this comparison regarding the other [shadow] among the parts is not applicable when those two are equal. The sine of the direction (*digjyā*) on the terrestrial horizon is equal; thereafter, it increases by that small amount.

In the northern hemisphere, [the latitude] is increased by the sum of the [ascensional difference] palas; when it exceeds one's own apamaṇḍala (oblique ascension), [the result is] 180° minus 23°. The difference between the [latitude and] natāṃśa (zenith distance) is the earth-sine (bhū). The two arms are determined from the arc-minutes of the dyujyā (sine of the meridian zenith distance).

Here, from the point of the gnomon's shadow (*śaṅku*) situated at the zenith, a vertical circle (*lambavṛtta*) is drawn above the ground at the limit of the depressed angles (*natāṃśa*), which indeed establishes half the interval of those depressed angles. Therefore, the sine of the angle facing the arc of half the depression is *pra-jyā* (the sine), and the cosine is *ko-jyā* (the cosine). This arc in degrees is converted into *nāḍīs* (time units); hence, the result in *ghaṭīs* and so forth is subtracted from that [total], and thus the calculation of the depressed *ghaṭīs* is established. And those desired parts of the gnomon are subtracted from that; the depressed angles are equal to the sky-measure (*khaṅka*). Alternatively, it is the square root of the difference between the squares of the latitude-sine (*svākṣajyā*) and the cosine of the altitude (*parakhyā*). || 359 ||

The natajyā (sine of the zenith distance) multiplied by the trijyā (radius of the celestial sphere) and divided by the jyā known as *parā* (the sine of the maximum declination) shall then be the *prabhā* (shadow). [1] Viśvanātha: Regarding *parā*, it is the measure of the arc produced at the intersection of the equator and the horizon; it is the maximum declination of the three circles. Now, according to one's own declination (*apakrama*), the degrees of the observer's latitude (*akṣāṃśa*) are subtracted from it; thus, the *parā* degrees are obtained. From these *parā* degrees, the degrees of one's own declination are subtracted; they will not be less than the degrees of one's own latitude. [2] Viśvanātha: When the *digjyā* (sine of the azimuth) has the form of the north direction and the declination is less than the degrees of latitude, then in both hemispheres (*kapāla*).

When the shadow is abundant, and due to the influence of the small circle (maṇḍala) attached at the intersection of the large circle of the earth and the long circle of the region of the Lord of Small Intelligence (the Sun), there arises a supreme state; then, when the water-circle (apa-maṇḍala) becomes greater than its own [meridian] points, it is indeed logical that it exists as a single hemisphere (ekakapāla). 298. This is from the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, the chapter on the "Three Questions" (*tripraśnādhikāra*). 299. But when the oblique ascensions (*svatakrānti*) and the degrees of latitude (*palāṃśaka*) are equal, no shadow shall appear here at all. 360.

Just as the light of the sun increases when facing away from it, so too does that light increase when facing toward it; likewise, even in the case of an equal [object], the nature of existence becomes non-existence for the wise. (361) If the degrees of the *khecarāpama* (the amplitude of the rising-setting points) were not slightly greater than those of the *parabhāga*, then even a dull-witted person would surely ask why this is so, for that would be a total contradiction. (362) Since Bhāskara and others, in their own works, have calculated two directions of the *digbhāga* (the azimuthal angle) starting from the northward-pointing line, there is a discrepancy.

Even when the rule for the oblique ascension (*digjyā*) is applied by means of the nine hundred and sixty degrees (*khanandabhāga*), that [result] is the ascensional difference (*iṣṭāpama*) here due to the addition of the oblique ascensions of day and night. (363) For whatever has been made by those [ascensions] through human convention, if there is equality between those two here, then that indeed exists; for there are divisions of the hemispheres (*kapāla-bheda*). Otherwise, O wise one, there is no equality here, but rather a single [hemisphere]. (364) In this case, the shadow (*bhā*) occurs in a single hemisphere, whereby it would be measured by a single human [unit]. Indeed, from the conjunction of the circle of the sun’s declination with the oblique ascension, and from the addition of two signs (*bha*), they both exist. (365)

That which was indeed stated occurs in the southern hemisphere (yāmyagola) below one's own horizon. And as for the calculation of the single direction (digbhāna) in the south when the digjyā (sine of the azimuth) is greater than the agrā (shadow-tip), that [occurs] correctly below the horizon in the sphere; now hear the proof regarding the configuration of the sphere. Having fixed the zenith and the nadir at the center of the sky, let there be the meridian, the prime vertical, the horizon, and the equator. Let the circle of declination (krāntivṛtta) be imagined upon the horizon.

Therein, the interval between those two would be equal to a degree of the horizon; the desired circle, fixed at the pole, is the locus of the right ascension points of the intersection of the meridian and the horizon circles.

The intersection of the ecliptic and the meridian is observed from the celestial pole (*dhruva*) along the visible arc. On the northern solstitial colure (*uttaravṛtta*), the degrees of the arc from the zenith to the pole are the *kṣetrāṃśas* (field-degrees). Having subtracted the desired degrees from those, the resulting complementary degrees are the *kāyāṃśas*. The junction of the visible circle (*dṛgvṛtta*) and the equatorial circle (*nāḍīvṛtta*) is the point where their respective arcs meet; the difference between these two circles—namely, the solstitial colure and the equator—is the precession (*ayanāṃśa*) on the desired circle.

Now, on the diurnal circle (*dṛgvṛtta*), the desired degrees of longitude (*iṣṭakṣāṃśāḥ*) from the intersection of that [circle] up to the zenith (*khamadhya*) are the field-angles (*kṣetrāṃśāḥ*). The poles (*dhruva*) are indeed the two celestial poles (*dhruvau*). On the meridian (*yāmyottara-vṛtta*), the degrees of one's own longitude (*svakṣāṃśāḥ*) extend from the zenith to the prime vertical (*nāḍīvṛtta*); they are not so on the circle arising from the two poles associated with the planet. The interval between the meridian and the diurnal circle (*nāḍī-dṛgvṛttayoḥ*) is the degrees of its own latitude (*svapayāṃśāḥ*). Here, the desired declination (*iṣṭakrāntyaṃśāḥ*) are simply the degrees of the [planet's] position on the solstitial colure (*śaivṛttastha*).

In that context, the two sides of a small triangle are the desired latitude and the radius on the ecliptic circle; its hypotenuse and the other side are the two chords arising from the declination of the questioner's location. The third is a chord arising from the declination of the sun mentioned immediately prior. Since these three form a right-angled triangle, it is easily understood that by means of the two sides of that triangle obtained through proportion, the values of the desired latitude and the obliquity of the ecliptic can be known. When the declination of the sun is less than one's own latitude, the declination-figure is contained within the latitude-figure, and the latitude-figure is contained within the declination-figure.

When the sum [of the latitudes] is negative, the declination circle situated outside the chest, field, and corners will touch those corners. The difference between the two sums divided by the equinoctial shadow (viṣuvat-chāyā) gives the number of degrees; from that, within the interval between the directions of their union, the calculation of one or two directions occurs above the earth in its own northern hemisphere. [End of Chapter 300 on the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, Chapter 3 on Tripraśna (The Three Questions). Chapter 301 begins: "O best of navigators, this is the neck of the ship."

When the northward shadow is corrected by its own northern shadow-component (*padacchāyā*), the resulting arm (*bhuja*) is correctly situated within the northern part of the meridian-line (*bhāgra*). The two arms [of the triangle] are determined by the northern component; at other times, the arm subtracted from that [meridian-line] becomes the equatorial shadow (*akṣabhā*), or the arm subtracted from it by that [equatorial shadow] is likewise obtained. The arm is correctly divided by the degrees of the meridian-line and multiplied by the hypotenuse-component (*karṇabhāga*); from this, the arc of the northern component is derived. The velocity of the arm established by the hypotenuse and the northern component is to be subtracted from the square of the shadow; from that, the square root shall be obtained.

Now, here on the celestial sphere (kheṭa-kapālaka), the eastern and western limits are the eastern and western conjunctions. The maximum distance between these two is equal to the complement (of the latitude). In the northern hemisphere, when the *agrā* is less than the equinoctial sine (*digjyā*), the degrees of direction for a planet situated below the earth’s surface are properly subtracted; in the southern hemisphere, they are subtracted from themselves. Thus, the desired latitudinal degrees (*iṣṭakṣāṃśāḥ*) are clearly established in the visible sphere (*dṛggola*) when the declination is small. There, the two day-and-night circles (*ahorātra*) meet at two points by way of the division of the hemispheres; thus, the initial shadow and so forth are well-known.

In the case of the *ādhaka* (the equinoctial shadow), the equinoctial shadow (*svapama*) is attached at only one point on the meridian; thus, the shadow and so forth are there, though even that is perceivable only through subtle calculation. However, in the case of the *paralpa* (the declination), the diurnal circle of the planet situated at the point where the diurnal circle intersects the local horizon is attached precisely there and nowhere else; thus, the shadow is singular and is understood through direct perception in the *agrakā* (the sine of the amplitude) along the direction of the equinoctial shadow.

In this matter, those who assert that the great doubt regarding the nature of the gnomon (*śaṅku*) is resolved by the shadow and other methods have been refuted; the remainder is clear from the source itself, so enough with further elaboration. Here, the sine of the direction (*digjyā*) multiplied by the sine of the zenith distance (*dṛgjīvā*) and divided by the radius (*trijyā*) results in the *bhuja*. Alternatively, the sine of the direction divided by the product of the shadow and the radius yields the *bhuja*; from that *bhuja*, the [other] elements are obtained in reverse order. (368)

(1) The *akṣaprā* (latitude sine) divided by the three sines (*tribhajyā*) is the *karṇanitrī*. (19) These two verses belong to Bhāskarācārya himself. Here, for the sake of demonstrating the reversed sphere (*vyastagola*), many people needlessly construct a "ear-sphere" (*karṇagola*). From the base point to the east-west line, there is the *bhuja* (side); that, however, arises from the correction involving the shadow of the gnomon's base (*śaṅkatala*), which is always established on the meridian without dispute.

Now, the hypotenuse is the distance from the tip of the shadow (*chāyāgrīya-bhuja*), and the side is the radius of the circle (*trijyā*). The arrow (*śara*) is the sine (*ijyā*), and the shadow is the gnomon of twelve *aṅgulas* (*chāyākarmī*, *chadaśāṅgula-śaṅku*). These two figures are similar triangles; therefore, the ratio is as follows: The hypotenuse is the distance from the tip of the shadow (*chāyāgrīya-bhuja*), the side is the radius (*bha*), and the base is the sine of the altitude (*dṛgjyā*). *Chāyāgrīya-bhuja* : *Bha* = *Chāka* : *Śīta* In this proportion: *Chāka* / *Śīta* = *Dṛgjyā* / *Chaka* Here, the first segment is *pa*... *cha*.

The base (*bhuja*) is twelve *chakratra*s; one *adhapalabhā* is always added to it for the sake of the proper correction. In the second segment, if the two hypotenuses (*karṇau*) are not assumed to be reversed, then the base would not be the same as the tip of the desired shadow (*icchāyāgra*); therefore, the statement regarding the "reversed sphere" (*vyastagola*) is indeed appropriate. Now, the surface of level ground should be prepared and marked with circles (*cakra*). There, the point of the shadow-tip (*chāyāgraka*), which follows the movement of the moon and is purified by the [shadow] distance, enters and departs. (372) (1) Viśvanātha Śarmā.

In this context, the statement "at the tip of the wood" (*kāṣṭhānte*) is due to negligence. (2) Viśvanātha: The base (*bhuja*) is from the tip of the shadow; *X* is from the tip of the radius (*trijyā*). Let *X* = *ka*, and the base = 7. Thus, having calculated the other base as *chāka* and the radius as *tri*, the measure of the difference between the arcs (*cāpa*) of those two—namely *chā* and *chā0*—is easily understood.

At this juncture, some, desiring to add the difference of the sides (*bhuja-antara*) to the circle according to Bhāskarācārya’s verse beginning with “*tatkālāpama-jyayā tu*,” etc., falsely claim that Bhāskara’s calculation is useless. In reality, however, the difference between the entry and exit points (*praveśa-nirgama*) is indeed known; that is the hypotenuse (*karṇa*). The calculated difference of the sides is the side (*bhuja*), and the square root of the difference of their squares is the perpendicular (*koṭi*). Thus, in the geometric construction (*kṣetra-yoga*), the addition of the difference of the sides is not difficult to establish. Otherwise, how could one determine the measure of the side even from a single degree?

This should be reflected upon by the wise; it is consistent with reason. [End of Chapter 302]. Chapter 303: On the Determination of the Three Questions. In the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, on the day following the full moon, two directions arise. The two arms (sides) are those reaching to the tips of the *dṛgjyā* (sine of altitude) at that time. These are multiplied by the hypotenuse derived from the shadow and divided by the measure of the shadow; the arcs of these two [results] are then taken. If they are in different directions, their difference; if in the same direction, their sum—these are the *kalās* (degrees) by which the eastern direction has shifted toward the south.

The [latitude] subtracted from the [zenith distance] shall be the declination; that, when situated in the desert (the meridian), becomes here the southern latitude. || 374 || From the observation of the sun at Aries, even at a difference of ten degrees [of longitude], there is one [consistent] east-west line. Since the pole-star is always in the north, the knowledge of other directions from this is easily understood. || 375 || Now, from a single point on the ground, one should place a gnomon of many digits in its own direction; likewise, another gnomon should be placed at the tip [of the first], and the intersection of their shadows will be in the direction of their respective points. || 376 ||

Therefore, the diameter of the circle is the form of the meridian line (*divadhyarūpa*), while its two ends have the nature of the east-west line. The side (*bhuja*) has the nature of the north-south line (*yāmyottarasūtra*); thus, the knowledge of the directions from that is easily understood. (377) Even without a magnet, skilled artisans here likewise determine the directions. The method for establishing the east-west line described here by the wise is the same as that for the equatorial circle (*samamaṇḍalīya*). (378) The east and west are determined at sunrise and sunset; however, some say that because there is a slight difference due to the rising of the sun at different locations, [the true east-west] lies slightly to the north of that.

379–380. If the direction [of the planet] is established at the time of rising from the conjunction known as *ādyapakārādayana*, there is a slight discrepancy here; yet this method for determining direction is adopted for the sake of practical usage. 381. That determination of direction performed by those who rely on the longitudinal difference (deśāntara) of the center of the disk is not yours, O Lord of Planets, because it occurs before or after midday by an amount equal to half the minutes of the disk’s radius. Indeed, for two human latitudes, there is an absence [of such a calculation], while for a planet situated in the sky, there is some small portion of the day remaining.

Since there is no increase or decrease from the center of that circle toward the east or west, it is the same as the previous [calculation]. (382) The distance between the base of the gnomon situated at the intersection of the meridian line and the point where the shadow-tip meets the east-west line is the *karṇa* (hypotenuse). The square root of the difference between the square of this *karṇa* and the square of the gnomon is the *koṭi* (perpendicular), which extends from the north to the south. (383) The sum of the *karṇa*, the gnomon, and the *koṭi* is said to be the base (*mūla*). Alternatively, here the *dṛgjyā* (sine of altitude) multiplied by twelve and divided by the gnomon situated on the surface of the earth gives the result clearly. (384)

The point on the surface of the Earth where the line of sight from an observer touches the center of the celestial sphere’s globe is called the *dṛkkṣepa* (zenith distance) in the Siddhāntas; this is the subject of the chapter on the three questions (*tripraśna*). The line of sight from the observer touching that point on the terrestrial globe is submerged within it. If one desires the true [geocentric] position, that point on the surface must be established by the wise as the *dṛkpūtraka* (the point of the zenith-distance). For practical purposes, due to the small difference, it may be calculated from the point on the Earth's surface directly beneath the observer's zenith.

The degrees of the bird [the planet] from the center of the visible horizon are considered to be the *matāṃśas*, and the degrees of the zenith distance (*khāntabhāgāḥ*) are likewise; their sine and its square root, multiplied by the radius (*trijyā*), are indeed the *yojanas*. (387) In that case, the gnomon-sine and the sight-sine (*dṛgjye*) arise from the nature of one-fourth of that; and just as knowledge of direction, place, and time may be obtained from an instrument, so do I describe it with precision. (392) Therefore, the segments of the sine-values for the purpose of the treatise are thirty-fold, arising from the radius (*trijyā*).

A simple instrument has been devised according to the measure of the radius of the terrestrial latitude-circle (khāgni-trijyā). This is a triangular instrument (jaya-yatra) whose two sides are equal to its radius; its third side is the arm consisting of one-fourth of the circumference of that circle. One of its angles is a right angle, while the other two are indeed unequal. At the right angle is the center of the circle; at the unequal angles are the Earth and the celestial pole respectively. Similarly, the other [unequal] angle is the zenith, while the Earth lies between the center of the circle and the terrestrial pole.

Likewise, within the center of the circle of space, the wise [astronomer] should fashion two compartments for the earth's sphere according to three circles, including the line of space and the rim. From the point of Mars (Kuja), thirty-six degrees (khaṅgalavā) on the rim, as well as thirty lunar days (tithi) in nāḍīs, and thirty equal divisions of the body of the earth, should be established. Then, the sines (jyā) extending from the rim toward the interior, with intervals equal to the lines designated as "space" (kha), are made by the wise in the instrument starting from the point of Mars up to the limit of space.

The eighteenth sine (jyā) is that which lies between the two ends of the chord; it is doubled from the center [of the circle]. In that [circle], why is it that at the tip of the arc equal to the latitude (akṣabhā), there exists a perpendicular line from the center? And where that perpendicular line touches the circumference, from that point to the earth [the center]—just as far as the degrees of latitude, so far are the degrees of the colatitude (lamba). The direct and inverse sines of these two should be known, as well as those for which the direct sine is desired. Those desired degrees should be applied to the circumference, and the sine which exists there [is what is sought].

On the ground, within those two centers, the segment of the gnomon (śaṅkukhaṇḍa) measuring 402 digits of successive sines should be subtracted; the remainder is called the "back" gnomon (pṛṣṭhākhyashanku). Then, the square root of the difference between the squares of that [back gnomon] and the hypotenuse (dṛgjyaka) shall be the measure of the "side" (tiryak) for you. Then, having subtracted the square of this "side" from the square of half the diameter of the circle (svayambhujanyāsadalasya varga), the square root thereof is indeed the "back-side" (pṛṣṭhatira); that is to be understood as the "visual cord" (dṛksūtraka) by the knower of the sphere (golavid).

When there is a declination for that planet moving through the sky, the sine of its altitude (natānatajīvā) should be calculated from the difference between the [ecliptic] image and the zenith. This resulting arc of the visual distance (dṛgbhavāstraka) is applicable everywhere in the sky as stated. (390) Likewise, one should draw lines upward, downward, and horizontally through the center of the circle. From those two [intersecting lines], four equal sectors should be formed here. By the 298th verse of this very section, it is stated that the midday gnomon-shadow (*dinamadhyayaṣṭi*) is equal to the sine of the amplitude (*jyāpakrāntya*). Just as the second segment increases, so too does the midday gnomon-shadow increase; therefore, the sine of the amplitude (*jyāpakrāntya*) is subtracted from the radius (*jyāla*). Here, due to a small difference, the sine of the amplitude (*jyāpakrāntya*) is approximately equal to the cosine of the amplitude (*ujyāpakrāntya*). The sine of the amplitude (*jyāpakrāntya*) and the radius (*jyāla*)—which are the values read for the purpose of the *paṭṭī* (table)—are such that their sum is thirty. Thus, half of thirty is fifteen.

"The measure of the sine is greater than ninety-seven."

Then, having destroyed that mechanism situated in the sky, the wise man should [destroy] the body like Vṛtra. Or else, one should enter the jar-hole through the Indra-hole. Therefore, the degrees of altitude (*unnatāṃśa*) and the degrees of depression (*bhūjanatāṃśa*) are to be known; likewise, the sines of those [altitudes] and the sine of the zenith distance (*dṛgjyā*) when the instrument is positioned like the horizon-circle (*dṛgvṛtta*). (423) The degrees of the earth-sine (*bhūjyā*) equal to its tip extend along the circumference from the tip of the ascensional difference; the hours of altitude (*unnatā nāḍikā*) are to be known, and the remaining [hours] are those of depression (*natāśca*). (424)

One should construct a circle (cara-ayana-yuta) with its diameter oriented opposite to the direction of the latitude (vicaloma). Then, the sine of the oblique ascension (tad-yan-jyā) situated on the meridian line is multiplied by the radius (rekha-saṃva-nata-jyaka) and divided by that [radius]; at its tip, one should then imagine a fish-figure (miga) representing the Sun. From there, the sky (kha) would be the degrees of altitude (unnatāṃśa) up to the Earth (kuja), which are the degrees of depression (natāṃśaka). On the circumference, from the Earth (kuja) to the tip of the degrees of latitude (palāṃśa), there is a cord (paṭṭa-pina-jyā) which touches [the circle] at a certain point; from there, the distance to the center (kendrāntara) would be the desired divisor (iṣṭahṛti).

In this manner, one should touch the edge of the gnomon-board at the point where the shadow falls; there, within those two centers, the board itself shall be situated. (428) The eighteen-fold [shadow] is located upon that board where the sun's image has gone; from that point to the earth, the shadow extends as far as the center, which is its distance. (429) Thus, on the board situated at the degrees of the palas of the zenith-distance, the measurement of the sky [is determined].

Where the sine (jyā) is cut off, the distance from that center is equal to the *nara* [430]. And its cloth-band (*paṭṭa*) is at the point where the cut-off sine reaches the end. One should mark a point on the circumference of the interior of the circle. Thus, when the ground is leveled by the equal gnomon, the sine (jīvā) reaching that point, extending from there up to the celestial zenith, is the declination (nata-śā) belonging to the equatorial circle (samamaṇḍalīyā); for this very reason, the calculation of the shadow (rāva) is appropriately performed there.

In the second [division], there are indeed sixty *vighaṭikās* (seconds); these are the divisions of the six *maṣas*. The fourth [division] consists of thirty parts; their names follow in sequence. Therein, how is that celestial pole related to the ecliptic (krāntivṛtta)? The declination (krāmya) portion is the complement of the oblique ascension (anyakramya) portion. Thus, the calculation of the true declination and the true oblique ascension is established according to the method of the previously stated declination-spheres. Likewise, the equatorial circle (nāḍīvṛtta) related to the planet is the axis of the celestial pole (kadambavṛtta); the circle of the celestial pole related to the planet is the precession of the equinoxes (āyanavalana), which is the oblique ascension portion at the terrestrial latitude of the planet's mark.

[52] By means of the calculation of the meridian distance (*abhā*), the true interval between the planet and the sun is to be determined from those two; for the planet moves toward the sun due to the influence of its terrestrial orbit.
