The line of conjunction of the orbs for those two planets that were mentioned in the section on *adhikāra* (spheres) should be applied here. When it occurs among the planets, it is exactly so; otherwise, it is as stated previously. || 54 || Out of fear of prolixity, I have not stated the entire rationale (*vāsanā*) here; let the wise understand it through the various distinctions of the celestial sphere (*golacakra*). Indeed, this alone is the fruit for the understanding of the sphere. || 59 || When the mark of the planet's longitude in the zodiacal sign reaches its own horizon from the center— || 60 ||

At that time, the orb of the planet situated at the tip of the arrow is not located there by its own power, nor is it situated along the arm. Its rising and setting are produced by its own nature; this secret depends on the force of the northward and southward arrows. This [process] described is for the northern course (uttarāyaṇa); in the reverse order, it is for the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana). When the arm is reversed, the setting occurs; thus, the rising of the celestial body is first at the tip of the *nāmana* (bending), and the reverse is for the setting planet. That line which emerges from the fixed point (dhruvasūtra) touches the orb of the planet.

Bhaṭṭa says: "That [longitude] at which the planet is on the horizon of the equator (nirakṣa-kṣitija) is its true longitude when it rises as a visible image. Indeed, that is the parallax correction (dṛkkarma). The minutes of arc between the [true] planet and that [point of rising]—added to the planet if they are of the same direction, and subtracted if of opposite directions—are known as the parallax correction. That very [correction] is the true declination (sphuṭa-śara), for the purpose of correcting the [true] latitude derived from the difference between the true declination and the declination calculated from the parallax-corrected planet. Alternatively, the deflection (valana) here is calculated from the parallax-corrected planet, as previously described."

The sine of one-twentieth of that [latitude] shall be the gnomon (yaṣṭi). Then, the product of the uncorrected sine of the arrow (śara) and the radius (trijyā), divided by that gnomon, is the corrected arc (anuh). This is the arrow (śara) situated along the meridian line (dhruvasūtra) between the observer’s latitude and the planet. It occurs within the difference between the true declination (apama) and the declination known as the "equal orb" (sama-vimbā) of the planet. That is described by the learned as the result of the parallax correction (dṛkkarma), and it is established in two ways: through the distinction of terrestrial latitude (akṣa) and precession (ayana). Up to the point where it reaches the equator (nirakṣara), it is called "precession" (ayanākhya); from there up to its own local terrestrial latitude (svīyaṃ kujaṃ), it is designated as "terrestrial latitude" (akṣasaṃjña).

Since the arrow (*vāṇa*) is always directed toward the *samākhyā* (the point of intersection) and never toward the *kadamba* (the center), it is stated by the ignorant that the *kṣepa* (latitude) resides in the *gola* (sphere) in two ways. These two [views] are not useful here for the wise who proclaim the true nature of the Siddhāntas, as stated in the *Śiromaṇi*. (66) [Note: For this purpose, the commentary on verse 38 of this very chapter should be examined. This concludes the section on Rising and Setting (*udayāstādhikāra*) in the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*.]

399. I shall now describe, in a different manner, the eight planets known as *ayāna*, which are even more accurate than those previously mentioned, for the sake of bringing joy to the calculators (gaṇakas). [Verse 68: The planet multiplied by the sine of the maximum declination (*trijyā*) and divided by its own hypotenuse (*koṭiśru*) is the *āya*. The sine of the other [planet's] declination, multiplied by three and divided by the sine of twenty-four degrees (*jināṃśamauryā*), is the *ācāpa*. [Verse 73: When the first [planet] is greater than the second, the first and second quarters [are used]; likewise when they arise from the second and third quarters.

Since there is a mutual subtraction of these two positions, this [result] is their difference; and that which was previously stated regarding the pair of signs should be applied here as well. In the third case, it would be up to the degrees of the sign; however, in the fourth, it should be reduced by the degrees of the zodiacal circle (the *cakrāṃśa*). Having performed the calculation starting from the planet in minutes and so forth, and having subtracted those from the degrees of the two [positions], or else, in this case, the other one would be called "correct" (*sphuṭa*), while that which belongs to the malefic and the non-living [signs] is "incorrect" (*asphuṭa*).

The *pada* (quarter) of the argument [of the anomaly] is multiplied by the difference in declination (*vaga*) and divided by the sine of the true obliquity (*sphuṭakrānti*) and the daily sine (*dinajyā*). || 69 || That [result], multiplied by the sine of the anomaly of the planet increased by three signs and quadrants, or alternatively by the sine of the anomaly, and divided by the sine of the true anomaly plus one, yields the sum of the results from the sines of the true anomaly. || 70 || Having applied that correction here, the planet is considered the "apparent-zenith-distance planet" (*apanadṛggraha*). Between that planet and the Sun, whichever is less than Aries is taken as the Sun, and the other as the ascendant; then, using the aforementioned method, the calculation should be performed. || 76 ||

Alternatively, the degrees of *kaṭī* (latitude) here—known as *agya*—are the arc obtained by multiplying the true obliquity (*sphuṭānyapama*) by three signs (*tribha*) and dividing by the sine of the true obliquity (*spaṣṭāpamadyujyakā*). || 71 || When the mean and true obliquities are of the same direction, their sum is taken; when of opposite directions, their difference is taken. These are the true equinoctial points (*viṣuvāṃśaka*), and the degrees of the [right] triangle (*kṣetrāṃśaka*) should be considered here as the arc. || 72 || The results of the parallax correction (*dṛkkarmaphala*) at the rising or setting of a planet are multiplied by those right-ascensions (*udaya*) produced at the non-equatorial location (*nirakṣaja*). || [End of verse] ||

The planetary motion situated at the zero-point of the axis [the equinox] is the arising of the planet ahead [in the east], by way of its velocity. In the southern course, it is with a northern arrow; however, in the north, it occurs through time. This which has been declared regarding the planet’s solstice applies when it is in the north; in the south, the reverse should be understood by the wise. Here, the aspect known as *vayana* (solstitial) should be placed before; that very same aspect, joined with six signs, becomes the station (*pada*) of the planet at the solstice. But the sin arising from that quarter is indeed produced from its foot.

In the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, Chapter 400, the section on the refutation [of errors] begins. Verse 79: Indeed, when a planet is situated at the non-axial equator (*nirakṣatijastha*) in the sky, its latitude becomes zero. Verse 80: That parallax correction (*dṛkkarma*) devised by the author of the *Śiromaṇi* through his own intellect—which he has abandoned as being devoid of value—has been refuted by me; for that which was stated by him is indeed incorrect. Verse 81: Alternatively, for a moving planet, the fixed and movable equinoctial points are increased or decreased by their own quarter-parts according to the degrees of time for the parallax correction of the precession (*ayanadṛkkarma*).

If, on a single day, the degrees of precession (*ayanāṃśa*) exceed 360, they should be subtracted from the circle [360]; if they are less than that, they should not be subtracted, but rather added to the circle. Those [degrees] arising from the observation of one's own [local] precession are the equinoctial degrees (*viṣuvāṃśaka*). From the knowledge of that [precession], there is the knowledge of that [equinox]; conversely, from the knowledge of the equinox, the precession is clearly determined. Now, I shall explain the calculation of the planet’s position at the end of its retrograde motion and the determination of the precession through observation, as well as the combination of subtle observations, in another way.

On the celestial sphere, those two points where the circle arising from the two poles of the celestial equator (the *dhruvavṛtta*) intersects the circle of the planet’s disk are indeed the points of intersection of the ecliptic and the equator (*ayanadṛgda*). The true longitude (*sphuṭapama*) is that of the planet at the intersection of the ecliptic and the equator; its declination (*krānti*) occurs within the interval between the equinoxes. Furthermore, the distance between the circles of the two poles of the celestial equator (known as the *vimba* and *acala*) is the so-called equatorial circle (*viṣuvākhyavṛtta*). These are the equatorial degrees (*viṣuvāṃśaka*) from the junction of the spheres (*golasaṃdhi*) for both the planet on its disk and the planet at the intersection of the ecliptic and the equator.

Now, for a planet situated on the eccentric circle (calavṛtta), which is always equal to that on the mean circle (bhaṭṭavṛtta) due to its conjunction with the same fixed line (dhruvasūtra), the celestial body is perceived as the "image-planet" (vimbagraha). This image-planet would be situated on the eccentric circle. The sine of the apparent declination (sphuṭakrānti) arising from the true [longitude] is multiplied by the daily sine (dinajyā) and divided by the sine of the true declination; the arc of the resulting quotient is the correction (phala) in minutes. The sum or difference of those two [corrections] constitutes the equatorial degrees (viṣuvāṃśaka). The sine of sixty degrees is multiplied by the sine of the latitude (trijyā) and divided by the sine of the zenith distance (apanadṛgjyā). This is the [sine of the] apparent zenith distance (dṛgrahaṇa).

Likewise, the equinoctial shadow (viṣuvāṃśa) of the planet's disc is equal to that of the precession-correction planet (ayanadṛggraha). When this is divided by the sine derived from its own co-latitude (koṭijyā), the result multiplied by the radius (trimaurvya) gives the obtained value.

(1) Viśvanātha: Just as one [value] is produced from the arc of the longitude of the apsis derived from the longitudinal degrees on the ecliptic, and another from the arc of the sine of the maximum latitude derived from the arc of the sine of the celestial latitude, and from these two the calculation of the oblique ascensions (*viṣuvat*) is performed according to the rule beginning with "The sines of the three houses starting from Aries," in exactly the same way, here, having assumed the true declination (*spaṣṭāpama*)—which is the circle passing through the celestial poles and intersecting the disc—as the ecliptic, and having assumed the sine of the maximum declination as the maximum sine of latitude (*paramāpajyā*), one should proceed.

The degrees of the equinox (viṣuvāṃśa) are easily calculated. Therein, the arc of the difference between the celestial meridian and the observed position of the planet in the ecliptic, as well as the shadow of the planet's disk, and likewise the declination (śara), exist in the kadamba-vṛtta (the circle of declination). Furthermore, in the dhruva-vṛtta (the circle of the pole), the true declination is the interval between the meridian and the planet; then, in the middle of the two disks of the two [celestial] bodies, it is the declination. In the Siddhāntatattvaviveka, Chapter on Rising and Setting (udayāstādhikāra): the arm (bhuja) of the planet according to the meridian is indeed situated in the quadrant of the moving planet. 2.

The degrees of the true obliquity of the ecliptic multiplied by ninety are the bāhu (sine of the amplitude) as stated in the first section; likewise, that which arises from the second and third sections is mutually transposed, for it resides in its respective position. (93) Indeed, the circle of the celestial sphere passing through the center of the shadow [the kadambavṛtta] is situated at the point of the celestial body on the ecliptic; this has been accepted here by the wise because of the difference between the shadow and the circle of the poles. (97) For the equinoctial deflection (āyanavalana) arising from the celestial body—that sine of it multiplied by the sine of the latitude (śara)—[is used].

The arc of that bow, obtained by means of the clearly defined sine of the amplitude, measures one-sixth of its span; from this, the extremely subtle correction for the aspect (dṛṣṭikarma) in ghatis and so forth arises, even more refined than that produced by the *śiṃśumāṇika* method. The square root of the product of the clearly defined sine of the amplitude and the co-latitude, multiplied by three and divided by the radius, gives the *śaṅku* (gnomon). From that [correction], the subtle precessional aspect (āyanadṛggraha) is obtained. Thus, the difference between the planet’s true longitude and the longitude of the equinoxial point is the aspect (īkṣaṇa).

When there is a deficiency or excess, the nodes of existence (bhavaśiphana) burst apart as they limp along; when obscured by passion (rasavṛta), the time of the eye’s movement becomes subtle, such as the state of being wealthy and so forth. (95) The degrees of motion (yācalāṃśa) added to three signs from the planet, multiplied by five and divided by twenty-four, yield the *doḍaka*. When obtained by dividing the difference between the true and mean [longitudes] by fifteen, it is the *vighajā* arising from the precession (*ayanabhava*), which is the sine of the word (*vacanajyā*). (96) Commentary: "The position born of the sky-goer" (khagajaṃ sthānam).

From the point of the disk, by constructing a vertical circle (lambavṛtta) above the fixed point (dhruva) located at that position, the central arrow (madhyaśara) is the hypotenuse (karṇa) on the axis of the celestial pole (kadambaprotā). On the axis of the fixed point, the perpendicular (koṭi) is the base (bhuja) on the vertical circle. Thus, in this right-angled triangle formed by the chords, the chord of the vertical circle is the same as the chord of the arc of the shadow (śataghnī) of the disk. Therefore, the chord on the vertical circle is derived from the following proportion: (Chord of the fixed point) × (Chord of the shadow) = (Radius) × (Chord of the shadow) (Radius) × (Chord of the disk) = (Disk) × (Chord of the shadow) [Note: The mathematical expressions provided in the source text appear to be fragments of a proportional calculation involving the radius (trijyā), the chords of the shadow (jyāsthā), and the disk (vi).]

9 (1) Viśvanātha Śarmā: By the word *kheṭa* (planet), "place" (*sthāna*) is meant. (2) Viśvanātha Śarmā: The moving-part planet (*calāṃśakhacara*) is the precessed planet (*sāyanagraha*) situated precisely on the ecliptic (*krāntivṛtta*). The oblique ascensional correction (*ayanavalana*) for the shadow-image (*chāyābimba*) is that which lies within the circle passing through the celestial pole (*dhruva*) and the nonagesimal point (*vaka*). For that purpose, the complement of the arc of the [precession] is the tip of the arrow (*śarakoṭi*), which is the degrees of the arc of the true declination (*spaṣṭadyujyā*). The angle between the celestial pole and the nonagesimal point is 84 degrees; thus, the calculation of the oblique ascensional correction for the shadow-image via trigonometric proportion (*koṇānupāta*) is easily understood.

(3) Viśvanātha Śarman: Regarding the phrase “jinalavothaguṇana,” the reading “lavajyakayā sī” is erroneous. Therefore, as the *upapakṣa* (2) Viśvanātha Śarman notes, since the radius of the shadow (*vimbīyayujyā*) was not calculated by Bhāskarācārya, there is necessarily a lack of precision in the Bhaṭṭa school; however, in the expression “sukhamam,” the word “su” appears as if it were a mere filler.

(3) Viśvanātha Śarmā: The hypotenuse (*karṇa*) is the sine of the oblique ascension (*ayanadṛgjyā*) up to the point of the planet’s true longitude; the middle arrow (*madhyaśara*) is the sine of the amplitude (*asphuṭajyā*) from the position up to the planet’s true longitude; and the base (*bhuja*) is the arc on the ecliptic from the position up to the planet’s oblique ascension. From these, the product of the sine of the base and the cosine of the sine of the amplitude is equal to the product of the cosine of the hypotenuse and the radius (*trijyā*). Therefore, the calculation of the single correction for the oblique ascension (*āyanadṛkkarma*) is established. [From] the *Siddhāntatattvāviveka*, Chapter on Rises and Sets (*udayāstādhikāra*).

100. From the square root of the square of the ascendant’s latitude diminished by the square of the sine of the oblique ascension, the sine of the amplitude is obtained. This is the correction for parallax (*dṛkkarma*) according to Bhaṭṭa; or else, it is the sine of the longitudinal correction (*āyanavalana*) derived from the diameter. 101. Multiplied by the sine of the true ascension and divided by the radius, the arc resulting is the longitudinal correction (*āyanakarma*). That [correction] does not indeed depend on that [parallax] here; for even the true ascension follows the method of the zodiacal circle. [Having subtracted the sine of the diameter from the sine of the planet's altitude, the sages have performed this calculation.]

The time of the [true] aspect (dṛkkarmakāla) is determined by one's own intellect through proportion; and the duration of the arc in the field is understood from its fearlessness. (102) Thus, the precession (āyana) and the aspect-induced correction (dṛṣṭijakarma) have been stated. Now, I shall explain the aspect-correction (dṛkkarma) as it truly is: the mean oblique ascension (madhyapama), the planet’s own precessional aspect (svāyanadṛggraha), and the true oblique ascension (sphuṭāpama) arising from the orb of the image (vimba) from its own planet. (103) From those two, the carakhaṇḍakas (ascensional differences) are as previously described; if they are equal and of the same direction, then their difference or sum, as the case may be, is the aspect here. This is indeed the well-established method among the wise. (104)

Now, in this case, the correction for the longitudinal parallax (*ayanadṛggraha*) should be added [to the planet] when it is in the northern course; that same correction, being of the nature of the ascensional difference (*udaya*), is subtracted when it is in the southern course. Then, by reversing the process, the planet becomes endowed with its own latitude (*sapabhāk*). (105) Viśvanātha: This statement regarding "by the sūtras" is appropriate only for Bhaṭṭa. In the very same way, the sine of the meridian distance (*natakālaja-jyā*) multiplied by the terrestrial sine (*akṣajyā*) and divided here by its own half-chord (*svopahṛtadala-vistṛti*) yields the sine arising from the terrestrial deflection (*ākṣavalanodbhava-jīvā*). (106)

The sine of the latitude (akṣalavajyā), multiplied by the radius (trijyā) and divided by the sine of the amplitude (vimbajaghuguṇa), is constant at the times of rising and setting; its arc is the axial deviation (akṣavalana). That which results from the proper correction of the longitudinal deviation (sampāmya), the solstitial deviation (ayanāṅka), and the axial deviation (akṣaja), is known as the "apparent" (spaṣṭa) deviation, which is of two kinds according to one’s own rising and setting. The sine of this [apparent deviation], multiplied by the cosine of the ascensional difference (iṣukoṭiguṇa) and divided by the radius (trijyā), yields the degrees of the resulting arc.

That [equinoctial shadow] multiplied by the sine of the latitude devoid of that [shadow], and by the radius, is the square root of the sum of their squares; this is the true equatorial arrow (*sphuṭaśara*). When this is always corrected by the horizontal arm of the planet at the observer's latitude, it becomes the body-arm (*vimvabhuja*) here; for it is indeed made manifest as the declination (*apama*). The sine of the difference between the desired degrees and the true value arising from the planet at the observer's latitude is [the vertical arm].

(1) On a great circle passing through the center of the sphere and the zenith, the segment from the center of the sphere up to the point where it intersects the ecliptic is the true latitude (*sphuṭaśara*). From the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, Chapter on Rising and Setting (Udayāstādhikāra): The planet attains its rising when its [longitude] is equal to the ascendant; otherwise, it always undergoes setting. When the ascendant at rising or setting is greater than or less than the triśalagna, the rising or setting is yet to come or has already occurred. The elapsed or remaining ghatis arising from that difference are the time by which it has moved from its own [right] ascendant or setting.

The time in *ghaṭikās* between the two points [of rising] is repeatedly multiplied by the number of *akṣas* (the sine of latitude); this product, divided by three, is the *puñjakā*. When multiplied by ten and divided by the *sphuṭatarā* (more accurate) *śara* (latitude), it becomes the more accurate *valanajyā* (sine of deflection). This, multiplied by the *guṇa* (radius) of the *sphuṭa-iṣu* (corrected arrow) and divided by the *trijyā* (radius of the celestial sphere), yields the arc known here as *sphuṭa*; this is the *dṛkkarma* (parallax correction) on the *bhavṛtta* (horizon circle). [This is determined] according to the method for the planet at the junction found in the chapter on "Questions and Answers."

Alternatively, having made the declination (vakana) true, one should bring the ascensional difference (dṛkkarma) to its true value. Depending on the sequence of the southern or northern course, the correction for the oblique ascension (astraka) shall be positive or negative when the deflection (valana) is northward; however, when the deflection is southward, it shall be the reverse. Apply that to the house; that planet becomes the local horizon-planet (ākṣa-dṛggraha). That same [planet], when added to six signs, becomes the ascendant at sunset here; that which is with six signs here is the eighth-ascendant (astavilagna), as has been stated according to the power of one’s own latitude. || 113–115 ||

The rising and setting of the planets occurs at the eastern horizon; likewise, their rising and setting would occur at the western horizon. Due to the daily revolution of the wind carrying the sphere [of the sky], there is a setting every day at the point known as the western horizon. (116) A planet is visible when its longitude is less than or greater than the longitude of the rising or setting point at midnight. If, at the time of the sun’s setting, the planet is greater than the sun plus six signs or less than the sun, it is within the range of one's own vision. (117) One should subtract the desired planet from the planet at the desired time, [calculated] between the desired time and the setting of the planet.

But Māya, standing nearby, [observed] that the restriction regarding his own vision was otherwise. (120) "Wherever I have brought another wife, surely in that place one must be restrained from that self-conceit by a wise person elsewhere. (121) Now, I shall speak of that which was said by the virtuous: how at the time of the rising and setting of the orbs of the moon-faced women and the suns, there is the attainment of the secret without even the use of the eyes. (122)

At the time of the sun's setting, the body [of the planet] here is like the sine of the latitude of its disc. (1) Viśvanātha Śarman: In whichever place the calculation of another object has been performed by me based on the triangle of declination (*jātya*) and so forth, from that place of declination, in another place where that declination is zero, it should be understood by the wise knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*).

In establishing the genus of that which consists of lying down, this "thorn" (logical flaw) is unavoidable because of the attainment [of the result]. 408. This concludes the chapter on Rising and Setting (*udayāstādhikāra*) in the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*. 409. Having calculated the declination (*krānti*) known as the true [longitude] derived from the aspect of the observer and the observed, and the ascensional difference (*cara*) and so forth from one's own location; and having determined the risen hours (*unnatanāḍikā*) of the planet from the horizon, the day-measure (*ahargaṇa*) should be computed. (1) When the planet is within three signs (*tribha*) from the cusp of the quadrant (*kendr*), it is the elapsed day of the planet; (2) when it is beyond six signs (*ṣaḍbha*), it is the remainder of the planet's night. 124.

Thus, at the time remaining of the night, the planet's longitude is determined by the stated method from the time of sunrise, or from the time of the rising of the *rekhā* (equatorial line), according to the previously mentioned calculation for past and future times. This should also be understood from the time of midnight; likewise, when the day exceeds six [muhūrtas], it is certainly so. In the same way, the measures of day and night are to be calculated through the well-known methods described for the two planets. Once the elapsed time is established, subtracting it from its own measure, the square root of that remainder is indeed used for its proof.

Therefore, this [calculation] for the immovable [ascendant] must be purified; thus, the elapsed and yet-to-come portions arising from day and night [are determined]. (126) When the elapsed and remaining portions of the day joined with the night are increased by the difference between one's own [longitude] and the [desired] time, the ascendant is obtained through the stated method as the "rising-point" (*udayāsyalamana*) at the rising of a planet. (127) Then, by means of one's own intellect, the elapsed and yet-to-come [portions] are calculated in sequence; indeed, the rising and setting have been declared in this way, and I shall now speak of them according to their proximity to the Sun. (129)

For those who previously had an uninterrupted vision of it here, the sages say that its non-vision or setting occurs due to the intense heat of the sun. (130) Then, even when it is not visible for some time, the sages declare that its reappearance is its "rising. Generally, this invisibility to men is caused by the impact of the light from the fierce rays [of the sun] upon the eyes. (131) When, due to proximity, it becomes appropriate for someone, its parts are indeed described by them as being of such a nature.

The [ascendant] arising at the time of sunrise always occurs above its own [longitude] when Mars is present, even if the orb is bright; however, when the Sun is below, [the ascendant] is below. (132) Viśvanātha (7):—By the verse beginning with "The quadrant [is calculated] by subtracting the ascendant from the longitude of the moon plus three signs," in this very section, the quadrant is determined. When the latitude of the sun is twenty-four degrees and the place is on the horizon, there is a fault; therefore, one must understand everything based on the *vitribha* point and the current position of the sun, and the resulting quadrant derived therefrom.

(2) Comment: Regarding the phrase "in the third part" (*tribhāge*), the three signs beginning with Aries (*vaharbha*) and the nine signs beginning with Libra (*navabha*)—which are the ascendant, the seventh house, and the descendant (*lagnāstarasaṃskṛta*) corrected by the tri-ascensional difference (*vitribha*)—should be examined as in the case of the determination of the results of the *śama* (conjunction). Otherwise, an error would arise; this must be discerned by those who possess [true] knowledge. The times of rising and setting, whether past or yet to come, should be calculated from their respective degrees of ascensional difference (*udayāṃśaka*). If that [calculated time] is greater than the actual time, it is gross (*sthūla*); if it is less, it is subtle (*sūkṣma*). [End of] Chapter 410: The Section on Rising and Setting (*udayāstādhikāra*), from the *Siddhāntatattvāviveka*.

411. From the time of its setting until its rising, the white appearance of the deer-marked one (the moon) is unprecedented; during its waning and waxing, those portions of time [of its visibility] would last as long as the day of the visible moon. (139) Indeed, the elders say this regarding the moon; the noble ones do not state merely the cause. For that which is gross is composed of less light, whereas that which is subtle is composed of more light. (134) The lunar orbs, though consisting of water, are both distinct and non-distinct by nature.

Likewise, those situated below [the sun] are difficult postures; from the sun onwards, there are gross and subtle divisions such as the *iyā* and others. Whatever is perceptible to the eye exists through these distinctions; their knowledge regarding the different strengths and times is not within my reach here. Indeed, those who know what is beyond the senses have perceived these divisions of time and distinguished them by means of yoga. Only they themselves, being independent in this matter, understand the logic of that conceptualization, and no others. The divisions of time are stated to be joined with the directions, consisting of two, seven, four, one, six, and eight parts.

For the Moon and others [the planets], when Venus and Mercury are retrograde, those two values are reduced by two; when they are direct, they are increased by their own [respective] time-portions. When the planet’s time-portion is greater than what has been stated, then the planet will be visible; if it is smaller than those, it will not be visible under any circumstances. Indeed, at a time equal to its own time-portion, the planet is set; after that, and before its rising, its disc is clearly visible. Therefore, the difference between the planet and the Sun as perceived by the eye has been determined here.

It shall be equal to the portions of the field produced from the degrees of the *bhoktṛ-kalā* (the eater-time). When the degrees of the field produced from the time-portions (*kālāṃśa*) are equal to the degrees of the field for the two visible planets, then it is visible; beyond that, it is even more so during the day. If its interval is greater, it is not visible by any means whatsoever. The maximum [interval] at the end of the eight time-portions for the visible planet is established through proportion (*anupāta*). Due to its connection with the [orbis] *śara*, it is proven to be distinct at every moment; therefore, that interval between the visible planet is difficult to know.

145. And it was stated otherwise by the compassionate Śrīravi as follows: "When the difference between the true planet and the sun becomes equal to the degrees of the field derived from the previously mentioned time-portion (kālāṃśa), then that very [position] is near; the interval between the visible planet and the sun will be minimal. At the end of the opposition, that moon is generally at its closest; therefore, the interval between the visible moon and the sun is said to be minimal. 146–148.

The determination of the *bimba* [diameter] is accomplished through the effects produced by the constellations. (9) The *kālāṃśas* (time-parts) are the portions of time; they are the third part of a *nāḍī*. In the *Vāsanābhāṣya* on the verse "The moon is twelve *kālāṃśas*" from the *Udayāstādhikāra* of the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi* by the venerable Bhāskarācārya, it is stated: "The moon has twelve *kālāṃśas*. From the time of its setting or rising, the moon becomes visible when it is at an interval of more than two *ghaṭikās*; if it is less than that, it is invisible because it is obscured by light."

Therefore, its time-portion (*kālāṃśa*) is twelve. In this very same way, the time-portions of the other planets have been stated. Even in the *Sūryasiddhānta*, the time-portions are exactly the same; thus there is no difference whatsoever. [From] the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, Chapter on Rising and Setting (Udayāstādhikāra): Whatever was composed by Sārvabhauma [in his work] regarding this context is now stated here as well: The true orb of Saturn, which consists of digits (*kalā*) and is determined by the conjunction of the distance and the radius vector (*karṇa*), is as follows: 412–413. [End of section]. 414. [Verse 149]. What was done by Sārvabhauma in that context is likewise stated here. The clear orb of Saturn, consisting of digits, is derived from the calculation of the distance and the radius vector.

The minutes of arc of the lunar disc are obtained by dividing the product of the sine of the latitude and the radius by the karṇa; these minutes, multiplied by fifteen and divided by their own kāṣṭhāṃśas, thus become the measure of the disc itself. That which has been stated by Bhāskara, arising from the strength of the variation in the *ujjātā* [equation] in reverse order, is not correct. Just as the disc of the lunar mansion corresponding to the degrees of the lunar day and the degrees of the *akhāṃśa* was calculated using the previously mentioned radius and disc, why is the determination of the discs of the planets not done in the same way here? For it is not so established here.

In this regard, having calculated the orb of a sign possessing an equal number of minutes and degrees from the heard orb of another planet, that which results is not the same as the orb of a sign possessing degrees and minutes derived from the lunar day (tithi). Therefore, that [calculation] is not considered pleasing. Furthermore, the time-measurements in units of three and one (fire and moon) would result in signs and so forth that are too grossly visible; whereas by the method mentioned from the origin of Saturn, the orbs resulting from the stated method of Saturn are even smaller.

For those possessing right vision, these [calculations] are not excessive, nor are they appropriate for those who see differently. (155) The true positions of the Sun and the planets should be calculated at the time of sunset as being in the west, and at the time of sunrise as being in the east; thereafter, the planet is to be treated as before. (156) In this system, that planet whose motion is greater than the Sun's is designated as "Swift" (śīghra); likewise, that whose motion is smaller is to be known by the name "Slow" (manda). (157) The "Slow" planets—Jupiter, Mars, and Saturn—are eclipsed from behind when their longitude is less than the Sun's.

O knower of yoga, people go toward the east before sunrise, and likewise for the two retrograde planets (Venus and Mars). The Moon, Mercury, and Venus set in the east when they are less than the Sun; moving swiftly, they rise in the west when they are greater [in longitude]. Thus, the times of setting and rising have been declared by the Sun in his own branch (the *Sūryasiddhānta*). Now, the knowledge of time pertaining thereto is being presented here. The nadīs produced from the difference between the true Sun and the planet, multiplied by six, shall be the desired minutes of arc (*kāṭhalava*).

If the [ascensional] differences for the desired planet at its rising are less or more than those stated, it is moving toward or away from the point of setting; otherwise, it is setting. (161) The seconds resulting from the subtraction of the stated and desired degrees are divided by the degrees of the planet’s position and its ascensional difference. These are again divided by the seconds of arc of the difference between the planet’s and the Sun’s motions, and further divided by the sum of their velocities. (162) The result is the time in days and so forth that has passed or remains; according to that time, the planet is subtracted from or added to the planet at the time of setting.

Having attained a curved motion by moving slowly toward the north, it reaches its established position right there; then, having moved swiftly toward the south, having reached a straight-curved path, both set right there. (170) It becomes stable and fit for practical use when its true motion is clear through its own rising and setting. (163) When the slower planet is less [in longitude], its rising is in the east and its setting in the west; but when the faster-moving one is greater, [the reverse occurs].

In the state of being rooted in the primary [cause], there is the exhaustion of the eightfold [suffering] in this world; in the absence of anger, there is prosperity in the east. Thus, through one’s own [effort], there is the singular realization of that. Whether the enemy is small or great, he who acts with excessive gentleness, having cast aside his own [self-interest], is intent on knowing the means for that purpose—the specific path desired by the wise.

The days past or yet to come for that [planet] are to be calculated by the minutes [of arc] from the sum of the desired [longitude] subtracted from the liberated [longitude]. (166) In this case, there will always be a conjunction with the planet when the [difference] is three [signs]; likewise, when the slower [planet] is less [than the faster], it is as stated before. When the enemy [planet] is greater, it is always set according to the previously mentioned days of the desired sum of persons and so forth. (167) For the fast-moving planet, there is a debt in the slow [motion], and thus the days of setting, rising, and the intermediate periods are also like this. However, this has not been stated by the gods because it was omitted from the primary subject matter. (168)

It is well known that the rising of a planet less than [the Sun] occurs before [sunrise], while the rising of one greater [than the Sun] occurs immediately after; however, if it moves above the horizon at night, it is visible otherwise (during the day). When the slower planet (Manda) is not very small, sunrise occurs after its rising; thus, when the remaining portion [of the orbit] is in the eastern direction, there is rising in the east due to the increase of that interval. But when it is greater, the rising occurs in the west during the elapsed night due to the decrease of that interval; for a superior planet, this is easily understood by reversing the process.

If the slower planet (manda) exceeds [the faster one], the conjunction will occur; thus, there would be no further setting (asta). From that time onward, there is a subsequent decrease in the parallax (prahāka) and an increase prior to it. In that interval between the two, the degrees of the *svedya* and *kaḍā* are the beginnings of the rising and setting (*udayāsta*). In that case, when the [longitude] is greater than the stated [value], then by the desire for a lesser degree, the setting occurs later; when the difference is small and the own [longitude] is greater, by that desire, the setting occurs earlier. In the case of the slower planet, there is an increase in the interval subsequently and a decrease previously. Thus, in the opposite case, there is a decrease.

In that case, when the desired [longitude] is greater than the stated [longitude], its rising occurs first by virtue of the desire for a smaller interval; however, if it is less, its rising occurs later by virtue of the desire for a greater interval. Similarly, even when the swift [planet] is greater than the other, there is an increase in their interval here, whereas previously there was a decrease; in that instance, when the desired [longitude] is greater than the stated one, its rising occurs first by virtue of the desire for a smaller interval, while if it is less, its rising occurs later by virtue of the desire for a greater interval. Likewise, when the slower [planet] is less than the other, due to the decrease in that interval, its setting occurs first; however, if the desired [longitude] is greater than the stated one, it is otherwise.

(1) Viśvanātha (Vi0), Śaka year 7—[refers to] a specific point not mentioned by others. The venerable Bhāskara accepts as the first [view] that which was stated by Āryabhaṭa in the *Graha-gaṇita-udayāstādhikāra* [chapter], beginning with: "If the planet seen in the east is greater than the sun... (1) Viśvanātha (Vi0), Śaka year 7—in such cases everywhere, coarseness arises precisely through proportion (*anupāta*); thus, out of fear and envy, he (Bhāskara) censured Bhāskara. 416. *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, *Udayāstādhikāra*: 417. "Where the sun at setting is greater than its own sun at rising..."

Because of their proximity, there is no disappearance of these [planets] by the sun in any way; rather, it occurs there due to the power of the earth's rotation. However, for those whose hearts are directed toward the zenith—such as the great devotees of Viṣṇu and Indra—their forms are not eclipsed by the rays of the sun because they remain situated in the north. But in the northern region, when the interval of the amplitude (śara) is greater than the additional time-portion (kālāṃśa), even though it has been stated that the disk is not eclipsed, it is not eclipsed because it is at a great distance. Here, the rising of the luminaries is said to occur in the east, and their setting in the west.

If the true declination (spaṣṭapama) in the northern hemisphere is greater than the latitude (lamba), then that [latitude] is added to the degrees; likewise, the arm of the interior (garbhabhuja) is below it according to the stated rule for true declination. If one desires to know the excess, it is as previously stated; if one desires to know the deficiency, the subtraction is performed as described.

Thus, when the *manda* [mean] is greater than the *śīghra* [true] or vice versa, their conjunction is then called *paramāsta* (maximum setting), which is the *agra*. Therein, the Sun, having conjoined with the *manda*, moves ahead of the *manda* by an interval of degrees derived from the *kālāṃśas* for the purpose of rising, until *paramāsta*. The first interval between these two is the *sveṣṭakālāṃśas*; they are stated thus, and it is clear that the rising occurs after those days have elapsed, having surpassed its own time of *paramāsta*.

In this very way, it is logical that the planet would be seen on the day following its own time of setting, once the doubt has been resolved by the calculation. This method for determining the gross time, up to the point of the planet's heliacal setting, is equal to the degrees of the arc of visibility. (171) If the difference [in longitude] should be greater than the degrees of the arc of visibility, then on that day, the planet will indeed be visible at night during its period of visibility. (172) Otherwise, if the difference is greater than the degrees of the arc of visibility, it will be visible at night.

Alternatively, the planet may be visible or set; likewise, [the calculation] is performed with a small degree of difference. (173) In the asterisms of Agastya, Lubdhaka, Trahṛdaya, Abhijit, Indra, and Citrā, the degrees are equal to the number of the Kākāṃśas (twenty-one). (174) In Bhaga, Aryaman, Adhīni, Dṛśa, Maśra, Dhātṛ, Bhagha, and Āśava, as well as in Hasta and Śravaṇa, the degrees are equal to the number of Śakra (fourteen), which is the same as the number of the Sun. (175) In the asterisms of Agni, Rudra, Ahi, Pitṛ, Ambu, Dhi, Svadevatā, and Mūla, the degrees are equal to the number of Tithis (fifteen); however, for Puṣya, Mṛga, and Yama, they are equal to the number of Mūrchanās (twenty-two). (176)

The products of the remaining signs are 17; by these, the ascendant is calculated from its own rising degrees as the solar portion. This is known as the "own-ascendant-sun" (svodayabhānu) and the "own-horizon-ascendant-sun" (svāstalagnāṭaṇa). || 177 || By those same degrees in the ascendant, the "sun at that time" (atadbhānu) is obtained, joined with the sign-pada. The difference between this and one's desired sun, converted to minutes and divided by sixty, is the result. || 178 || This result represents the elapsed or remaining portion of the day, depending on whether the desired sun is greater or less [than the current sun]. Since sunrise and sunset are determined from the rising of the sign Khara-vāk (the 10th sign), || 179 || [it follows accordingly]. Now, here:

On the first day of the bright fortnight, when the sun has set, one should calculate the true positions of the moon and the sun, as well as the moon’s node (pāta). From these, the latitude (śara) will indeed be north or south. Then, having determined the true oblique ascension (vilagna), the quadrant (kendram), the declination (dṛkkṣepa), and the time of rising (udayamāśa) there according to the prescribed method, the calculator should determine the degrees of the moon’s meridian distance (vidhitanatāṃśa). Then, having calculated the time of the moon from the sun according to the method of the *Tripraśna*, [the result is obtained].

If that [value] consisting of ghaṭīs and so forth, when multiplied by six, should be greater than the *kālāṃśakas*, then this Moon—having the form of a bee about to die—is white, bestowing complete bliss upon the hearts of men. (Siddhāntatattvaviveka, Chapter on the Occurrence of Parvas, verse 187). Now begins the Chapter on the Occurrence of Parvas (verse 188): It cannot be otherwise; rather, it will undoubtedly occur at the time of the setting of the Sun, provided that [the value] is less than the aforementioned *kālāṃśakas*. Even if it is slightly less than the stated *kālāṃśakas*, one who is bold in his own estimation regarding the celestial bodies may declare it so.

Who would not be an object of ridicule for looking at the dull moon? (189) Those who, exhausted by the various views regarding the determination of its appearance, offer their own conclusions, are merely deluding themselves for its sake. (190) Whether it occurs after the time of its setting or before the time of its rising on the first day of the lunar fortnight, the primary definition of its appearance or non-appearance is as previously stated. (191)

If that [eclipse] should occur before or after sunrise, then a lunar eclipse begins; I shall correctly explain its occurrence beforehand, so that by knowing it, the effort regarding it will not be in vain for those who possess the knowledge. (1) When the degrees of the arc of the moon’s longitude with its node (the *pāta*) are eleven degrees (*indrapaka*), an eclipse occurs; this applies at the time of full moon for the moon, and likewise at the time of the end of the new moon for the sun. (2)

The sign and other divisions (gṛhādika) of the elapsed nāḍīs at the time of the [lunar] eclipse, which indeed constitute the *vedabhāga* (quarter-part), are added to the Sun when the [ecliptic] latitude (*nata*) is eastward, and subtracted when it is westward. Those resulting intermediate degrees (*madhyanāṃśaka*)—which are well-corrected by one-sixth part (*rasāṃśa*) of them—become the true longitudinal degrees of the Moon with its node (*sapātendu*). If the Moon's longitude is less than seven signs (*naga*), it arises from the [mean] motion; this should be multiplied by six, as it is said to be very effective. The monthly additive (*māsakṣepa*) in signs and so forth is added to the Moon conjoined with its node: Earth (1), Sky (0), Sky-oceans (4), and Five-moons (15), making 10;40;15.

Within five months, or even within a fortnight, its occurrence must be observed. (5) However, in that case, the time of rising is fixed; likewise, its setting occurs at the same time as its rising in the previous birth. (192) If it is situated at the time of rising on the first day of the lunar fortnight, then for one situated there, there is no certainty regarding the non-appearance of the deity or the fire. (193) Even from the appearance of one situated there, there is no certainty regarding the setting in the previous birth.

However, by means of one’s own reasoning, one should establish the reality of this [eclipse] on the two lunar disks through the sequence of visibility and invisibility; otherwise, one would be an object of ridicule like a man appearing in the spotless sky at the place of the moon. Thus ends the chapter on Rises and Sets in the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka* composed by the illustrious Kamalākara. (1) The investigation into the possibility of eclipses follows the method of Bhāskarācārya, and its proof has also been demonstrated by Bhaṭṭa Śeṣānanta.

520. Chapter on Lunar Eclipse in the *Siddhāntatattvāviveka*. 421. Since the Earth and the Moon always remain situated upon the line of sight even at a point on the surface of the Earth, there occurs an eclipse of the Moon at the end of the full moon; but it is not so for the Sun at the conclusion of the new moon. (6) The true longitudes of the Sun, Moon, and their nodes produced at that time, as well as the true audibles (longitudes) of the Sun and Moon, constitute the measurement of the line of sight; from that arises the apparent orb of the Moon in its true aspect. (2)

That [time] would be the true time of the end of the lunar day for the Sun; it is here the true [time], corrected by parallax, because at the moment of the end of the visible period, both the Sun and the Moon are situated on the plane of the horizon. (7) If the end of the lunar day for the Moon occurs at night, or if that for the Sun occurs during the day, then an eclipse is observable there; otherwise, it is not, due to the position [of the observer]. (8) As has been stated regarding the Sun and Moon in an eclipse, their true positions on the lunar day are likewise determined by means of parallax.

I do not perceive any superior logic in the calculation of the lunar eclipse therein by Śrī Jiṣṇu and Jaya regarding the celestial sphere. (9) Thus ends the chapter on the possibility of eclipses in the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka* composed by Śrī Kamalākara. The digits and so forth of the Moon are as before; likewise, the calculation of the Earth's [shadow] is indeed subtle. Having understood this first, one should perform the calculation of a lunar eclipse at night. (3)

Due to contact with the rays of the sun, this mass of water shines with shimmering moonlight toward the direction of the sun; but in the opposite direction it does not shine thus, for the cool-rayed one (the moon), like a stone, remains in the heat by means of its own shadow. 5. That portion of the lunar orb which stands facing the earth is visible to the eye; no other part is visible, for at the end of the full moon, the entire disc is indeed white. 6. If [it were otherwise], there would be fear of the earth being situated six signs (90 degrees) away from the sun...

That entire lunar orb exists outside [the Earth]; when the lunar disc is within the Earth's body, then during its eclipse it would be devoid of light (non-white). That which is unfit for observation here should also be understood as unfit for calculation; indeed, at the end of the full moon, the lunar disc is free from defects such as the horizon at its own rising or setting. Now begins the chapter on the lunar eclipse (*candragrahaṇādhikāra*). Now, when the true Sun and Moon are equal in degrees and so forth, being separated by six signs (*ṣaḍbhāntarita*), [the eclipse occurs].

That [mean moon] at the end of the full moon (pūrṇimānta) is established once; that very same value is to be first calculated for the purpose of the lunar eclipse.
