When the moon’s disk is positioned above the clear sky and its rays are arranged below, and when there is a difference of six signs (ṣaḍbhāntara) from the point of conjunction, then the observer situated on the earth sees the moon’s orb as eclipsed by the earth, just as it was previously seen.

It has been seen that the shadow (tadla) is devoid of length and breadth; therefore, [the moon] is without conjunction (yoga). || 17 || How can that which is deformed, lacking hands, feet, and wealth, cover the thousand-rayed sun? Surely, when the rays of the hundred-petaled [lotus] shine forth, how could that [darkness] not perish? Listen: the whiteness of the moon is inherent; it arises from the contact with the rays of the sun. || 9 || Deformed by its own parts, deformed, and with its rays obstructed by a bad mouth (kubhā), the rays do not fall upon the moon; therefore, the moon is dark. || [End of verse] ||

O fortunate one, they say that those two [the Sun and Moon] are visible to each other when they are conjoined with Kuja (Mars). (10) In this system, the solar orb is always larger than the lunar orb; therefore, the shadow of the Earth is like the point of a needle, and the portion of the Earth [in darkness] is constant. (11) Indeed, it extends far beyond the orbit of the Moon, for it lies outside. Thus, according to the method of calculation, it is well known among those who understand the spheres. (12) And for those situated within the shadow of the Earth, there is night, because of the non-perception of substances.

And they describe that [darkness] as being of the nature of night, which is designated by the term "darkness" (tamas). Therefore, because of the delusion that it is that [darkness], when one perceives it, one thinks the moon is being eclipsed; thus, their view that there is a "falling of the moon" (candrapāta) here is not at all acceptable. Even during a solar eclipse, one does not see the sun because it is situated in the shadow of the moon. And the solar disc is obscured by the moon, which has entered its own shadow. That alone is logically the obscuring agent, for it is that which causes the desired obstruction.

It is not that the moon falls [into the earth], but rather that planet (Rāhu) approaches it with great speed. (16) But how is the form of the fall to be seen? (18) Why does he not swallow [the moon] at times other than during an eclipse? When the planet is situated at the point of the *pāta* (node), it does not swallow [the moon] because of its own power. (19) Having reached the intersection of the orbits, the planet, assuming a subtle body, covers the object to be swallowed; thus it is in accordance with the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*. (20) They perform this as a solution to the "Crown Jewel" (of the system), which is certainly not false. (1)

Since that eclipse occurs even when [the moon] falls outside the sphere of the perceiver, it is indeed the moon itself, situated within its own nature, that obscures the sun; for this capacity to obscure the cognition of the sun is established by the fact of the solar eclipse. However, according to the ancient authorities, such a capacity belongs to the shadow of the earth (bhūbhā) in the case of the lunar eclipse, because in both types of eclipses, the obstruction is determined to be caused by darkness (timira). (Viśeṣāvaśyakabhāṣya 7)

Regarding what was stated by the venerable Bhāskarācārya in the Golādhyāya—namely, "Rāhu is situated in the circle of the Earth's shadow upon the Moon"—it is not there that Rāhu is described as the node (*saṃpāta*) of the ecliptic; rather, in Varāhamihira’s *Bṛhatsaṃhitā*, it is said: "The sons of Rāhu, known as the Tāmasakīlakas, are thirty-three comets (*ketus*)," and so forth. If one assumes that among these many Rāhus of erratic and portentous motion, one is located in the circle of the Earth's shadow, then how can the refutation of Bhaṭṭa [Śaṅkara] be considered valid?

In the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, Chapter on Lunar Eclipses (424–425): The head and tail of that [Rāhu] are situated above and below the Earth’s equator, respectively, and are considered to be equal to the Earth itself. Therefore, it is indeed this shadow (*tamaḥ*) here that is Rāhu, the obscuring agent, as declared in the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, and other scriptures regarding lunar and solar eclipses. Since the Moon, moving toward the east, enters [the shadow], contact (*sparśaḥ*) occurs first on the eastern side at the end of the full moon. 32–35.

Liberation [from the eclipse] occurs after the lunar eclipse, whereas in the case of a solar eclipse, the first contact (*sparśa*) and the subsequent release (*vimukti*) always occur before the sun has risen. (21) Since the moon is always situated below the sun, it approaches from the west and, having covered the orb of the sun like a thick cloud, departs. (27) The knowledge of the *ku-bha* (the base of the ecliptic) has been handed down through tradition, yet it is not directly perceived by the wise. Therefore, having understood that which is consistent with logical reasoning, I shall now explain it. (28)

The segment of the Earth's diameter minus the separation [of the observer from the center] is the base (*bhuja*); the distance to the Earth's surface is the hypotenuse (*karṇa*), and the height of the Earth's radius is the perpendicular (*koṭi*). The difference between these two is thus established for the purpose of determining the Earth's shadow. (29) The hypotenuse multiplied by the Earth's segment and divided by the base gives the distance from the Earth's center to the tip of the shadow. The square root of the sum of the squares of the Earth's segment and the perpendicular, when divided by the base, gives the distance from the Earth's surface to the tip of the shadow. (30) Alternatively, the distance from the Earth's surface to the tip of the shadow is the square root of the difference between the squares of the Earth's radius and the Earth's segment.

The square root of the difference between the square of the "bad segment" (kukhaṇḍa), the moon’s rays (śītadyutikara), and the ear (karṇa) is called the first (ādyasaṃjña). When divided by the product of the earth's radius and the hypotenuse (pṛṣṭha), it becomes the sine of the result (phalajyā); or else, when multiplied by the base (bhuja) and divided by the hypotenuse, it is indeed the same sine of the result. Multiplied by three and divided by the moon’s radius (indukaṇa), half of that result is the diameter of the earth on the lunar sphere. 31–33. The square root of the difference between the square of the "bad segment," the moon’s rays, and the square of the hypotenuse shall be known as the first (ādyasaṃjña). Divided by the product of the earth’s radius and the hypotenuse, it becomes the sine of the result; or, when multiplied by the base and divided by the hypotenuse, it is indeed the same sine of the result. Multiplied by three and divided by the moon’s radius, half of that result is the diameter of the earth on the lunar sphere.

Situated on the surface of the sphere, having the form of a bow drawn to its limit at the flank, and resting upon the horizon-line smeared with its own [shadow], it is always separated from the Sun by half a zodiacal sign according to the very subtle method of the spherical field. Its center is that point (pada), and by its motion it reaches the direction of the lords of the quarters (the cardinal points). That line which is drawn from the vertical meridian line toward the east, appearing as a straight horizontal arrow, is subtler than what was previously stated; I shall describe it as being separated from the Earth's center by the distance of the Moon’s radius.

This [Earth's shadow] has the form of a cone with a thick base at the Earth and a sharp point at the Sun; therefore, the corrected shadow-tip (koṭi) is clearly obtained by multiplying the radius of the Earth by the sine of the latitude (ākṣajyā). (37) Viśvanātha: During a lunar eclipse, the Moon is eclipsed by its own shadow. The row of digits (liptā) consisting of the minutes of arc that constitutes the circumference of its orbit is the extent of the Earth's shadow (bhūbhā-vyāsa) expressed as an arc. However, the contact and release of the lunar disc do not occur solely by this extent of the Earth's shadow; rather, it is well known to astronomers that the lunar orbit lies below [the ecliptic].

426. The Chapter on Lunar Eclipses, which ascertains the essential principles of the Siddhānta. 427. Those [points] situated on the terrestrial surface at equal distances from the fruit-line (phalanayugbhūmi), where the earth is intersected by a line parallel to the celestial equator (khāsamānāntarā), there the point *la* is located; this is the lunar node (*labindu*). Thus, that straight line which is equal to the radius (*ramanala*) and serves its purpose is the human line (*nararekhā*). Now, on the circumference of the earth centered at the point *bhu*, there is a line parallel to the human line; where another line drawn from the very point *bhu* intersects it, there they know the point *tha*.

A line *thapa* is drawn; it is the intersection of the circumference of the solar disc with the terrestrial surface, which is extended until it meets the line *bhūra*. From that point of contact, another line drawn parallel to the solar disc reaches the point known as *ṭa* on the lunar orbit where the line *rabhu* intersects it. A line drawn from the moon (*ṭabindu*) parallel to the terrestrial surface meets the extended line *phatha* at the point known as *ṭha*.

O Lord of Sages, the half-chord of the arc corresponding to the latitude of the observer (bhūbhāvyāsārdha) arrives at the point where the line drawn from the center of the Earth (bhūcandra) intersects the extended radius at a distance equal to the Earth's radius. This is because the triangle formed by the Earth’s radius, the observer’s latitude, and the hypotenuse is similar to the triangle of the celestial sphere. When the segment of the chord is subtracted from the sine of the latitude, it is divided by the square root of the difference between the squares of the radius and that segment; and that result, when divided by the product of the radius and the sine of the latitude, yields the corrected value. (38)

That shadow (bhā) is clearly visible on the surface of the earth and on the pot; it is the portion of the rays falling upon the curved surface. (39) The moon is situated at a much greater distance, while the thousand-rayed sun is nearby. To the extent that [the observer] is here within the lunar sphere, to that same extent the terrestrial shadow (kṣitibhā) should be considered small. (40) Therefore, if the shadow is greater, it is due to being situated far away; if it is smaller, it is due to being situated near.

It may be that [the earth's diameter] is established by the relative proportions of the sun and moon, situated on the surface of the middle orbit. However, the subtle [diameter] of the earth, which was calculated by the son of Raṅganātha according to the method of Āryabhaṭa and others, is incorrect; for he, by his own intellect, stated it in his own commentary (*bhāṣya*) as being equal to the diameter of the moon. Here, I shall correctly state that [diameter], which is the field of its face. The diameter of the earth divided by the diameter of the sun—[the result is] *vi* (the sine of the parallax). [Note: Although the word ends in the vowel 'a', it is written as *śravaḥ*; therefore, the form *śravonitam* is correct.

(2) vi0 śa7—In the phrase "prapaśya," the reading "pradvā" is a scribal error. (3) thi7 śa7—The point *bhū* is assumed to be the center of the Earth (*bhūkendram*). The point *ra* is the center of the Sun (*ravikendram*). Lines are drawn from the point *bhū* to the point *ravi*, and from the point *indu* to the point *ravi*. The intersection of the line from *bhū* perpendicular to the line joining *ravi* and *indu* is *ta*. The intersection of the line from *indu* perpendicular to the line joining *ravi* and *indu* is *pha*.

From point *na*, a line of darkness (*tama-rekhā*) should be drawn parallel to the terrestrial radius (*bhūrarekhā*). Where that line of darkness meets the obtainable line (*labhyarekhā*), which is the perpendicular from the center of the solar disc (*ravibimba-dhyāsa*) to the line designated as *rapha*, there is the point *ma*. That line of darkness, when extended to the circumference of the solar disc on the side facing the earth, meets it at the point *na*. From point *na* to point *pha* along the *rapha* line, let *na-ra* = *na-la* = *x* and *ra-na* = *y*. Then *y* × *ra* is the minimum result (*phalādhama*). Since the triangle *bhū-tha-ca* is a right-angled triangle, *ca* × *ra* [is the hypotenuse].

Let *v* be the point where the line drawn parallel to *thaca* intersects the line *rabhū*; let *ravikarṇa* be the distance from *v* to *ra*, and let *kalpitaravikarṇa* be the distance from *v* to *ca*. Then let *bhūra* be the distance from *v* to *b*, and let *kalpitacandrakarṇa* be the distance from *v* to *ca*. Let *vindu* be the point where the line drawn parallel to the line joining *ra* and *vi* intersects the line *tha*. Let *pabindu* be the point where the line drawn parallel to the line joining *tha* and *vi* intersects the line *rapha*.

Line *thapa* is equal to the assumed solar radius (*ravikarṇa*), and line *ṭaya* is equal to the assumed lunar radius (*candrakarṇa*). Therefore, the two triangles *thapapha* and *ṭavaca*—namely, *karcaka*, *paka*, *baca*, *karaka*, *rakhā-ka*, *ceka-thaca*, and *baca*—are similar. Consequently, *baca* = *karaka* × (*rakhā-ka*) / (*ceka-thaca*). Now, from the Siddhāntatattvāviveka, Chapter on Lunar Eclipses (428): "When the square roots of [the quantity] increased by one-quarter of that product and decreased by one-quarter of that product are respectively the solar and lunar radii, then those two [radii] are established. (429)

43–44. The solar disc diminished by its [own] result, struck by the lunar digit, and divided by the solar radius; diminished by the quotient obtained—this result here becomes the subtle extent of the Earth's shadow (*kubhā*) on the path of the moon. Thus, that opinion exists there because, in his view, the illumination of the earth does not reach the moon. Therefore, he always stated that the moon is indeed situated within the body of the Earth's shadow. 45. In this case, since the Earth's shadow is the veil, how could an eclipse of the moon produced by it occur?

Now, his names are indeed based on the well-known succession of refined [traditions] and the descent of the moon (46). As for that manifestation performed by him, which is beyond measure and free from limits—what gain is there for me here through opposition to that, when he is skilled in moving through the constellations? (47) The removal of the moon’s orb by Rāhu and so forth, occurring at the ear-region of the sky where the moon had risen, is a beautiful [event]; yet the removal of the wicked woman is far more excellent than that, even if it causes slight distress (48).

Since it is said that from an ear situated within oneself, whatever is spoken would be heard accordingly, so too was that [distance] described for the Sun and Moon respectively as being equal to the diameter of the Earth. (Commentary: *karka*, *karaka*, *batha*, *kā*, *ṭaṭha*, *bhūbhā*—*pha*, *kara*, *ka* [the calculation: *pha* = *kalaṅka*]). Therefore, it is established that "the result diminished by what is obtained here becomes the subtle extension of the Earth's shadow on the path of the Moon. Here, the subtlety [of this calculation] has been stated by the Lord of Sages himself.

Furthermore, this statement regarding the path is like an incoherent discourse; for since it possesses the form of being situated within the crescent moon (*candrakaṇa*), it is clear that it exists precisely above the lunar orbit. Indeed, this [eclipse] is not caused by the contact of the rays of the solar disc with the shadow of the earth.

(1) Viśvanātha’s commentary (*vi0*): Regarding the phrase *tadudītirītitaḥ kubhāgram*—"by that lord of sages (*munīśvara*), the manner (*rīti*) which was spoken (*udīritā*) or described" connects with the first half [of the verse]. In that case, the statement "the moon is always below the earth's path (*māgadadha*)" would not be tenable; therefore, in that lunar eclipse, the manner (*rīti*) which was spoken (*udīritā*) or described—by that [manner], the portion of the earth (*kubhāgam*) which is the part of the terrestrial sphere useful for the lunar eclipse, is in reality always below the moon's path (*śaśimārgāt*), that is, below the lunar orbit (*candrakakṣāyāḥ*), by which auspicious [alignment] there occurs contact with the lunar disc.

The root of that shadow of the earth (bhūchāyā) extends as far as the solar radius; however, the arc of that [shadow] lies precisely along the line of contact with the terrestrial disc, and thus it belongs to the lunar orbit. (9A) The center of the earth's globe is situated at a distance equal to the solar radius from the center of the solar orb. Therein, those solar rays which are obstructed by the earth and do not reach the surface of the earth are absent; due to that absence, the object of sight is indeed darkness possessing a blue form. Because it is perceived through observation, it is designated by the term "night" and called the "shadow of the earth" (bhūchāyā).

And that shadow is as follows: because the terrestrial globe is smaller in dimension than the solar globe, there will necessarily be a connection between the rays emitted from all sides from the surface of the solar orb and the terrestrial globe when they reach the earth-dwelling Rāhu; therein, the entry into the shadow of the earth occurs. Since the terrestrial globe is covered by the solar rays, the nature of the shadow of the earth within the shadow-region is established as being filled with those rays.

In that context, the rays not being obstructed [by the moon] touch the surface of the earth; the circular area on the ground along that path is the "face" (*mukha*) there. The penetration (*vedha*) is the distance from the center of that circle up to the shadow-limit, appearing like a long needle-shaped shadow due to the absence of connection with the internal rays. [From the *Siddhānta-tattvaviveka*, Chapter on Lunar Eclipse: Herein is the demonstration of the shadow-cone (*chāyāpyatana-kṣetra*) for the purpose of knowing the earth. There exists half the diameter of the earth.

Outside the rays, everywhere, shadow exists due to the cessation of the connection with the rays. That extent of the shadow on the spherical surface of the ball (the Earth) is precisely what is utilized for the purpose of a lunar eclipse. To understand this, one should construct a long thread from the center of the various celestial spheres (golakas) touching the center of the terrestrial sphere, extending as far as the tip of the Earth's shadow; this shall be the central thread. Wherever that thread touches the surface of the lunar orb and the surface of the terrestrial globe, those points shall be the respective centers of their surfaces.

From that center, on its own rear side, the circle formed by a fourth part of its own circumference—acting as the diameter—is its respective semi-diurnal arc (pṛṣṭhārdhavṛtta). Now, on the sphere of the solar disc, the portion of the sphere above the semi-diurnal arc is indeed obstructed by the Earth's shadow, because there is no connection with the sun’s rays there. Next follows the consideration regarding the semi-diurnal arc. It is as follows:

From the center of the solar disc-globe, extending as far as that specific point, a line equal to half the diameter of the solar disc-globe serves as the *bhuja* (base). Then, the line parallel to the central meridian (*madhyasūtra*) that touches that very point and no other is also not useful for the present purpose; for, being parallel everywhere, it lacks a connection with the central meridian.

That which is the form of the limit (koṭi), even if it touches the half-circle of the sphere's surface at the point where the solar disc is situated, such a seasonal thread (ṛtusūtra) would touch the central thread; however, due to the obstruction by the lower region of the hemisphere in the form of the earth (thāpara), this could not happen in any way. Even if it were established by force according to the statement of the ancients, that too would be untenable without piercing the surface of the sphere; thus, it is incapable of its own function because, in that manner, the rays of light cannot possibly exist [there].

Therefore, because there is no connection with the rays even from the circle of the hemisphere of the surface of the solar disc, that shadow has been imagined by those who are ignorant of its impossibility. Now, from the lower region of the circle of the hemisphere of the surface of the solar disc and the terrestrial globe, starting from the point situated at the end of the interval—which is the form of the *bhuja* (the base) from that center of the dark [shadow]—there is a ray-line in the form of the *koṭi* (the perpendicular); that indeed would be capable of touching the central line, and it would certainly be so.

Since one may assume that the distance from the center of the sphere to the point on its surface is equal to half the diameter of the sphere and take it as the *bhuja* (the base), then the *yaju-sūtra* (the chord) extending from there is the *koṭi* (the perpendicular); however, it is very well known that this [chord] exists only at that specific point on the sphere's surface and not elsewhere. In this context, the state of being "above" or "below" is to be understood by the relative position of being distant or near to one’s own location.

For that purpose, there is one straight line known as the *pṛṣṭhasūtra* (surface-line), as follows: the straight line passing through the center that touches both the point on the surface of the celestial sphere (*vivigolagola*) and the point on the surface of the terrestrial globe (*bhūgola*)—wherever it touches, according to the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, that line is such that the sun’s position (*ravisaṃciḍae*) should be determined sequentially at the points where that line touches the surface of the solar disc and the surface of the terrestrial globe. Furthermore, wherever that same line touches the central meridian line (*madhyasūtra*), there is the entry of the earth’s shadow (*bhūcchāyā*).

On the celestial sphere, the circle drawn at a distance equal to the Sun's semi-diameter from the center of the Earth’s surface opposite the Sun is indeed the *āvṛtta* (the ecliptic); likewise, on the terrestrial globe, it is the terrestrial circle (*bhūvṛtta*). Thus, it is established that only those rays of the Sun which emerge from the solar circle and meet the sky situated upon the terrestrial circle within the path of the solar rays constitute the actual nature of the Earth's shadow, and no others.

From the center of the solar disc to the edge of the earth's shadow at the limit of the sun's path, the radius of the solar disc-sphere is the large base (*bṛhad-bhuja*) along the central meridian. From the center of the solar disc-sphere to the point marking the tip of the earth's shadow, the large hypotenuse (*bṛhat-karṇa*) is formed. Along the posterior meridian, from the same starting point to the limit of the earth's shadow at the sun's zenith, the large perpendicular (*bṛhat-koṭi*) is formed; thus is the large triangle established. Now follow other triangles of the same kind.

From the center of the earth (kugarbha) to the mark on the circumference of the terrestrial circle (bhūvṛttacihna), half the diameter of the earth (bhūvyāsārtha) is the hypotenuse (*karṇa*) along the median line (*madhyasūtra*). The distance between the center of the earth and the portion of the earth's surface is the base (*koṭi*), which is the segment of the arc from the back of the earth to that mark. Thus, from the center of the earth to the mark on the circumference of the terrestrial circle, half the diameter of the earth is the hypotenuse; then, up to the median line, the perpendicular mark equal to the earth's [radius] is the base (*koṭi*); the distance between those two along the median line is the earth's [radius].

Thus, from the terrestrial circle (*bhūvṛtta*) to the end of the earth’s radius (*kubhāgra*), the arc on the surface of the earth within that middle line is the hypotenuse (*karṇa*). The distance between those two [points] along the middle line is the perpendicular (*koṭi*). Similarly, from the end of the earth’s radius to the lunar sphere (*candragola*), the arc known as the last segment (*antyasaṃjñaka*) is the hypotenuse; then, the sine (*jyā*) of the segment of the earth’s diameter situated on the lunar sphere is the base (*bhuja*), and the distance between them along the middle line is the perpendicular (*koṭi*). In this way, for the purpose of establishing all calculations here, there is a proportional field (*pramāṇakṣetra*) of the same kind.

And it is said in the *Sahasrabhujastotra*: "The side [of the triangle] opposite the earth's diameter is the radius of the sun; the hypotenuse is the solar distance (*ravikarṇa*). The square root of the difference between those two squares is the perpendicular (*koṭi*), which is the line situated at an equal interval from the center of the earth to the two lunar ornaments. Likewise, from the interior of the earth, there is another dissimilar figure: the side is the distance from the center of the earth to the moon; the hypotenuse is the distance from the surface of the earth to the moon; the square root of the difference between those two squares is the perpendicular, known as the first segment of the line from the surface of the earth to the lunar sphere."

This [shadow] is not purified by the line from the tip of the Earth’s shadow (kubhāgra) to the back [of the Moon]; the remainder would be the doubt regarding the other [parameters]. Now, for the determination of the true position of the eye (kunayana), there is a proportion: if the hypotenuse (karṇa) from the tip of the Earth’s shadow to the back [of the Moon] is equal to the Earth’s radius, then what is the hypotenuse known as the "mouth" (āsya)? This is the sine of the extent of the Earth’s shadow situated on the lunar sphere; this is the section on the lunar eclipse (candragrahaṇādhikāra). It would be 433.

Thus, by means of this proportional calculation (*pramāṇanetrānupāta*), when the ear-measure is secure (*pramāṇakṣemakarṇe*) and the field-measure (*pramāṇakṣetre*) is the side, then what is the other side known as the arm? That which is established is multiplied by three times the sine (*trijyā*) and divided by the lunar radius (*candrakarṇa*); that resulting quotient, doubled, shall be the extent of the Earth's shadow (*kubhāvistāra*) upon the lunar sphere (*candragola*).

Thus, when the base (bhuja) is the standard measure, the hypotenuse (karṇa) is likewise the standard measure; then, when the base is measured by the earth's radius (bhūvyāsārddha), what would the hypotenuse be? That [hypotenuse] would extend from the center of the earth to the surface of the earth (kubhāpradeśa). However, that [surface] lies far outside, having passed beyond the moon’s orbit (candrakakṣā). In this way, the calculation of the corresponding base, perpendicular (koṭi), and hypotenuse belonging to a similar figure (jātīyakṣetra) through the proportion of the standard field (pramāṇakṣetra-anupāta) is easily understood.

In this regard, Bhāskara and others maintain that on the lunar sphere (*candragola*), the shadow-cone (*kumbha*) is formed by straight lines drawn perpendicularly from the vertical-horizontal central axis; however, their method of calculation is considered approximate. The actual reality is as follows: it was previously stated that the path along which the rays of the sun strike the terrestrial globe (*bhūgola*) is itself a circle parallel to the equator of the earth.

Now, regarding the "Great Story" (*Bṛhatkathā*) which is the interval between the terrestrial latitudes (*bhūbhā*) at the center of the Earth's cavity (*kugarbha*): just as the "Great Arm" (*vṛhadbhuja*) serves the purpose of the diameter of the Earth's surface in the form of the terrestrial latitude at the center of the Earth's cavity, so too, when the "Small Ear" (*laghukarṇa*) is equal to the "Great Ear" (*bṛhatkarṇa*)—which is the radius of the lunar sphere—the "Small Story" (*laghukathā*), in the form of the interval between the terrestrial latitudes at the center of the Earth's cavity, becomes the "Small Arm" (*laghubhuja*) measured from the gross terrestrial latitude; its two ends are the segments of the triangle on the back of the Earth. Thus, the difference between the Great Arm and the Small Arm is the "Arm" (*bhuja*), the "Ear" (*karṇa*) is the radius of the Moon, and the "Perpendicular" (*koṭi*) is the line drawn parallel to the line passing through the back of the Earth.

This field is of the same nature as the *pramāṇakṣetra* (standard field); thus, just as in the case of the Sun’s radius, if the half-diameter of the Earth is the side (*bhuja*), then what is the [resulting] Moon’s radius? Having subtracted that from the diameter of the Earth, it is found to be equal to the "gross" half-Earth-shadow (*sthūlabhūbhārdha*) mentioned by the ancients. However, that which is the side (*bhuja*) corresponding to the hypotenuse (*koṭī*) formed by the distance between the center of the Earth and the limit of the Earth's shadow is actually the true half-Earth-shadow; whereas this [other] hypotenuse (*koṭī*) is of the nature of the gross half-Earth-shadow, and the full shadow-hypotenuse (*bhākarṇa*) would be the complete one. This [calculation] occurs through the proportion of the standard field (*pramāṇadoṣānupāta*).

The true calculation of terrestrial latitude (*bhūbhā*) is also easily accessible. Thus, having set aside the configuration of the celestial sphere (*kṣetra-saṃsthā*) as joined by a series of half-arches, [the author] proceeds otherwise according to Govindaśiva (Go Vi0 Śa7): "Subtracting the terrestrial latitudes, multiplied by the lunar sine and divided by the solar radius... and so forth. From this, the line obtained on the back-side meridian from the intersection of the middle orbit of the Moon is doubled; the terrestrial latitude derived from that measure differs from what is stated by Bhaṭṭa. This is the firm conviction found in the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, verse 434.

The Chapter on Lunar Eclipses (Candragrahaṇādhikāra). 435. Those who calculate the duration of the eclipse (*muhūrta*) using inconsistent half-chord lines (*lārdhasūtra*) are incorrect; for such a method lacks the factual basis required to establish the relationship between the true positions of the moon and the earth’s shadow, as well as the configuration of the relevant geometrical figures. Regarding this point, the sons of Raṅganātha hold the following view according to the intention of Sārvabhauma.

In reality, when the distance between the rays from the circumference of the Earth's sphere and the circumference of the solar disc is equal to the Earth's radius, then by inverse proportion, one determines the distance between those two rays on the Earth's sphere for the desired solar diameter. Having thus established the interval between the rays, one adds to it—respectively—the true distances in *yojanas* of the Sun and Moon, which are represented by the square root of the difference of squares of half that ray-interval and half the Earth's radius, as the distance between the center of the Earth and the midpoint of the line of the ray-interval.

There are two *karṇas* (sides) useful for the calculation of the Earth's shadow (*bhūbhā*). From these, by means of the hundred-ray interval produced from the position of the Earth's diameter, the determination of the Earth's shadow is obtained through the method already stated; they say that its true nature is such. However, regarding the Moon's diameter, they state that the "swallowing" (*grasana*) is the half-sum of the measures minus the *śara* (latitude). But those of subtle intellect always consider this [half-sum] alone as appropriate, not the well-known half-sum of the measures. (53) The contact or the swallowed portion of the Moon arises from the points of conjunction falling upon the Moon's disc.

Since the shadow of the earth (bhūbhā) is fixed at the gross level for one situated below, I shall therefore state another logically consistent method regarding the interval between the neck of the moon and the earth: how the neck of the moon touches the back of the earth’s shadow here correctly. (55) The neck of the moon is always smaller than the measurement of the earth, while that situated below it is always larger. Furthermore, when the earth’s shadow is positioned below, there would first be contact with the entire sphere of the moon. (56)

Then, having first reflected upon this regarding the Earth situated within the lunar sphere, the wise [author] considered it with his daughter: "When the lower part of the Earth touches the lunar sphere, the distance between the centers of the two spheres would be twice that [radius]. (57) At the time of the eclipse, the Sun and Moon are separated by six signs; thus their conjunction occurs. Then, as the Moon's disc moves toward the south or north along the *ikadambavṛtta* (the ecliptic), (58) the interval between the centers of the Earth and Moon here is nine [degrees], while the east-west distance is indeed south-north. (59)

The difference between that [latitude] and the center is always the arrow (*bāṇa*) at the time of the middle of the eclipse. When the measure of the Moon (the lunar disc) is equal to a quarter of the measure of the jar (*kuṃbha*), the arrow is three quarters; here, as long as the planet is not within the body of the half-measure of the conjunction, its arrow remains situated within the earth. That same neck of the Moon exists there, and it is appropriate for their positions at conjunction and release; nothing else is found here. Therefore, for the sake of the happiness of those who possess the knowledge of the divisions, I shall speak here according to the method of the sky-dweller (the Moon) situated in the field.

Viśvanātha (vi0 śa7) states: "When the earth-shadow (bhūbhā) situated below—that is, situated below the orbit of the moon—is greater than the calculated earth-shadow, the moon has indeed set; this is extremely clear from observing the field [of the sky], as was first understood by Bhaṭṭa himself. Viśvanātha (vi0 śa7): "The true ecliptic latitude (bhabhe) is that which lies within the vertical line (lambarekhā) on the meridian line (madhyasūtra)."

In this matter, who indeed knows what is the truth? — 436. *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, Chapter on Lunar Eclipse. 437. Everywhere, that which was done by those ancient masters [is accepted]. Whatever has been done here by the ancients for the sake of practical application, even with slight differences, is accepted; whereas that which has been done here by moderns out of their own intellect and pride, my opinion stands against that. 65–66. The radius of the Moon’s orb increased by the Earth’s radius shall be the sum; by that [sum], here...

The square root of the difference between the squares of the hypotenuse and the [perpendicular] of the Moon will indeed be the [other] side. Then, the *kubhāva* (the sine of the argument) multiplied by the *bhujaphala* (the result of the correction), divided by the hypotenuse, and having subtracted that from the sum as appropriate for the remainder; that [result], multiplied by the cube of eight (*ibhākoṭi*) and divided again by the hypotenuse, and further multiplied by the radius (*trijyā*) and divided by the hypotenuse of the Moon; the arc of that [result] becomes the correction to be applied to the Moon during the conjunction or separation.

Then, the square of the difference between the other [latitude] and the earth-sine (kubhā), increased by the square of the sine of the argument, is the square of the distance from the center of the Earth. From that, the arc [of the distance] is calculated; when doubled and added to that, it becomes the distance from the center of the Earth at the time of contact or emergence. This line of sight, in the form of a straight line, meets the surface of the Earth at the point where the moon's disk rises. Because the velocity produced at the surface of the Earth is directed toward the rising of the lunar orb.

63–64. A wise person should apply this elsewhere as well, according to the nature of the different forms [of the problem], having correctly observed the calculation of the "unprecedented" (apūrva) through the method of the *saṅketa* (convention). Even though it is not present here, I have established it within the interval; for it is indeed not suitable everywhere in its true form. The measure (*māna*) is a segment, easily understood as the year. The central line between the center of the earth and the portion of the earth's shadow (*bhūbhāga*) is where it meets the lunar sphere (*candragola*); there is the center of the earth's shadow (*bhūbhākendra*). At the point of contact and release, the center of the lunar disc-sphere (*candrabimbagolakendra*) is also situated within its own sphere.

The circle of three sines (trijyāvṛtta) attached to those two [sides] is designated as the *sthiti-karṇa* (duration-circle). The distance between its center and that [circle] is called the *sthiti-karṇa*, which is suitable for determining the duration (*sthiti*). The method for its calculation is as follows: At the points of contact and release, the shadow of the Earth situated on the lunar sphere is below it; on the surface [of the moon], there is contact with the lunar orb by the shadow of the Earth, which is greater [in extent] and situated below. There, from the surface of the Earth’s shadow situated above and below, the center of the lunar orb exists on the lunar sphere at a horizontal distance (*bhuja*) equal to the diameter of the moon, measured from the point of contact and release, which serves as the perpendicular (*koṭi*).

Thus, the *kubhāpṛṣṭha* line is perpendicular; from where it is fixed, the center of the Earth also exists at a distance equal to half the Earth's diameter in the form of the base (*bhuja*), in a direction opposite to the Moon's center. Furthermore, how can there be such stubbornness in the deluded regarding that which is clearly seen to be small?

"I have discovered through calculation that the maximum horizontal parallax (*haralambana*) is four *ghaṭikās*"; thus [the author] increases his pride. But for one who has skillfully calculated the eye-parallax (*netravatti*) as being equal to the Earth's radius, his obsession with composing this treatise is indeed in vain. (26) When the Sun is situated on the terrestrial horizon (*kṣitija*), the difference between the line of sight (*dṛksūtra*) and the vertical line (*nāḍīsūtra*) is the Earth's radius. From that, the difference between the vertical line passing through the center of the Earth (*kugarbhanāḍī*) and the line of sight is indeed the horizontal parallax (*apakrama*). (27) Therefore, in this case, the former [maximum parallax] is the greatest.

Therefore, by means of proportion, it was calculated for the desired time. That [calculation] would be [correct] on the surface of the earth; however, according to the method stated, it is less than that at the center of the earth. Indeed, it is even more deficient when compared to the observed [value]. How then can the wise not investigate this, given that the greater value is established by direct perception? (28–29) Furthermore, those who accepted that the maximum [longitude] occurs when the [true] position is equal to the observed [position], and then applied that [maximum] to the time of the desired moment via proportion—that was not done correctly. (29)

30. And as it has been said: "The bhalandhana [correction] arising from the back (pṛṣṭhaja) is always very small. Now hear the correct method regarding those arising from the interior (garbha) and the face (āsya). 31–32. In the case of the Sun, the hypotenuse (karṇa) is at the ear (karṇa), while the perpendicular (koṭi) is at the interior (garbha). At the back (pṛṣṭhaja), there are two hypotenuses (karṇakoṭī); the side (bhuja) of those two is the segment of the earth's curvature (kukhaṇḍa). 33. There, the hypotenuse is joined with the sides (pārśva) according to their respective positions; likewise, the sum of the interior perpendicular and side is equal to the sum of the back-side and side.

The conjunction of the Moon and Mars should be calculated at the point of their union; this is to be done by adding [the longitudinal difference] and dividing by six. When the Moon is on the terrestrial meridian, the result is clearly evident from direct observation as being less than the longitude of the point on the meridian. Therefore, because the Moon is situated at the center of the terrestrial sphere, the ancient reading "garbhajī" is unsatisfactory.

(2) Bhaṭṭa has demonstrated the perceptibility of a celestial body situated in its own orbit according to its own system; however, if one now places the koti of the subsequent knowledge—which is a conceptual construct—merely by joining it with the center at the base of the hypotenuse such that it is equal to the solar radius, it clearly swears an oath that even the sixteenth proposition of the first chapter of the *Rekhāgaṇita*, namely "the perpendicular is greater," is violated. [End of] the section on Solar Eclipses in the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*.

35. Between the center of the earth (*kṣitigarbha*) and the ecliptic (*sūtra*), there is no observation of its [the planet’s] rising or setting. 38. For the purpose of observing the *laṅbana* (parallax), there is a diagram. That *laṅbana* is stated to arise from the center of the earth, and indeed from the very sphere accepted by it. 39. Although that which is produced by the grasp [of the planet] is considered unsuitable because it is situated below the local horizon (*kṣitija*) and due to the influence of the improper line of sight, nevertheless it is stated to be on the terrestrial plane. 40. Since the knowledge of the observed planet here depends upon that [line], therefore it is logical.

The rising and setting [of a planet] occurs naturally from the east; its effect is not accepted below Mars. (40) Now, the true nature of parallax and its calculation are stated: This is not the same as the circle of the zodiac situated on one's own [local] horizon. From the center of the earth, at that point on the zodiacal circle, there would be a degree of arc for the mark of that planet. (41) One situated on the surface of the earth sees that planet at that degree of arc along the line [from the center], but one situated on the terrestrial surface does not see it there.

He sees the woman’s eye-marked arrow [the planet] at that very point and nowhere else, because it bears the mark of the observer's sight. (42) This is not another thread extending as far as the celestial sphere (bhagola), piercing through to the mark of the planet situated in its own orbit; rather, the observer always sees the lord of the sky-dwellers at that point on the celestial sphere where it is intersected by that thread. (43) That [planet] which is established in the degrees of the zodiacal circle is indeed seen here as if reflected in a mirror. It is precisely here that the calculation of parallax (helambana) was performed by those skilled in the methods of the *Kṣetrajña*. (44)

Listen now to that which is unfit [for calculation] and beyond the scope of investigation, due to the marks on the back of the earth (the terrestrial latitude): When the hypotenuse (śravaṇa) is joined with the two arms (doḥkoṭi) at the ear (latitude), the support (avalamba) is likewise established in the small segment (kukhaṇḍa). The large segment (vṛhatkukhaṇḍa) diminished by the square root of the product of the interval between the support and the hypotenuse (lambandukaṇāntara) is reduced by its own foot (pada). That [large segment] diminished by its own hypotenuse (koṭi) and divided by the hypotenuse (śravaṇa) yields the arc; thus it is to be established. [This concludes the section on the determination of the sun's position according to the Siddhānta. The Chapter on the Determination of the Sun’s Position within the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*.

455. Since the visible [point] is situated within the observer, this [parallax] established on the celestial sphere (bhagola) is fixed. || 44 || And the parallax of that planet is correctly [calculated] from the interval between the line from the center of the earth and the line from the center of the eye; for that [interval] which is drawn as a single straight line from the center of the earth to the degrees of the planet situated on the zodiacal sphere (bhacakra). || 45 || Likewise, the second point of observation is indeed the opening made in the sphere by piercing it; the parallax of vision (dṛg-lambana) on the ecliptic (imaṇḍala) would belong to the planet situated in its own orbit (kakṣā). || 46 ||

In the calculation of the true longitude (yathābhūta-dharmayoga), the first parallax is determined by the interval of the *kalikā*. If the planet is situated ahead of its own [mean] degree, then those degrees of depression (*natabhāga*) occurring at that time, when combined with the parallax below the sky (*khādhaḥ-lambana*), shall become the depressed degrees of the planet at that moment. Some say that for the sake of achieving the conjunction (*tadyoga-siddhi*), these [depressed degrees] are not indeed the second [true] degrees of the planet itself. Thus, in the case of an eclipsed rising (*grastodaya*), if the [calculated] value is greater than that, the other [correction] would be the *haṭṭisapa* (or *haṭṭisarpa*).

Immediately thereafter, when the celestial body is situated in the middle of the sky, its nature [is such that] it diminishes there. (49) Viśvanātha: This very thing is the parallax of vision (*dṛglambana*). Viśvanātha: This indeed is the second parallax of vision. Viśvanātha: On the horizon, the circle is equal to the line of sight. Just as the planet becomes further away from the observer, so indeed does the parallax decrease; just as it becomes closer to the center of the earth, so this [parallax] becomes somewhat greater. (10)

Thus, during a solar eclipse, the obscuration of the sun is twofold; for the moon, however, it is indeed the distance between the two disks of the sun and the moon. (51) They say that in that case, [the calculation] should be performed using only the first [two] disks and not the others. In the central conjunction of the sun and moon, it is not [calculated] from the first two nor from the second two. (52) Those [disks] which are above the moon and facing upward, and likewise the sun below, facing downward, are respectively the "womb-born" (*garbhaja*) and the "external" (*bāhya*). Since the distance between those two—the spheres of the sun and moon—occurs here, it is designated as "first" and "other" (*prathamānya*). (53)

The visual support (*dṛglambana*) is declared to arise from the position of the ocular film; likewise, that same value derived from the tri-ascendant (*tribhonalagna*) is designated as *nati* (parallax). (14) In a location where the Moon and Sun occupy the same degree [of longitude], they are seen on the meridian line at the moment of new moon (*darśānta*), yet the Sun is not seen at that very spot. (52) That Moon is indeed delayed by the distance [from the observer], because it is situated below the horizontal line (*bhasūtra*) at that point. (56) When the interval between the ears [the zenith distance] is small, the delay (*vilambana*) is small; likewise, when it is greater, the delay would be greater.

The Noble One, however, has prescribed that very same form of simulation for the sake of ease in his independent treatise. (57) Now, I shall state the parallax (*lambana*) that exists at the time of rising and setting: let the square root of the product of the Earth’s diameter and the distance [of the Moon] be divided by the hypotenuse (*śruti*) of the Moon and Sun respectively. (58) [End of page 451 of the Viṣaya-śataka]. In the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, this is the chapter on Solar Eclipses. (427) The difference between those two roots, multiplied by half the Earth’s diameter and divided by the Sun’s radius (*ravikarṇa*), and then further divided by the Moon’s radius (*candrakarṇa*) after being multiplied by the radius of the celestial sphere (*trijyā*), [is the parallax]. (59)

Likewise, when situated at its own elevation, the parallax for the solar disc is stated to be the difference between the hypotenuse and the latitude. (60) The sines of the latitudes of the Moon and the Sun, multiplied by the radius and placed separately, are divided by their respective terrestrial hypotenuses (*yojanakarṇa*). Alternatively, the parallax in arc is equal to the difference between the arcs of those two [sines]; it stands as the true parallax at the rising of the Sun. (61) Thus, the parallax of a planet at its rising is derived from the latitudes of the star and the planet. When the planet's longitude-mark is at the center of the Earth, that very value is always the subtle and ultimate [parallax].

62. The Lord of Sages has explained in his own work that the shadow (valmī) and the accepted latent impression (svīkṛtavāsanā) lie on the line situated at the surface of the earth within the cavity of the earth, at an interval equal to half the diameter of the earth. 63–64. When [the sphere] is made greater than the sphere of the stars (bhagola) by those two, whatever empty space (vimbara) occurs within its own sphere (svagola), the wise declare that to be the arc in minutes of the terrestrial obscuration (kuchannatrasa) for the planets.

Having understood that the difference between the two—one arising from the vertical line of the stationary observer and the other from the vertical line of the planet situated on the ecliptic—is equal both on the celestial sphere (bhagola) and on the planetary sphere (grahagola), [one finds] the divisions of the arc of the latitude of the planet’s position; this is the derivation of the parallax of the moon based on the difference in the arcs of the great circle. Therein, within the visual depth of the observer, it occurs at the degree of the planet’s position. Thus, because in this case the vertical lines do not coincide with the verticals of the entire sphere, equality does not occur here.

Regarding the three [corrections] arising from Kṣitigarbha, it should be understood that this is so; thus, one should examine this with one's own intellect and with care. (67) Likewise, even at the desired time, when the Sun and Moon are situated in their middle [longitude], the state of the Moon [is determined] by its own internal difference, for it resides in its own house or exaltation. (68) The difference [between them] is found in one’s own work through one’s own intellect, due to other specific factors; there, the son of Raṅganātha has always correctly stated this according to the opinion of the masters of Gauḍa. (69)

That which was stated by Īśvara as being established according to his own school’s doctrine—that there is no other object of perception (ālambana) [for the cognition of the sky]—is indeed untenable, because when the sun is present, that [cognition] occurs through portions devoid of an object of perception. Furthermore, even that which arises from the sun’s light does not produce a result here in the context of the subject at hand; for he has indeed accepted the logic of another object of perception in his own work. Thus ends the section on Solar Eclipses in the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*.

469. Since the difference between the two [corrections] is always equal to the sum of the parallax in latitude, that [calculated correction] does not arrive at the true value; how then, O Sovereign, can it be so? This must be reflected upon in many ways by those who follow this path. (72) When there is a difference between the parallaxes of the Moon and the Sun, that parallax indeed lies within the lunar sphere. Therefore, because of the difference in the directions of the lines arising from the observer's eye at that time, it is incorrect there. (73) Just as the parallax in the sum of the latitudes [is calculated] by means of the difference in the initial parallaxes... (74)

Because that [error] is diminished by that [correction], and because there is a difference in the other reference point (*ālambana*), those who are intent on binding themselves with knots—though they do not perceive this—are reduced to a state of ridicule in the assembly of the learned. (745/70) Furthermore, this which I have stated as the reference point is equal by virtue of its similarity; it is established through observation, being joined with the same logic as the "eye-born" [correction], even without the various other corrections for that specific case. (746/71) However, this [correction] which pertains to the circle of vision (*dṛṣṭivṛtta*) is merely an error arising from the confusion of the observer. (747/72)

Greater than that on the curved surface of the earth, and even greater still on our own [local] surface. (77) If the rising [longitude] is different from the longitude of the curved surface of the earth, this [parallax] would occur; otherwise, if there is no difference between the two, the parallax arising from the sun’s rising and setting is itself the maximum parallax on the curved surface of the earth. (78) Having conceived a segment of the earth’s diameter extending upward from the point on the earth’s surface marked by the gnomon, and reaching as far as the distance to the sun, the parallax appropriate for the sun’s rising and setting is derived from that [segment]. (79)

That which was established as the supreme definition is situated at the two sharp points by means of the *ilyāvṛtti* (the ecliptic); from that position, there is always a decrease in the depression (*huglambana*) both before and after. (80) The square root obtained from the product of half the Earth’s diameter and the hypotenuse (*karṇa*) is termed the "perpendicular" (*koṭi*). Half the Earth’s diameter multiplied by the Sun’s distance and divided by the perpendicular results in the "base" (*bhuja*). (81) From the center of the Earth, having subtracted that base halved from the surface of the Earth, [one reaches the point of interest].

Now, the sign of the aspect is that the observer constantly gazes at the one situated on the opposite side; for here, the back-ascendant is the opposite of the day-ascendant, since the so-called "rising of the hand" (hand-ascendant) indeed belongs to the womb of the earth.

(1) Viśvanātha Śarman: "In the case of a difference [of parallax], when the [Moon] is within the [Sun's] orb, the solar parallax produced by the line from the back of the orb is subtracted from the lunar parallax; thus it is rightly stated that the true horizontal parallax does not exist on the lunar sphere. (2) Viśvanātha Śarman: "At the conjunction of observation, at the end of the [Moon's] diameter as seen from the back, the difference between the solar and lunar parallaxes is the parallax on the lunar sphere. This is certain because, according to the thirty-second proposition of the first chapter of the *Rekhāgaṇita*, the parallax is the difference between the individual parallaxes corresponding to the angle of the terrestrial horizon."

(3) Viśvanātha Śarmā: "By that lord of sages" (*tena munīśvareṇa*). (4) Viśvanātha Śarmā: "Such as this, etc., is like a tautology" (*ityādi punaruktavad iti*). (1) Viśvanātha Śarmā: "Situated at some distance from the surface of the earth, standing upon the local horizon (*garbhakṣitija*), the chariot-borne one [the Sun] is five *upavas* [fingers] away," and so forth; this is indeed the first case (*bhaṅga*). This concludes the section on solar eclipses (*sūryagrahaṇādhikāra*) in the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*. 83. Here, however, due to the influence of another latitude (*anyadṛkchada*), there is no observation of sunrise from one's own back [side]. *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, 460–461.

Indeed, the point on the celestial sphere where the image [of a planet] is located at the local horizon is that very same point where the thousand-rayed sun is perceived by the wise. (84) Where there is the rising or setting [of a planet], there is the local horizon; at that point, the parallax (*nāśyapāta*) is produced from the arm of the rising-setting circle. (85) Having abandoned the coarse [parallax] mentioned below, that which arises from the subtle geometry is declared for those two [planets] at rising and setting; likewise, it is stated for the desired time. (86)

In a triangle where the sides are the Earth’s radius (*kṣiti*), the Earth’s extension (*vistṛti*), and the Moon’s distance (*candraka*), the perpendicular from the Moon’s position (*śaśidṛṣṭijamūtra*) upon the Earth’s radius is the *kamba* (base). And here, that which is large in this Earth-segment is as follows: || 87 || Now, the square root of the product of the *lambaka* (perpendicular) and the Moon’s distance shall be the second segment. The difference between these two segments, divided by the Sun’s distance (*ravikarṇa*), is the *lamba* (sagittal) here. || 91 || The sine of three signs (*tribhajyā*) multiplied by the sine of the ascensional difference (*āśikaṇa*) and divided [by the hypotenuse] yields the sum of results known as the parallax arising from vision (*lamvanaṃ dṛguttham*). || 92 ||

This [calculation] is distinct from the first method of derivation, and here it has been prescribed by means of a second method of derivation. (92) Thus, by the transposition of the "ball" (*akanda*) and the "thread-drop" (*kūtrakaṇa*), those two have been made mutually interchangeable; that pair should now be understood by different names. (93) In this manner, the first parallax (*vilambana*) is to be calculated using the moon’s degrees of depression (*natāṃśa*); however, the second parallax is to be calculated here by means of the moon’s degrees of altitude (*unnatāṃśa*). (94) The first [parallax] arises from the sine of the latitude (*analabhava*), while the second is produced from the sine of the moon’s latitude (*candratala*).

In the *Dṛggaṇita* section of the *Antargarbhasūtra*, [the following] is joined: (95) Because of the influence of various signs (*cihna*), the calculation of the visual elevation (*dṛglambana*) must be performed in diverse ways. Therefore, in this context, all of this has been explained by everyone starting from the sign on the surface of the earth attached to the eye. (96) Now, that interval which is difficult for those of subtle intellect to accomplish—(95)—if one takes the square root of the product of the two intervals of the gnomon's shadow, it becomes the second segment. From where [does this come]? The difference between the two segments, divided here by the solar radius (*ravikarṇa*), is the gnomon (*kamba*).

88. The arc of the result obtained by dividing the distance from the moon’s center by the sine of the moon’s latitude is indeed the parallax arising from observation. This is calculated according to the first method; at the desired time, another [value] is derived from the second [method]. 89–90. In the triangle formed by the radius of the Earth, the distance to the Sun, and the solar ray, where the two sides are the Earth and the solar ray, the line drawn from the point on the Earth's surface is the perpendicular (lamba). Here, in the segment of the Earth, that which is greater is the depth (agha), and that which is smaller is the hypotenuse (sadhya). (1) Viśvanātha: "The end of the ten [digits] on the surface."

(2) Commentary: Among those of subtle intellect, that which is *asādhya*—impossible to accomplish—and that which is *sādhya*—fit to be accomplished, yet is *nyūnatara* or very slight—these two things the wise who know the vital points (*marmajña*) do not mention at all; they do not include a discussion of these two in their own treatises. Alas! When it was said that there is no fault on their part, Kamalākara declared himself to be "well" (*svastha*). [End of] the Chapter on Solar Eclipses in the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*. (58 462)

The wise say, "Not at all"; the fault of these [calculations] does not reach the level of the truly intelligent. (97) Thus, I have explained the determination of the field [of observation] through methods of subtle calculation; however, the first [method], established by worldly convention, was made coarse for the sake of ease. (98) For what is the use of that labor here, whose fruit is exceedingly small? Therefore, this coarse [calculation] has been composed for the purpose of practical application. (99)

This *nirukta* (derived value) obtained from the moon and sun is indeed the means for determining the non-preceding hypotenuse (*apūrva-hag-lambana*). For a planet, its position in the subtle ecliptic circle (*sūkṣma-bhacakra*) and the asterism (*bha*) therein—even when conjoined with that planet—are treated in this same way. [100] The large segment (*kukhaṇḍa*), the hypotenuse (*śravaṇa*), and the earth (*mahī*) are present there; among them lies the line of the planet’s shadow (*iṭisūtra*). Here, the hypotenuse (*avalamba*) is to be calculated; of the large segment that exists there, the first-named segment is used. [101] Indeed, that which is the square root of the square of the hypotenuse (*bhakarṇa*) diminished by the square of the equinoctial shadow (*tulyāmbudharma*)—that is the result.

Then, the difference between that apakhaṇḍa and the khaṇḍa, multiplied by the *lambaka* (sine of the latitude) and divided by the hypotenuse (*karṇa*) of the planet, is the result; when divided by the trijyā, it is the *nidhana*. When divided by the *bhakarṇa*, it becomes the *upaka*. Indeed, the *vilambana* (parallax) equal to that arc is the *haja* of the planet according to the first method. Likewise, having assumed the planet as the asterism and the asterism as the planet, one should similarly calculate its velocity.

That which is produced by the calculation according to the stated method for the parallax of vision (*dṛgjya*) shall be the second parallax of vision (*vilambana*). Thus, by the power of their own natures, the parallaxes of vision for those [planets] preceded by Mars are certainly of two kinds; they arise correctly through the first and second methods respectively, as the sequence of the circumference of their respective spheres. And when they are joined with the [longitude] arising from the center, they indeed always become equal; furthermore, this occurs during the solar eclipse.

The first parallax occurs when [the planet] is situated between the Moon and the Sun; due to the difference between those two initial parallaxes at the time of their conjunction, the correction for the observed parallax at the moment of the end of the lunar day (darśavirāma) must be accomplished in this manner. The degrees of the Sun's longitude calculated for that specific time, when added to the first parallax derived from the observed parallax by means of a single calculation, result in the second parallax determined according to the degrees of depression. That which is produced from the first calculation is called the "first parallax" (*ādyalambana*), while the second is not equal to it in any way. 106–108.

In this manner, the second parallax (vilambana) is subtracted. Thus, the degrees of the *darśāntaja* [longitude at the moment of apparent conjunction] should be calculated; by means of these, the true [longitude] is produced, and that becomes the second [parallax]. [From the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, Chapter on Solar Eclipses: The parallax generated by that [second value] would not occur at all at the moment of *daśantī* [the point of true conjunction]; thus, the end of the new moon (*amānta*) would not be equal [to the time of conjunction], and that is what is called the second parallax.

Now, one might ask: "In this case, since there is a difference in the points of parallax (lambana), how can there be a simultaneous observation of the center of the sun and the moon? Listen: at the moment of the conjunction (cūti) of the moon and the sun, both are always situated within the field of vision. Because of their proximity, the difference between them would be the parallax (lambana) occurring along the great circle. Therein, when the sun is situated on the horizon, for the purpose of calculating parallax, the configuration of the diagram is as follows:

On the terrestrial globe (*bhūgola*), the point where the thread—marked with its own limb and extending from the Sun—touches is precisely the central point of that [limb]. Similarly, the face [of the instrument] is fixed obliquely; from that position, at equal intervals on both sides, there are points on the ground separated by the same distance. Because that [thread] has no connection to the points of contact on the terrestrial globe, the Sun appears as if joined at the point of the eastern or western horizon (*udayāsta-kṣitija*). From that limit up to the center of the Earth and reaching the Sun is the "Sun's radius" (*ravikarṇa*), which serves as the hypotenuse (*karṇa*).

The square root of the difference between the squares of those two [sides], extending from that point to the invisible mark on the moon's sphere (the *dṛk-sūtra*)—which is the hypotenuse (*koṭi*)—constitutes a large triangle. Similarly, from the center of the earth to the mark on the moon’s sphere where the line of sight meets it, the moon’s distance (*candrakarṇa*) is the hypotenuse; that same [distance] is the base (*bhuja*). The square root of the difference between the squares of those two is the segment of the arc from that point to the mark on the moon’s sphere where the line of sight meets it, which is the perpendicular (*koṭi*); this constitutes a dissimilar triangle.

This koti is the distance from the previous limit (pūrvakoṭī) to be subtracted; the remainder, when divided by twelve, will be the difference between the spheres of the Moon and the Sun. Here, in the radius-line (racihnasūtra), that difference is the hypotenuse (karṇa). In the lunar sphere, the sine of the depression angle (lambajyā) of the horizontal line from the center is the base (bhuja). The square root of the difference of their squares is the perpendicular (koṭi) along the central line (garbhasūtra). This triangle should be understood as being similar to and contained within the previously described large triangle.

In this case, one should not suspect how the hypotenuse-line of this [triangle] corresponds to the side-line of that [other], and the side-line of this corresponds to the hypotenuse-line of that, for they are suitable for proportionality. Even with such an arrangement of two similar triangles, the actual result is established; indeed, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in the first and subsequent calculations. It should be noted that the Moon is marked by the point where the line of sight from the observer’s eye meets the lunar disc. (112)

Now, the demonstration of the *dṛglambana* (parallax): An observer situated on the surface of the earth who perceives the sun as touching his own location at a certain distance [from the zenith] must necessarily assume that the line of sight from his position extends to the point on the celestial sphere directly opposite his location. For this very reason, by virtue of the point of contact between the line of sight and the earth's surface, the observer sees the sun as if it were actually touching that point on the celestial sphere directly opposite him, and not at some other distance.

Now, from the point on the Earth's surface directly beneath the observer's zenith, up to the point where the rising and setting horizon meets the celestial sphere, there is a curved path that touches the terrestrial globe; because it follows the line of sight, the Sun appears as if it has set at that location on the Earth's surface touched by the visual ray, due to the convergence of the line of sight. From the point on the Earth's surface, the circle drawn at a constant distance all around that limit is the horizon of rising and setting (*udayāsta-kṣitija*).

For the sake of marking the celestial equator (svaṅgacihna), by virtue of its connection with the point where the local horizon (tatkṣitija) touches the sphere of the sun (ravivṛtta), the solar sphere is to be understood as being entirely surrounded by the rising and setting horizons. However, that portion of the sphere above [the horizon] is visible to humans, while that situated below it is invisible. Now, wherever one may be situated, when a thread is applied to touch the surface of the earth, those two points where it touches are known as the "local zenith" (garbhadṛk). Those very same points, where the thread touches the lunar sphere, are designated as the "zenith-marks" (garbhadṛksūtracihna).

The sun’s distance (ravikarṇa) multiplied by half the earth’s diameter (bhūvyāsardha) is the base (bhuja). Then, from the subsequent [proportion], let *ka* be the form of the infinite interval; this is the sine of the depression (lambanajyā) in yojanas and so forth. Again, there is a proportion: if the moon’s distance (candrakarṇa) corresponds to the radius (trijyā), then what corresponds to this [base]? This is the sine of the depression (lambanajyā). The arc of this [sine] will be the depression as perceived (dṛglambana) when the sun is situated on the eastern or western horizon. Now, for the justification of the second method: when the sun is situated on its own eastern or western horizon, that depression of the sun is to be assumed as the first quantity (*ādyasaṃśa*).

Then, extending downward from that point everywhere with a width equal to half the diameter of the earth, there is a second line drawn from the center of the earth to the edge of the celestial sphere (*ahaṃgola*). And a third [line] extends from the center of the earth to the edge of the terrestrial globe (*īpagola*). There, in the solar sphere (*arkagola*), the distance between the second and third lines is the arc of the sun's terrestrial obscuration (*kucchanna*) as established in the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, in the chapter on solar eclipses.

That same interval of 467 *kalās* exists even between the two lunar spheres; therefore, when subtracted from the second sūtra-interval—which is the portion of the moon's sphere situated within the moon's body—it results in the first-third sūtra-interval. It is thus established that the *dṛglambana* (visual displacement) is the distance along the central axis (*garbhasūtra*) at that point, as previously stated. By this very method, the underlying principle (*vāsanā*) for obtaining it in the case of an equal circle (*tulyavṛtta*) should be understood by the wise.

In this context, since there are many points marked by circles (*dṛk*) on the surface of the earth in the order of the twelve *urdhvaka*s (elevations), the establishment of the locations of the eastern and western horizons as described above is possible everywhere according to the observation of those circles; for it is seen that, apart from the difference in the hypotenuse (*karṇa*), the types of geometric figures (*kṣetra-prakāra*) are identical everywhere.

Therefore, when the observer is situated on the terrestrial horizon (kṣitija) at a point where the nadir is depressed by the amount of the earth’s radius, the method for calculating parallax (*lambana*) remains the same as that used for the rising and setting points; however, due to the depression caused by the respective radii of the observer's location, that [parallax] would otherwise be different. Now, according to the first method, the rationale for parallax on the horizon-equal circle (*dṛktulyavṛtta*) is as follows: from the center of the Earth to the observer's own zenith is the base (*bhuja*), equal to the measure of the observer's own radius; from the Earth's center to the Sun is the hypotenuse (*karṇa*); and the square root of the difference between their squares, divided by the Sun's distance, is the perpendicular side (*koṭi*). This constitutes the large triangle.

If this small, dissimilar area lies within that [larger circle], then the distance from the center of the earth to the point where the line of sight reaches the lunar sphere is the hypotenuse, measured by the *drakarṇa* (the distance to the moon). That same [distance] is the base (*bhuja*). The square root of the difference between the squares of those two is the perpendicular (*koṭi*), extending from the point *ra* on the horizon to the point where the line of sight reaches the lunar sphere. This perpendicular is to be subtracted from the previous perpendicular; the remainder will be the distance between the centers of the lunar and solar spheres at the point *ra*. Since the base is infinite, it is obtained as such. Thus, there is a proportion (*anupāta*).

The sun’s distance (ravikarṇa) being multiplied by its own sine (svahṛc-cid-dha) and divided by the sine (ka) obtained immediately thereafter, the resulting quotient is the sine of the parallax in latitude (lambanajyā). This [sine] multiplied by the radius (trijyā) and divided by the moon’s distance (candrakarṇa) shall be the sine [of the parallax]. Thus, the parallax in longitude (dūglambana) occurs on the epicycle of the anomaly (dūlyavṛtta). Now, the determination of the parallax for the sun situated anywhere is stated by means of a single calculation.

The two arms should be assumed as having a measure equal to the increase of the earth-center’s own hypotenuse; the sun’s face is the base, and the perpendicular therein should be calculated for the two segments. Likewise, from the center of the earth, a line reaching the mark on the visual ray situated on the lunar sphere should be made, measuring the moon’s hypotenuse.

In this context, the large segment (*bṛhat-khaṇḍa*) is the interval from the point of true conjunction (*samyak-pāta*) up to the limit of the Sun; the square root of the difference between the squares of the *lambacandra* (the Moon's projection) and the *karṇa* (the hypotenuse) is the interval from the *layapāta* up to the limit of the *drus-traciḍa* (the point of intersection) on the auspicious sphere (*bhadra-gola*). The distance between these two points would be the distance between the spheres of the Sun and the Moon at that moment. From that, the calculation of the parallax (*lamvana*) is established as follows:

The *lambajyā* (sine of the colatitude) is equal to the radius (*ka*) multiplied by the *lamba* (the sine of the latitude), which has been derived from the formula for the difference; this *lambajyā* is then multiplied by the radius of the celestial sphere (*trijyā*) and divided by the moon’s distance (*candrakarṇa*), resulting in the *labhyajyā*. The square of this is established as the parallax in longitude (*duglambana*). Now, if it is asked: "Previously, the parallax was stated to exist at the eastern and western horizons; why is it greater on the surface of the earth? Why is it even greater on the local horizon (*svahkulyavṛtta*)? And why does it reach its maximum there, only to decrease until it vanishes at the zenith? Listen. [The text continues with the mathematical derivation of the parallax. ...Thus, the parallax is zero at the zenith, and it increases toward the horizon. This is because the parallax is proportional to the distance between the observer and the center of the earth, and that distance is greatest at the horizon. Therefore, the parallax reaches its maximum value at the local horizon and diminishes accordingly until it becomes non-existent at the zenith. Thus, the calculation is consistent. (Note: The provided text contains technical astronomical terminology related to the calculation of lunar parallax in Indian Siddhānta literature.)

One circle should be drawn with a radius equal to half the Earth's diameter from the center of the Earth; likewise, a second circle should be drawn from the Earth's center with a radius equal to the distance to its own horizon-mark. From that [second] center, a third circle should be drawn with the radius of the Moon, and a fourth circle with the radius of the Sun; these are to be designated as their respective "ocular spheres" (*dṛṅmaṇḍala*). In all cases, one should mentally mark a north-south and vertical line starting from the Earth's center. Among these, the north-south line is the "terrestrial equator line" (*kṣitijasūtra*) passing through the Earth's interior.

On the meridian line (*ūrvarekhā*), at the intersection with the first circle, is the surface of the earth (*bhūpṛṣṭha*); at the intersection with the second circle, however, is the mark of one's own body (*svaṅgacihna*). From these two points, lines should be drawn parallel to the east-west line (*pūrvāpararekhā*) at equal intervals everywhere; this is the intersection of the meridian line and the horizontal circle (*kṣitija-vṛtta-sūtra*). There, from the mark of the earth on the meridian line, a thread is raised up to the mark of one's own head, and from there, a thread extending as far as the sun is the "thread of one's own face" (*svadvaktra*).

The line passing through the point where the thread, extended from the zenith in the direction of the observer's back, touches the lunar sphere is known as the *udayāsta-lambana-sūtra* (the thread of the rising-setting parallax). This is because, on the lunar sphere, one observes that this thread is separated from the central thread (*garbha-sūtra*) by the amount of that parallax. When the Sun is situated on the horizon of rising or setting, the *udayāsta-lambana-sūtra* itself becomes the *nata-sūtra* (the thread of altitude). On the lunar sphere, the distance from the center up to that limit would constitute the parallax (*lambana*).

Then, as the Sun moves away from the zenith, the parallax at the points of rising and setting relative to its own heart (the observer's position) would be excluded from both inside and outside. In the lunar sphere, the parallax at the points of rising and setting—measured up to the line connecting the center of the sphere to the points of rising and setting—is indeed [the same], but it becomes greater up to the limit of the observer's own visual ray; thus, an increase in parallax is observed up to the horizon of the Earth's surface.

Then, as the sun moves from the horizon (dūlyavṛtta), just as it declines, so too its own line of sight (svadṛksūtra) would lie outside even the line of sight that establishes the vertical support upon the surface of the earth; thus there is an increase [in the distance]. This is as follows: when the sun is situated on the terrestrial horizon (bhūpṛṣṭhakṣitija), one should draw lines from the points where the center of the earth and one's own eye meet the vertical line up to the sun. Among these, the line from the surface of the earth is the line of support; with respect to that limit, [the calculation is made] on the celestial sphere (gola).

The locus of the rising and setting [of the sun] from the terrestrial sun (garbhasūrya) is as stated in the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, in the chapter on solar eclipses (sūryagrahaṇādhikāra). It is indeed so. However, up to the limit of one's own line of sight (svadṛksūtra), it would be greater than that.
