A single line drawn from the center of the earth toward the sun, extending upward from the terrestrial horizon (bhūpṛṣṭhabhittija) to the limit of the horizon-circle (dṛgvalayavṛtta), and brought to touch the circumference of the earth at its own surface-direction, would be the line of the rising and setting locus. Furthermore, a line from the center of the earth touching a point on that [line] should be made to meet the horizon-circle.

The line situated on the back of the celestial sphere from the point of the local meridian (tallagna) up to the nadir is the line for calculating parallax (*lambana*). On the lunar sphere, the distance from the central line (*garbhasūtra*) to that point is precisely the parallax at the terrestrial surface. However, one’s own face located there is further extended beyond it; thus, the parallax would be even greater than calculated. In this way, the parallax when the Sun is situated on the horizon coincident with the observer's latitude (*dṛktulyavṛtta*) would be the maximum.

Then, as the Sun rises higher and higher, the single thread [drawn from the observer] touches the ecliptic; until that point, for one situated on the ecliptic, there is indeed parallax (lambana) due to the support of the Sun. However, since the local meridian (svadṛktra) lies lower and lower than that thread, a decrease in that parallax is observed.

Thus, when the Sun’s thread (sūtra) passes through the center of the terrestrial meridian at Laṅkā, the parallax there is difficult to perceive; otherwise, it is clearly small. Likewise, where the face [of the observer] lies on the very line that establishes the horizon and the zenith of the local meridian, the parallax there would be equal to the parallax of the zenith. Similarly, when the Sun is at the eastern or western horizon, since its own visual thread takes the form of the rising-setting parallax line, the parallax at rising and setting occurs precisely there.

From that vertical line of the zenith-south direction, as one moves progressively downward along the observer’s own visual line (*svadṛksūtra*), there is an increase [in parallax]. Thus, when the observer’s visual line coincides with the center of the Earth, there is an absence of parallax; because of the difference [from that point], its presence is acknowledged. In this way, when the Sun is situated at a certain place on the terrestrial horizon due to some force, for that observer, there exists a parallax equal to the zenith-parallax caused by that very force; there is no other parallax apart from the influence of that force.

In that regard, the ancient authorities such as Bhāskara and others maintain that the maximum parallax occurs when the line of sight has been brought to the limit of the moon’s sphere within the womb of the earth by piercing through the back of the *balāḍhya* and the back of the *viḍaṅka*; this is because, from the line of the rising-setting-parallax at the equator, the sun situated on the terrestrial surface at the limit of the *viśa-garbha* (the interior of the earth) lies below that line of sight, resulting in a smaller parallax. Thus say the ancients.

Because the object is situated on a circle parallel to one's own horizon, its parallax is exceedingly small; thus, its maximum value cannot be established. Furthermore, for an observer emerging from the cut at the Earth's surface, the line of sight cannot be established as a straight line [from the center]. Thus, for one whose fixed line of sight is indeed attached to the Earth's surface, the horizon located on the Earth's surface is the limit of rising and setting; and since that [horizon] is a circle parallel to one's own horizon, the parallax obtained at the points of rising and setting would be the maximum there.

When the observer's zenith is elevated above the surface of the earth, then by virtue of that elevation, at a point raised above the local horizon, there occurs a maximum *layana* (obliquity) equal to the observer's latitude and corresponding to the celestial equator; this is the true zenith distance. However, all calculations everywhere are performed based on the zenith as if it were coincident with the terrestrial surface, because this approximation is sufficiently close for practical purposes at locations near the Earth's surface, and because calculating it by other methods involves excessive labor.

Thus, this investigation into latitudinal parallax (*vāsanā*) can be understood here only by one who is highly proficient, and not by anyone else; therefore, enough with further elaboration. This second method for the parallax-circle is established through reasoning; likewise, the first method for the parallax-circle is also for the sake of the wise alone. For it is observed here that the difference between the true and the apparent parallax occurs when the Sun is on the ecliptic; however, for those situated on their own orbits, that difference would be the true parallax. (113)

Since the revolution of a celestial body occurs precisely within its orbital circle (*kakṣāmaṇḍala*), the observation (*vedha*) is certainly established according to that very circle. (114) In this context, that which is situated on the visible horizon (*dṛgga*) is to be understood as "visible" (*darśanayogya*); therefore, for the sake of establishing the time [of observation], the interval between that point and the point situated on the revolution circle (*bhramaṇḍala*)—which lies along the line of the celestial pole (*kadamba*)—is well known. (115)

(1) Viśvanātha: The clarity of the parallax (*lambana*) itself is to be observed directly; however, here in the *Bhaṭṭotpala*, the clarity of the statement regarding the parallax has been appropriately set forth. [Siddhāntatattvaviveka, Sūryagrahaṇādhikāra, verse 470]. 471. "Since that parallax which is produced by us in our own Sanskrit [treatise] is clear at the time of mean conjunction (*daśantakāla*), the calculation of the true, manifest parallax (*saṃsphuṭa-vilambana*) is now stated therein. (Verse 116). First, the previously mentioned calculation of the manifest parallax (*pūrvokta-sphuṭa-lambana*).

(1) The sine of the difference between the tri-bhonalagna and the sun, multiplied by four and divided by the radius, is [the result]. The quotient obtained here, multiplied by the natural sine of the latitude and divided by the radius, gives the parallax in ghatis and so forth. Alternatively: "The square root of the sum or difference of the squares of the sines of the zenith-distance of the tri-bhonalagna and the sun, multiplied by four and divided by three, shall be the parallax in nāḍīs. "How is the arm in minutes of arc derived from the minutes of depression? How are the minutes of parallax for those two [obtained]?"

The square root of the difference between the other term and the square of the *koṭi* is the *sphuṭalambana* in minutes of arc. (119) Now, I shall state here in a subtle manner, derived from the *muvimalagola* sphere, that which constitutes the form of the *koṭi*: the product of the maximum sine (*paramaguṇa*) multiplied by the sine of the ascensional difference (*akṣepaka*), divided by the sun’s *dṛgjyā* (sine of altitude), results here in the *parā* value; from that and the resulting quotient, the square root of their difference is the *koṭi*, and the square root of the sum of their squares is the *maurvī* (sine) here. (120)

(1) These are the verses marked with "1" as stated in the Sūryagrahaṇādhikāra of the *Graha-gaṇita* by the venerable Bhāskarācārya, [composed] in the year 1442 (Vi0 Śa 7). (2) Vi0 Śa 70—The magnitude of the angle resulting from the intersection of the horizon-circle (*dṛgvṛtta*) and the celestial equator (*krāntivṛtta*) is the maximum (*para*). 9. The true sine of parallax (*lambanajyā*) is divided by the maximum [sine]; its arc here shall be the true parallax. 12. Thus is the calculation of the depression (*nati*); the sine of horizontal parallax divided by the sine of three signs (the radius).

Once this has been obtained, there shall be a calculation for those two, either designated as *nati* (deflection) or otherwise. [Verse 122] The square root of the product of the sines of the altitude (*dṛgjyā*) and the co-latitude (*avagava*) of the Sun and the non-trigonal ascendant (*dvibhonalagna*) shall be the *nati*. Alternatively, it is the sine of the difference between the non-trigonal ascendant and its complement (*aṅga*), multiplied by the *nati* and the velocity of observation (*dṛggati*). [Verse 123] Or, the sine of the difference between the non-trigonal ascendant and the Sun, divided by the radius (*tribhajyā*), is the *dṛtinī*. Then that *dṛtinī*, multiplied by the sine of the non-trigonal ascendant and divided by the sine of the altitude of the Sun, shall be the *jīva*; that is the true sine of the difference between the non-trigonal ascendant and the Sun. [Verse 124]

The product of the firm *vanajyā* divided by the sine of the Sun's altitude (*dineśadṛṣṭika*) yields the value here; that is the motion of the aspect (*dṛggati*). When divided by three and its arc taken, it is called the true parallax (*sphuṭasaṃbala*). The square root of the difference between the squares of the parallax (*dṛglambanā*) and the *avanatijyā* (zenith distance) is its [true] value; its arc is the true parallax here, and thus the calculation of the zenith distance (*nati*) should be performed. The parallax in longitude (*dṛkṣepaka*) divided by the sine of the Sun's altitude (*ravidṛgjyā*) shall be the parallax in latitude (*dṛglambanajyā*), and the zenith distance (*avanatijyā*) shall be as follows.

472. In the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, this is the section on solar eclipses. 473. The visible parallax in latitude (*dṛśeṣakanī*) is divided by the corrected horizontal parallax (*sphuṭalaghanacyā*), or it is known by the name "parallax in altitude" (*dṛṅnati*). 127–128. And here, that which is the difference between the observed parallax in latitude and the parallax in altitude—whether it be the arc of the sine of the parallax in altitude, or its chord—the arc of that [sine] is the parallax in altitude (*nati*). This should always be applied as directed toward the Moon. 128. When the two points arising from the nonagesimal (*vitribhalagna*) are situated on the surface of the spheres occupied by the Sun and the Moon respectively...

The latitude of your moon and likewise that of the sun arising from the parallax of the observer’s position [is found] by means of the two ears (the two latitudes) of those two; others also state the deflection (*nati*) of the second parallax of the observer’s position. Whatever has been done here by me in this *Sphuṭādhikāra* may it be for the betterment of the world. Having performed the calculation of the parallax of the observer’s position through a rough method of proportion, the ancient masters have stated the determination of the clear parallax using precisely the well-known reasoning.

Or rather, having clearly established here that which is merely a mockery of observation, they have calculated the true parallax at the desired time by means of a gross approximation. (132) Thus, in accordance with the previous [method], the sine of the true parallax and its arc—the true parallax—have been stated. Now, the true [parallax] itself is being described. (133) As for those who say that the parallax of the first rising point is increased by the sine of the angle [formed by] the [ecliptic] pole minus three signs (90°): [they are mistaken].

The calculation of parallax mentioned by Śaka is indeed useless, for the arc [of parallax] exists within the sphere of the stars (bhacakre). (124) The sine of the deflection known as *sphuṭālambana* (apparent parallax), which is directed toward the eastern horizon, is indeed the form of the cosine; however, that [sine] is not the cosine on the circle arising from the product of the cosine in the stellar sphere (*bhamaṇḍala*)—so it has been stated by the wise. (131) Furthermore, the clear parallax calculated by those who subtracted one degree from the sphere of the stars is not correct; for the difference between the Moon and the Sun in that stellar sphere is vast, and therefore the parallax-sine derived from that is not accurate. (136)

The latitude of the moon is multiplied by the sine of the maximum parallax and divided by the radius; the arc of this result is the true parallax here. This is my view of the true parallax, whereas otherwise it would be the mere mouth-tradition of the cowherd-paṇḍitas. (137) Indeed, when the sum [of the latitudes] is multiplied by the radius and divided by the sine of the maximum parallax, the result is the sine of the arc of the zenith-distance. When ninety degrees are subtracted from that arc in the zodiac, the difference between the sun and the moon will be the true parallax. (118)

Thus, the effect is the clear kiss; in that regard, for the sun and moon, when divided by the difference [of their latitudes], it shall consist of *ghaṭikās*. But know this repeatedly here: [the calculation] according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is as follows. (139) When the ecliptic appears circular, then those two—the apparent [longitude] and the latitude—are equal; in that case, there is an absence of declination (*nati*). When the sun is at the third point of the sign (*tribhona-lagna*), however, there is indeed declination. (149)

By means of the visual parallax (*dṛglambana*) alone, the [parallax] is equal on the circle passing through the observer’s eye and the *kadamba* (the zenith), due to the force of the ecliptic; and there, on the circle passing through the *kadamba* situated at the horizon mark, it is equal by virtue of their non-difference. A more distinct parallax is observed when there is a difference between those two; indeed, in the absence of that difference, there is no parallax at all. (140) That [parallax] would certainly be zero when [the Sun] is equal to the tri-une ascendant (*trirāśilagna*), provided there is no deviation toward the north or south from the meridian. That region of the central circle lying between the ascendant and the setting point is indeed what is called the "mid-heaven" (*madhyalagna*) in the system of the Sun (*Ārkatantre*). (141)

Indeed, that parallax which is accepted by taking the sine of the zenith distance is not correct. Those who do not understand this through their mental conditioning (vāsanā) possess a useless obsession with the scriptures. (142) [Objection: But then, how is it stated in the *Sūryasiddhānta* by the Sun [the author] that the "clearness" (*sphuṭatā*) of the latitudes of the mid-heaven (*madhya*) and the prime vertical (*unnata*) is further [discussed]? (143) If it is argued that the term "mid-heaven" (*madhyāṅga*) is not used at all in the calculation of parallax—[referring rather to] the statement beginning with "the sine of the base and the perpendicular of the depressed degrees" (*natāṃśabāhukoṭijye*) and so forth—[then our position holds]. (144)

Thus they say: in that context where the sword [of calculation] is perfected, those which are the zenith and nadir are to be known as the clear [values] arising from the tri-une ascendant (vitribhalagna). Therefore, the meaning of the statement regarding the Sun—that which concerns the sight-lines and the motion of the aspect—is clearly stated as the hypotenuse and the perpendicular arising from the tri-une aspect. Thus, the degrees of the zenith and nadir at the location of the tri-une Sun are clearly the motion of the aspect of the Sun; this is indeed certain. Therefore, at night, the sky is useless; rather, that [sky] is the tri-une point.

For the purpose of establishing the means of perceiving the application of the middle [reasoning] and logic... (148) Vi0 Śa7: "Because of this, from this"—[it follows that] non-existence itself is the clear objective support (*ālambana*) for perception, provided it is distinct from what is perceived as equal; however, that would be the ultimate. (190) That state of non-attainment (*apada*) is seen to be of many kinds due to the distinction between what is heard and what is perceived. Furthermore, because of the difference from the two previously mentioned [cases] regarding trees and so forth, there can be no other "otherness" (*paratva*) elsewhere. (151) That which was accepted by the ancient ones in the *Ga* and *Bakuṇe* [texts] is suitable for conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), even if it possesses only a slight interval.

Due to the absence of any distinction between those two elsewhere, that which arises in the form of a clear or delayed [perception]—therein, for the most part, there would be a dissolution of the visual [cognition] arising from the eye, because [the object] exists in front of the circular arrangement of the *kadamba* flowers; likewise, because the dense [object] is situated behind, it is seen by the eye as being at the back, and furthermore, O protector of the earth, [this occurs] at the terrestrial horizon behind the celestial sphere; therefore, the sine of the latitude (*jyapāla*) is the sine of the amplitude (*jyāila*).

Now, elsewhere than this, [it is said]: "O Jyāila, this is indeed superior; let the degrees of the back (pṛṣṭhīyanta) be calculated from the degrees of the center (garbha). There, the degrees of the center itself should be understood as being directed eastward by the ancients. [End of] Chapter on Solar Eclipses in the Siddhāntatattvaviveka, verse 476. [Verse 477: Even according to the *dṛg-gomūtra* (the visual-cow’s-urine line), it is established here by virtue of the *garbha-sūtra* (the central line) that the statement of the wise is thus: "When the celestial sphere follows the *dṛg-gomūtra*, whatever interval exists between those two in the circle of the sky (*bhacakra*)... [Verse 154].

That [parallax] exists in those two lines [of sight] just as a bird [appears displaced] on the celestial sphere according to its position; therefore, in this case, the parallax should be clearly calculated between the line of sight and the ecliptic. (155) At the moment of new moon, the Sun is situated on the line of sight and the Moon is located on its own orbit; however, when positioned on the central axis, it is displaced from the line of sight. (156) The Moon is ahead of the Sun in front, while being delayed behind at the rear; when the Moon is in front, the conjunction is past, and when it is behind, it is yet to come. (157)

Therefore, when the Sun is equal to the tribhonalagna (the nonagesimal point), there is no parallax; otherwise, parallax exists. When the Sun is less than that [tribhonalagna], it is additive, and when greater, it is subtractive; by this sequence, the time of the true aspect (sphuṭadaśākāla) is obtained. (158) This very thing is well known here by the name *citra* (mark/spot), for you two [the Sun and Moon] become united at the point on the line of sight (*dṛksūtra*) where the lunar mark (*candracitra*) would be located. (162) Hence, a line drawn from the center of the Earth touching the point on the line of sight becomes the "central line" (*garbhasūtra*), which passes through the center of the Earth and the center of the Sun.

163–166. Here, the distance between the two centers of the orbs on the visual sphere (dṛgvṛtta) is indeed the same as the distance between the two centers of the orbs from the center of the Earth. Because of this difference in the positions of the visual spheres, there occurs for those two the time of conjunction. In that case, the difference between the Moon and the Sun, which arises from the center of the Earth, is observed through the medium of time in the form of *ghaṭī*s for the sake of establishing the conjunction. For that [difference] is suitable there, situated between the center of the Earth and the sky. Just so has *lambana* (parallax) been declared by the wise for the purpose of establishing the conjunction.

Therefore, the parallax arising from the conjunction of the Sun and Moon is known to be produced by reasoning (yukti). (167) This [parallax] is stated to occur when there is a coincidence of the ecliptic and the horizon; however, even when there is a difference between them, the determination of the Sun and the planet is achieved here, and it is explained accordingly. (168) The horizontal parallax (*dṛglambana*) which exists for the Sun and Moon at their respective points of contact with the Earth’s center—that very parallax must undoubtedly be investigated for the purpose of the three-dimensional observation of those two points of contact. (169) In the case of the first [parallax], there would be a discrepancy at the time of observation; whereas in the case of the second, there is agreement.

Therefore, that which was uttered is the resonance of the *Dṛggarbha-sūtra*. (160) But those who have gone to the Sun in the Sūtra marked by the signs of the evil views of the Kuga-bhadra, and those who are in the eighth month of the womb within the lunar sphere (*candragola*) of those two; (161) Where there is no fault in the calculation of the *bha*, *vṛtta*, *daṇḍa*, *laya*, and *āra*, there the Lord of Rays (*sūrya*) and the Lord of the Night (*candra*), situated on a single line of observation (*dṛgjai-ka-sūtra*), would have a conjunction produced from the centers of their orbs. (162) In all cases where there is a difference between those two [planets], and where the other directions and the descriptions are equal, [the conjunction occurs]. (163)

In that case, there is conjunction when [the Moon] is on the *kadamba*-circle (the vertical circle passing through the zenith and nadir) as seen along the line of sight; otherwise, it would be different. When the Moon situated in the stellar sphere (*bhacakra*) lies on the same line of sight from the observer, or from that point, there is no difference; this is stated in the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka* in the chapter on solar eclipses. Furthermore, that very time is declared to be the moment of conjunction when the Moon’s disc is positioned on the *kadamba*-circle at the tip of the arrow (*śara*).

In the same way, for the sake of establishing the true [longitude], the moon is at the tip of the arrow on the *dṛktra* (the line of sight). The difference between that moon and the point situated on the arc of the *dṛksūtra* (the visual axis) is called the *nati* (latitude). Therefore, the true arrow of the moon, corrected by the *nati*, is used for the determination of the solar eclipse. Due to its absence, the sun and moon discs are located where they are; by means of the depressed portions situated there, the method for the *lagna* (ascendant) and the *dṛkkarma* (parallax correction) is stated.

If that parallax calculated for the moon and sun were clearly [based on] the true parallax, there would indeed be no difference between them. Likewise, if the parallax at the tip of the arrow (the shadow) of the lunar disc were the same as the parallax stated by Dadhi, then the distance between the sun and moon would not be so; how then could the calculation of their conjunction be made? However, the parallax performed here from the point of the eye-line to the moon is what should be used; thus, the conjunction of the moon and sun is determined by the parallax as perceived by the observer.

The [angular] distances are indeed determined from the north-south direction. However, it has been stated that the sum of the diameters of the orbs at the centers of their respective spheres constitutes three-fourths of a degree. (174) The ecliptic lies east-west, while the celestial equator is situated north-south. This is the state of the two orbs of the Sun and Moon when they are positioned on those respective circles. (175) The true distance between the two orbs is measured along the line of their mutual separation. At the moment of conjunction, there is always an absence of east-west separation. (176) Having understood this, one should observe the Moon’s orb with the eye; thus, the calculation is established.

Just as the lunar disc might appear within the enclosure of a *kadamba* tree, so too, when the Moon’s mark is situated within the lunar orb, the time at which the longitudinal difference between the Sun and the Moon vanishes is recorded by the learned. (177–178) When there is a separation between the two luminaries of the lunar orb, the mark of the Moon’s shadow at that time should be calculated; and the first [longitude] derived from that should always be equal to the [true longitude] corrected for parallax. (182)

Therefore, since the sun is established by its own nature, the doubt regarding its position is indeed dispelled; for it is that very [sun] which, situated at the point of the mark on the meridian line, makes the lunar disc clearly manifest. (183) Now, at the time of the end of the eclipse, there is no difference between the two due to their lack of conjunction; therefore, when the sun and moon have ceased [their motion], whatever clear parallax exists between them, the difference there is exactly equal to that. (184)

The convention (*samaya*) which consists of the *ghaṭī* (forty-eight minutes) should be understood as being both prior to and after that [moment]. In the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, in the chapter on solar eclipses: If their sum is negative, it is a debt; if positive, it is a credit. Such is the state of affairs in the *Viḍambana*. The result of the ten-fold correction, well-adjusted by the true obscuration (*vilambana*) at that specific time, is certainly that very time itself; it is designated as the "conjunction" (*yoga*), the time of the actual observation.

First, however, the calculation of the conjunction of the moon and the planet at that time, which is to be accomplished by oneself, must be performed from the previously determined *darśānta* (end of the lunar month) and the previously established *alambana* (parallax correction). From that established *alambana*, the conjunction should be calculated again, and so on repeatedly, until the two *vilamghanas* (interpolations) are equal; the time of the conjunction should then be determined by the wise. That first interpolation which arose during the conjunction is indeed the one to be considered for further analysis.

However, at that time, there is no moon apart from the sun due to parallax; if there were, then the point of contact arising from observation would coincide with the conjunction of the moon and the sun. Therefore, because the two parallaxes are equal, the wise have declared that their conjunction is established. Having abandoned the clear [calculation] for the sake of seeing the actual reality, whatever error exists here regarding the previously stated true distance, the resulting parallax is distinct from the parallax arising at the time of setting.

The time of the end of that [period] refined by that [correction] is also clearly not distinct from it here; for its establishment occurs only through a delay produced at that [specific] time. (192) Thus, all delays arising from various times are always distinct from one another. Because their difference is very slight, the proximity of the subsequent one indeed prevails there. (193) No equality between them has ever been observed here, even by those of noble intellect and great insight.

Because the equality of all minute parts is not established by those who lack the perception of subtle characteristics, [the calculation] is not truly accomplished. (194) Nevertheless, for the sake of establishing worldly convention, that which was formulated by the ancients through their limited vision has been correctly executed; otherwise, the very means of proving the conjunction would be utterly destroyed. (195) Thus, in accordance with the tradition of the ancients, this has been stated here for the purpose of calculating conjunction. However, one who understands the true nature of the celestial sphere (*golajñāna*) must reach a definitive conclusion based on reality. (196) [The distance between the true Moon and the planet, as corrected for parallax, shall be...]

That very conjunction-time (*yutikāla*) here is indeed that which is equal to the sum of the time of its own meridian-transit (*svayalambana*) and the [calculated] conjunction-time; this is due to the joy [of the result] from the maximum position of the two times established at the beginning. (197–198) [This concludes] the section on Solar Eclipse (*sūryagrahaṇādhikāra*) within the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*. (482) Even by means of the established equality of the latitudes (*lambana*), the determination of the eclipse occurs through their influence. (483)

The *vṛtta* (circle) is indeed the circle of declination (*krāntivṛtta*). Likewise, with reference to the center of the *kadamba*, it is possible to construct a circle touching the point of the *dūṣa* mark; for in that case, deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is joined [with the calculation], since—199—the circle of the sine of the latitude of the *natikoṭi* is likewise named "similar to declination" (*krāntisadṛśasaṃjña*), and similarly the circle situated at the zenith (*khamadhyasthugvṛtta*). This arises from the distinction between the spheres of the eclipsing body (*chādaka*) and the eclipsed body (*chādyagola*). It is known as the circle of the shadow of the non-oblique ascendant (*vijibhalagnaśaṅku-vṛtta*).

Thus, with the intention of [the point] being at the center of the *kadamba*, the circle of the sine of the maximum limit (*parakoṭyaṃśajyāvṛtta*) should be constructed; here, the established position is that the *kadamba* is indeed situated close to the center of the sky (*khamadhya*). Without the non-difference [of these points], the determination of the latitude (*nati*) and parallax (*lambana*) would not occur. In that regard, on the ecliptic (*krāntivṛtta*), the distance between the two circles passing through the center is the true parallax (*sphuṭalambana*), due to their being situated together at one place within the central point.

Even when the Earth is spherical, at the time of opposition, the *nati* (deflection) is equal to the difference between the ecliptic and a circle parallel to it; its sine is the *bhuja* (base), and the *dṛglambana-jyā* (parallax sine) is the *karṇa* (hypotenuse). The square root of the difference of their squares is the sine of the interval between the center of the Earth and the point on the circle parallel to the ecliptic where the planet is situated. That [sine], converted to that same circle, exists as the *koṭi* (perpendicular side) in the form of the true parallax. It is not the case that there is no parallax during a lunar eclipse. (201)

The distance between the center of the earth and the ecliptic, measured as the sine of the interval between the two circles, constitutes the field of parallax (*lamvana-kṣetra*). When the Sun is situated within its own orbit, this field is contained within a similar triangle. On the celestial sphere centered at the earth's core, that which is clearly the parallax is accepted as such; the sine of the interval between the celestial equator and the ecliptic, as obstructed by the zodiacal circle, is the base of the triangle of observation (*dṛkkṣepa-bhuja*).

In the *iṅgaṇḍala*, between the center of the sky and the central point of the circle, that which is measured by the *dūjyā* (versed sine) of the sun is the hypotenuse (*karṇa*). You take the square root of the difference between those two as the gnomon (*śaṅku*); we do not know what has been done out of the delusion of your own intellect. (202) The *dṛti* (sine) is the perpendicular (*koṭi*) between the center of the sky and the central point of the circle. From this, the hypotenuse is greater than the arm (*bhuja*), and the shadow is the *upanati*. For many who are ignorant of the sphere (*gola*), there is an error in establishing the *talajyā* and *naḍajyā*. How then could the small arm and small perpendicular be established?

Therefore, I shall explain that inclination (*vāsanā*) of the sphere which lies within the heart of the matter. The difference between the two lines passing through the center of the sun’s motion on the lunar sphere is the *lambana* (parallax). Thus, from the lunar sphere, this small triangle is contained within a larger similar triangle; its nature is as follows. On the ecliptic (*umaṇḍala*), the distance between the point where the line through the center meets it and the point of the [sun's] distance is known as the *dūglambana* (distance-parallax); this much is well-established.

From the point of intersection of the ecliptic and the equator, the intermediate arc between those two [circles] on the central circle is likewise [measured]. The method for calculating the true obliquity and declination from that is as follows: On the lunar sphere (candragola), whatever is the circle of the horizon (kāśāvṛtta) is the obliquity; the intermediate arc between that circle and another circle situated at a third of the quadrant (tribhāntarita) obtained by proportion is called the "maximum" (parā), which is the maximum circle (paravṛtta). That very circle should be taken as the ecliptic (krāntivṛtta). Then, the horizon (kadasyā) should also be assumed upon that plane.

In that context, what is the "gata" (the traversed part)? It is precisely the sine of the interval between the ecliptic and the circle of the maximum declination at the point of the *garbhacihna* (central mark). Having drawn an east-west circle through the two points of intersection (*damya*) of the [ecliptic] with the movable circle (*calavṛtta*), one should lead that circle to the point of the central mark (*garbhacihna*). There, at that time, that sine is the base (*bhuja*); the radius (*trijyā*) is the hypotenuse (*karṇa*) in the triangle; and the square root of the difference of their squares is the sine of the maximum declination. In that same manner, having led the movable circle to the point of the central mark, its form is the perpendicular (*koṭi*). Thus it is said.

Therefore, when the hypotenuse is the trijyā (radius) and the sides are the *yūha* and *vajra*, then the hypotenuse is the *dṛglambana-jyā* (the sine of the parallax in longitude), while the circle is indeed the *duḍhaivṛtta*. Thus, that moving circle (*calavṛtta*) is to be brought to the point of the *tribhonalagna* (the nonagesimal); there, those two—the *bhujā* (sine of the arc) and the *koṭi* (cosine)—become established as the *upanati* (parallax in latitude) and the *sphuṭalambana-jyā* (corrected sine of the parallax in longitude). In this manner, the *dākāravṛtta* (the circle of the observer's position) is the central circle; it necessarily touches the center of the sky.

From the rising and setting points of the horizon, the sines of the co-latitudes (koṭi) and the sines of the degrees of altitude (natikoṭyaṃśa) on the circle parallel to the equator are all equal, because that circle exists at an interval of one degree from the meridian. Thus, that moving circle would be a circle drawn on the sphere at right angles. However, what is required is the sine of the altitude on the ecliptic; therefore, having fixed a point on the central axis (garbhasūtra), it must be led to an interval of one degree [from there], where that circular figure is the secondary circle (paravṛtta) relative to the celestial poles (kadamba).

On the [great] circle, what is this [arc] at that time? It is established on the ecliptic as the degrees of the arc between the observer's latitude and the equator. That point on the central line reaching the ecliptic is made into a chord by those degrees; its sine is the form of the *tarajyā*, which is the clear result of the calculation. [Chapter 484: The Section on Solar Eclipses, ending with the subtraction of the sky. Now it is stated otherwise: At the point of the observer's line, there are two circles similar to the horizon and the ecliptic.

Indeed, from the mean [longitude] the true [longitude] is seen quickly; from that, the node (*pāta*) is seen on the visual sphere (*dṛṅmaṇḍala*) up to the secondary circle (*paravṛtta*). The perpendicular distance (*koṭi*) of the parallax (*duglambana*) is the sine (*jyā*) thereof, and likewise the parallax in latitude (*sphuṭalambana*) is derived from the declination (*krānti*). On a similar circle, the sine of the interval between the ecliptic (*cidvṛtta*) and the secondary circle is not the same as that belonging to the ecliptic (*krāntivṛttīya*). Therefore, here, through repeated calculation (*asakṛtsādhana*), the sine of the interval between those two [circles] is likewise established. However, the radius (*trijyā*) would be the measure of the sine of the perpendicular of the true parallax; this is consistent with direct observation and is established there by the method of iteration (*sakṛtprakāra*).

This is established. Hence, there is a proportion: if on the circle of the koti of the natikā (the meridian distance) the koti-jyā of the *dṛglayana* (the arc from the zenith to the rising-setting circle) is measured as *kṛta* (4), then what would it be on the circle of the trijyā (radius)? Thus, by means of the [proportion] belonging to the ecliptic, the same applies here to the parallax (*vilambana*). The *koṭi-jyā* of the parallax, which takes the form of the *antarajyā* (sine of the difference) between the two circles, shall be so; and likewise, subtracting that from the [mean] latitude, just as at midday, the resulting true latitude is indeed the true parallax. This is proven.

Or rather, the point of the *lagna* (ascendant) is three signs away from that. Here, the meridian circle (*draṅamaṇḍala*) is like the declination circle; the ecliptic (*krāntivṛtta*) is the equatorial circle (*nāḍīmaṇḍala*). When the [ecliptic] is three signs away from that, the celestial equator (*ayana-maṇḍala*) becomes very similar to the declination circle. The *yujyāvṛtta* (circle of latitude) is at the *kadamba*, while the poles (*dhruvau*) are at the *lagna*. The planet situated between those two, when calculated by the sun's rays, has a declination consisting of its [spherical] altitude; the rising measure of the division of the celestial sphere, which consists of the visual parallax, is indeed the true parallax.

This is easily understood by those who know the sphere. (1vi7 śa7) Even for the illustrious Bhāskarācārya, the maximum [parallax] occurs precisely at the terrestrial horizon. That which is shown here in the lunar sphere (*candragola*) for the purpose of parallax is intended as the parallax reaching the center of the Earth along the line of the true angle; and since it is established and concluded by means of the sine of the zenith-distance on the surface, which is equal to the radius (*trijyā*), that same true value would also apply to the solar sphere (*sūryagola*). Thus, the parallax and equation of time are determined by the degrees of the Sun's zenith-distance alone.

However, at that time, due to the contraction of the expansion of the calculated arc, the calculation of the parallax in longitude and latitude should be performed by the wise. For this very purpose, the knowledge of the distance from the eye-line (*dūglayana*) and so forth is required; therefore, because the difference is small, the parallax in latitude is derived from the parallax in longitude itself. Now, by this method, the determination of the parallax is accomplished in a single step. It is as follows: since the parallax in time is first obtained, the parallax in the visual ray (*iṣudraglambana*) is then found through the repeated method; thus, following that repeated procedure according to the opinion of Dṛgmaṇḍalacaṭṭa, the parallax in the visual ray is combined with the parallax in time, and the single-step method is established.

It has been demonstrated: "That which is the maximum parallax (*vilambana*) of the nonagesimal point (*tribhonalagna*), as stated in the *Narabīja* and other texts, is clear from an investigation into the rationale of the [parallax] line, as follows: The third arc measured along the circle of the burning ship (*dagdhapotavṛtta*)—which lies below the nonagesimal point of the planet situated at the celestial cross-staff (*khasvastika*)—is the parallax. And the sine: The sine of the [arc] multiplied by the radius (*trijyā*) and divided by the sine of the obliquity of the ecliptic (*krāntihṛt*) shall be the maximum [parallax]. (204) In this case, the parallax on the plane of the meridian is that belonging to the ecliptic."

The interval between the ascendant and the third house is the arc of the difference between the longitude of the ascendant and that of the third house. Let this be *jyā* (the sine). Let *jyā* (the sine) be divided by the radius (*trijyā*) and multiplied by the sine of the desired time-interval. This result is again divided by the radius and multiplied by the sine of the desired time-interval. Thus, the sine of the desired time-interval is obtained. This is established as follows: if, from the sine of the equation of center for the swifter planet, [the following is calculated]... ॥ 205 ॥

Then, the sine of the arc [of the argument] is the sine of the complement; hence, by assuming the sine of the maximum equation of the center as the *jyā* for the apogee, and placing it below the center of the celestial sphere, one should construct another circle equal to the ecliptic. Therein, the *jyā* of the arm-result of the planet called "swift" (*śīghra*) is produced. By assuming the non-triangular point (*vitribha-lagna*) as the apogee and the point three signs away from that as the ascendant (*lagna*), and so forth, [the calculation] becomes exceedingly clear.

61. [In the year] 486, on the 4th day of the waxing moon, this work on solar eclipses was completed by Vaśī, the author of the *Svaviveka* Siddhānta. 209. Thus, having constructed a circle called the "Swift Epicycle" (*śīghramaṇḍala*) and placed it upon the [deferent] circle, one should apply the parallax (*lambana*) once, according to the method for the swift motion, along the line passing through its extremity and the center of the [deferent]. 210. Thereafter, the square of the arc of the string (the sine) subtracted from the radius is to be added here; or else, the square root of the sum of the squares of the interval between the ascendant and the sun and the [perpendicular] distance (*koṭi*) shall be the measure of the hypotenuse (*śruti*).

The sine of the ascendant at the time of greatest [eclipse] is stated to be the product of the radius and the sine of the latitude. That parallax is the true value; it is equal whether calculated once or repeatedly. (211) When the sine of the difference between the sun and the non-triangular ascendant is multiplied by the hypotenuse and divided by the radius, the resulting arc will be the true, corrected parallax. (212) If the true parallax is established by the "once-said" method, then the time of observation is corrected accordingly. The true parallax is established for that specific time without the need for repeated proportional calculations. (213)

Then that very [longitude] becomes the true longitude for the observer, and that same [true] planet is indeed suitable for the calculations mentioned therein. Even though the time is established by a single observation, that which was done by those who performed a single observation for the sake of the true [longitude] is not correct. (214) The sine of the altitude of the ascendant diminished by three signs is the [ascensional] difference (*ṛkṣepa*) of the Sun and Moon. From that, the parallax (*nati*) should be calculated as before, which is of the nature of the base when subtracted from the radius. (216) In this matter, some say it should be known as the "stone" (*dṛṣat*); having applied the parallax of the aspect (*dṛglambana*) to their [sine of] ascensional difference, they state the parallax as the interval between them. (217)

Those by whom [the correction] arising from the side of the *rasa* (six signs) is called "the embryo" (*garbha*) as the supreme [correction], have here utterly rejected it by the removal of the sound of the *ḍagla*. (218) Therefore, the Sun is devoid of declination (*krānti*), while the Moon has its declination at the tip of the arrow (*śara*). Between those two, the difference in visible declination (*dṛg-īṣa*) is distinct; hence, for the Moon, [the correction] is joined [to the declination]. (219) Otherwise, why was it stated by Brahmagupta as "three parts of the *bhā* (fifteen degrees)"? In the absence of an arrow, even though [the Moon's declination] is distinct, it is said to be non-distinct from the Sun! (220) But when there is an arrow, in his opinion, the difference in visible declination of the Moon is observed.

Therefore, let the intention of those who hold that the [celestial sphere] is outside the *gola* (the celestial globe) be considered. However, the solution provided here by Bhāskara is inconsistent; for that very point was refuted by his own followers, who were opposed to his view. But some [hold that] the movable circle of Jupiter (*jña-vṛtta*), which is fixed upon the gnomon of the local meridian (*lagna-asta-vilagna-kīla*) and situated at the center of the lunar disc, is indeed where the *dṛkṣepa* (visual declination) occurs. From there, up to the zenith, are the degrees...

Having first accepted the coarse and slow [motions] from the beginning, they then repeatedly [apply] the subtle according to the logic established for what was not yet proven; yet, do they truly know whether that subtle [motion] exists or not? (215) The true parallax (*dṛkṣepa*) would be clear; however, the difference between the ecliptic and the circle of parallax should be calculated as that which is termed *calabāṇa* (the "moving arrow"). (224) By this logic, the moon’s true form becomes well-corrected through that parallax.

488. The Chapter on Solar Eclipses in the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*. 489. Therein, in the *Dhṛṣṭabha-cakra*, that which was devised for the sake of establishing the true latitude (*avanati*) is stated as follows: || 229 || The modern scholars say that what was spoken regarding the revolution of the field of one's own circle is [as follows]: || 225 || (1) Since the multipliers and divisors are not truly so, there is indeed a deviation. When the Ascendant and the Moon are equal, O friend of the Moon’s color, the moving arrow is always measured by the sword (five). || 226 ||

This [longitude] seen by means of the golārīya instrument would not be according to the method described by him. Just as the movable circle of the tri-bhonalagna is displaced from the celestial sphere (bhacakravṛtta) upon the kadamba-vṛtta, so too, if the circle is at an interval equal to the calavaṇa, then the point of the kadamba is likewise on that very circle. Here, by that same interval and in that same direction from the kadamba, another circle is designated; and just as it is in the celestial sphere from the center of the kadamba, so too is the circle known as the *sucala* drawn from its own center.

The Sun’s motion from the point of Makara [Capricorn] is suddenly added to the longitude; then, from that, the parallax in latitude (*dṛglambana*) is to be calculated. That which was previously made the depression (*natī*) in the ecliptic circle is indeed the sine of the arm (*bhuja*) in the celestial sphere (*dṛṣṭirvṛtta*). || 230 || In the case of the Moon, the cosine is five hundred and sixty-eight; this is the first method for the true parallax. Having assumed another [method] here, the depression (*natī*) which results is in the other celestial sphere (*kadambavṛtta*). || 231 || From the mark of the visual line (*dṛksūtra*) to the edge of the lunar disc, at a distance equal to the true parallax, there exists [a point] on the celestial sphere (*kadambavṛtta*).

The parallax (nati) is not distinct when [the planet] is within the arc of the moving apogee (calakhyadṛṣṭi), each on its own kadamba-circle. (232) That parallax which exists transversely by virtue of the moon's displacement (tākṣepa) from the circle known as the "moving" (calasaṃjña-vṛtta)—the true parallax of the moon arising therefrom is not increased by it anywhere. (233) Here, the sun situated in the direction of the line drawn from the moon to the sun’s point of observation is seen half-visible; therefore, that [parallax] does not belong to the moon, for it is not other than that. If it were otherwise, why was it prescribed here by you yourself? (234)

If the latitude (nati) resulting from the moving declination-circle is accepted within the calculation of the true altitude (dṛgbhaṭṭatta), then Viśvanātha Śarmā Munīśvara also adopted the "moving circle" (*calavṛtta*)—that is, the arc between the true celestial latitude and the zenith—as being exactly half [of the total]. However, there is an error in that method of derivation; for in the sūtra stated by Munīśvara, the square root is obtained from the product of the sine of the latitude and the sine of the co-latitude, diminished by the square of the sine of the moon's [latitude]. By that [root], the sine of the co-latitude of the moon added to the ascendant, multiplied by the sine of three signs (the radius), and divided [by the hypotenuse], [gives the result].

"The square root of that [value] which has its color (magnitude) derived from three times the sine, divided by this [sine], multiplied by the radius and the sine, shall be the correction for the purpose of refinement. Here, *jyā* is the sine. Here, in the phrase "from the square of the multiplier of the broken [sine]," the inverse operation is simply *X = koṭijyāśa*. This is from the *Siddhāntatāttvaviveka*, in the chapter on Solar Eclipses. [Question: Without the base of the *vilambana* triangle here, how can that [correction] be determined for the sake of ascertaining the eclipse? 235.

In the calculation [of the moon's longitude], the difference between the circle arising from the *kadamba* (the equatorial plane) and that which is attached to five, three, one, and six signs (5316°) is what remains; yet therein, the other [circle] remained for as many signs. Even a small difference between those two is like an eon. (236) Then, when the *balacakra* was made by the clever [astronomers] to be known through the throat [of the system] upon the universal monarch [of astronomy], what was achieved by them? (282) In the process of subtracting the squares, the sum of the squares of the *nati* (latitude) and the *śara* (ascensional difference) remains as twice the square of the sine of the amplitude (*kaṇa*). The equinoctial circle is the interval from the solstitial point; likewise, the declination (*cakṣaja*) is the interval from the solstitial point on the ecliptic. The true *valana* (oblique ascensional difference) is the interval from the intersection of the ecliptic and the equator. (283) But when [the point] is outside the junction of the spheres (*golasaṃdhi*), if it is with the equatorial circle—(1) the two respective square roots of the *viṣuva* and *śara* have been shown there; whichever is the smaller root is where [the calculation proceeds].

There is no precession (*ayana*) at all there; how [could it be] so? (284). [The values are: *yāva* = 6, *he* = 2, *yāva* = 6, *vi* = 9. Likewise, another square root of the light [term] is *vi* = 9. [there is no precession there]; for this reason, how is it to be established? [Thus says] Bhāskara. *na* = 0, *ba* = 8, *va* = 5.

[Response: No; there is no equalization between these two positions. One's own connection [to the truth] is established by the very fact that the method for solar eclipses (*sūryagrahaṇavidhi*) is a part of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). As for the statement of Ācārya [Brahmagupta], "The sum of the *yujyāvṛtta* and *apavṛtta*... and so forth, it is merely the prattle of Bhaṭṭa’s imagination; however, the refutation of *utkramajyā* (versed sine) has been demonstrated in many ways, and one such instance here is as follows.

In his own *Vāsanābhāṣya*, Bhāskara Ācārya has demonstrated the consistency of the underlying rationale (*vāsanā*) for the section beginning with "placing the solar disc in the form of a ring upon the sphere at the junction of the conjunction and apogee" and ending with "the difference between the [latitude] and the [oblique ascension]," by somehow accepting the non-difference and thickness of the lines of contact between the sines and arcs of its own minute-parts. Regarding that, the venerable teacher has presented a specific, faultless rationale, which is as follows:

Having placed the solar disc in the shape of a ring upon the plane tangent to that sphere above the point where the latitude circle intersects the meridian, the edge of the disc is at a distance from the point of tangency on the ecliptic equal to half the diameter of the disc.

On the plane of that point of tangency, there is a third line of tangency passing through the center on the back of the diurnal circle (ahorātravṛtta) which passes through the celestial pole (dhruva) and the center of the image; this is known as the line of tangency of the vertical circle (lambavṛtta). This is because it is the single line of tangency common to both the diurnal circle and the vertical circle, and it is also the line of tangency for the circles passing through the celestial pole and the nadir (kadamba). Since the angles formed by the lines of tangency arising from the planes of the circles are equal, the measure of the angle produced by the line of tangency of the declination circle (krāntivṛtta) and the vertical circle is the deflection of the meridian (ayanavalana).

The perpendicular from the edge of the disk onto the line of contact (sparśarekhā) of the vertical circle (*lambavṛtta*) is the versed sine of the deflection (*valanajyā*), measured from the point on the edge of the disk where it meets the equator. This is not the chord of any arc belonging to the edge of the disk itself. Similarly, the horizontal line from the edge of the disk onto the plane of the equatorial circle (*viṣuvavṛttadharātala*) is the declination sine (*krāntijyā*) of that point on the edge of the disk.

And that [sine] would indeed proceed by cutting the plane of the *dyujyā*-circle; for there exists an interval on both sides equal to the *apamajyā* (sine of declination) between the center of the image and the planes of the *viṣuvavṛtta* (equator) and the *dyujyāvṛtta*. Thus, here, the segment of the *krāntijyā* (sine of latitude) at the edge of the image, extending from the edge of the image to the plane of the *dyujyāvṛtta*, can be stated as the difference between the *pratāpamajyā* (sine of the distance from the center of the image) and the [other] *apamajyā*.

In this matter, there is one simple case: where the versed sine of the oblique ascensional difference (*viṣuvāyanavalana*) is the hypotenuse, the difference between the sines of the obliquity (*krāntijyā*) is the perpendicular (*koṭi*), and the square root of the difference of their squares is the base (*bhuja*) in the plane of the terrestrial circle of the day-and-night (*ahorātravṛtta*). Since the angle produced by the line of contact with the sine of obliquity from the center of the sphere is equal to the obliquity itself, the magnitude of the angle produced by the hypotenuse and perpendicular—where the hypotenuse is equal to the difference between the sine of obliquity and the sine of the oblique ascensional difference—is also equal to the obliquity; thus the doubt is resolved. And how is this stated as a single coherent statement?

In this manner, O crest-jewel of our own [tradition], we have established the circle of the latitude (yujyāṅgalāpavṛtta) using unprecedented arrays of suns (bhāskara). One should place the solar disc there; that would be the oblique ascension (valana), which is the interval between those two circles. The difference arising from the declination (krānti) and the amplitude (pauṣṇya) at the meridian of the [solar] orb is the destruction of the Sun’s misfortune (arkadorbhāgyakhaṇḍana). Increasing that by the sine of the ascensional difference (asra) and dividing it by twenty-four (jinajyā), and then dividing by the radius (trijīvā), one obtains that very interval. Multiplied by the diameter (bimba) and divided by the radius (tribhajyā), and then again divided by the radius (trijyā), it becomes as it was originally obtained.

288–289. When the square root of the product of the sine of the argument (guṇahara), the radius (vimbārdha), and the radius (trijyā) has been taken, that [result] multiplied by the sine of twenty-four degrees (jināṃśajyā) and divided by itself [the same], [yields the result]. Then, from the tenth verse of the eleventh chapter on calculation (khāgaṇita), the measure of the angle between the hypotenuse and the side is equal to the arc of the corresponding sine (yujyācāpa).

Now, since all the right-angled triangles produced by the co-latitude, the latitude, and the equinoctial shadow are similar, that [triangle] which arises from the sum or difference of those [segments] is also similar to the right-angled triangle arising from the difference between the co-latitude and the declination-sine and the equinoctial shadow-sine; therefore, it is appropriate that this [difference] be considered similar. The difference in co-latitudes favored by Bhaṭṭa is obtained through the current segment of the arc traversed: *bhaurca × viveka* divided by *kojyādā* (4235).

From the *Sphuṭabodha*: Let *ke* be the sine of the obliquity of the ecliptic (*krāntijyā*). Then: *ke* × *jyāji* / 4 = 225/229 The sine of the precession (*āyanavalanajyā*) is: *tri* × *tri* / 4329 The sine of the precession is: *jyāja* × 4 / *ke* × 4325 Then: *vā* × 3 × *ka* × *tri* / *tri* × *tri* × *tri* × 229/4 The sine of the precession is: *jyāji* × *kojyā* / 4 × 225/4 × 6/3 × *ka* × *tri* × *āyanavalanajyā* × *tri* × *oṃ* / 225/4 Thus, the precession as stated by Bhāskara is established. *Viveka*: *jyāji* × *kojyā* / 4 Therefore, the precession as stated by Bhāskara is proven.

Therefore, the intersection of the Sun’s [orbit] with Mars is called *lagna* and is designated as *samābhidha*. From that point, one should lead [the calculation] as far as the center of the Sun; then, at the point where it is touched upon the arc of the half-sum of the diameters (*mānaikyakhaṇḍavṛtta*), the latitude (*krānti*) measured in the direct order from the triad of signs (*satribhākā*) becomes equal to that. Or else, having observed the interval between the direct and reverse latitudes, the foolish ones have fallen into error; that is incorrect, because the Sun’s [motion] is understood throughout the entire year.

The occurrence of another [eclipse] while situated within the middle of a visible disc is impossible. Likewise, when the moon is at the point of conjunction (apana-sandhi), an absence of interval is observed within the solar disc at the location between the two discs, according to the method of the *saṅgola*. Furthermore, non-existence would become existence at the point of occurrence; thus, how can there be a calculation based on such a deviation from reality? Even that which is stated regarding the difference in the sines of the latitudes derived from the proportion of the shadow is certainly not produced from the difference between the middle points as described by you.

The difference between the *krāntijyā* (sine of declination) situated at the center of the disk from the three [parameters] is taken; from that, the *valana* (deflection) is derived for the planet's latitude through proportion. (295) Due to the distinction between the eastern and western halves of the disk and their unequal latitudes, the *valanas* would be different; however, in this system, they are considered non-different. (296) When the center of the solar disk is situated at an interval of eight signs or three signs from the ecliptic or the horizon, there arises a difference between those two circles. (297) And when the half-sum of the disks [of the sun and moon] is equal to that difference, [the eclipse occurs].

By means of the addition of that [equatorial] measure, one should draw a circle upon the celestial sphere starting from the center of the solar disc; even without the ecliptic, the horizon (samamaṇḍala) is seen situated in a different location. (2) Viśvanātha Śarman: Regarding the grammatical rule *dūde dvivacanaṃ praṇudyam*, Bhaṭṭa’s perspective is encountered in many places. Considering that [the rule] originated from that direction, the correction known as *valana* was accepted; and that *valana* is conceived as being directed toward the center of the Sun. (303) This is appropriate for a solar eclipse according to the diagram (*parilekha*), but it is not suitable for a lunar eclipse. If you ask why, then listen to this.

304–307. During a solar eclipse, the correction for deflection (*valana*) is indeed that which is derived from the [longitude of the] Sun; it is [zero] at sixty degrees [of the Sun's anomaly]. During a lunar eclipse, it is zero when the Moon’s latitude is zero. Even though the correction called *valana* is derived from the [longitude of the] Sun, it does not belong to the lunar orbit (*vimaṇḍala*), because it would otherwise be suitable for the configuration of the lunar disc. However, since that *valana* is derived from the Moon’s longitude by adding three signs (*tribha*), one then applies proportionality to find the [correction] within the circle situated at the center of the lunar disc.

How can that which is performed and given by them through the application of honor be [otherwise]? That sūtra which reaches the tip of the *valana* (deflection) is the *vimaṇḍala* (eccentric orbit) of the lord of the [planetary] sign. 308. Therefore, the arrow (*śara*) is given as having the form of the arm; at its tip, the center of the terrestrial shadow situated on the *krāntivṛtta* (ecliptic) is conceived. 309. The arrow is indeed multiplied by the declination (*krānti*); for that is the *vimaṇḍala*. And the sūtra reaching the tip of the *valana* is forcibly accepted as being turned away. 310.

[Objection: Then, how is it that in your own work, immediately following the *Samākhyāpaṇḍala*, you have stated that the deflection (*valana*) occurs from the north? [Response: Indeed, in the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka* (verse 504), the chapter on solar eclipses (verse 505) states that the clear eastern deflection is suitable for the procedure of drawing the lunar disc; and whatever reasoning (*vāsanā*) was declared by the Lord of Sages (*munīśvara*) regarding the northern deflection in his *Nijasārvabhauma*, I shall now explain that as well. The koti-sine of the apogee plus the moon’s latitude, divided by the sine of the arc of three signs (90°) minus the ascendant, is multiplied by the [sine of] the remaining degrees of the moon; the resulting arc is the latitude, which becomes the face [of the shadow]. || 313 || In the direction of the epicycle of declination, those [distances] from the equinoctial points toward Bharatavarṣa arise from that very [latitude]; that is the more precise declination for the planets beginning with the Moon. For Mercury, however, it is said to consist of three distinct parts. || 318 ||

On level ground, from the point of the *saṃskṛta* (the corrected position), one should draw a circle using the radius equal to the true body of the planet [the Moon] and the half-sum of the [orbis] dimensions; this circle has the same center as the first [reference circle]. ||219|| In this circle, the sine of the deflection (*valana*) is the north-south arm. From the point of contact, the east-west arm of the Moon is produced. O wise one, it should indeed be applied to the left or right, south or north, and likewise from the west. ||220|| But for the Sun, those two arms are respectively toward the southwest and northeast, starting from the points marked by the directions of Varuṇa (west) and Indra (east). ||220½||

The direction of the Moon’s node is opposite to that of the Sun’s; the direction of the Sun’s node is indeed the same as that of the Moon. The conjunction and liberation (of an eclipse) occur at the points of the nodes. The true latitude (*spaṣṭa-vaṇa*) is equal to the full sine (*pūrṇaguṇa*) when it is zero; for the Moon, it is the reverse of its own [node’s] value. Thus, the mean [latitude] is directed toward its own node. From the apogee (*kendrataḥ*), these values should be applied toward the front of their respective nodes at the points of the arrow-tips (*iṣujāgravinduṣu*). The circle arising from the segments produced by the true body of the eclipsing planet (*grāhaka*) is distinct; thus there shall be three [circles].

The sine of the correctional arc (*saṃskārabhāga*) derived from the bow of the longitudinal parallax (*śarāsanākṣabhavalaṇa*) should be multiplied by the radius and divided by the sine of three signs (*tribhajīvā*). This result should then be applied there as the true [longitude], which indeed stands in the place of the [true] image (*vimba*), for it is stated with logical justification that the longitudinal parallax arises from the [true] image. From this correction, the true longitudinal parallax (*sphuṭavalana*) shall be obtained.

The calculation of the *ayanāṃśa* (precession) should be understood through the method of the *candranavāṅga* (nine lunar digits) correction; likewise, the calculation of the *śaravalana* (latitude correction) is to be known by that same principle. || 316 || If, in this context, the point on the ecliptic circle is stated to be at a certain distance from the eastern or western directions, that declination (*valana*) is called "clear" (*sphuṭa*) when it is equal to the interval in a different region. || 317 || The pair of points arising from conjunction and liberation is the ascendant (*lagna*) held here by the planet; therein, those two—the beginning and end of the eclipse—occur, and thus it is obscured within the central disc. || 318 ||

Chapter 529: On the Conjunction of Planets. In the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, it is stated that when the conjunction of the observed planet has already occurred at a certain time, the correction for precession (*ayanāṃśa*) should be applied at that very moment. By this means, the conjunction of that [planet] would be as previously described. However, if the conjunction is yet to occur (*gamya*), then what was "already gone" (*gata*) becomes "yet to come" (*gamya*), and conversely, what was "yet to come" becomes "already gone. Consequently, the conjunction of the two celestial bodies cannot be established [in that manner]. The first group [of scholars] have stated that for planets moving in direct or retrograde motion, the status of being "yet to come" or "already gone" regarding their conjunction is as previously explained.

That [correction] arises from the conjunction of the apsis and the node; how could it possibly occur here otherwise? That correction for the moon’s latitude is not like that of the sun, for it is derived from the true longitude. However, the parallax (dṛkkarma) arising from its rising is not like that of the sun.

For the sake of achieving success, it should be understood that the calculation of the true place of a planet from its own *śruti* (mean longitude) has been stated in the same manner by the wise.
