For that purpose, the cosine of the ascensional difference (*cāpajya*) is the hypotenuse (*karṇa*) on the horizon; the sine of the amplitude (*dambapreta*) is the base (*bhuja*), and the sine of the declination (*krānti*) is the perpendicular (*koṭi*) here on the ecliptic. Thus, the measure of the angle formed by the intersection of the declination circle and the horizon circle is the visual motion (*dṛggati*). Therefore: The sine of the arc of the complement of the ascensional difference (*utacāpatyasya bhujajīva*) is equal to: \[ \frac{\text{cojyālū} \times \text{ga} \times \text{bhūtra} \times \text{dṛgga}}{\text{mṛxḍagga} \times \text{trijyā} \times \text{lotri} \times \text{jyalaṃ}} \] Of this [arc]: [End of fragment]

Wherever those very circles intersect with the ecliptic (*bhamaṇḍala*) and the equatorial circle (*samamaṇḍala*), there the [sine] values would be their own respective sines; thus, this is also the third variety. (112) The sine of the maximum interval between the two is established from this. (2) Viśvanātha Śarman—From the intersection of the ecliptic and the equator, the ascendant at the time of the solstice is 70° 59' 8". In the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, in the chapter on Great Questions (Mahāpraśnādhikāra), 599, the multipliers for one and so forth up to five are thirty.

The remaining degrees here shall be the sign of wealth (the second house). 116. From the northern or southern *agrā* of the ascendant, the sum or difference of the night-side sine (*kṣapabhuja*) and the *śaya* should be determined; this is the *dṛkkarṇa* (hypotenuse of vision), being south if the *agrā* is south, and otherwise (north) if it is north. 117. Having likewise calculated the *agrā* of the ascendant and multiplied it by the *agrā* of the [second] ascendant, one should determine the *dṛgjyā* (sine of vision) obtained by dividing the *tribhajyā* (radius) by the *śruti* (hypotenuse). 118. Then the *śruti* and *bāhu* (adjacent side) measures should again be computed by the wise. If the stated degrees of the *agrā* are greater than thirty, then—

118–121. [The degrees] calculated from the lord of the house (bhāveśa) are likewise subtracted from the lords of the houses; those [results] are then combined with half the [respective] houses. If the remainder is greater than eighteen (āṭhavaḍā), then the difference arises; otherwise, it is the difference between the two ears (karṇas). The two ears of the first [house] are then [calculated], and otherwise the difference. The two degrees (lavayam) should be added to the ascendant for the sake of the house-lords; they are thus made manifest (sphuṭa). Those [degrees] along with their own houses are known as the death-houses (mṛtyubhāva).

The ascendant increased by two signs is the setting point; furthermore, the sine of the other arm [of the triangle] is the equatorial sine (*samamaṇḍala*). Thus, incidentally, the many states [of the planets] have been established. || 122 || For the states [of the planets] joined with the Sun, that which lies between the visual sine (*dṛgjyā*) and the sine of the arm is the interval between them, which is indeed the third sine of the equator. || 123 || Even if it is not minute, one should know that by its power there is an interval of states; and that which exists is due to the measurement of the state suitable for the equatorial arrows. || 124 || By means of a coarse proportion (*sthūlanupāta*), the determination of the states from the ascendant is indeed accomplished. || 124 ||

That [calculation] performed by Sārvabhauma, however, lies outside the established position of the celestial sphere (Golādhyāya). If there is a method for calculating the ascendant (bhāva), then that of Śrīpati is superior; yet even with his degrees of the ascendant (bhāṃśas), it is not the same as this [method], because of the discrepancy in the stated results regarding the *alagna* (ascendant). When the non-trinal ascendant (*avitribhalagna*) is at the meridian, the income (*āya*) and expenditure (*vyaya*) situated one or two signs apart from it do not belong to the equatorial circle, nor are they known to you in their true rising points (*sanmadraṇi*).

For the sake of the unshakable state of existence, which is firmly fixed by the equal stakes, one should abandon the abode here from within the supreme equanimity. Having understood the measure of the swift movement of the planet through the force of its own desired conjunction, one should proceed.

(1) Viśvanātha: From the perspective of the nature of the house, even at the time of calculating the houses on the equatorial plane (*samamaṇḍala*), the sine of the arc (*bhujajyā*) is not used; rather, by means of the *kapī* (the cosine), that [sine] is obtained. When bringing forward the houses starting from the first house (*śrīpaśya*), this is the method. Thus, having accepted the sine of the aspect (*dṛgjyā*) as situated between the arms, which is nearly equal to the sine of the equatorial circle (*samavṛttīyaśiñjinī*)—though it is not subtle—and having transformed it into the semi-circumference of the circle formed by the hypotenuse of the arm and the perpendicular (*bhujakoṭibhyāsārdhavṛtta*), the elevation of the house resulting therefrom is considered equal to the house on the equatorial plane by means of a coarse proportion (*sthūlānupāta*).

The statement by Bhaṭṭa that "the conjunction is made at the zenith" is indeed appropriate; for, up to the eastern point of the cross (pūrvasvastika), there is equal respect [for the degrees] on the prime vertical circle (samamaṇḍala). Since the third part of the ascendant is on the horizon (kṣitija), the distance between two angles minus one side is easily understood as the hypotenuse when the respect [for the degrees] is great. (1) Viśeṣa: Starting from the eastern point of the cross, twelve parts of the prime vertical circle are equal to thirty degrees; these are the six parts, and the remaining degrees are the lords of the signs. (2) Viśeṣa.

From the correction of the [longitude] by the [ascensional] difference (*kṣepabhujasaṃskāra*), at the point on the equatorial circle (*samamaṇḍala*) measured thirty-two degrees east from the intersection with the ecliptic (*ṛtasama-maṇḍala-saṃpāta*), that which constitutes the state of being intersected by the equator—when combined with its declination—is assumed to be the sine of the angle at the intersection-point (*saṃpātalagnakoṇajyā*). By means of this, when the hypotenuse and side are calculated through proportion (*trairāśika*), the correction obtained from the arc of the hypotenuse (*karṇacāpa*) should be added to the obtained [longitude] if it results in a positive value; thus, the calculation of the [true] position is easily understood. This concludes the chapter on the determination of the true positions in the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*.

561. The sines of the latitudes (natājyās) multiplied by the [sine of] the ascensional difference (guṇa) and divided by the radius (dhanurlambā) should be corrected here as before. Indeed, from the sines of the longitudinal distances (diglānām), the degrees of the co-latitude (koṭyaṃśaka) are obtained; from that, the direction-sine (digīśa). 136. Then the sine of the amplitude (svabāhu) follows, and then the correction for the circle's diameter (viṣkambhadale) as previously described. All this arising from the oblique ascension (viṣa) should be performed by the wise here for the sake of generating the [astronomical] results. 137. The equinoctial deflection (āyana-valana) has indeed been declared; now tell me its clear derivation (vāsanā) so that it may be well understood.

Having calculated the *khecara* (the planet) in the middle of the sky, and likewise its longitudinal difference (*tāpamala*), [one finds] the degrees of latitude (*palabhāga*) from the knowledge of its own degrees of declination (*svakṣabhāga*) and its celestial motion (*khacara*). From these two—the sine of the arc of the longitudinal difference (*bhogavibhva*) and the product of the sine of the oblique ascension (*bhavasaṅguṇita*)—if you are skillful in composing a treatise whose meaning is churned by sound discernment, tell me quickly the value of the *dṛgjyakā* (sine of zenith distance), the *nara* (sine of altitude), and the measure of the *bhuja* (sine of amplitude). Then, having subtracted the *lagna* (ascendant) from the lord of the planets with the three signs added, one should determine the *kendram* (quadrant) and its *koṭijīvā* (sine of the co-latitude).

A person’s own aspectual motion (*svadṛggati*) divided by three becomes its aspectual sine (*dṛgjyā*), as previously stated. (131) The aspectual sine of the [ascendant] cusp multiplied by the sine of the argument (*kendrajyā*) and divided by the radius (*tribhajyā*) yields the degrees of the result. If these are less than thirty, they are the degrees of the planet; otherwise, they are subtracted from sixty. (132) In the case of a northern aspect, if it is southern, the reverse applies: the degrees of the waist (*kaṭibhāga*) are subtracted from ninety. The resulting degrees in their own direction are then to be calculated further as before. (133)

When the planet exceeds three signs, this [calculation] is stated as before; likewise for the Sun. When the subtractive quantity (śodhya) exceeds the arc, it should be understood that the subtraction is reversed due to the inverse nature of the operation. || 134 || When the planet is five [signs apart], its diameter (bimba) is produced according to the previously mentioned method. Here, the wise one should calculate the sines of the depressed and non-depressed arcs; the sine of the anomaly (kendrajyakā) is the square root of the difference between the squares of the sine and cosine of the remainder. || 135 || Indeed, the ascendant (lagna) plus three signs is always equal to the Sun plus nine signs (kujagaja). || 135 ||

In that context, the correction for obliquity (*valana*) arising from the ascendant is indeed the same as that produced by the *ayanāṃśas*. Some say that the true *valana* occurs even without the *ayanāṃśa* and *akṣavalana*; having observed this discrepancy in the astronomical treatises (*kalpa*), I consider him to be a great authority. First, the calculation of the house-positions (*bhāva*) must be performed; then the calculation of the *dṛkkṣepaka* (parallax) should be done according to the ear and mind. O dear one, when the *dṛkkṣepaka* is situated in the southern direction, it proceeds sequentially through the southern and northern hemispheres.
562. In the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, the chapter on Great Questions (Mahāpraśnādhikāra). 563.
That deflection (*valana*) of the celestial body shall become clear.

In that case, when the sine of the latitude (dṛkkṣepaka) is equal to the radius (sāmyagata), the conjunction with the planet occurs in reverse; indeed, at that same time, there is no longitudinal difference (bhujā) for the planet. (142) Likewise, the first sine (ādya-śruti) multiplied by three and divided by the sine of the obliquity (ijyā) gives the tip of the ascendant (lagnabhavāgraka). Therein, the sine of the deflection (valanajyakā) known as *phuṭa* is equal to the sine of the difference between the equinoctial and the solstitial colures (*samākhyāpamavṛttayośca*). (143) That would be the maximum sine of the interval (paramāntarajyā) produced at that time, just as the sine of the quadrant (jinajyā) is the maximum interval between the equator and the solstice.

The circle known as the equinoctial (viṣuvakhyavṛtta) is indeed that same ecliptic (bhavṛttaka). And the maximum sine of its [the Moon's] declination is the sine of the obliquity; that is the latitude. Now, the arm (bhuja) here between the two orbs is the true declination, and that is on the equinoctial circle.

In this regard, there is a specific rule: (1) One who knows the sphere (*gola*) should first calculate the ascendant, the junctions (*sandhi*), the planets, and so forth, situated on the ecliptic; then, from the hypotenuse (*bhuja*) of the planet corrected for the [precession] anomaly (*pāta*), one should calculate the sine of the complement (*koṭijyā*). The product of that [complement-sine] and the other [sine] should be divided by the square of the radius (*tribhajyā*); the result is the lower [value]. The product of the other complement-sine and the radius (*trijyā*) should be divided by the divisor’s complement-sine; the resulting arc-complement is the first [value]. That same sine of the anomaly-corrected planet, multiplied by the divisor and divided by the first sine, is the [resulting] sine.

That planet, diminished by the arc of the result when its longitude is not yet clear, should be determined as the planet [at the desired point]. Likewise, the sine of twenty-four degrees (the *jinajyā*) is the bowstring of the equinoctial shadow; it is the cosine-sine (*krāntijyakā*) of the universal planet. Multiplied by the cosine-sine of the planet designated as "desired" and divided by the sine of twenty-four degrees, the resulting value for the *yujyā* shall here be the sine of the deflection (*valanajyaka*) on the plane of the ecliptic at the time of the rising of the secondary circle (*kṣepavṛtta*).

(1) (Viśeṣa-śloka) Now, the arc of the interval between the central meridian and the prime vertical circle on the projection of the celestial sphere is either the declination corrected by the obliquity of the ecliptic, or it is precisely the interval between the vanished central meridian and the projected circle.

Then, by drawing the circle of the celestial sphere (bimba-upavṛtta) from the center of the bimba up to the point equidistant [from the poles], and from that same equidistant point on the axis (kadamba-samasthāna) constructing the arc of half the diameter of the bimba-circle as the *yujyā* (sine of the co-latitude), one should draw the maximum declination (*parama-krānti*) and the intersection of the *vimaṇḍala* (eccentric circle) with the east-west circle as the *golasaṃdhi* (sphere-junction). Having thus projected the *vimaṇḍala*, the *krāntimaṇḍala* (declination circle), and the east-west *viṣuvavṛtta* (equator), the sine of the planet's longitude (*kheṭakoṣṭima-jyakā*) is obtained by dividing the *jinajyā* (radius of the sphere, 90° sine) by the *yujīvā*. This is indeed easy to understand.

In this context, the arc between the positions of *vikalpa* and *vikadamba* is denoted by the first term (*ādyapada*) and is that which is to be determined. Furthermore, the point of intersection of the *vimaṇḍala* (eccentric circle) and the posterior meridian must also be known. On the plane containing the celestial sphere, the side (*bhuja*) or arm extending from the center of the sphere to the eastern-western meridian is well-known as the *visvīya*; it is easy to ascertain through the *śaṅku* (gnomon), the *hasta*, and other such means.

On either the southern or northern side, at a point equidistant from the *kadamba* and *vikadamba*, the distance between the *kadamba* and *vikadamba* is equal to the maximum sine of the oblique ascension (*parama-śaracāpa-jyā*). The diameter measured from the center of the *kadamba* is the sine of the oblique ascension (*udayajīva*). In that context, the sine of the correction for the equinoxial deviation (*ayanavalana*) as previously stated shall be the same as the so-called "apparent" (*sphuṭa*) sine of the deviation; we shall now describe its calculation. That [sine] is multiplied by the cosine-sine (*koṭijyā*) of the node of the planet at the junction [of the signs]. This is the maximum sine of the difference.

The arc of the result is stated by Vyāsa, who has explained the divisions, as being equal to 565 and 564. In the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, the author of the *Mahāpraśna* states: "Just as the precession known as *āyana-valana* was previously mentioned, that which is well-known in the calculation of *bhāvanā*—the divisor of the sine of the difference of arcs—is called *āḍana*, [referring to] the degrees of the arc of the difference between the two positions."

Thus, by these three methods—whether by the *Galaprakāśa* composed by the Maithila Paṇḍita Śrī Nīlambara Śarmā, who established the astronomical system (*Jyotiṣasiddhāntabhāskara*), or by the *Cāpajaya* composed by Paṇḍita Śrī Yādeva Śāstrī (S.I.I.), according to the rule stated therein: "The earth [radius] multiplied by three, divided by the sine of the arc," or as stated in the calculation of the arc: "In this case, the earth [radius] multiplied by the cosine, divided by the sine of the arc"—the first arc is the earth [radius], and the remainder is the arc.

Then, the arms are: the cosine of the angle facing the earth (*dharaṇisaṃmukhakoṇakoṭijyā*), the cosine of the hypotenuse (*kojyā*), the product of three cosines (*tri-kojyāpaśa*), and the cosine of the hypotenuse (*kojyāha*). Here, the divisor is the sine (*jyā*). Since the sine of the hypotenuse is the divisor, the cosine of the hypotenuse is the dividend; thus, the cosine of the hypotenuse is equal to the cosine of the angle facing the earth. The cosine of the angle facing the earth is the negative cosine of the junction-point planet (*pānasandhigraha*) because it is the cosine of an angle exceeding ninety degrees. Therefore: *kojyā* (from the *Saṃgraha*), *kojyā*, *tri-kojyāpaśa*.

Someone has said: "The wise man should calculate that [distance] situated in the direction of the three junctions, the eclipses, and the rising and setting of the planets. When that [distance] is divided by the diameter of the epicycle arising from the [planet's] orb, it becomes the distance arising from the zenith. Then, multiplied by the sine of the interval between the planet at the junction and the [other] planet, and divided by the sine of three signs (the radius), it shall be the maximum sine of the interval. This should always be performed joyfully as a playful exercise on the surface of the observational sphere known as the horizon-circle."

110. Now, regarding the point of intersection of the solstitial colure and the equator on the sphere of the Moon as found in the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*: since you are ignorant of the true nature of the oblique ascensions (*carakhaṇḍa*) and the right ascensions (*tāna*), this has been stated for your benefit. (151) If you are indeed a wise man, tell me the subtle point of intersection of the obliquity (*apama*) at the location of the true center of the image, which consists of the union of the ecliptic and the equatorial circle—provided you possess the discernment of the true essence of the Siddhāntas. (152) And what is the point of conjunction of the two circles—the celestial equator (*vibhṛtta*) and the ecliptic (*bhavṛtta*)—which are situated in different directions? (153)

And the mutual distance between the planets is six signs; then the node (*pāta*) is at the end of Capricorn (*himāṃśugoka*). Since there is a sextile from the beginning of Aries (*rābikramataḥ*), it is situated in Virgo, having moved from the circle of the nodes (*bhavṛttāt*) toward the north. Therefore, *kājya* = *kojyāpaśa* × *ha* / *kojyā* (multiplied by the sine of the argument). From this, the first arc is obtained. Now, [the calculation] arises from the conjunction of the planet and the node.

Just as, by means of the sine of the angle at the junction of the *pāśa* (noose) and the *prahālagna* (pre-ascendant), which is the sine of the current ascendant, one obtains the sine of the planet at that junction minus the *pāta* (node) from the *krāntivṛtta* (ecliptic); so too, by means of the same sine of the angle at the junction of the *pāśa* and the *prahālagna*, the sine of the *vimaṇḍala* (ecliptic-circle) is obtained. When the seventh house from the true planet situated on the *sapātavimaṇḍala* (the ecliptic-circle with the node) is subtracted from the true planet, then the sine of the planet at that junction minus the *pāta* is equal to the sine of the *vimaṇḍala*.

Having conceived [the planet] as a bird, it is like an ant found by digging into a mountain; thus are established the specific rules stated in the *Sūryasiddhānta*, refined by the correction of the autumnal combustion (*śarajvalana*). In the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, this constitutes the great chapter on the determination of the nodes. For they say that Rāhu is that which exists in the past, while the wise always call Ketu that which is in the future. By means of its motion and knowledge, this node moves in the opposite direction to the planets, while the other [node] moves in the same direction.

In the case of both [the Sun and Moon], when their longitude exceeds six signs, that very position becomes the point of descent (*adhuraha*) in reverse order. In the circle, however, by subtracting the degrees of motion from the circle and then adding them to the circle’s half, the two points known as the *ādyanya* (initial and final) are indeed the nodes of the sphere; they are like the nodes of the sun and moon for the purpose of calculating the duration of eclipses. By subtracting those [nodes] from three signs and then adding the degrees of motion to the three signs in reverse order, one obtains the *aṅkagṛha* (house of the mark) in sequence. Those two [nodes] of the Moon are certainly situated at some distance for the sake of determining the true apogee, as established by the ancients.

Then, for the [mean] sun corrected by the sequence of precession (ayanāṃśa), one calculates its sine (rāśisaṃjajyā) and its declination-sine (apamaśiñjinī). From that, the cosine (dhṛjyakā) is derived; then, the sine of the latitude (tribhajadyumaic) is multiplied by the sine of the [precessional] correction and divided by the radius (dyumoṭhyā). The arc of the resulting quotient is called the equinoctial degrees (viṣuvāṃśaka); likewise, the precession (ayanārūpa) is the value in minutes of arc. These, when properly corrected, are added to or subtracted from the [longitude of the] sun according to whether it is in the first half or second half of the zodiac starting from Aries and Cancer respectively. Then, the sine of that [corrected longitude] is calculated. 158–159. The sine of the complement (koṭyaṃśakāḥ) of that [longitude] is multiplied by the degrees of the moon’s parallax (candrapareṣubhāgaiḥ). Whether the sun is in the first half or second half of the zodiac starting from Aries and Cancer, it is to be subtracted or added [to the mean moon]. Then, the sine of that [resulting true longitude] is taken.

That product is to be divided by the sine of three signs (the radius); the divisor shall be the product of the degrees of the arc and its complement. || 160 || But when the sine of three signs and the sine of the maximum declination are the divisor, then the two [results] will be the hypotenuse and the base, starting from the degrees of the [ecliptic] longitude; the difference between the degrees of the base and the degrees of the [ecliptic] latitude is the complement. || 161 || The dividend is multiplied by the sine of three signs; then, this is multiplied by the hypotenuse, the sine of the maximum declination, and the sine of the [ecliptic] latitude. Divided by the sine of the complement of the degrees of the [ecliptic] latitude, it is the dividend; and when divided by the sine of the complement of that [latitude], it is the arc. || 162 ||

The junctions of the Sun’s sphere and solstice are at the points of Aries and Libra; endowed with these, those two [junctions] of the Moon occur in the six signs beginning with Libra, while in the six beginning with Aries they are subtracted from them. (163) The degrees of the result obtained by multiplying the square of the sine of the other ear [latitude] by the radius and dividing by the square of the sine of that [latitude], when subtracted from thirty, are the [degrees of] declination. Alternatively, the radius may be divided [by that sine]; the result is as previously stated. (164) The junctions of the Moon’s sphere and solstice are designated as the first and the other [second] according to the method of the Sun.

When Rāhu is situated at the junction of the Moon’s path, Karṇa is always the maximum. (165) Viśeṣa-śiromaṇi: The degrees of the arm (*bhujāṃśa*)—the increase in the form of the arm—have now been established as the equinoctial degrees (*viṣuvāṃśa*). Those equinoctial degrees, together with the precessional degrees (*ayanāṃśa*), constitute the equinoctial degrees of Rāhu. [End of] the chapter on Great Questions in the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*. In the *Bhaṭṭadīpikā*, however, the *kadamba-vṛtta* (the circle of the celestial pole) is located where the sum of the intersection of the ecliptic and the meridian meets.

From the beginning of Aja (Aries), the node of the Sun (Rāhu) is at [the end of] Gaja (Leo); from that, the node of the Moon (Ketu) is at the end of Tula (Libra). Thus, as stated, the nodes of the solstices (ayana-sandhi) occur in the third sign. || 166 || Since those two nodes arise from the orbs of the [solar and lunar] disks, they exist within the solar and lunar disks respectively because of the absence of any distinct degrees of obliquity (krānti-lava) for the disks themselves. || 167 || Having calculated Rāhu by subtracting the true apogees of Mars and the other planets from the circle (360°), the true nodes of the planets are derived from that; these two [nodes] become true through the conjunction or separation of their respective orbits as previously described. || 168 ||

The sine of the declination (*krāntijyā*) at the unmentioned junction (*anākhyasaṃdhi*) is obtained by adding three times the value of the ear (*karṇa*) to the [sine of] the apsis; it arises from the square root of the difference between the square of the maximum declination and the square of the sine of the apsis. From that junction, the three corrections—precession (*ayanavalana*), obliquity (*nata*), and the latitude derived from the moon’s longitude—are calculated. Furthermore, the difference between the [mean] Sun and the Moon at the junction of Capricorn and Cancer is indeed the sine of the [true] Sun. That which remains after subtracting the conjunction of the planets is called Rāhu; this has been stated by the Brahmins on account of its influence.

In what [position] is the moon eclipsed when not prepared for the transit? Rāhu is said to be at the distance of ten thousand *karṇas*. (171) If the circle of lightning is at the first quarter, then in the second quarter; if it is increased by the digits of the sky (90) in the third; and if it is at the end of the void (0) in the fourth, then in both cases, in due order, Rāhu is said to be at the distance of ten thousand *karṇas*. (172) The junction of the moon's prescribed sphere would be at the center; indeed, when that is diminished, the moon is struck by lightning.

In the case of Rāhu, however, since the consciousness [of the planet] begins at Karṣa (the first point) and the Yuga-beginning (the fourth point), the centering [of the orbit] occurs at the beginning and end of the quarters. The arc obtained by multiplying the sine of that [longitude] by the sine of Rāhu’s latitude and dividing by the sine of the radius is the [true] longitude of the Moon. This centering is in Aries, Libra, and so on; it is north or south depending on whether the Moon is in the six signs beginning with Capricorn. If Rāhu is situated in the opposite direction from what was stated, the wise say it is in the first sign and so forth. It should be understood that, due to the absence of the Ārya’s statement, even a minute correction for establishing the true node is of no consequence.

Thus, the point of the solstice-conjunction (ayanasaṃdhi), which is of the nature of the equinox (golayana), has been correctly established by me through its underlying rationale (vāsanā). Those experts in calculation have been deceived by those skilled in the practical application (karaṇa) of crude approximations. Three [units], ten, one; zero, one, three; zero—these are the degrees of the precession of the equinoxes (ayanāṃśa); this is the Rāhu of the house (the first point of Aries). It always resides at the initial solstice-conjunction of the Moon; yet, according to the statement of Bhāskara, it is not established here. [End of] the Mahāpraśnādhikāra in the Siddhāntatattvaviveka.

571. This [longitude] has been stated for Rāhu when it is slightly less than two or three lunar [diameters] (2, 3, or 1 degrees) prior to the Moon. Since the node known as *ayana* is not established by observing the conjunction, the [eclipse] caused by it is therefore not logical. Now, the method of *kuṭṭaka* (pulverizer): Whatever multiplier exists such that when the dividend is multiplied by it and increased or decreased by the additive constant (*kṣepa*), and then divided by the divisor (*hara*), it results in an exact quotient—therein we shall explain the knowledge of the multiplier (*guṇa*) and the quotient (*āpti*). ॥ 179 ॥

If there is a remainder when the divisor is divided by the dividend, let the divisor become the dividend and the remainder the divisor; here too, that remainder must be further reduced, and the process continues in this sequence until the divisor becomes the dividend and the remainder the divisor. The quotients [obtained] from below are placed one beneath the other; then, below that, the constant term (*dṛḍha*) is subtracted. In this way, when the quotients obtained here are equal, then [the solution is reached]; however, if they are unequal, then [the process must continue].

(3) Having subtracted the multiplier and quotient obtained from their respective divisors, those two remainders become the multiplier and quotient when [the original values] are subtracted from their divisors. 178. Since the precession known as *ayanāṃśa* is not established due to its being situated at the junctions [of the solstices], the *pāta* (node) produced by it has also been declared [by some] to be incorrect. 179–180. When there exists some unknown multiplier (*guṇaka*) by which the dividend (*bhājya*), when increased or decreased by the additive (*kṣepa*), and then divided by the divisor (*hara*), yields an exact quotient, the knowledge of that multiplier is the essence of this instruction. If the remainder obtained when dividing the dividend by the divisor is non-zero, one should then assume that remainder as the new dividend and the divisor as the new divisor; then the remainder from that division must again be determined. This process is repeated in sequence, such that the divisor becomes the dividend and so forth.

181. Since the last two [divisors] must necessarily divide each other, let the number by which they are firmly divided be the *apavarta* (common divisor). By that, the dividend (*bhājya*) is raised; the divisor (*bhājaka*) is likewise made firm by being divided accordingly. 182. The additive (*kṣepa*) also certainly becomes known as "firm" (*dṛḍha*), just as the dividend and divisor were reduced by the *apavarta*. That for which no further reduction of the additive is possible is declared to be the "remainderless" (*akhila*) case. 183. Otherwise, it is indeed "with remainder" (*sakhaṇḍa*). Those [values] which were previously obtained by mutually dividing [the numbers] are used here.

The fruits are below the *dṛḍha* [divisor]; the lamp is below that; and the last [quotient] is below that. The penultimate [quotient] is multiplied by zero (0). When the penultimate [quotient] is added to the last [quotient], one should repeatedly discard the other. Thus there would be a pair of values (*rāśiyugma*). Divided by the *janavabhājya* and reduced by the *dṛḍha*, the quotient would be the multiplier (*guṇa*), and the other would be the remainder (*caraṇa*). (Siddhāntatattvaviveka, Mahāprasnādhikāra, verse 184). If the remainder is zero, the remainder of the seconds (*vikalāvaśeṣa*) would be the remainder of the [corresponding] count (*gaṇāvaśeṣa*). (Verse 14).

When the *viliptikā* and the *śapa* arise, they are equal to the previously stated result; however, the understanding of the planets in the form of *viliptikās* here is easy to grasp and not a secret. (185) When the *dṛḍhakka* and *ddaścakra* are divided, if the remainders (*vicinnikā*) there are small, then the *dṛḍhakka* is small. 185. Those [results] which arise from conjunction enter through subtraction; those arising from disjunction occur through addition. And those two [results] would indeed be obtained by their respective multipliers. In the case of a moving [value], the pulverizer rule for a stable [value] should be understood; at the point of annihilation, the result is always zero.

From the desired [multiplier], the multiplier and quotient for their respective [divisors] shall be obtained; and by those, the divisor and multiplier possess the properties of the original [divisor and multiplier]. (190) Thus ends the method of *kuṭṭaka* (pulverizer). [The calculation of] the days of the cycle (*cakravāsara*) starting from the beginning of the Yuga should be performed very firmly according to what has been stated.

(207) First, observe the methods for the square-root as stated there: the root of numbers increased by the product of a multiplier and a divisor shall be obtained. (208) That which is the square of a quantity in relation to the multiplier is called the *prakṛti* (nature/base).

The square root of the sum [of the square of the least root and the constant] shall be the least root; multiplied by two, it becomes the square of that [least root]. By means of the original [least root] joined with the additive, the greater root shall be obtained. Having placed the least root, the greater root, and the additive in a row, and then below them—[one should proceed]; however, having established them in equal pairs, the composition (bhāvanā) should be performed. Indeed, through the sum and the difference, those [roots] will then become manifold. The sum of the products of the respective greater roots and the least roots [is the new greater root].

The difference [of the two] would be the least root, and thus the greatest root would be obtained. (112) Whatever is the square of the original least root and whatever is the square of the greatest root, the sum and the difference of those two respectively become the greatest root and the difference [between the squares]. (212) If there is an error regarding the additive constants (*kṣepa*), it occurs in both cases of the square roots. Therefore, the calculation of the sum and the difference is performed according to the sum and the difference [of the roots]. (214) The additive constant (*kṣepa*) derived from the square of the desired number, when divided by that same desired number, yields the quotient; the square root of that [quotient] is the additive constant for the original [number], and then the square root [of the product] is the root. (915)

One should divide that [product] by an arbitrary chosen square; the quotient is the *iṣṭa* (chosen), and its square root is the *kaniṣṭha* (lesser root). With these increased by one, the *jyeṣṭha* (greater root) is obtained; thus there is an infinite variety according to the chosen value. In the case of a residue (*akhila*), if the sum of squares is not a multiplier, then the given residue divided by two square roots in two ways yields two values for the *svapada* (its own root); from that, the *jyeṣṭha* is found by subtracting the residue. The square root of the product of the base (jātabhūmi) and the hypotenuse (koṭi), multiplied by the arm (bāhu), when divided by one hundred, is the result; O Narada, that result added to the circle (cakra) is the measure of the bamboo (vaṃśamāna), which is the height (lambaka). ||330|| Now listen to how it is even without piercing (vedha); in the case of the simple measure of the bamboo, as well as in the case of the piercing by the sixth [digit], and likewise when seated, the measures of the arm and the hypotenuse are to be accomplished. ||331|| And those two hypotenuses, multiplied by zero-zero-arm (khakhabhuja), are divided by the difference between their results; this is the value for the two sights (dṛṣṭyoḥ).

The distance between the two heights shall be the terrestrial latitude, measured in ten-thousandths from the city [of Ujjayinī]. The terrestrial latitude, multiplied by ten million and divided by its own polar altitude, is increased by the product of its own polar altitude and the sine of the zenith distance; this is the value in ten-thousandths when the places are on the same side of the meridian. This same method applies to the observer's location as well for determining the depth of the reflection; however, in this case, the correction for parallax must not be applied at the point of conjunction, nor should it be done even from the depths of the respective poles.

The product of ten million and the sun (1,200) shall be the *bhujaphala* (the sine of the arc); the light (the cosine) is derived from its square root; and the degrees of altitude (*palāṃśāḥ*) are obtained from those [degrees] divided by ten. This result, however, comes into agreement with all that [is observed] through the influence of very subtle *doḥ* (sine) and *koṭi* (cosine). That which, when multiplied by various [factors], attains purity among these, and which is exceedingly small yet superior to calculation—that I have truly declared as the "Day" (*ahaḥ*), when it stands upon the path of the sixty [parts of a day]. This is the Great Chapter on the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*. [End of Section] 406–407. *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*.

If you are skilled in this great ocean [of calculation], then first write down the smaller number; subsequently, all [the larger numbers] are to be reduced by that [smaller one]. If, according to the initial sequence, the larger is divided by the smaller, then the quotient is the subtraction of the smaller from the larger. Alternatively, from those two firmly established factors, one should be reduced here so that they remain very firm. In this way, through the sequence, they become firmly established factors, and their product is the desired smaller number.

O Jalaṅgola, how could the moon, which is subject to destruction, not lose its own coolness when mixed with the horn [of the sun] and heated by the rays of the sun? O you who are skilled in discernment, provide an answer to this. (339) The heat does not reside in the rays of the sun; rather, it exists in fire itself. Likewise, the rays are hot by their very nature. When they come into contact with a certain object, that object becomes fire; otherwise, it would simply be fire. (340) Therefore, by virtue of its position in the sky, that heat may exist there; but how could it possibly exist here in a liquid state?

It is said that heat is produced by the combination of earth, water, fire, and air; it is not produced by the planets, nor is it due to the rays of the sun. (341) Those who claim that the heat of fire is established through a conjunction with the heat of the sun’s rays—surely that opinion does not appear correct, for that [heat] is never observed elsewhere without fire. (342) Having understood the underlying principle (*vāsanā*) in this manner, I have spoken out of fear of prolixity. Those who know the manifest and the unmanifest should understand that which has not been explicitly stated here. (343)

Having set aside the ancient and obsolete [works] that have arisen at the beginning, and having discarded the new well-spoken [treatises] lacking the methods of *anugra* and *caṅgola*, may the long-standing [works] previously stated in the world always serve to establish the novelty of my own exposition for the conviction of all. (344) He who, being ignorant of his own system, imagines the superiority of another’s, quickly meets with ruin and is reborn in other wombs. (245) Thus ends the chapter on questions and answers in the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka* composed by Śrī Kamalākara. Now follows the conclusion of the work.

Now, here [is the location] where the Godāvarī river flows, situated at thirty-six degrees and thirty minutes south latitude, and which is known as Durgā, the divine city of the gods. It is famous among us as being one hundred and fifty *yojanas* to the east, where the Pārthā river lies within its interior. This beautiful city, situated in the midst of the kingdom, is located within the Vidarbha country. And it is said to be just a little beyond that, at two and a half *yojanas*.

The Godāvarī flows perpetually; it is the Gaṅgā whose fame is established through the song of the Unbegging One (Śaṅkara). (3) Near the banks of this [river], there is a village of virtuous people well-known by the name of Goṇa. Likewise, to the south is the city named Puruṣottama; between those two is he himself. (4) In his abode of eternal bliss, virtuous young women—though consumed by the fire of their homes—delight themselves. They are intent on conversing with one another, engaged in the playful arrangement of water-sprays. (5)

The birds, independent and free from desire for food, are always delighted here in that excellent lake; they are as pure as the best of the twice-born, those dear friends who take refuge in the nectar-like banks of the Godāvarī. (6) On the nearby bank of the Godāvarī, at the place known as Godā-saṅkama where all things are easily accomplished, there lived a Brahmin renowned as Mahārāṣṭra, Rāma by name, the ornament of the lineage of Bharadvāja. (7) His son was Bhaṭṭācārya, honored by all, highly skilled in the scriptures, and pure. (8)

His son was Divākara, who always joyfully served Bhārgava (Śukra). His son was Siddhasārvabhauma Viveka, who held a position of great authority. Having abandoned his body through the merit accumulated from the study of the Vedānta branch in Kāśī, his son was Arthabhūṣaṇa, renowned as Śrīkṛṣṇa Daivajña. His son was that pure Sattīrtha, a knower of the scriptures; his son, moreover, was Saṅgrāmavidāṃ Vara.

There was a group of scholars named Nṛsiṃha who spoke words concerning the task; by them, here, the commentary on the *Śiromaṇi*—which is endowed with unprecedented reasoning and establishes its own meaning as well as that of others—was composed for those of discerning intellect. (10–11) But from a mere fragment of his grace, Khañjeṣṭha, whose heart is virtuous, having obtained the understanding of the *Siddhāntaśekhara* through the instruction of his friend Rāyaḍuru, has written this for the satisfaction of the assembly of astronomers. (12)

And the king, known as Śrī Kamalākara, who was endowed with the skill of the *trairāśika* method as previously described, produced this work which contains the essence of the discernment of all established astronomical systems and the true nature of the celestial sphere. (13) When one thousand five hundred and eighty (1580) years of the Śaka era had passed, he, residing on the banks of the Ganges near the city of Haridvāra, composed this entire treatise according to the principles of the Siddhāntas. (14) This effort exists solely for the sake of those whose intellects are absorbed in the sacred grass (*darbha*) [of Vedic tradition].

This entire work is to be investigated with the very method of sound reasoning; otherwise, like a honey-bee, one would not find the nectar without encountering a stinging insect. My transgressions here must indeed be forgiven, for this [work] is intended for those who are firm in their capacity to understand. (16) In the system of the *Kāraṇaprāya-siddhānta*, the ancient masters declared themselves to be poets based on their own statements regarding their own excellence. (17) Only those are truly poets here who, like farmers, cultivate the field of speech and extract its essence. (18)

But those poets who merely tear it apart will never [attain its essence]. (18) This poison, however, consists of compositions charming with the resonance of the *ṭuṅkāra* word; that flattery which masquerades as a garment is indeed a hundredfold [more harmful]. (18) In this world, an ancient enemy might cast blame upon my face; I feel no sorrow because of that, for I have many kinsmen on earth. (20) This secret of the gods must not be given to just anyone. This supreme knowledge should be imparted only to a disciple who has been thoroughly tested. (21)

Otherwise, for those who have resided here for a long time under the guidance of their preceptors and teachers, as well as for sinners, there would inevitably be a depletion of their merit and lifespan. (22) Having understood the movements of the planets and constellations and the celestial sphere (*gola*) in its true essence, one attains the state of the Sun through successive stages, like a soul within. (23) This structure of Vivasvat has arisen in each successive age; by the grace of someone, this knowledge manifests from time to time. (24) For those by whom this discernment of truth (*tattva-viveka*) has been composed through various efforts and according to the principles of the celestial sphere (*saṅgola-yukti*), [it serves as a guide].

O Lord, no one other than You possesses such omniscience as Your own; therefore, this [work] has been dedicated by me at Your lotus-feet for Your satisfaction alone, so that the joy of Your companions may increase. Henceforth, amidst the assembly of the virtuous, may these words of mine—bearing the essence of deliberations on the compendiums of calculation—bring delight to those whose minds are ever-dwelt upon by the True Being. (25–27)

Those who teach, recite, and write this entire work—having examined it together with its meaning and its latent impressions (sāthai savāsanam)—possess fame, humility, and skill that increase through the grace of the Goddess of Fortune (Śrī). Thus ends the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, composed by Śrī Kamalākara, the son of Śrī Siṃha, the sovereign of all astronomers (gaṇaka-sārvabhauma). Now follows the supplement (*śeṣavallī*) to the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*. Salutations to Śrī Gaṇeśa.

Salutations to Śrī Sarasvatī. Victory to the venerable Guru! I shall now explain that Lord who bestows speech, the cause of the movement of the luminaries, by whose grace Brahmā became the creator in the worlds. (1) Whatever has been conceived here is stated according to its true nature along with its underlying rationale (*vāsanā*); there is no falsehood in this Siddhānta, nor is there any need for further elaboration through words. (2) Now, first, the rationale (*vāsanā*) is explained in the section on the Mean Motion (*madhyamādhikāra*). Since that [section] is already very clear, the remaining [rationale] regarding the True Motion (*sphuṭa*) is being stated. (3)

(9) "The remainder from the face of the year" means as follows: When the day-count (*ahargaṇa*) starting from the weekday, namely 4;45, up to the sunrise of the desired day, and the day [of the year] is 0;15, here the sun at the start of the year consists of sixty *chadmas* (units). In the day-count, there is invariably a remainder. Since the *ghaṭī*s of the year are 15, the sun is understood from that point; therefore, until the end of the *ghaṭī*s of the day-count, it remains the solar weekday (*ravivāra*). This is certain because of the sixty-fold cycle of the *pakṣa*.

Immediately after, it has been stated that when four days have passed from Monday up until sunrise, the operation belongs to Śakra alone; thus it would be said that [the weekday] has passed according to the Apāṇimat system. According to the ancient method, by counting the doors starting from the year-lord (*abdapa*), it would be Mercury by the current method and Jupiter by the "passed" method; however, this too is impossible. [Verse 9: "In the calculation, the year-lord's *ghaṭīs* added to the day-count (*ahargaṇa*)—or else from that same day-count—the weekday passed by the year-lord shall always be determined in the day-count starting from the beginning of the year. [This refers to] the verse numbered twenty-five on page fifteen.

The remaining portion of the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*: 77. (1) The rationale for adding one or subtracting one from the *karaṇa*. If the current mean lunar day (*tithi*) exists at the rising of the mean Sun, then the *ahargaṇa* (count of days since epoch) is established for that rising. If the true lunar day exists at the rising of the mean Sun, then the *ahargaṇa* required is for that [true] rising. The interval between these two is the time produced by the correction of the slow-motion equations (*mandaphala*) of the Moon and the Sun; it is precisely due to this correction that a difference in the weekday (*vāra*) sometimes occurs. Thus, the addition or subtraction of one from the *karaṇa* is well-reasoned.

Here, by the word "rising" (*udaya*), the meaning is as follows: the mean sunrise at the equator (*madhyama-arkeodaya*) occurs when [the planet] is situated on the meridian circle (*yāmyottara-vṛtta*) six *ghaṭīs* below the horizon; by that, the mean planet produced from its own velocity-correction (*svavīrya*) is also situated there, namely at the middle of the day or at midnight. (2) Now, regarding the phrase "in the *ahargaṇa* by mean civil time" (*madhyama-sāvanena*) and so forth: the "stellar day" (*nakṣatra-dina*) within a single solar day consists of the revolutions of one zodiacal sign (*ekabhabhrama*) added to the days of rising at the equator (*nirakṣodaya*) produced by the mean motion of the asterism corrected for its [precession] motion (*calaśiṣa*). They call these its "civil days" (*sāvana*).

However, they say that the purely solar motion situated in the middle of the sun's path, which is equal to the sum of the [mean] revolutions and the rotations of the earth, is called the mean *savana* day. Having accepted that the true *savana* day-count (*ahargaṇa*) situated at the time of the mean rising of the [ecliptic] point is produced from the mean [longitude], and that the day-count derived from the knowledge of the true [longitude] is the mean solar [day-count], they prescribe the correction for the difference in rising (*udayantara*) for the sake of clarity. A day always consists of sixty *ghaṭīs*; when it is joined with equal breaths (seconds) of the sun, it becomes so.

If it be argued that the midday *savana* (period) occurs thus at the end of the year due to the revolution of the asterisms through that same number [of days], then by stating "without calculation" (*vinā gaṇitena*) while speaking clearly regarding the commencement of the solar year devoid of precession (*nirayana-varṣādau*), the author has effectively stated the measure of the mean civil day (*madhyama-sāvana-māna*). However, by taking the measure of the mean civil day according to the rule "the mean [longitude] is endowed with precession" (*sāyana-śāñcita-madhyamānau*), and because of the difference between that and the true [longitude], the statement regarding the absence of the interval between risings (*udayantara-abhāva*) at the end of a quadrant (*padānte*) would be contradicted; for elsewhere its existence is stated. How can these two be reconciled?

First, regarding the interval between the rising of these very [planets], for example: at the time of a single rising, there exists both the *sāvana* (civil) and the *nākṣatra* (sidereal). In that regard, the *sāvana* is indeed real (*vāstava*), whereas the *nākṣatra* is not real; this is clear from the source. If the unreal were equal to the real sidereal, then that very one who has arrived would be without parts and devoid of calculation. This is because the doubt "I am" is established through counting.

Therefore, at the time of obtaining that [mean] and its ascensional difference (*āsanaka*), how could there be any difference whatsoever between the true *kathastava* and the true *revantara*, or between those two and the *kalikā* and *ahargaṇa*? If one were to insist [on such a difference], then because of that correction, the rising of the *avargaṇa* would occur; thus, how could it ever be established as being without fractional parts? In reality, however, because the two measures of the *avargaṇa* are distinct and belong to different times, there is no difference in their *sāyana* nature; hence, the error arises from perceiving a difference in their other natures.

Furthermore, at the point of sunrise, the true [longitude] of that which is not known through its own group of revolutions would not be truly called "true" if it were not corrected by the difference between the two [mean and true] suns. In reality, however, the ignorant display their own superiority over the ancient sages by imagining that the simultaneous difference between the true and mean [longitudes] is equivalent to the difference between two mean suns at different times; they thus conclude that if there is a discrepancy in the calculation of the revolutions, there must likewise be a discrepancy in the *daśā* periods.

Furthermore, since the determination that the mean sun is situated at sunrise occurs precisely through its movement from the middle of its own [mean] position, the *varga* (degrees) of the time [of calculation] are indeed identical to those of the mean sun at the moment of rising. However, the mean sun at the subsequent rising is different due to the difference in mean motion; thus, that interval between risings (*udayāntara*) is not real. The collection of nadīs (degrees) is not distinct from the mean civil day (*savana*), but rather, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that it is either situated at the actual rising or remains stationary there. Now, regarding the occurrence of the interval between actual and non-actual risings, this is the underlying principle (*vāsanā*) for the impossibility [of such intervals] in the case of lunar days (*tithi*) and so forth.

(1) In fourteen *putra*s [1504], seventeen for Śrīśoka; (2) in fifteen *pūḍa*s [1500], thirty for Śrīśammita. According to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) of his own *Viveka*, the remainder of the cloth [the calculation] was as follows: when the interval obtained by the *nākṣatra* [sidereal] degrees of the Sun is equal to the *kalā*s of the *sāyana* Sun, out of fear of error and due to delusion, Bhāskarācārya and others have made the interval equal to the *kalā*s of the *sāyana* Sun for the sake of the "correction for rising" (*udayāntara*). In that case, if the interval were calculated by the *kāryā* [corrected] degrees of the mere Sun...

When [the calculation] is being performed, that day-count (*gaṇa*) would be separated by a time equal to the degrees of the solstitial point (*ayanāṃśa*) and its minutes; for there exists a discrepancy between the [calculated] sweetness and the rising-time difference (*udayāntara*). By this [reasoning], if twenty degrees of the solstitial point correspond to sixty *ghaṭīs* of an *ahorātra*, then by four degrees of the solstitial point [the difference is] 1620 minutes; thus for the Sun, the discrepancy is four minutes, and for the Moon, fifty-two minutes. The difference is 48 [minutes] and the sum is 56 [minutes]. These are the measures related to the lunar days (*tithi*) and so forth, according to the motions [of the planets]: 731 and 780.

If there were 850 *ghaṭī-ghaṭikās*, then by those [divisors], what would be the difference in *tithis* and so forth, being slightly less than 48;52;56? Or rather, what would be the difference in four *ghaṭīs*? Thus, in the source [text], which consists of the presence and absence of destruction, the intended group (*vargaṇa*) should be understood. Whatever destruction is desired at a particular time, that should be understood through the power of the group (*vargaṇa*) acting at that time. The rest is clear. All the expertise in the Siddhāntas has been destroyed by the noble Aryabhaṭas.

Therefore, those of dull intellect have been deceived by that which is always contrary to the doctrine of the Sun and others, which is to be rejected. (1) Now, regarding "the transits of the true Sun" and so forth: here, according to the true measure, from the end of Āmānta until the end of Āmānta is a lunar month (*candramāsa*). If, in the middle of that [month], there is an entry into Aries (*meṣasaṃkramaṇa*), then it is Caitra; if there is an entry into Taurus (*vṛṣasaṃkramaṇa*), then it is Vaiśākha; likewise, if there is an entry into Gemini (*mithuna*), it is Jyeṣṭha, and so on in order. Thus, by virtue of the twelve entries into Aries and the other signs, the twelve lunar months beginning with Caitra are pure.

It is the established conclusion of all authorities that whatever month is formed by the transference [of the solar ingress] is the intercalary (*adhika*) one. And it has been said: "Whichever lunar month is completed while the sun is situated in Aries and the other signs, that is to be known as Caitra and the rest; when there is a double completion, the other is the intercalary month. If the true measure [of time] is not accepted, then the commencement of the intercalary month would occur on the second day of the dark fortnight at four *ghaṭīs* past [midnight], when the mean [longitude] is at 32° 16' 4". In that case, the violation of the conduct of the learned (*śiṣṭa*) would be the fault.

"Spaṣṭa" (apparent) refers to the occurrence of the subtraction of the fruit of the five-fold correction (*pañcāṅga*). Now, in this context, in reality, there is neither mutual excess nor deficiency in number between the years, months, and so forth of the Sun and Moon within their respective periods; rather, they would be equal in both cases by means of a single count. Thus, by means of the single count of mean solar days, the mean solar measure is 26; 21; 50, and the mean sidereal measure is 30; 2; 17.32; 52.

Since there is always an excess [of lunar days], how could its state ever reach exhaustion? Thus, the first [type of intercalary month] is not established, nor is the second intercalary month established. Therefore, when the duration of a solar month exceeds the duration of a lunar month by even a single day, then—within the interval from one solstice to the next—a single lunar month would contain two transits (saṃkrāntis). This would result in a "double-transit" month, which is unbearable for the world-cycle (yuga), because it was previously determined that such a thing occurs due to the deficiency of one [solar month] over another.

That [lunar month] is considered "short" (kṣaya) precisely when its duration becomes less than that of the sun's transit through a sign; for by the rule that the measure [of a month] is determined by the time taken to traverse a zodiacal sign, a shorter duration implies a faster motion. Since such a shorter duration is possible within the interval of a karpa in all months, there is the possibility of a *kṣayamāsa* occurring at any time. As it is stated in the *Śiromaṇi*: "In the triad of months beginning with Kārttika, however, such a [short month occurs] according to its own time, provided the Sun’s [longitude] and the Ascendant are as follows: 2;18;0."

The rule regarding the determination of the year based on the month of Śrāvaṇa as stated by Bhāskarācārya is also valid here only in accordance with its own specific time and not elsewhere; thus say the wise. In this matter, dry scholars who are ignorant of the underlying principles (*vāsanā*) of the Siddhāntas, as well as those performing sacrifices nowadays, consider only the *Caitra* year to apply to all times and, relying upon that, compose works of definitive calculation (*nirṇaya-grantha*), yet they do not accept his [Bhāskara’s] opinion as authoritative.

Now, having thus described the intercalary month (*kṣayamāsa*), [the author asks] how it might not be directly perceived. In response to the twenty-first question, regarding the single *cala* [month], [it is said]: "The fasting and clothing [are for that]. Even though the difference between the lunar and solar [months] is not small in the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, there is no possibility of a single intercalary month occurring twice because the true [longitude] at that time is far from the end of the [solar] transit (*saṃkramaṇa*), and thus there is no room for two transits within one lunar month.

Now, regarding the possibility of an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) resulting from the destruction of the interval between two successive *saṃkramaṇas* (solar transits) as previously described, when such a conjunction occurs, it may happen at some time or not; this should be understood by the wise. And that is the purification of the true [longitude] for the sake of calculation only when the true intercalary month would have occurred previously.

Therefore, an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) is certain before the month of Śrāvaṇa; furthermore, because there is an excess of eight lunar days (*candramāsa*), another intercalary month may occur again, since its end falls within the two *saṃkrāntis* (transits). Thus, two intercalary months are certain after the month of Śrāvaṇa. Now, the intercalary month that follows immediately thereafter always consists of six days; it is either impure (*aśuddha*) or pure (*śuddha*).

The *pūrva* (first) month is that which is delimited by the [preceding] *śaya* (intercalary) and so forth, and is named after the [constellation] such as *ghaṭi* (Aquarius); the *avyavacita* (uninterrupted) month consists of thirty days. Since both the interrupted and uninterrupted months exist here, for the sake of determining both of them, if an intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) should occur within that [period], one should treat it as part of the year belonging to that [location]. Even if there is a suppression (*kṣaya*) [of a month], according to the statement "the wise man should act thus," this is the meaning.

By the phrase "connected with *prakāśa*," it is understood that the intercalary month (*adhikamāsa*) indeed does not exist; otherwise, the word "if" (*yadi*) would become redundant. Since there is no other recourse, one must regard this [intercalary] month as lacking authority (*aśraddheya*), for how could its year be diminished by that day? For that which has already been determined as an intercalary month on a previous day is certainly not to be accepted as such by virtue of being "that" (*tadvattvena*). This is because it possesses the characteristic of being connected to that [prior determination].

Precisely because the statement regarding the excluded [kṣaya] month is made for the sake of brevity, the determination of that [excluded month] is stated separately from the statement regarding the non-excluded [adhika] month. Therefore, since the two—the excluded and the intercalary—are combined, the determination of this [kṣaya] month is indeed like that of an additional month (*adhikamāsa*) occurring later; however, its exclusion (*kṣaya*) occurs through a transposition (*visaṃkrānti*) at the beginning of a pair [of months], such that even though it is mentioned as being among the two months, it must be treated as such by necessity.

Even in the case of including an additional month preceding the intercalary one as a Śūdra month, the flaw is that it would violate the scriptural injunctions regarding the Śūdra months associated with the *saṃkrānti* (solar transits). Furthermore, the subsequent months following that [intercalary period] would lose their respective designations, as the names of the successive months would lack authoritative basis; for there is no text by the divine sages (*devarṣi*) in the *Dharmaśāstra* that establishes such a determination.

In the investigation of the words of Vairocana, regarding the rule that "the preceding *śara* (five) is to be taken," the word "preceding" (*pūrva*) refers specifically to the immediately preceding one, not one separated by an interval. Although the statement concerning the intercalary month in the *Āryabhaṭīya*, such as "after thirty-two months have passed," is repeated for the sake of clarity and utility within the discussion of the intercalary month, it does not serve as an authoritative basis for the calculation of results.

In this regard, the views of many contemporary individuals—who, being outside the purview of the *vāsanā* (underlying principles) of the *Jyotiḥśāstra*, are ignorant of the supreme teaching, lack the traditional lineage of the sages, are proponents of non-theism (*anīśvaravāda*), arrogant, and engaged in false deliberations—manifest their own respective biases; such opinions are not to be respected by the wise. Specifically, those who, following the statement regarding the "intermediate intercalary month" (*madhyamādhikamāsa*), have proceeded with their own determinations based on the view that the preceding [month] is the intercalary one (*naiṣādhika*), while others maintain that the subsequent [month] is the intercalary one because of the impossibility of two intercalary months occurring consecutively. These views are to be disregarded.

The sphere that exists at an equal distance all around the earth, serving as the support for the revolution of the planets, is the *yajñakaśā* (sacrificial tether). However, they do not revolve there by their own motion; rather, moving every day at a speed of one *yojana*, the distance in *yojanas* they traverse during a *kalpa* constitutes their respective *khakaśā*. Thus, if by one *kaṣpaku-dina* (day of a *kaṣpa*) there are *kha-kha* (*100,000*) *yojanas*, then by that same multiplier, how many *yojanas* of the traversed distance would there be? (2) Regarding the "crooked segment, sun, and ear": the line from the center of the earth to the zenith is the meridian line (*madhya-sūtra*). On the solar sphere, the line drawn from the center touching the celestial sphere does not reach as far as the meridian line.

From that very point of intersection, a line drawn through the center of the circle to the point on the circumference opposite the observer serves the purpose of determining the true altitude. Therein lies the determination of the true position. The distance from the center of the circle to the point on the circumference is the base (*bhuja*). The sum of the segments of the arc from the center of the circle to the point where the sun's rays intersect the horizon is the side (*koṭi*). The line from the point on the horizon to the sun is the hypotenuse (*karṇa*). By means of these, the corresponding base, side, and hypotenuse for the similar triangles are also determined.

The lamba (perpendicular) from the center of the earth (*kukendra*) touches the terrestrial globe at the point where the line of sight meets it; thus, the arm (*bhuja*) is indeed the form of the earth-segment (*kukhaṇḍa*). The hypotenuse (*karṇa*) is the distance from the sun. When the hypotenuse is measured from the point where the line of sight from the sun intersects the surface of the earth, the perpendicular (*koṭi*) corresponding to this hypotenuse is the distance from the center of the earth to the sun. Therefore, the interval between the center of the earth and the point of observation on its surface—namely, the reduction by the earth-segment—is established as the height of the observer above the earth's surface. Consequently, it is logically proven that the sun is visible even to one situated within the interior of the earth.

Just as one perceives the remaining points of the earth below the observer's location from the mark on the surface of the terrestrial globe, so too does one perceive them from the center of the celestial sphere (the *garbhakṣitija*) by means of that same mark. For the sake of that knowledge, the method is as follows: one’s own line of sight and a thread should be extended from the point of contact with the terrestrial globe up to the limit of the solar globe; that is the "thread of the solar globe" (*raviḍakasūtra*). Since the back of the earth at that point is different from the other [visible] part of the curved surface, the line from the center touching that point where it meets the solar globe is the "other meridian" (*anyakhamadhya*).

Just as the distance between one's own back-surface and the center of the sky, and that other back-surface and the center of the sky, increases respectively, so too the distance between one's own back-zenith and another back-zenith must increase; thus, the sum of the obscured and visible portions (kucchannadṛśyāṃśa) is necessarily the interval between the meridian line of the center of the sky and the meridian line of the other [point]. Here, the sine of that [interval] is used.

The arm (*bhuja*) is the cosine of that [angle] at the zenith distance; the hypotenuse (*karṇa*) is the sine of the co-latitude (*koṭi-trijyā*) along the meridian line through the center of the sky. Thus, between the center of the earth (*kukendra*) and its surface point (*tatpṛṣṭhastha*), the segment of the earth is the *koṭi*, the segment of the arc from the sun to the horizon is the *bhuja*, and the arc from the center of the earth to the observer's position (*hukacā*) is the hypotenuse. Having understood this triangle with these sides, one should subtract the segment of the earth from the total radius; the remainder will be the distance from the observer's position to the horizon (*svabhapṛṣṭhacihnadrk*). By observing this, the visibility of the sun from the center of the earth up to the observer's position is also logically consistent.

For those situated below [the equator], the ecliptic itself is the meridian (kujam). Then, the degrees of obliquity (*ḍagyāṃśa*) are indeed the maximum declination (*parāpama*). Therein, the establishment of the point of rising (*ukacihna*) is as previously described. Now, the method by which the sun is always visible in every location is stated: from the meridian up to the ecliptic, the degrees of latitude (*svāṃśa*) are subtracted; from that, twenty-four degrees (*jinaśaḥ*) are added, and the resulting arc, situated below the meridian, is brought forward as the point of rising as before. Thus, it will certainly be suitable for the observation of the sun at its rising.

However, your portions [of the sphere] are only a small fraction of a crore, neither more nor equal. It is certain that the eye-mark lies precisely on the meridian line. Therefore, the line of sight from the sun touches the terrestrial globe; yet, on the spherical surface, it touches only at the point designated as the fourth part, not at the full extent. That which is situated at the fourth part and directed transversely is separated from the meridian line by the distance of the eye-mark.
