The equinoctial points (*viṣuvāṃśa*) at the end of that [longitude] are indeed those *niraya* [points]. In the northern hemisphere (*uttaragola*), since the celestial pole (*svakuja*) is below, they have already risen by the time of their own rising due to the inclination of the horizon; in the southern hemisphere (*yāmyagola*), since the celestial pole is above, they will rise immediately after, so those [points] are not joined with the ascensional difference (*cara*). Those equinoctial points situated at the rising of their respective celestial poles (*svakujodayastha*) would be the [true] rising points (*khodayāya*). They are written at the base for the sake of ease, and those equinoctial points which are desired for the [specific] kalaśa [instrument] are indeed the rising points.

The portion of the desired *kalā*s from the *yojana*s is indeed the fraction of the total mass of the shadow; thus, by the force of the necessary implication (*anyathānupapatti*), one should calculate the portion of the *vyasta-cala* (the reverse motion) as it reaches the point of intersection. In this context, the portion [of the earth's shadow] is such that, when the sum of the portions of the lion (*siṃha*) and the earth-shadow (*kucchanna*) is equal to the hypotenuse (*koṭi*) of the earth-shadow, then in a location further than that, it is less. Thus, what was stated is logically established.

When the terrestrial latitudes (kujorvīpṛṣṭhakujāḥ) are below the visible latitudes (dṛśyalaṅkā), then from their difference, as previously stated, [the correction] on the surface (pṛṣṭhe) would be added to the terrestrial latitude at the center (garbhakujoyaḍacijñādhaḥ). From the knowledge of that, the visibility (dṛśyakhaṇḍanaṃ) is in reverse order; that is the obstruction. (1) "The solar day-time (sāvanābhaṭakāla)" means: at sunrise, the degrees traversed by the sun (sūryabhuktarāśyaṃśaka) are increased by the minutes of arc (vikalāṃśa) present at that time; its declination (krāntimaṇḍala) remains constant.

Therefore, since the degrees of the Sun's remaining arc of motion are destroyed by the time of its rising at the local horizon, the point on the horizon (*lagna*) is determined by subtracting that [remaining] time from the desired time of destruction; thus, even though the Sun has not yet reached the horizon, it is understood that the *lagna* has been attained. Furthermore, those ascendants (*lagnas*) that have already passed are considered "risen" (*udita*), while the one immediately following them is the current one, being equal [to the desired time]. Consequently, even if it has not yet been explicitly stated, it follows from the calculation of the remainder; such is the conclusion of the ancients: "From the interval between the time of destruction and the desired time, measured against the time of the Sun's remaining arc of motion at the horizon."

Now, in this context, if the interval between the two [mean] suns when they are together or when they are apart is equal to some desired interval, then that desired interval—produced by the movement of the sun during the savana-period—is assumed. Within that savana-interval, it is equal to the degrees produced by the motion of the sun; at the desired time, it is equal to the degrees produced by the sun's displacement. As long as this is subtracted from the beginning of one’s own desired savana-time, it will result in the exact desired savana-time. Therefore, at the desired savana-time, the *lagna* (ascendant) calculated from the mean sun for that moment shall be equal to the *sphuṭa-lagna* (true ascendant).

(9) The *ayāpa* (declination difference), the *utkramajyā* (versed sine of declination), and the radius (*trijyā*) form a triangle: the middle [side] is equal to the *yujyā* (sine of the oblique ascensional difference), the hypotenuse is the *kakarṇa*, and the staff (*yaṣṭi*) is the perpendicular (*koṭi*). The base (*bhuja*) is the measure of one hundred minus the segment of the tip [of the shadow]. This is the "staff-figure" (*yaṣṭikṣetra*). In the "side-figure" (*pakṣakṣetra*), if the sine of the latitude (*ślatha-jyā*) is the perpendicular when the radius is the hypotenuse, then what is the perpendicular when the *yujyā* is the hypotenuse? Therein, the *yujyā* is the radius multiplied by the versed sine of declination (*krānty-utkramajyā*) and divided by the radius. Thus, it is established as stated: "by the sine of the moving sun's [latitude]," etc. The shadow on the prime vertical (*unmaṇḍala-chāyākarṇa*) is now calculated.

In that regard, according to the method of Devarāja: Let *kr* be the radius of the equinoctial shadow circle (*uvṛtta*), *ka* be the hypotenuse of the shadow (*chāyākarṇa*), *tri* be the base, and *pa* be the perpendicular. Here, the square of the sine of the latitude (*ji*) multiplied by twelve and divided by the sine of the colatitude (*jinajyā*) yields a result of 177 digits (units). When this is divided by the sine of the latitude (*do*), the result is called *para*. This, when multiplied by the hypotenuse of the shadow (*palakarṇa*) and divided by *para*, is established as the proof.

Now, regarding the calculation of the shadow-hypotenuse (*chāyākarṇa*) from the sine of declination (*krāntijyā*) for the purpose of equalizing the gnomon-shadow (*samaśaṅku*) in the *Samamaṇḍana*: having established the equal gnomon as previously stated, it is proven that the shadow-hypotenuse is indeed obtained by multiplying it with the radius (*bhāvaravyaya*). This is established as stated [in the verse]: (2) "Having divided... the *itālīyaka*. Here, twelve is the hypotenuse, the shadow is the base (*bhuja*), and the gnomon is the side. As stated on page 1258 for the first case and on page 369 for the second case, this is logically proven. The rest is clear from the source text. (2) Now, regarding the other methods for those who desire to calculate the shadow and so forth.

Bhaṭṭa Sampātamegha, page 181, verse 18; Ākāśa, page 215, verse 12; Siddhāntatattvaviveka, verse 18: "The entire *vāsanā* [explanatory commentary] on the *Yākarṇa-karṇa* [the hypotenuse of the ear]. 19. The small shadow-area (*chāyākṣetra*) is reduced by the factor of *cūcaka*. In that [reduction], the gnomon (*śaṅku*) is the perpendicular (*koṭi*), the sine of the zenith-distance (*dṛgjyā*) is the base (*bhuja*), and the radius (*trijyā*) is the hypotenuse (*karṇa*); this is the shadow-area of the pole-star. That by which this is to be reduced is the same for all three."

If the gnomon is reduced by one-twelfth [of itself], then that same [proportion] applies to all three; if it is twelve, then it applies to all three as well. From the reduction of the radius (trijyā) by the hypotenuse of the shadow (chāyākarṇa), if it is the hypotenuse of the shadow, then it applies to all three. From the reduction of the sine of altitude (dṛgjyā) by one-sixth of the shadow, if it is the shadow, then it applies to all three. Thus it is understood: that which is one-twelfth of the gnomon is the same as one-sixth of the radius in relation to the hypotenuse of the shadow, and that very same [proportion] is one-sixth of the sine of altitude in relation to the shadow.

Now, the arm (*bhuja*) is the segment of the east-west line, the perpendicular (*koṭi*) is the gnomon-shadow (*chāyā*), and the hypotenuse (*karṇa*) is the radius (*ijyā*). Thus, the Buddha-field (the circle) is reduced by the twelfth part of the radius; in place of the radius, the arm belonging to the shadow-hypotenuse circle is stated. Depending on whether the addition or subtraction of the *agrā* (latitude) parts occurs during this reduction, the shadow-hypotenuse should be calculated. However, when reduced by the twelve [parts] of the gnomon-shadow, the arm is the twelfth part of the gnomon-shadow, and the gnomon is the perpendicular.

When the *ka* is subtracted, the resulting value becomes the hypotenuse of the shadow (*chāyākarṇa*) through reduction by a tenth part; its square root is the shadow itself. Even after reduction by a tenth part, that [shadow] would be the hypotenuse of the shadow-circle. Therefore, the arm (*bhuja*) of the shadow-hypotenuse must be derived precisely from the correction of the *agrā* (the sine of the altitude) belonging to the shadow-hypotenuse circle. Since the shadow is in the opposite direction, the arm—which is obtained by reversing the five parts—is clearly greater than the shadow measured from the east-west line of the celestial sphere. And thus it is said: "And this is the circle."

Having established one's own location as the center, just as the horizon is a circle, so too is the circle of the celestial equator (takakendrādivṛtta) a circle produced by the sine (śiñji). Therein, when the sun is situated in the eastern direction, the shadow-mark (chāyāgra) will be situated in the western direction; when the sun is situated in the western direction, the shadow-mark will be situated in the eastern direction. Thus, it is clear that the entry of the shadow is at the western mark and its exit is at the eastern mark. On the circle of the equatorial plane (samamaṇḍala), there is a single line from east to west.

The lines that run equally spaced from south to north are also of the same nature as the east-west lines of the equatorial circle (samavṛtta); for the observer, with respect to each respective location, perceives the sun situated on the equinox exactly as if it were positioned on the east-west line of the equator. Now, here, it is established that from a fixedly assumed western point, the eastern point of emergence [of the sun] lies at an equal interval from the east-west line of that equator. This is because the sun moves according to the direction of its solstice.

For the sun moving toward the north when situated in the western direction, the shadow-tip moves eastward along the line of equal altitude (*samasūtra*). Wherever it has moved from that point, because the tip of the shadow moves in the opposite direction, there are two lines drawn obliquely on the circle from the east-west points of the equatorial circle (*samavṛtta*) to the respective eastern marks; these are the directional sines (*digjye*) at the times of entry and exit, and their arcs are the degrees of those respective directions. On the circle, these extend from the respective eastern mark to the east-west points.

On the shadow-plane (śayāpīṭha), when the base (bhuja) is established according to the measure of the hypotenuse (śaku) and the shadow (chāyā), then the base of the chord (jyāyabhuja) corresponding to the shadow-hypotenuse (chāyotkarṇa) is equal to the radius (trijyā). For the purpose of converting these into arcs on that circle, one must apply the radius as the scale. Thus, the base of the chord corresponding to the shadow-hypotenuse becomes equal to the product of the shadow and the radius divided by the hypotenuse; this is established as stated.

If it is asked: "How is it that there is an equal interval between the rising points of the centers of the many sūtras established daily through their prior and posterior movements of entry and exit, even though they are situated on the equator? Listen: although they are not actually equidistant when located very close together, they are treated as being equidistant for this purpose. Just as when two vertical lines are held by the hands, or when two gnomons are placed in such a way within the center of a circle, even though they are not truly equidistant, they appear equidistant to the eye.

Just as, even though the two gnomons (*śaṅku*) and their two shadows (*chāyā*) are not at equal intervals, they appear to be at equal intervals to the observer; or just as, for example, in the case of the gnomon and shadow of a commoner (*vṛṣala*) and a low-caste person (*laghu-śaṅku*), although there is a difference in shadow due to the lack of connection with their respective castes, yet to each person's own perception it appears as if the shadow were the same—understand that here too it is so. This is the *Upapatti-vāsanā* (explanatory rationale) of the *Siddhānta-dīpikā*.

21. Here, the hypotenuse (*karṇa*) consists of the distance in *yojanas* from the center of the terrestrial globe (*kupṛṣṭhabimba-kendra*) to the point where the line from the center of the earth (*garbhadrksūtra*) meets the surface; the base (*bhuja*) is likewise in *yojanas*, and the perpendicular (*koṭi*) is the distance in *yojanas* from the center of the earth to the surface of the terrestrial globe. In this right-angled triangle on the surface of the earth, the hypotenuse is the line from the center of the earth; the square root of the sum of the squares of the other two sides is the clear circumference of the terrestrial globe at that point.

The sūtra reaching from the point on the surface of the earth to the zenith of the opposite side is the *bhuja* (base), extending as far as the diameter of the earth in *yojanas*. The *garbha-sūtra* is the *karṇa* (hypotenuse). From the curved surface of the earth to the point of contact, the *koṭi* (perpendicular) is formed; the square of the *karṇa* minus the square of the *koṭi* results in the square root which is designated as the *pṛṣṭha-dvaka-sūtra*. Thus, what was stated is established. Now, [the explanation of] the method for determining one's own location using the celestial instrument (*golayantra*).

If the gnomon previously established by the maximum equinoctial shadow (*krāntyaṃtakrāma*) is calculated using the maximum declinational sine (*parakrāntyutkramajyā*), then it would belong to that [other] location. At midday, the hypotenuse is always the radius (*trijyā*) when the gnomon-shadow is the perpendicular (*koṭi*). What would the hypotenuse be when the gnomon-shadow is the perpendicular? It would be another [value]. In that case, even the gnomon-shadow would be understood as being maximally equal to the radius; thus, the maximum declination and the gnomon are held such that one's own location possesses the maximum amplitude (*adhikānti*).

In whatever part of one's own country this [latitude] is greater than another, it is said to be "superior" (*para*); that [distance] is measured as six *danda*s, which is the maximum extent. Now, for the purpose of determining the gnomon-shadow: having placed a stick (*yaṣṭi*) made of *kujana* or *palāśa* wood, from the center of the circle situated at its tip, one should apply the *dyujyā* (cosine of latitude). From the point where the sine attached to that [circle] touches the ground, up to that center, the midday gnomon shall be determined. By the proportion: "If the radius (*trijyā`) is the hypotenuse, what is the perpendicular (*koṭi`)?", then by the same proportion, "if the *dyujyā` is the hypotenuse, what is the [perpendicular]? [the result is obtained].

In this case, the sine of the arc situated where the chord (jyā) attached to that [latitude] meets the circumference (nemi) shall be the same as the sine of the arc situated on the cloth (paṭī), once it has been converted from the radius (trijyā). Since the hypotenuse (karṇa) was established at the tip of the gnomon (yaṣṭi-koṭhe) for the purpose of calculating the shadow, that cloth is designated by the term *dinapa*. Thus, what was stated is proven. Now, the derivation of the *parakuñcā* (the sine of the maximum declination): the sine of the maximum declination (12; 19) multiplied by the *palabhā* (equatorial shadow at local latitude) and divided by twelve shall be the *parakuñcā*.

In that case, since the shadow obtained from the calculation involving the *spaṣṭa-yaśa* (corrected declination) is the result, it is established that this [shadow] is equal to the product of the radius (*trijyā*) and the sine of the latitude (*akṣajyā*). That same [shadow], when multiplied by the desired day-sine (*iṣṭadyujyā*), would be the desired sine of the ascensional difference (*carajyā*). That [desired sine of the ascensional difference] would be the sine of the latitude (*akṣajyā*) divided by the radius (*trijyā*). In that context, having assumed the maximum sine of the ascensional difference (*paramacarajyā*) itself as the product of the radius and the desired day-sine, it was calculated as being multiplied by the sine of the co-latitude (*dojyā*) and divided by the radius; for there is no difference in the resulting value.

However, that [distance] is not actually the parācarajyā; for its determination is accomplished by the jyā itself. It is established, therefore, that it is employed merely for the purpose of calculating the *parācarajyā*. Now, [regarding] "the rising of the sky" (*khodaya*): the time of the sun's depression or elevation is known from the instrument. Having determined the sun’s depression or elevation on the ecliptic using the instrument, one should take the distance along the dial-plate from the point touched by the sine of the depression (*natajyā*) to the center; this shall be the desired other [value]. In the case of the gnomon’s end, if the hypotenuse is equal to the radius (*trijyā`), then what is it when the gnomon is the side? This is determined by proportion.

The thread [drawn] from the center along the latitude-line (paṭṭī) according to the sequence of the sphere (golakrama), added to or subtracted from the ascensional difference (cara), shall be the sūtra. Having thus fixed the thread on the circle and holding the instrument, wherever that thread touches the rim (nemī) of the circle—whether above or below—that is the arc of the bow (cāpāṃśa). These are the degrees of the time of altitude (unnatakāla-bhāga) on the equatorial circle (kharātravṛtta) above the prime vertical (unmaṇḍala). Due to the sequence of the sphere, they are [calculated] from the local horizon (svaśitija) as being added to or subtracted from the ascensional difference. Therefore, for the purpose of the correction involving the ascensional difference, it is stated that "the ascensional difference is obtained"; the rest is clear.

The *Natakalaśa* [is] easy to understand through its reverse order. Here, in all cases, according to the statement of the *Tripraśna-gaṇita*, that which exists in the calculation of the *carārdha* is the measure (*pramāṇa*). Having made the product and the multiplier clear by means of zero (*khacchaya*), the result is clear; thus, by proportion (*anupāta*) on the instrument, the results are as stated for the verse (1) 157, the previous (388), the verse (1) 198, and the verses 404–406 of the previous [section].

(3) On page 155, verse 400 of the *Śokasya* (1); on page 155, verse 411 of the *Dhokasya* (1); and from page 100, verse 1 to 424 of the *Ākānām-asiddhāntatattvaviveka*, the establishment [of these] is clear to those who know the sphere of astronomy (*golavid*). Now, regarding the author of the *Bīdhikāra*, the underlying rationale (*vāsanā*) is clearly stated here and there.

In the case of a universal eclipse (sārvabhauma), where the circumference of the disc is eclipsed, the point where the center of the shadow (bimba) lies is the center of the world-circle (viśvanemi), and where the center is located is the middle of the disc. The line joining these two points is the chord of the full arc situated on the shadow-path; it is the full sine-line (jīvāsūtra) of that arc. Thus, when the day is divided into two such arcs, their sum shall be the disc in its measure of minutes.

In that case, it was observed that the method is simply to multiply that [radius] by four to obtain the diameter. Therein, the calculation of the radius (*karṇa*) of the full earth-circumference, measured at twenty-one thousand *yojanas*, is stated as follows: "The radius of the sun and moon's apogees, multiplied by the sine of the argument (*koṭijyā*) and the trijyā (radius of the celestial sphere), is divided by the respective semi-chord of the epicycle (*calakhaṇḍakarṇa*) and the trijyā. The product of the other semi-chords arising from the central terrestrial radius and the divisor, when reduced to minutes of arc, is the measure of the orb. However, in reality:

The statement that the trijyā (radius of the celestial sphere) is derived from the clear calculation of the sacrifice (*yajana*), and that the arc obtained by dividing the difference between the terrestrial diameter and the [celestial] orb by four is multiplied by four—how can this be? This is my objection. Now, when the orb is seen to be greater than the midday [measurement], the method stated by Saira is as follows: One should divide the degrees of the oblique ascension (*dikṣepa*) by the result of the day-measurement at sunrise; those [results] are indeed the unblemished [values]. One [unit] is marked by three *kalās* at sunrise, and by four *kalās* at midday; the difference between them is one *kanna*.

One *kalā* is obtained by dividing a day by 60. What is obtained by multiplying that by eight? Thus, by the rule of three, the effort [required] in the abode of *kalās* for three days would be half a day; however, since that is indeed a full day, it is added to the time of rising and divided by sixty to yield the *kalās*. From those, one *aṅgula* is determined; thus, in the case of the planets, the measures in *aṅgulas* are to be calculated at that time. (1) Now, when the lunar disc is smaller than the solar disc, the shadow—due to its influence—assumes a shape such as a complete circle, and so forth, resulting in the appearance of an eclipse.

The disc [of the moon] is visible when it lies within the line of sight, while other [objects] are invisible. When two rays of light, emerging from the solar disc and touching the spherical disc [of the moon], have equal velocities, and the observer's eye is situated there, a line drawn through that point along the path of those rays constitutes the line of sight. Because the discs of the moon and the sun lie on this same single line, and because the moon’s disc is larger than the shadow-tip of the sun at the point of the observer's eye, [the moon] eclipses the sun.

Because the shadow-tip is situated on the surface of the [celestial] sphere and the circle of the ear is marked by the *ḍaka* [point], and because the lunar disc is of such a nature, it is very clear that the lower disc would be obscured by the sun due to the excessive force of conviction. Those who, out of a desire to reject the discus [of the moon] as being contrary to the scriptures, do not perceive the maker of the night [the moon] as clearly manifest—[their view is flawed]. Now, in the section on light (*prabhādhikāra*), follows the rule for calculating the shadow on the celestial sphere. The distance in *yojanas* between the centers of the spheres of the sun’s and the observer’s discs, each situated within its own sphere, is the "line of interval between the discs" (*bimbāntarasūtra*).

Just as on the terrestrial globe, here too the difference between the centers of the orbs (*bimbāntara*) is the base (*bhuja*), the line connecting the centers of the orbs is the hypotenuse (*karṇa*), and the square root of the difference of their squares is the perpendicular (*koṭi*); by this very proportion, the calculation of the shadow is well-established. Now, the difference between the true Sun and the Moon, known as *spaṣṭa*, which is useful for determining the line connecting the centers of the orbs, is stated; its rationale is as follows: the Moon and the Sun are situated upon the ecliptic (*krāntivṛtta*).

On the arc of the planet's longitude (*bhoga*), there is the solar disc; above that disc is a circle with a radius equal to the trigonometric sine (*trijyā*). Therein, the distance between the centers of those two discs is the *spaṣṭārcā* (apparent arc), which serves as the hypotenuse (*karṇa*). The difference between the planet's longitude and the sun is the base (*bhuja*) on the ecliptic (*bhavṛtta*), while the latitude (*śara*) is the second base on the *kadambavṛtta*. However, the *bakaśāvṛtta* is the equator of declination (*krāntivṛtta*); there, the solar disc is at that point [of intersection] (221° 15′ for the Śrīkās; 224° 5′ 15″ for the Auokās).

On page 217, line 126, regarding the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka* of Dhoka: 24. [The term] *doṣavāsanā*. 25. It should be understood that this is due to the connection with the *katrikugarbhaka-sūtra*. In the *Cāpaśānya*, the correction known as *sphuṭa*—the difference between the [true] apsis and the [mean] apsis—is easily understood through the method for calculating the radius (*karṇa*). Here, because it is separated from the sun by the distance of the [true] apsis relative to the *kadamba*, when situated in the first quadrant (*prathamapada*), the true anomaly (*spaṣṭāya*) will be situated solely in the first quadrant.

In the second quadrant, however, its accomplishment is through *saṣajhrkatat* (the addition of the correction), as stated by Cakreśvara; for it is necessary to understand that [the correction] is due to being separated by the sun (*arkāntaritatvena*). Likewise, in the third [quadrant], it is joined with *bhāīṃ*, and in the fourth, it is said to be diminished. When the *ejapada* (the point of Aries) is reached, because of the separation from the sun, the true [longitude] is increased; when equal, it is decreased. Thus, to whatever extent the difference in the arm (*bhuja*) exists, to that same extent is the difference in the perpendicular (*koṭi*), which also accords with what was stated as "by the interval between the sky and the perpendicular" (*kha koṭyorvivareṇa*).

Now, when the Sun is below the horizon, the circle of the trijyā (radius) passing through those two points is the base (*bhuja*) in *yojanas*. The difference between that and the true [distance] is the result in *yojanas*. When the argument (*kendra*) is in Capricorn and so forth, it should be subtracted from the true difference; when in Cancer and so forth, it should be added to the Sun’s radius (*ravikarṇa*). The square root of the sum of those two is the hypotenuse (*karṇa*). The difference between the light and the shadow is the side (*pakṣa*). If they are reversed, the result should be understood as such. Now, it is stated otherwise: the distance between the centers of the discs of the Moon and the Sun situated in their respective spheres is the base.

It is so. Having calculated the *yojanas* by means of the intervals between the east-west line and the arms (*bhuja*), one should then determine the clear arm (*spaṣṭabhuja*) as either the difference or the sum of those intervals, depending on whether they are of the same or different directions. Likewise, having calculated the clear hypotenuse (*koṭi*) in *yojanas* and so forth from the difference or sum of the corresponding perpendiculars (*koṭi*), the square root of their sum should be taken as the hypotenuse (*karṇa*). A distance equal to that, in *yojanas* and so forth, shall be the interval between the enemy's base and [one's own] position on the earth.

Because the gnomon is situated at equal intervals from the lunar disc up to the horizon, that very lunar sphere is the side (bhuja) designated as "first" (ādya). When the sum of the verticals (ūrjādharaikya) is in the opposite direction, the difference between the two is the other side (koṭi) designated as "second" (anya). The square root of the sum of their squares is the line of interval between the two (viśvāntarasūtra), which is the hypotenuse (karṇa); thus it is established. (1) According to Bhāskarācārya, by those sines of depression (natajyās) for which the shadow would be equal to the gnomon (śaṅku), the method of understanding this is as follows: on the back-gnomon (pṛṣṭhaśaṅku), the measure of the sine (jyāpramāṇa) is exactly equal to that shadow.

Let *yā* (the unknown) be one unit. The segment (*kukhaṇḍa*) multiplied by the radius of the circle (*trijyā*) and divided by the hypotenuse of the sun's ray (*ravikarṇa*) becomes the sine of the obscured portion (*channajyā*). This, when added to the gnomon (*śaṅku*), becomes the "central gnomon" (*garbhaśaṅku*: *ka* = 1, *yā* = *ka*). The square of this, when added to the square of the sine of the obscured portion (*irajyā*), becomes the square of the radius of the circle (*trijyāvarga*: *ka* = 1, *yāva* = *ka*, *va*). Since the square of the radius (*triḥ* = *kuba* + *ghi* = *va* = 1) is equal to the square of the radius, these two sides are equivalent. Thus, the two sides of the equation are: *ka* = 1, *yāva* = *ka*, *va* = 1, *triḥ* = *kuba* + *ghi* = *va*. These are the two sides of the equation.

Let *ka* be 1. Let *yā* be such that *yā* + 1 = *ku*. Then, having formed the product of the squares of the radius of the circle (*trijyā*) and the cube of the side of the triangle (*kukhaṇḍa*), and divided by three times the square of the difference (*ba*), the equation is established by taking the square roots of those two values and equating them; thus, what was stated is indeed proven. This is the proof for the calculation of the "back-gnomon" (*pṛṣṭhaśaṅku*) according to the ancients. The moments of motion (*gatikalā*) are always [determined] by the yojanas of motion, when the numerator and denominator are reduced by a common factor using half the circumference (*kudala*).

In the opinion of others, ten degrees have been obtained; therefore, according to that view, the degrees of the lunar day (*tithyaṃśa*) of the motion (*gatitithyaṃśa*) are the terrestrial obscuration (*kucchannaka*). The shadow behind (*pṛṣṭhachāyā*) would be the difference between that and the degrees of the obscured part (*ga'aśa*); thus it is established. (1) Now, in order to demonstrate the nature of the single horn (*ekashṛṅgākṛti*) as if on the same celestial sphere (*ekagola*), the following is shown: A single thread should be drawn from the center of the disc-sphere (*vimbagolaka*) at the point of observation (*hakacihna*) to the edge of its circumference. That point where the thread touches the other side of the disc-sphere should be known as the center of the visible sky (*dṛgyaviśvakendra*).

That which is the point of intersection on the horizon (lagna) is the center of the invisible hemisphere of the sphere. From those two points, the circle drawn through them and the four cardinal points is the visible-invisible meridian (dṛśyādṛśya-bimba-nemivṛtta) of that globe. The small circle passing through the zenith and the center of the sphere's globe intersects the surface of that globe at a certain point; the circle drawn from that point to the center of the visible and invisible hemispheres, situated within the sphere of the image, would be the small circle of visibility (dṛśya-ṛkṣuṇḍala). There, at the junction with the meridian circle, the vertical circle (ūrdhvavṛtta) should be conceived.

Now, those two circles which are drawn through the centers of the Sun and Moon—namely, the vertical circle and the horizontal circle—should also be constructed upon the orb-sphere (*bimba-gola*). At the intersection of these two with the prime vertical circle (*tanemivṛtta*), a horizontal mark should be made; likewise, the interval between them along the prime vertical circle on the orb-sphere is one-fourth [of the diameter]. Now, when that horizontal circle conforms to the ecliptic (*krāntivṛtta*), then the line of the interval between the centers of the lunar and solar orbs is horizontal... [as stated in] verse 49–50 on page 225 [of the first part], and verse 43 on page 236 [of the second part]. This is the explanation for the remainder (*śeṣavāsanā*). 27.

The *garu* (the gnomon-circle) itself becomes the *siddhāntatattvaviveka* (the circle of truth); from that, the *bimba-gola* (orb of the image) is given as a fourth part, and that *arka-vṛtta* (sun-circle) would be at its end. At the time of the new moon (*amā*), the *tarka-vṛtta* (reasoning-circle) is the *nemi-vṛtta* (rim-circle), and thus the visible form lacks the shape of a parrot (*śuka*). To the extent that the sun is obscured by the moon, to that same extent the *arka-vṛtta* becomes attached to the upper mark, separated from the *nemi-vṛtta* by a transverse circle. The visible orb becomes a parrot-shaped fragment equal to that interval.

The middle point between the two *śṛṅga* (peaks) is the highest. From there, on both sides, there is a decrease until the base (*śṛṅga*). In the calculation of the segments of duration (*sthiti-khaṇḍa*) during a lunar eclipse, the arm (*bhuja*) is the arrow (*śara*), the difference between the hypotenuses (*koṭi*) is the segment, and the hypotenuse (*karṇa*) is the sum; from these, the derivation of the segments of duration is easily understood through all the methods for calculating the arm in this right-angled triangle (*cāpajāti*). (1) Regarding "originating from light" (*jyotiḥ-prabhava*): at sunrise, because of the impact [of light], the sky appears as if it were below; therefore, even when this [sun] is in the middle of the sky, it appears so due to the greater intensity of the impact.

Therefore, the difference between the two small differences [of the longitudinal parallax] at the respective zenith distances is calculated by the proportion: "If this difference corresponds to these zenith distances, what would it be for those [other] zenith distances? This result, when added to the interval between the rising and setting points, becomes the observed difference between the visible and invisible portions of the orbs. Thus it is established that when half of that is eclipsed, the eclipsed portion cannot be perceived by men. Just as the method for calculating total parallax according to Bhāskara’s system has been clearly stated in the *Yārkagavaṇa*, so too is it here in the case of the parallax of the sky. The sine of the amplitude is divided by the product of the sine of the latitude and the correction for parallax.

In this case, the result obtained by dividing the radius by the koti-jya (the sine of the complement) of the sun’s heliacal setting is not to be assumed as the final value. Rather, following the method of the *aphalīyakakṣā-pratiyukti* (the calculation of the apsis-line), one should calculate the parallax using the anomaly (*kendra*) derived from the difference between the true and mean positions of the sun and moon. According to the *Tattvaviveka*, that parallax will be the correct value when calculated according to the first method. Now, regarding the calculation of the displacement of the moon’s node (*candradvakkṣepasādhanam*), it has been stated by Marīci at the end of his work that the very clear and well-founded reasoning is found in the *Siddhāntasārvabhauma*. Therefore, even though it is in the *Sārvabhauma*, that reasoning should be understood by the wise.

(2) Now, according to the opinion of Devarṣi, the rationale for the drawing of the Moon and Sun [is as follows]: When there is no *śara* (latitude), the Moon is at its conjunction, and its orb is at that same point on the ecliptic. However, when there is a true deflection (*valana*), the difference between the two points on the ecliptic arises from proportionality. On the circle of half the sum of the diameters, the distance between the two points on the directions of the ecliptic and the meridian—measured along the lines drawn from the center of the Moon’s orb—is the [deflection] on that circle. Those two lines are indeed the lines of the directions of the equator and the meridian on that circle.

In that case, the circle of the inhabited world (*bhūvṛtta*) is real, whereas the equal circle (*samavṛtta*) is imaginary. Here, when the moon is at the zenith (*viśva*), from the center of the lunar disc along the line marked by its direction on the circle of the sum of the [sine] segments, [the distance] is as stated in verses 50–55 on pages 250–251; in verse 37 on page 344; in verses 366–367 on page 366–367; and in verse 36 on page 275 of the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*. One should draw two lines parallel to the lines marked by the directions of the moon and the sun.

In that deceptive [circle] which resembles the respective directional sūtras, there exists within it a certain clear statement. Therefore, in the lunar sphere, one should know that the circle passing through the center of the moon’s disc—which corresponds to the sūtra at the interval of the rotation of the signs of the directions—is not visible. For some reason, that circle is not perceived; this is because, by its presence, the position of the moon on the earth would be untenable. However, by means of a thread perpendicular to that similar sūtra, the actual point (cihna) exists, which is always suitable for the location of the moon on the earth.

If it is asked: "Why has this not been stated here by way of the equation of the center (kujavalana) itself?"—the answer is as follows: Even when two directions are assumed on the horizon, there exists a circle passing through the centers of the images of the objects being grasped, fixed by some observer, which is clearly defined by the radii reaching the centers of the images on one's own celestial sphere (*svakāśagola*). One such circle is the *bhuvṛtta* (terrestrial circle), whose radii are everywhere equal and parallel to the *śara* (latitude/deflection), and which resembles the circle of declination (*krāntivṛtta*). The second is indeed the *dṛgvṛtta* (visual circle).

The first [result] is the arc of the segment of the sum of the sines (mānaikyakhaṇḍavṛtta) on the circle of declination (krāntivṛtta); the second is the arc of the segment of the sum of the sines on the circle of the interval between the declination and the similar circle (sadṛśavṛtta), which has a radius equal to the diameter of the disc (bimba). The interval between the circles of the segments of the sum of the sines on the oblique circle (durvṛtta) is the diameter of the disc. On the circle of the disc (doṣavṛtta), the sine of the latitude (sphuṭakakṣepa) from the zenith to the point of declination is the base (bhuja); the sine of the disc’s own latitude is the hypotenuse (karṇa), and its corresponding cosine on the similar circle is the perpendicular (koṭi). From this proportion, the first result is established within the interval of the diameter of six signs (ṣaḍaṅgula-vyāsa).

Otherwise, the arrow (*śara*) is the base (*bhuja*), the sum of the sines of the latitudes (*mānaikyakhaṇḍa*) is the hypotenuse (*karṇa*), and the sine of the latitude (*koṭi*) is equal to that; thus, the knowledge [of this] is easily understood. In the case of the solar eclipse, a proportion (*anupāta*) is made based on the latitude arising from the same class [of calculation], such as: "If the latitude at the point of visual parallax (*dṛgalambana*) is so much, then what would it be for a distance of six *aṅgulas*? Another [proportion] is: "If the true latitude corrected by the declination is so much, then what would it be for the moon? Thus, the circle of the sine of the latitude from the *kadamba* (celestial pole) is similar to the moon’s declination; however, in the solar eclipse, the circle of the sine of the latitude is the circle of the arrow (*śaravṛtta*).

In whichever direction the circle of the apparent path (*dṛgvṛtta*) lies, another [circle] lies in that same direction. The circle of the sum of the sines of the latitudes (*i-vṛtta-mānaikya-khaṇḍa-vṛtta*), which is the circle of the correction for declination (*haravalana*), lies in the direction of that [apparent path]; thus, the clear observation of what is within the field of vision is established. (1) Now, the rationale for calculating the parallax in longitude (*halambana*): In the celestial sphere of the lower planet's orbit, the point where the line from the center of the earth meets the ecliptic and the point of the planet's true motion—whatever the distance between these two is, that is the parallax in longitude.

For the purpose of knowing that [latitude], having constructed a point (*cihuṃ*) on the horizontal meridian line (*dṛksūtra*) at the position of the moon, the perpendicular from it to the horizon is the *nata* (zenith distance), and the arc below it is the *natajyā* (sine of the zenith distance). From the point marked *ha*, the sine of the zenith distance (*natajyā*) exists as a vertical line within the sphere; however, from the central axis (*garbhasūtra*), there is a line drawn horizontally toward the center of the sky.

Now, even if a single thread touches the mark of the *kugarbha* (the earth's center) and extends upward to the limit of the celestial sphere (*ūrdhagola*), this [shadow] remains in the form of a side-arm (*bhuja*) despite being drawn downward by gravity; for, due to the non-perception of the true ecliptic circle within the interval of the forty-five *śoka*s, that [calculation] is untenable. Furthermore, even the solar disc situated in its own space is seen at a distance from the lunar space.

Therefore, from the two lines marked by the directions on the prime vertical (bhavṛtta) and the meridian (atyabhavṛtta), another line of direction-marking should be drawn at the same interval as the latitude (natya). At the intersection of those two, the center of the celestial sphere (kaibimbakendra) is located; there, using those measurements, the segments of the equator (kyakhaṇḍa) should be made if they exceed [the required length]. Between those two, there is a deflection (balana), which has been described there as being caused by the interval between the meridian and the point of the horizon. That line of direction-marking, separated by half the equator from the meridian, is the line resembling the prime vertical (bhavṛtta) for the observer’s location relative to the visible sun.

The ecliptic and a line parallel to it passing through the Moon intersect at the point where the Moon is situated on the celestial sphere. The distance between these two is the *sparśarekhā* (line of contact). When the difference between the true latitude and the latitude derived from the first method is equal to the difference between the true latitudes, their sum on the circle of half the sum of the diameters (*mānaikyakhaṇḍavṛtta*) is the fixed position of the Moon's disc. Here, if the *valana* (deflection) line is assumed to be the ecliptic, then because the calculation of the true latitude would be untenable, the determination of the Moon's disc-position would be difficult; thus, everything stated by the author is proven.

The true nodes (pātas) occurring at night, when the Moon is near the meridian, are to be determined. Therein, when the true and mean longitudes of the Moon are equal, that is the time of the true node. According to the rule beginning with "multiplied by the trijyā for the sake of the declination," etc., even the absence of the difference between the arcs related to the sine is observed there; because the declinations would be equal, the time of the true node is then sought through the understanding of attaining proximity to that time, according to the sequence of whether the node is past or yet to come from that time, being separated by the arc [of the difference] either before or after.

The Moon is to be calculated; however, since its node (pāta) at that time is also [derived] from the Sun’s node, how can this be? For in your system, the motion of the Moon is established by the *anupāta* (proportionate calculation) based on the node alone, whereas the motion of the Sun and the node is derived from that [lunar motion]; thus, they would only be true for that specific moment.

Now, even here, in the absence of equality between the true and mean latitudes of the Moon and Sun, the Moon, Sun, and node must again be calculated at a time interval equal to the previously stated difference in arc; thus, by repeating this process until the subsequent occurrence of the node's time, that difference in arc becomes small. When that state occurs, because the two latitudes are equal, that very time is established as the true time of the node's occurrence; for the Moon is known to be separated from the node by that same difference in arc when the node is distant.

In the case of a *satva* (odd sign), when the difference between the apogee and the [longitude of] the planet is subtracted repeatedly until the result is zero, the fruit is indeed a single point of descent (*pāta-sthāna*). The method for calculating the elapsed and yet-to-be-traversed portions is as follows: in an odd sign (*ojapada*), there is an increase in declination (*krānti*) at the beginning and a decrease thereafter; in an even sign (*samapada*), there is a decrease at the beginning and an increase thereafter. By this, it is clear that in an odd sign, when the Moon is greater than the apogee, the declination is "elapsed" (*gata*), whereas in the opposite case, it is "yet-to-be-traversed" (*eṣya*); and in an even sign, it is the reverse.

In this context, at the point where the true declination (*spaṣṭakrānti*) is zero, it is appropriate that the direction of the true declination associated with the Moon at the commencement of the solstice (*saṅkrānti*) should indeed be the same as its own [mean] direction. Therefore, the true declination situated in the direction of the mean declination is the very *pada* (foot/position) of the Moon; if it is in the opposite direction, it is the other *pada*. The declination-sine (*krāntijyā*) is of two kinds—either when the Sun and Moon are in conjunction (*cakra*) or in opposition (*cakrārtha*)—and it is established by the authority of the sages that it arises from their conjunction when they are situated on the equatorial circle (*viṣuvadvṛtta*).

The *antaraja* [conjunction] is not authoritative when it is not based on the words of a seer (*ārṣa*), but both are authoritative when the sun and moon are situated at the equinox (*viṣuva*) or the solstice (*ayana*), due to the authority of the seers’ words. The *yogaja* [conjunction] is produced by virtue of the moon and sun being situated on opposite sides of the equatorial circle (*viṣuvavṛtta*). The *antaraja* [conjunction] is said to occur by virtue of the moon and sun being situated on the same side. It is clear that the knower of conjunctions (*yogajña*) calls it *yogaja* when they are on the same side, and *antaraja* when they are on opposite sides. (1) Now, the rationale for the question and answer: the radius (*trijyā*), the latitude (*akṣabhā*), and the declination (*natī*).

When the gnomon is situated on the equinoctial circle (*viṣuvavṛtta*), the shadow there is zero; consequently, the base (*bhuja*) is equal to that [radius], because of the absence of the hypotenuse (*āyā*). However, on the shadow-attraction circle (*chāyākarṣavṛtta*), which consists of the *palabhā*, if the radius (*trijyā*) is the hypotenuse when the base is the radius of the celestial sphere (*dijyā*), then what is the hypotenuse when the base is the *palabhā*? The result is the difference between the tip of the base and the center of the gnomon.

How is the desired palabhā obtained from that? Then, by the proportion "if the palabhā is the base, what is the trijyā?", the arc of the resulting desired akṣajyā is the desired akṣāṃśas. These are the degrees of obliquity between the equator situated at the zenith and the equinoctial circle. Between the equinoctial point and the desired [latitude], the degrees of declination are the natīśās within the interval between the zenith and the equinox. The squares of the segments of this [arc] are expressed by these terms: *trijya* (the square of the radius), *bruvaḥ* (the square of the sine), *vaga-gaṇa* (the square of the cosine), and *dyajyā-vaga-bhaktaḥ* (divided by the square of the sine). The square of the chord (*sūtra-varga*) is given by: *yāva avanava1 aśaṃtri triyaśavatrivava1*. The lower term is in the place of the unmanifest group; on page 365, verses 23–25 are for the *cakras*; on pages 365–366, verses 26–27 are for the two *yogas*; on page 368, verse 43 is for the *śloka*; and verse 42 is the remainder of the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*. 43. e.

The square of the divisor multiplied by the string (jyā) is negative and placed in the position of the dividend; the square of the unknown (avyakta) is positive and placed above the square of the constant (akṣaya). Therefore, by subtracting the negative from the positive, their sum indeed results in that which is termed *cara*. When the two sides are equal, by dividing them, the square of the known becomes distinct and negative in the northern declination (*saumya*), while in the southern (*yāmya*) it is positive. There, for the sake of equalizing the two sides, the declination-sine (*krāntijyā*) is clearly obtained as stated for both the southern and northern cases.

Sometimes, in the northern hemisphere, that [result] may be of two kinds; if it were not so, it would be impossible due to its nature as an unmanifested posterior operation. Now, among those of the same genus (*sajātīya*), one should assume the sum of the arms (*bhuja*) as the arm, the sum of the sides (*koṭi*) as the side, and the sum of the hypotenuses (*karṇa*) as the hypotenuse; whatever is thus produced is also of that same genus, and is to be sought through the proportion of the same genus. Here, even the knowledge of the arms, sides, and hypotenuses through the sum of two [elements] by means of the sum of three is produced by proportion; for those who know this, the proof of the "same-genus" and so forth is indeed established. (1) Regarding the phrase "of the two stars":

The proof for this is as follows: On the ecliptic (krāntivṛtta), at intervals from the beginning of Aries (meṣādi) equal to the respective polar longitudes (dhruvaka) of the constellations and their respective latitudes (śara), there exist respective points on the celestial sphere (kadambavṛtta). Among these, one is designated as the first (ādya) and the second as the other (anya). The maximum interval between the two points on the celestial sphere—corresponding to the first and last [constellations] on the ecliptic—is the difference between their respective polar longitudes.

When the interval between the two ears (the extremities of the radius) is equal to the tip of the autumnal bow of another *kadamba* circle, the distance between those two *kadamba* circles is the base (*bhuja*). That base is obtained through proportion from the difference between the known polar longitude (*dhruvaka*) and [the desired point]; its perpendicular (*koṭi*) is as follows: from the point situated at an interval of three signs (*tribhā*) on the circle of the first known degrees of the planet, up to whatever distance there is from the point designated as the *kendra*, that arc on the circle of sines (*tajyāvṛtta*) exists in the form of the hypotenuse (*karṇa*).

The other latitude (anyakṣa) is the arc situated between the circle of the trijyā and the circle arising from the quadrant, which is the interval between their respective hypotenuses. However, when the interval is three signs (90 degrees), that interval between those two is maximum; this is established by proportion. But the interval up to the point of the first longitude (ādyajña-bhoga)—where the equatorial circle and the celestial equator meet—is the interval up to the first latitude (ādyakṣa). Through the correction of the first latitude, there would be an interval up to the first shadow (ādyachāyā). From the union of those, however, in the interval of the previous arm (bhuja), there is the other latitude (anyakṣa); thus, through the union of those, when the arms and sides are mutually separated, they become the first and the other latitudes.

That distance between the two ends of the arc should be the trijyā-circle. Then, having determined that interval and making its center the zenith, one should mark that degree of altitude on the trijyā-circle in the visible hemisphere at another point; the difference in right ascension (viṣuvāṃśa) between those two points is the altitude of the other point on the diurnal circle. Then, the complement of that altitude on the declination circle (phalavṛtta) is the sine of the co-latitude; this should be calculated as the interval between the meridian and the east-west circle passing through the zenith and the nadir. This would be the interval in degrees.

Then, the cosine of the latitude (lambajyā) multiplied by the co-latitude of the meridian (digaṃśakoṭijyakā) and divided by the radius (tribhajyā) gives the latitude (akṣāṃśa) according to this method; this is easily understood. If you ask how, listen: The ninety-degree arc drawn from the intersection of the celestial equator (vṛtta-viṣuvavṛtta) and the prime vertical (svastika) toward the south, passing through the pole (dhruva), is perpendicular to the horizon (kṣitija). The sum of these two [arcs] forms a right angle (samacihna). From there, moving northward, at the ninety-degree interval is the location of the observer (akṣāṃśa); the distance between that point and the prime vertical (svastika) is the latitude (akṣa).

By the statement "the equatorial sphere" (*samamaṇḍala*), it is very clearly understood by the wise that the distance from the pole (*dhruva*) to the point on the horizon where the ecliptic intersects it is equal to the latitude (*akṣāṃśa*) of its own location; for here, what is called the "equatorial sphere" (*samamaṇḍala*) would be the horizon (*kṣitija*) relative to that place, and it is clear that the latitudes measured from the pole are indeed the same as those at the prime meridian. Now, if it is asked: "How is this so, given that the difference in the equinoctial midday shadow (*viṣuvat-śaṅku*) exceeds nine digits?"—the answer is: although the locations separated by six signs from one's own position differ, the horizon remains one and the same.

A constellation and a non-constellation exist within an interval of ninety degrees, and even within an interval of ninety minus that [interval], it exists as if separated by sixty. Since Mars and so forth are situated below the *dhruva* (pole), while other *dhruvas* are situated above, there is no inconsistency here because there is no difference between the degrees obtained through calculation and those established by tradition; thus, everything stated is logically consistent. (1) "The knower [is known] from the region of the knowable itself."

In this context, the other location is indeed the planet; [the calculation] of that [longitude] is on page 66 of the *Graha-karaṇa* (1.71). In the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, the determination of the shadow is as follows: the difference between the two locations is in degrees with parts (*sāṃśa*), while the degrees of direction (*dig-aṃśa*) are in whole degrees. Having understood the latitude (*ayanatāṃśa*) on the ecliptic through the sine of the zenith distance (*karṇa*) and the degrees of direction, one should divide by the sine of the degrees of direction. Then, having made the quotient of the division the hypotenuse (*dṛgjyā-karṇa*), the correction for the degrees of latitude (*akṣāṃśa*) results in the desired declination (*kānti*). Thus, the declination is calculated from the degrees of latitude.

[The calculation] would be defective for a location other than that [reference place]. This is clear from the source text regarding "the two places. (From one's own place by the degrees of the moon...): Here, the difference between the degrees of the other place and one's own place is the latitude (*lambāṃśa*). The difference in the degrees of the meridian is the meridian zenith distance (*nata*) on the diurnal circle. Then, having determined the declination (*kānti*) and the amplitude (*bhuja*) via the resulting *phalavṛtta* and the meridian zenith distance, and having known the amplitude derived from that, the degrees of azimuth (*dig-aṃśa*) are to be calculated.

The square root of the sum of the squares of the sines of the latitudes of the two places is the sine of the distance between them; the arc of that [sine] is the difference [in longitude], or otherwise it is clearly known by calculation. (2) Now, the proof for finding the right ascension (*samamaṇḍala*) and declination (*nata*): The point of intersection (*lagna*) is indeed the horizon; from there, the terrestrial equator becomes the celestial equator (*bhavṛtta*), which is the same as the ecliptic. Likewise, at three signs [90 degrees], the maximum distance is the greatest declination (*paramāpama*). From the intersection of the ecliptic and the celestial equator, the degrees of the triangle are those of the *yāmyottarīya* (meridian) circle.

In the case of the equinoctial circle (*samavṛtta*), the arc from the point of intersection (*kuja*) up to the meridian is the declination (*apamāṃśāḥ*). From the meridian up to the point where the ecliptic intersects the equator (*svastika*), the oblique ascensional difference (*viṣuvāṃśaḥ*) from the rising point (*lagna*) occurs. Or rather, by the rule "whatever is the arm (*bhuja*) is the arc of the [oblique] ascensions," those degrees of the sector (*kṣetrāṃśa*) are to be calculated as the hypotenuse (*śruti*) and arm (*bāhu*) of the right-angled triangle (*jāṃśāḥ*). Here, when the intersection of the equinoctial circle and the celestial sphere (*bhavṛtta*) lies at the end of the equal circle (*samacinnavṛtta*), the hypotenuse and arm are derived precisely from that intersection.

In that context, the *bhuja* (sine of the amplitude) is the sum of the remaining degrees of the ascendant (*adyavāhu*) and the degrees of the [ascendant] interval; its square root is the form of the *nagna*. The maximum difference and the decrease between the oblique-sphere (*bhavṛtta*) and the equatorial-sphere (*samavṛtta*) are stated as before by others, and the *śrutibāhu* (hypotenuse and sine) are to be calculated there. The *bhuja* at that point is established from the shadow of the gnomon (*śaṅkatalāṇa*). Whatever [correction] arises from the equatorial-sphere for the ascendant, when added to the form of the interval between the first house (*ādyabhāva*) and the tenth house (*daśama*), it becomes the house (*bhāva*). Here, the consideration of the proximity of the houses is very clear through the observation of examples; thus it is for those who know the method.

(1) Having indeed conceived the planet as being in the sky, [one considers] the "middle of the sky. Here, when the ascendant (*lagna*) is at three signs [90°] from the planet, then the *ayanavalana* (precession correction) sine does not exist, because it lies within the circle of declination (*krāntivṛtta*). This is as follows: the co-latitude sine (*lambajyā*) is the side and the radius (*trijyā*) is the hypotenuse; the declination sine (*krāntijyā*) is the side—what is the hypotenuse? Thus, here the co-latitude sine itself is the planet-sine (*grahajyā*), and the declination sine of the ascendant (*lagnakrāntijyā*). The sine of the planet at three signs [from the ascendant] is the result; this is exactly what was stated regarding the calculation of the *ayanavalana*. (2) Now, the rationale for the conjunction planet (*sandhigraha*).

The conjunction (*sandhi*) is the sum of the true ascendant and the true ecliptic point (*bhavṛtta*). From that limit, the conjunction and the ascendant follow the order of the signs starting from Aries (*meṣādi*) in direct sequence (*anuloma*). The difference between those two is the current *karṇa*. If the conjunction is situated in front of the ascendant, it is added to the *karṇa*; if it is situated behind the ascendant, the ascendant is subtracted from the *karṇa*. This will be the position of the conjunction. When the declination is south (*yāmya*), the conjunction is correctly [ahead] of the setting point; when the declination is north (*saumya*), the conjunction is behind the ascendant. In the case of the opposite [northern] declination, the conjunction is behind the ascendant. Thus, the derivation is established as stated.

(4) Now, regarding this point as it appears in the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi*: In the sphere (*gola*), there is a descending node (*pāta*) at the beginning of Aries and the other signs in the sky. That [node] is calculated from the junction of the Sun’s sphere (*arkagolasandhi*) by applying the correction for the retrograde precession (*vyastāyanāṃśa*). Rāhu, however, is calculated in the direct order (*anuloma*) from that same junction by applying the correction for the prograde precession (*kramāyanāṃśa*). Because these two occupy the same location, when the circle and half the circle are corrected by the retrograde precession, that becomes the junction of the Sun’s sphere starting from Aries. Likewise, the junction of the precession (*ayanasandhi*) also exists in that very sign.

The conjunction of the ecliptic and the equator is the *pāta*, which is Rāhu; it is situated ahead of the ecliptic in the direction of the north celestial pole (*saimyakadaṃba*), but behind it, it is fixedly situated in the direction of the south celestial pole (*yāmyakadaṃba*). Now, [the following verses appear]: (1) on page 379, line 138, of verse 1; (2) on page 379, line 142, of verse 2; (3) on pages 381, lines 151–152, of verses 3. (1) On pages 370, lines 77–78, of verses 1; (2) on pages 376, lines 111–112, of verses 2. In the supreme state of the junction of the *kaṅga* and *nasa*, the water is considered at night by those who possess discernment.

Just as it exists within that interval from Aries onwards when [the sphere] is rotated, so too does it exist constantly within that same interval from Aries onwards even when it is turned back (vivṛtta). Now, when turned back, at the point where the turned-back nāḍī intersects behind the mark of that degree, the junction of the lunar disc-sphere exists; in that turned-back state, the ear (karṇa) is within that interval. Thus, it would not be ahead in the second quadrant, nor would it be behind in the third quadrant, and it would be at the end in the fourth; this is clear in the sphere (gola).

In that context, the node (rāhu) moves along the middle of the ecliptic; where it is not displaced, there is no latitude (*śrava*). Where it is displaced, that very [displacement] is the ear (*karṇa*), and on the ecliptic, the interval between that and the [node] is the arm (*bhuja*); thus the *cāpa* (arc) is produced. Therein, for the purpose of calculation, there is a pentad of circles: the *kadamba*-circle, the celestial meridian (*dhruva*)-circle, the ecliptic (*kānti*)-circle, the displacement-circle (*vivṛtta*), and likewise the terrestrial horizon (*kṣitija*)-circle. From the point of the node (*pātasthāna*) on the *kadamba*-circle and the celestial meridian-circle, the oblique ascensional correction (*ayanavalana*) occurs at the horizon.

Its limit is the interval between the *krāntivṛtta* (ecliptic) and the *dhruvavṛtta* (celestial equator). This maximum interval, measured from the point of the apogee (*śara-śayana*), is obtained by subtracting the distance from the *pāta* (node) mark to the *dhruvavṛtta*. When held at the Earth's center, this maximum interval takes the form of the *krānti*; it is the junction of the forms of the *pāta* and the *gola* (sphere). Furthermore, that junction is the interval of that [circle], and its arc is also as stated.

Therefore, here, the equinoctial degrees (viṣuvāṃśa) are a certain fraction of those [degrees]; from them, the sides of the triangle are to be calculated by means of the *bāhu-jīvā* (sine of the base). The radius (*trijyā*) is the hypotenuse, and the sine of the maximum [latitude] is the base. Then, using the previously mentioned sine of the hypotenuse, let *ka* be the result; this is the sine of the arc between the equatorial plane and the pole-circle in the celestial sphere (*dhruvavṛtta*). Its arc is the base (*bhuja*), and that shall be the [latitude] of the place (*paśasya*). The same applies to the other positions as well.

Regarding the second and third terms, it has been stated that when followed by the word *śayana* (solstice), the maximum [latitude] occurs between those two; this determination was made based on their positions in the *rāyapuṃgaka* and other [tables]. At the node (*pāta*), the maximum declination (*śara*) lies within the ecliptic (*vivṛtta-krāntivṛtta*). However, at the tip of the radius (*karṇāgra*), the declination—which is established through proportion—is perpendicular to the ecliptic.

Who indeed possesses the deceptive mode of life? That one alone is the enjoyer of knowledge (*jñānabhuja*). Having calculated that which exists from the point of the equinoctial arc (*viṣuvāṃśa*)—the place of the fall of the spheres—to the limit of the zodiacal circle (*arkagocara*), how can one determine it? From that and the ear (the hypotenuse), a second side consisting of the arc is established on the ecliptic (*krāntivṛtta*). That would be the difference between the junction of the sphere resulting from the calculation today and the junction situated at the sun.

When the Sun is situated within six signs from the stated point of intersection (saṅkrānti), the [longitude of] the Moon should be added to the Sun’s solstitial point (golasaṃdhi); however, if it exceeds six signs, the [longitude of the Moon] should be subtracted from the same. This is because, starting from the Sun’s solstitial point, the Moon is situated behind it; since the Moon resides on the ecliptic (krāntivṛtta), this is indeed the intersection arising from its motion (bhoga). When the Moon is at that same point, its node (viṣuva) must necessarily coincide with the tip of its latitude (śara) upon the equatorial circle (nāḍīvṛtta).

In that case, there is an absence of distinct declination (*krānti*) because, on the celestial sphere (*bimba-gata-kadamba-vṛtta*) or the meridian circle (*dhruva-vṛtta*), the celestial latitude (*kha-kha-śara*) and the declination (*krānti*) have different directions; thus, there is no interval between them. Now, when the Sun is at the equinox (*atri-bha*), the maximum interval between them is the greatest declination (*parama-spaṣṭāpama*). By the proportion: "If the declination-chord of the node (*pāta-krāntijyā*) is the side corresponding to the previously stated hypotenuse-chord (*karṇajyā*), then what would it be for the radius-chord (*trijyā*)?", the point of the solstice (*ayanasaṃdhi*) is established.

Alternatively, the difference between the sum and the product of the strength of the bimba situated at the junction of the *gola* (hemisphere) and the strength of the *nāyana* (equatorial) circle should be applied to the stated declination (*rāci*) when it is negative; that shall be its measure. The *vivṛtta* (diurnal circle) starting from Aries, the *viṣuvavṛtta* (equator), and the *sphuṭa* (true) Moon are well known in the calculation of the *svalīkāra*. Likewise, Rāhu is also [well known]. According to the determination made in the four quarters of the source text, Rāhu is the difference between the intersection of the *karṇanāḍī* (ear-cord) and the *vivṛtta* starting from Aries, and the intersection of the *vivṛtta* and the *viṣuvavṛtta*.

When the Moon is situated at its apogee (vivṛtta), it is then touched by Rāhu from that very point; the entry of Rāhu occurs within the interval of the ear (karṇa) from that conjunction. If one asks what the *bhuja* (the sine of the arc) is when it is thus intercepted, it is simply the sixty-fold declination (*krānti*); thus everything is established for those well-versed in the celestial sphere (*gola*). The rest is clear in the original source (*ākara*). (1) Regarding the phrase "at the beginning of the Yugas" (*yugādijau*): here, "at the beginning of the Yugas" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*). Other times, such as the completion of a day of the gods (*kudina*) or a revolution (*bhagaṇa*), should also be taken; the rest is clear.

If *yugādi* days correspond to one revolution (*bhagaṇa*) of a planet, what would they be for *iṣṭakudina* days? In this case, the revolutions of the planet are the dividend (*bhājya*), the desired *iṣṭakudina* days are the multiplier (*guṇaka*), and the *yugādi* *kṛtadina* days are the divisor (*para*). The quotient obtained there is 386 (as seen on page 172–152 of the verses). This is the *śeṣavāsanā* from the *Siddhāntatattvaviveka*, verse 49: the elapsed revolutions and the remainder constitute the "remainder of revolutions" (*bhagaṇaśeṣa*).

If, in this case, the quotient and remainder from the revolutions and the remainder of revolutions multiplied by the *iṣṭakṛt* (the chosen square) are divided by the *kudinās* (terrestrial days) of the *yuga* and so forth, they become zero; thus, the quotient itself would be the elapsed revolutions, and the multiplier would be the *ahargaṇa* (the accumulated days). Since in this *kuṭṭaka* (pulverizer) calculation there must necessarily be a divisor and a dividend that are firm (*dṛḍha*), here the revolutions of the *yuga* and so forth and the *kudinas* are taken such that the quotient remains unchanged.

The *bhagaṇa* (revolution count) here is made firm; that [firm revolution count] multiplied by ten and divided by the firm *kudina*s (mean solar days) yields the signs (*rāśi*) as the quotient and the remainder is the sign-remainder (*rāśiśeṣa*). That [sign-remainder] multiplied by thirty and divided by the firm *kudina*s yields the degrees (*lagna*) as the quotient and the remainder is the degree-remainder (*aṃśaśeṣa*). That [degree-remainder] multiplied by sixty and divided by that same divisor yields the minutes (*kalā*) as the quotient and the remainder is the minute-remainder (*vikalāśeṣa*). Thus, the product of all the multipliers is the total number of minutes in a circle, 1,296,000; the product of that [remainder] is indeed the revolution-remainder (*bhagaṇaśeṣa*).

The quotient obtained by dividing [the remainder] by the *ḍṛḍhakudināni* (firm lunar days) is the motion (*cara*) in seconds; the remainder is the residual seconds. Here, the quotient found is multiplied by the divisor and increased by its own numerator; this should equal the dividend multiplied by the multiplier. Thus, O King, the seconds [of the planet] multiplied by the *ḍṛḍhakudināni*, added to the residual seconds, and divided by the total seconds in a revolution (*cakravikalikā*), yield a quotient that leaves no remainder, which is the residue of the revolutions (*bhagaṇaśeṣa*). When the residue of the seconds is added to the residue of the revolutions, the quotient will have a remainder; thus, the residue of the revolutions becomes one less than the actual value.

Since it is otherwise impossible for there to be no remainder in the division, the remainder of that [division] must necessarily be a fraction (*vikalā*). Thus, the remainder of that [division] is indeed called the *vikalā* remainder here; the quotient with its integer part is the *bhagaṇa* (revolution) remainder—this is the path that follows the reasoning of the ancient authorities. Here, the *cakrāgra* (remainder of revolutions) is designated as the first term, while the *vikalā* remainder is assumed as the other term. If the *vikalā* remainder were less than the fixed number of *kudina*s (terrestrial days), and if that other term were indeed called the "fixed *kudina*s," then everything would remain exactly as the *vikalā* remainder.

The remainder of the revolutions (bhagaṇa-śeṣa) is known as the "vādi" (initial). However, when it exceeds the firm solar days (dṛḍha-kudina), it should be understood as a "khila" (residue). But when that same residue in seconds (vikalātmaka) exceeds the revolutions and the minutes (cakravikala), it can also arise from the remainder in seconds after subtracting multiple revolutions; the method for knowing this is as follows: here, the remainder in seconds of the firm solar days may be either less than or greater than the sum of the revolutions and the minutes.

Since the other [quantity] designated as *saṃjñā* has the nature of a remainder in minutes (*vikalāvaśeṣa*) due to the smallness of the revolutions (*cakra*), it is understood to be that very remainder in minutes. The first designated quantity is the remainder of revolutions (*bhagaṇaśeṣa*). This is established because those two have the nature of unity and the number of civil days (*kudina*), respectively. Now, this [remainder] plus one is that very multiplier consisting of minutes which, where there is a remainder of revolutions, is applied to the excess of minutes in the revolution for the remainder in minutes, according to the previous calculation.

If the remainder of the *vikalās* (seconds) is equal to or greater than the product of the number of revolutions (*cakra*) multiplied by six, then the remainder of the revolutions (*bhagaṇa-śeṣa*) shall be the first [quotient] plus one; however, even that remainder of the *vikalās* must be less than the firm *kudinās* (firm solar days), otherwise it is not so. In that case, the following procedure applies: the firm *kudinās* should be made less than the *vikalās* of the revolution, and the remainder should be set aside as the constant remainder (*stabdha-śeṣa*).

In this context, since the remainder obtained by subtracting the divisor from the quotient (the *labdhi*) added to its own square is equal to the *dṛḍhakaca* (the constant), it is established that when the seconds of arc (*vikalā*) are increased by the smaller of those remainders, they will indeed be less than the *dṛḍhakaca*. Therefore, in the present case, when the sum of the remainder and the other [term] equals the *dṛḍhakaca*, the remainder of the revolutions (*bhagaṇaśeṣa*)—being equal to the *dṛḍhakaca*—will necessarily be equal to the *dṛḍhakaca* minus the quotient plus one; it cannot be otherwise. If it is asked, "What is the proof for this *dṛḍhakaca* being even? listen: [The proof follows].

In this context, whatever remains of the *bhagaṇa* (revolutions) that is assumed to be greater than the initial [value] is also included within the remainder of the firm revolutions (*dṛḍhakakṣā*) and the small degrees (*vikalā*). As stated, it is large, and nothing else; however, that [remainder] is small compared to the revolutions. Because it cannot otherwise be accounted for, the remainder of the *bhagaṇas* is indeed the firm revolutions. For if the remainder of the *bhagaṇas* were equal to the firm revolutions, there would result the attainment of a subtraction equal to the revolutions.

If one were to subtract [the divisor] from the dividend, then in the case of a remainder that is deficient by a multiple of the divisor, it is entirely logical that what remains deficient is the true remainder; thus everything stated in the source is well-founded. (1) Now, in connection with the counter-example for squares, we shall explain the rationale (*vāsanā*) for the rule in *Kuṭṭaka* [verse 10]: "That which is irreducible by a common factor... The meaning is that even for the purpose of *kuṭṭaka* (pulverizer), that [number] is not without reduction (*anapavartana*); it is not intended as such. In the *vargaprakṛti* (square-nature) method, only the reduction of the remaining [coefficients] is taught through the statement of the problem (*uddeśa*), for the sake of the remainder. Otherwise, if there were no reduction, the statement regarding the application of the square would be contradicted by the resulting error. However, that [number] is not unreduced when it is employed for the purpose of arranging the sequence of results (*phalapaddhati*). In that case, it is employed as it has been made firm (*dṛḍhīkṛta*).

Now, as for the statement that [the method] does not apply when the roots are not reduced: those [steps] were indeed stated on the basis of the relationship between the dividend and divisor being firm. When the dividend and divisor are inherently firm, all the steps as they have been arrived at are valid.

The original problem is this: $5y^2 + 2 = 16$ or $5y^2 - 2 = 16$. In both cases, the assumed coefficient (*prakṛti*) is 5, and the additive constant (*kṣepaka*) is $2y^2 + 16$ or $-2y^2 + 16$. Here, the color-term (*varṇa*) of the same kind as the additive constant—whether with or without a positive sign—is considered the "smaller root" (*kan-iṣṭha*) according to Bhāskara’s view; likewise, the "larger root" (*jyeṣṭha*) derived from it is also established. That smaller root consists of two parts, one manifest (*vyakta*) and one unmanifest (*avyakta*). The square of that smaller root consists of three parts.

The group of natural numbers (*prakṛtigaṇa*) consists of the squares of the integers starting from one: 1, 4, 9, 16, and so on. This middle segment, when added to the square of the lower [number], shall become the square of the upper [number]. Conversely, the square of the lower [number] shall be the product of the natural number and the square of the lower [number]; the sum of those two [products] is indeed the [result]. The middle segment, however, remains exactly as it was. Here, there is a consideration regarding the extraction of the square root: if the middle segment were the product of the roots of the two [squares], then its root would be obtainable; otherwise, it is not.

Since the sum of the two segments on either side of the square root is greater than the product of those two roots, the middle segment cannot be equal to the square root of that product. That middle segment, however, consists of the product of the difference between the square of the smaller of those two segments and one; thus it is less than, and not equal to, that [product]. If, however, one makes one of the two numbers slightly less and the other slightly more and then calculates the middle segment, then equality is possible; for the middle segment is of the nature of a product, and such a product can arise from two unequal factors as well as from two equal ones.

Therefore, a method has been observed wherein, having designated one of the two segments as positive and the other as negative, their sum results in the equality of the middle segment. Thus, when performed according to the order of the subtraction (udāvaraṇa), the squares of the first and last [segments] also become the squares of the others. For example: by means of the smallest segments and the additive segments consisting of the additive forms, those which are the squares of the respective variables become the squares of the first and last [terms].

In such a way that even upon subtraction, that very same middle segment remains, so should the two smaller segments be assumed for the sake of finding the [other] two; this is the method. Having made the squares of those [values] the defect (doṣa), one makes the desired smaller and larger [segments] manifest. Therein, the manifest smaller segment itself is the smaller [root].

The first unknown quantity (*avyakta*) is *yā* (yāvattāvat). The square of the smaller segment consisting of two parts, *yāva pra le*, is the "prakṛti" (the coefficient) in the calculation. The middle segment, *yā khyapa*, is to be added to the first [term], and the larger segment, *yāvapralepavarṇayaḥ*, is the additive (*kṣepa*). From these two [segments], the product of the roots is the square root; this must necessarily be added as the additive (*kṣepa*). Here, in the first example, the nature of the larger square is as follows: *yāvapra*.
